Mega Evolve Metagross and Bullet Punch Whimsicott to break its Focus Sash at +1 priority. Incineroar uses Parting Shot on Basculegion to drop it to -2 Atk, neutering its Wave Crash, then pivots to Rotom-Wash which resists Water and threatens both foes. Bullet Punch goes before Basculegion; even if Whimsicott Tailwinds first (Prankster +1, faster), Sash still breaks. Next turn Mega Metagross finishes 1 HP Whimsicott with priority while Rotom-Wash Volt Switches Basculegion.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Incineroar has 1% HP remaining, and Metagross enters. Basculegion is locked into Wave Crash, which easily KOs Incineroar (foe 2) or heavily damages Metagross. Meanwhile, Whimsicott can use Encore on Incineroar to lock it into Fake Out or Parting Shot (if it tries to move) or use Tailwind / Moonblast. Wait, Incineroar used Fake Out last turn (Turn 3) and Parting Shot/Flare Blitz before; if Incineroar tries to switch or use an attack, Encording Incineroar is incredible. Alternatively, Moonblast into Metagross or Incineroar. But let's check Incineroar: Incineroar used Fake Out on turn 3, so its last move was Fake Out (wait, no, Fake Out can't be used twice in a row normally, but Encording Incineroar forces it to repeat whatever it did or fails if not allowed? Wait, Encore forces the target to repeat its last successful move. Incineroar's last successful move on Turn 3 was Fake Out!). If Incineroar used Fake Out on Turn 3, encording Incineroar forces it to use Fake Out again, which will fail because Fake Out only works on first turn on the field! That's a classic and devastating lock. Meanwhile Basculegion uses Wave Crash into Incineroar to finish it off immediately, or into Metagross. Let's finish off Incineroar with Basculegion Wave Crash into foe 2, and Whimsicott Encodes foe 2 (Incineroar).

Bullet Punch breaks Whimsicott's Focus Sash (guaranteed KO from 34% but Sash leaves it at 1 HP). Volt Switch into Basculegion does 45.8–86.2%, threatening a KO and forcing respect. Whimsicott's likely Prankster Encore locks Metagross into Bullet Punch — which is fine, as +1 priority lets it finish the 1 HP Whimsicott next turn. Basculegion's Wave Crash is manageable: 26–39% into Rotom-Wash or 37–56% into Metagross, and even a double-target into Metagross (Moonblast 13–20% + Wave Crash) cannot KO. After this turn we have a 2v1 or a heavily damaged Basculegion with a Sash-broken Whimsicott easily picked off.
Whimsicott Protects to stay safe against Metagross and Rotom-Wash. Basculegion is Choice-locked into Wave Crash and hits Metagross-Mega.

Bullet Punch is +1 priority and guaranteed to KO Whimsicott from 34% (50.3-97.8% range, Focus Sash irrelevant below full HP). Whimsicott's only counterplay is a 1/3 consecutive Protect; even if it succeeds, Moonblast does at most 20% to Metagross and we win next turn. Volt Switch is a safe secondary click that finishes if anything unexpected happens.

Whimsicott is alone against Mega Metagross and Rotom-Wash with 34% HP. Moonblast hits Rotom-Wash for neutral/good damage or Metagross for 0.5x, but Moonblast into Rotom-Wash is the only meaningful offensive option. Basculegion is fainted so slot 2 must pass.

reflections.summary: We won the series 2-0 by effectively neutralizing the opponent's rain offense. In Game 2, we traded Serperior for their Mega Swampert early, removing their primary rain sweeper, then used Rotom-Wash's Volt Switch and Metagross-Mega's Bullet Punch to pick off Pelipper, Basculegion, and Whimsicott. Intimidate from Incineroar and the chip damage from Fake Out helped control Basculegion's Wave Crash recoil. Our between-game adjustments—bringing Rotom-Wash as a dedicated rain check and preserving Metagross's Bullet Punch for priority—worked perfectly. The team-preview plan was well-suited: we correctly identified rain as their win condition and brought the optimal four. Mega Evolving Metagross was the right choice as our only Mega Stone holder, offering priority and bulk against their squad. Our preparation was solid; the registered six had all the tools needed, and the chosen sets (e.g., Sash Incineroar, Sitrus Rotom) performed exactly as intended.
reflections.adjustment: In a future series, consider bringing Corviknight over Serperior if Tailwind control becomes more critical, as Whimsicott's Tailwind could threaten our slower core. However, Serperior’s ability to OHKO Swampert and pressure Basculegion was game-winning here, so only adjust if their team composition changes. Klefki could also be an option if screens are needed against a more aggressive Primarina or Ampharos-Mega, but the current core of Incineroar, Metagross, Rotom, and Serperior proved highly effective.

reflections.summary: The series and game were lost (0-2) due to unfavorable matchups against Rotom-Wash and Serperior, which disrupted the Swift Swim rain offense spearheaded by Mega Swampert and Basculegion. Serperior's Contrary Leaf Storm snowballed quickly after trading Swampert on turn 2, and Rotom-Wash's Electric-type moves and Levitate effectively checked both water and ground options.
reflections.adjustment: Bring Whimsicott and alternative special attackers like Primarina or Mega Ampharos earlier or in team selection to deal with Rotom-Wash and counter Grass-types, rather than relying solely on Pelipper and Mega Swampert rain setups.

decisions.rationale: Lead Charizard and Torkoal to immediately establish the Drought + Heat Rock sun core, enabling Charizard-Mega-Y and Venusaur's Chlorophyll speed. Back Venusaur as the primary sun sweeper with Growth-boosted Giga Drain/Sludge Bomb, and Aegislash to wall opposing Psychic and Dragon types (Farigiraf, Armarouge) while providing flinch pressure via Sacred Sword and King's Rock.

Lead Altaria and Mamoswine to suppress opposing sun, establish Tailwind, and immediately threaten Charizard, Torkoal, and Flying types with Rock Slide. Armarouge provides Wide Guard against spread Fire attacks, while Archaludon supplies powerful special coverage into the opponent's Fire- and Flying-heavy roster.

Charizard's Fire Blast is 2x super-effective against Mamoswine, the most dangerous foe due to Rock Slide's 4x threat to Charizard and High Horsepower's 2x threat to Torkoal. Eliminating Mamoswine early is the highest priority. Torkoal uses Protect to avoid damage this turn, preserving its HP to maintain Drought ability for sun extension across future turns. Mega Evolution is not needed since sun is already active from Torkoal's Drought on entry, and Mega-Y's Speed drop from 167 to ~100 would sacrifice Charizard's key speed advantage.

Set Tailwind while protecting Mamoswine from Charizard’s likely immediate Fire Blast or Torkoal’s Eruption. This preserves both core members and ensures Mamoswine outspeeds the opposing threats next turn for Rock Slide pressure.

Prioritize eliminating Mamoswine (notebook priority target). Charizard's Solar Beam (Grass, 120 BP) is 2x super-effective vs Mamoswine's Ground typing and fires with no charge turn under active sun—outclassing Focus Blast (70% accuracy) and Fire Blast (neutralized to 1x by Thick Fat). Torkoal's Earth Power (Ground, 90 BP) is also 2x super-effective vs Mamoswine's Ice typing with perfect accuracy. Hitting Mamoswine with two simultaneous SE moves maximizes KO probability and removes the Pokemon threatening both active team members with Rock Slide (4x vs Charizard) and High Horsepower (2x vs Torkoal).

Venusaur with Chlorophyll in Sun reaches ~290 effective Speed, outspeeding Tailwind-boosted foes and activating the win-condition sweep. Switching Charizard out for Venusaur preserves the sun anchor plan. Torkoal at 43% should pass to attempt a final hit (Body Press or Earth Power) before likely fainting to Mamoswine's super-effective Ground move.

Helping Hand boosts Mamoswine's spread Rock Slide enough to guarantee a knockout on Charizard if it does not Protect, while also heavily damaging Torkoal. Mamoswine moves first under Tailwind and Rock Slide pressures both foes simultaneously.

Focus-fire Mamoswine, the biggest remaining threat: Venusaur's Giga Drain is super-effective (2x) and provides healing, while Torkoal's Body Press is also super-effective (2x vs Ice/Ground). Eliminating Mamoswine removes the Rock Slide/Icicle Crash threat to both of your Pokémon and preserves Venusaur's HP for its Chlorophyll sweep under sun.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.
Helping Hand makes Mamoswine's Icicle Crash a guaranteed OHKO on Venusaur, removing the fastest major threat before Torkoal can matter.

Double-target Mamoswine to eliminate the biggest physical threat. Aegislash's Sacred Sword is 2x super effective into Ice, and Torkoal's Body Press leverages its 160 Defense stat for massive damage also 2x super effective. Removing Mamoswine neutralizes the primary Ground/Ice offensive pressure on both remaining Pokémon and is essential before Altaria's Cloud Nine can further disrupt the sun gameplan.

Helping Hand boosts Rock Slide enough to guarantee the KO on Torkoal while also damaging Aegislash and preserving a chance to flinch it. Removing Torkoal's spread Fire pressure is the strongest immediate position.
Bring Armarouge as the stronger immediate answer to Aegislash and retain its Wide Guard utility for future spread Fire threats.

Shadow Sneak targets Armarouge with a 2x super-effective Ghost hit and +1 priority, striking before Armarouge's Heat Wave/Armor Cannon and potentially removing or heavily damaging the biggest offensive threat to Aegislash. Torkoal has fainted so the only legal action is pass.
Double-target Aegislash with Moonblast and super-effective Armor Cannon to maximize the chance of removing it this turn.

reflections.summary: The sweep package (Charizard, Venusaur) was dismantled before it could function — Mamoswine's Rock Slide/Icicle Crash eliminated both Charizard and Venusaur by turn 3, both super-effective and aided by Altaria's Helping Hand. Torkoal Body-Pressed for useful chip but also fell to Rock Slide. Aegislash successfully cleaned Mamoswine on turn 4, but with only one Pokémon remaining against Altaria plus Armarouge (and an unrevealed third), there was no staying power left. Altaria's Focus Sash + Helping Hand + Tailwind made Mamoswine nearly unbreakable early, and the team lacked a defensive backbone once the sun sweepers were gone.
reflections.adjustment: Replace one of the redundant sun setters or the fragile Venusaur slot with a physically bulky pivot or a dedicated Altaria/Mamoswine check (e.g., Skarmory to threaten Altaria's sash and absorb Rock Slides, or Meowscarada for speed-tier revenge killing under sun). The team needs at least one durable member that can survive Mamoswine's coverage after Helping Hand and still threaten back.

reflections.summary: Won through an excellent anti-sun plan: Cloud Nine Altaria removed the weather advantage, Tailwind plus Helping Hand enabled Mamoswine to eliminate Charizard, Venusaur, and Torkoal quickly, and the back line finished Aegislash. Piloting was clean with no recorded decision errors. The four brought were well suited to this opponent; no Mega Stone holder was available or evolved, which was appropriate for this roster.
reflections.adjustment: After Mamoswine secures an early knockout, avoid leaving it exposed to Aegislash's physical pressure. Transition sooner to Armarouge or Archaludon to handle Aegislash while preserving Mamoswine for remaining sun threats.

decisions.rationale: Charizard leads to OHKO Altaria with Fire Blast, removing Focus Sash / Cloud Nine / Helping Hand immediately. Skarmory is the second lead for hazard support (Spikes/StealthRock) and phazing (Whirlwind). Meowscarada is the fast sweeper with Protean, LeafStorm for Mamoswine/Archaludon super-effective coverage, and SuckerPunch priority. Venusaur rounds out the team as the Chlorophyll sun sweeper with EarthPower for Electric/Fire/Steel targets. One sun setter (Charizard-Y Mega) avoids the weather redundancy that cost game 1.

Lead Altaria and Mamoswine to suppress sun, establish Tailwind, and apply immediate spread or super-effective pressure to Charizard and Venusaur. Bring Armarouge for Wide Guard against sun-boosted spread Fire attacks and Dedenne for fast Nuzzle or Helping Hand support.

Protect shields Charizard from Mamoswine's 4× Rock Slide (boosted by Expert Belt and Helping Hand). Whirlwind forces Altaria out at –6 priority after Altaria's Helping Hand resolves, removing the series threat of Helping Hand enabling Mamoswine next turn. Skarmory survives neutral-bonus Rock Slide at 211 Def. Turn 2 Charizard at 167 Speed can swing Focus Blast or Fire Blast against a Mamoswine that has lost its support.

Set Tailwind while Cloud Nine suppresses the opposing sun, then use Rock Slide to pressure both foes and potentially OHKO Charizard. Mamoswine survives a likely Charizard Fire Blast, and Tailwind gives the team strong speed control for the following turns.

Mamoswine is the primary threat with 4x Rock Slide in doubles. Charizard Mega Evolves for Drought-boosted Fire Blast to OHKO Mamoswine (FlashFire-immune Fire Blast, super-effective). Skarmory sets Spikes to pressure the opponent's switch-ins and punish Mamoswine's ExpertBelt/ThickFat advantage. Even in a trade scenario, removing Mamoswine is the highest-value play for series win probability.

Meowscarada to slot 1 for SuckerPunch priority against Sneasler threat; Venusaur to slot 2 where chlorophyll doubles Speed to ~290 in sun, outspeeding all Tailwind-boosted foes for Mamoswine cleanup with EarthPower/LeafStorm.

Mamoswine uses Rock Slide first under Tailwind, giving a strong chance to immediately KO Charizard and possible flinch support. Armarouge then uses Armor Cannon on Skarmory, which is guaranteed to KO it from 92% HP.

Both Pokémon target Armarouge, the biggest remaining threat due to Armor Cannon (120 Fire/Special, already super-effective vs both my Pokémon). Armarouge is already at -1 DEF/-1 SPD, making it the ideal elimination priority. Meowscarada's Sucker Punch (Dark, +1 priority, 2x super-effective) ensures a fast, powerful hit. Venusaur's Earth Power (Ground, 2x super-effective) provides heavy coverage. Neither move triggers Armarouge's FlashFire. After removing Armarouge, Mamoswine can be cleaned up next turn with Leaf Storm/Earth Power while preserving both Pokémon.

Armor Cannon guarantees the Venusaur KO, while Icicle Crash guarantees the Meowscarada KO. This removes both threats despite Venusaur potentially moving first, securing the best chance to take both opposing Pokémon down this turn.

Switch Armarouge to Altaria to preserve the healthy Cloud Nine user, suppress the sun and Chlorophyll advantage, and maintain strong board control alongside Mamoswine. Keep Mamoswine in position to threaten the weakened Meowscarada with Icicle Crash.

Sucker Punch (+1 priority) on Mamoswine lands before Mamoswine's Icicle Crash, adding 22–40% damage. Combined with Venusaur's Giga Drain (64–124%, super-effective, healing), the total 86–164% gives a strong chance of KOing Mamoswine before it retaliates. If Mamoswine falls, Meowscarada survives (unlike Brick Break which resolves after Mamoswine's attack). Removing Mamoswine is the top priority — it threatens guaranteed OHKOs on both remaining Pokémon next turn, especially if Altaria's Helping Hand boosts it.
Moonblast guarantees the knockout on the weakened Meowscarada, while Icicle Crash applies the strongest immediate pressure to Venusaur and has a possible OHKO despite its range.

reflections.summary: Lost 0-2 in the series. Game 2 was decided by the opponent's Altaria (Focus Sash / Cloud Nine / Tailwind / Helping Hand) enabling Mamoswine as a devastating breaker. Both Mega Charizard Y and Skarmory fainted on Turn 2 to simultaneous super-effective hits (Mamoswine Rock Slide OHKO'd Charizard Y; Armarouge Armor Cannon OHKO'd Skarmory), leaving only Meowscarada and Venusaur to clean up. Cloud Nine shut down sun, negating Venusaur's Chlorophyll and Charizard Y's value. Altaria's Helping Hand boosted Mamoswine's Icicle Crash past our remaining Pokémon, and Altaria's Moonblast finished Meowscarada on Turn 4. No hazards were ever set because Skarmory died before acting offensively. The opponent's speed control (Tailwind + natural speed) meant our revenge kills were unreliable.
reflections.adjustment: 1) Replace Skarmory with Toxapex or Swampert: Skarmory never set hazards and died uselessly on Turn 2. Toxapex offers Scald burns and bulk against Mamoswine; Swampert's Water/Ground typing walls Mamoswine and Ice coverage. 2) Consider leading with Venusaur or Torkoal instead of Charizard Y + Skarmory to guarantee hazard setup before committing the Mega slot. 3) Bring Aegislash over one of the weaker links — King's Shield baits Mamoswine's Rock Slide and threatens Swords Dance sweeps. 4) Against Altaria specifically: carry a faster Taunt user or a Pokémon that can 2HKO Altaria before Focus Sash activates (Meowscarada's Leaf Storm would OHKO but risks accuracy; a neutral Earth Power from Venusaur does not). 5) Sun team viability is questionable against this opponent — Cloud Nine hard-counters the entire sun strategy. Consider a balanced or rain pivot instead for a rematch.

reflections.summary: You won Game 2 and the series 2-0 by executing a strong anti-sun plan: Altaria established Tailwind and revealed Cloud Nine, while Mamoswine applied immediate Rock Slide and Icicle Crash pressure to Charizard, Skarmory, Meowscarada, and Venusaur. The four brought were well suited: Altaria and Mamoswine were the key pieces, and Armarouge traded itself for Skarmory after removing it with Armor Cannon; Dedenne was not needed. No friendly Mega Stone holder was registered or evolved. There were no decision errors or substitutions. The supplied evidence does not identify a specific between-game adjustment from Game 1, so its effect cannot be proven; the observable Game 2 plan clearly helped rather than backfired. The six registered were broadly appropriate, but no evidence shows that Farigiraf, Sinistcha, Meowstic-F, or Qwilfish offered a materially better four or set into this opponent.
reflections.adjustment: Against this opponent in a future series, preserve the Altaria-plus-Mamoswine core and prioritize early weather control, speed control, and spread or super-effective pressure on Charizard and Venusaur. Keep Armarouge available to punish Skarmory, but avoid exposing it unnecessarily to Meowscarada's Sucker Punch and Venusaur's Ground coverage. Consider bringing Dedenne only when its paralysis or support is specifically needed; the unused alternatives have no demonstrated advantage from this series. Since no Game 1 details were supplied, make future adjustments from confirmed scouting rather than assuming a particular between-game change worked.

events.text: Floette used Light of Ruin → Tyranitar
Gholdengo used Make It Rain → Garchomp

decisions.rationale: Lead the Sand core: Tyranitar sets Sand Stream immediately, and Excadrill at 308 Spe in sand outspeeds the entire opposing roster including Tailwind-boosted Garchomp. Excadrill's Rock Slide is 4x SE on Talonflame (Focus Sash saves it, but sand chip + recoil breaks it) and Iron Head is SE on Mega Floette. Tyranitar's Rock Slide also threatens Talonflame and provides general spread pressure. Gholdengo is the defensive anchor on the bench, resisting Fairy (Floette Moonblast), Dragon (Garchomp), and Water (Milotic Scald) while Make It Rain chips Steel-types like Metagross. Gengar-Mega rounds out the four as a Shadow Tag trapper that resists Fairy, outspeeds most of the field at 178 (165-200 Mega), and can Taunt screen/Tailwind setters or pick off weakened targets with Shadow Ball. This four covers all six opposing mons: sand Excadrill handles Garchomp, Talonflame, Metagross, and Scrafty; Gholdengo walls Floette and Milotic; Gengar-Mega traps and cleans late.

Lead Talonflame + Metagross for reliable Tailwind pressure and immediate Mega Gengar counterplay through Bullet Punch, while preserving Mega Floette until Steel/Poison pressure is weakened. Garchomp remains a strong back-line answer to Tyranitar, Excadrill, and Gholdengo.

Excadrill High Horsepower on Metagross (58.8-104.5%, possible OHKO) plus Tyranitar Rock Slide breaks Talonflame's Focus Sash (guaranteed 4x KO damage → 1 HP) and chips Metagross (9-16%). Sandstorm then KOs Talonflame at 1 HP. Combined Metagross damage (~74-127% with sandstorm) likely KOs it too. This play is robust: if Metagross Protects, I still eliminate Talonflame via Sash break + sandstorm rather than wasting both attacks. If Talonflame Flare Blitzes Excadrill, Sash saves it but sandstorm KOs Excadrill — a favorable 1-for-2 trade. If Talonflame Tailwinds or Brave Birds (NVE), Excadrill survives and I likely sweep both foes. Tyranitar survives Meteor Mash at 9-35% HP and gets Rock Slide off before fainting.

Set Tailwind with Gale Wings while protecting Metagross from Excadrill's immediate Ground pressure. Talonflame is highly vulnerable to either Rock Slide, so preserving Metagross and enabling the back line to operate under Tailwind is the safest opening.
Bring in Garchomp under Tailwind to immediately pressure both opposing active Pokémon with its Ground STAB while retaining Mega Floette for later once Steel pressure is reduced.

Protect Tyranitar to block Metagross's Meteor Mash (its only meaningful target—all its moves are NVE on Excadrill) while Excadrill hits Metagross with High Horsepower (59-105%, possible KO). If Garchomp Earthquakes, Metagross takes EQ (47-103%) + HHP (59-105%) = near-certain KO, and Excadrill survives via Focus Sash. Metagross Protect is unreliable (used last turn). This preserves the sand setter and removes the Metagross threat in one turn.
Bullet Punch chips Tyranitar before Garchomp’s faster Earthquake, maximizing the chance to remove Tyranitar before it can use Ice Punch while Earthquake also forces Excadrill to its Focus Sash.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Go for the potential game-ending double KO: Tyranitar Ice Punch (4x SE, 72.6-131.1% vs Garchomp's 90%) and Excadrill Iron Head (2x SE, 79.6-154.4% vs Floette's 100%). If both connect, opponent has zero Pokémon remaining for an instant Game 1 win. Excadrill at 1% HP is a dead slot regardless — attacking extracts maximum value. Tyranitar survives any single attack (Light of Ruin max 89.9%, Earthquake max 86.5%), guaranteeing Ice Punch resolves unless double-targeted. Garchomp's Earthquake also damages ally Floette, potentially deterring its use and letting Excadrill survive to attack. Gengar and Gholdengo remain fresh in back as insurance if the double KO fails.

Opponent has only Garchomp left at 80% — heavily winning position. Gholdengo is the better send-in over Gengar because Shadow Tag is useless (no switches available), Gholdengo has Recover+Leftovers to outlast Life Orb recoil, and keeping Gengar fresh in back provides insurance. Excadrill at 1% is already a sacrifice piece. Even worst case (Garchomp KOs Excadrill + Gholdengo), Gengar cleans up easily.

Mega Light of Ruin plus Dragon Claw concentrates guaranteed combined pressure into Tyranitar before it can remove Garchomp; Mega Floette also gives the best chance to withstand Excadrill's Iron Head if Tyranitar protects.

Garchomp's Earthquake threatens a possible OHKO on Gholdengo (72.2–104.6%). With only Garchomp remaining at 80%, the series is nearly secured—playing safe is correct. Gholdengo Protects to guarantee it stays at 100% regardless of Garchomp's choice. Excadrill (1 HP) fires High Horsepower into Garchomp for 32.1–56.3% if it moves first, chunking Garchomp to 24–48% for an easy cleanup next turn. Even if Garchomp outspeeds and KOs Excadrill with Earthquake, Gholdengo is preserved at full and Tailwind expires, leaving Gholdengo+Gengar vs a Life Orb–chipped Garchomp with no speed boost—an essentially guaranteed win.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.
Earthquake is the only play that guaranteed removes 1% Excadrill while also giving Garchomp a meaningful chance to immediately KO Gholdengo.

Garchomp is the opponent's last Pokémon at 70% HP. Gengar (178) outspeeds Garchomp (134–169) and Mega Evolution pushes Speed to 200 and SpA to 222, still outspeeding. Mega Gengar Shadow Ball (~34–63% est.) plus Gholdengo Make It Rain (35.3–63.9%) totals ~69–127% of Garchomp's max HP, giving ~94% effective KO chance even accounting for Make It Rain's 95% accuracy. Garchomp's Earthquake guarantees KO on Gengar and can OHKO Gholdengo (72–105%), but the probability of both being KO'd AND Garchomp surviving both hits is ~1%. Mega Evolving has no downside here—Shadow Tag is moot with one foe remaining, and the SpA/Speed/Bulk boosts all help. Sludge Bomb is NVE (0.5x) and Taunt doesn't stop Earthquake, so Shadow Ball is the clear best attack. Make It Rain outperforms Gholdengo Shadow Ball despite the 5% miss chance due to higher effective BP.
Earthquake is the only play that immediately guarantees the Gengar KO if it does not Protect while also threatening Gholdengo for heavy super-effective damage.

reflections.summary: Won through favorable trades and opponent self-damage. Garchomp's Earthquake friendly-fired Metagross (super effective), accelerating its KO. Sandstorm chip finished sashed Talonflame after Rock Slide broke the sash. The trade sequence left Garchomp alone; Gholdengo survived the final Earthquake at 10% and finished it with Make It Rain. Gengar-Mega contributed only chip damage before dying to Earthquake—Shadow Tag was never utilized since opponent had one Pokémon left when it entered.
reflections.adjustment: Gengar-Mega is extremely vulnerable to Garchomp Earthquake and should not be brought in while Garchomp is on the field unless Protect is guaranteed. Prioritize removing or weakening Garchomp before Gengar enters, or lead Gengar-Mega early to trap and remove a target before Earthquake pressure mounts. Consider Protect reads on Garchomp to create safe Gengar turns.

reflections.summary: Lost to the Tyranitar–Excadrill sand mode's favorable trades: Rock Slide plus sand removed Focus Sash Talonflame immediately, High Horsepower removed Metagross, and Excadrill's Iron Head removed Mega Floette. Garchomp then nearly reversed the endgame but was finished by Gholdengo's Make It Rain. The four brought were only partly suited: Garchomp and Floette pressured Tyranitar, but Talonflame's Sash was unreliable in sand and Metagross was exposed to Excadrill. Mega Floette was a reasonable Mega choice for Tyranitar pressure, but it needed protection from Iron Head.
reflections.adjustment: Against the sand lead, preserve Floette with Protect while using Garchomp to pressure or remove Excadrill first; do not commit both attacks into Tyranitar while Excadrill can freely Iron Head Floette. Favor a Garchomp-centered lead over Talonflame–Metagross when expecting Tyranitar–Excadrill.

events.text: Gholdengo used Make It Rain → Floette
Gholdengo used Make It Rain → Scrafty
Floette used Light of Ruin → Gholdengo
Floette used Light of Ruin → Gholdengo
Floette used Light of Ruin → Gholdengo

decisions.rationale: Lead Tyranitar+Excadrill sand core: Excadrill (Sand Rush, 154→308 in sand) outspeeds the entire opponent roster, is immune to Garchomp Earthquake, and threatens Floette with Iron Head SE. Tyranitar sets sand automatically and provides Rock Slide spread pressure. Back: Gengar-Mega (Shadow Tag wincon, 178 Spe outspeeds most of the meta) and Gholdengo (Steel typing resists Floette Fairy, Make It Rain spread, Good as Gold blocks Taunt/status). This covers opponent's likely Milotic/Scrafty adjustments—Gholdengo walls Scrafty's Drain Punch via Steel resist and Gengar-Mega is immune to it; Excadrill under sand outspeeds Milotic's Icy Wind speed control. Only real concern is Talonflame Gale Wings Tailwind giving Garchomp 268-338 Spe, but Protect scouting and sand chip vs Focus Sash mitigate this.
Lead Scrafty + Milotic to disrupt the sand opener with Intimidate/Fake Out pressure while Milotic attacks Excadrill; retain Garchomp and Floette for the midgame after Excadrill is controlled.

Excadrill Protects to waste Scrafty's likely Fake Out (standard turn-1 play, most likely targeting Excadrill at 308 Spe). Tyranitar Crunches Milotic for 21–41% neutral damage plus 20% Def-drop chance, targeting the bigger threat (Scald is SE vs both my mons). Milotic likely Scalds Tyranitar for 30–44% which it survives comfortably. Risk: Scrafty could Drain Punch Tyranitar (70–106%, possible OHKO), but Fake Out is the standard play and Excadrill is the natural target. This preserves Excadrill at 100% and chips Milotic for turn 2.
Deny Excadrill’s immediate Sand Rush attack with Fake Out while Scald applies major damage and a burn chance; this most directly limits the sand lead’s pressure before bringing Floette in.

Switch Tyranitar to Gholdengo to escape the 4x SE Drain Punch KO range (70-106%); Gholdengo is immune to Drain Punch (Ghost) and can Recover off Scald damage. Excadrill at 308 Speed moves first and lands High Horsepower into Milotic (34-64% of max HP), bringing it to ~11-41% before it can be KO'd. This preserves Tyranitar for late-game, maximizes Excadrill's Sash value by getting damage off first, and brings in a safe Gholdengo that threatens Make It Rain / Shadow Ball against the weakened foe field.
Split pressure: Drain Punch heavily damages Tyranitar while +2 Scald can remove or force Focus Sash on Sand Rush Excadrill, setting up cleanup next turn.

Double-target Milotic with Excadrill HH (308 Spe, moves first) + Gholdengo Shadow Ball to guarantee KO (combined 60-109% vs 35% HP). Removing +2 SpA Milotic is top priority. Shadow Ball chosen over Make It Rain to avoid self-SpA-drop (would be -2 with Snarl) and deal more to Milotic. Excadrill is at 1% and dies anyway, so spending its last action to help KO Milotic is optimal. If Milotic Protects, Excadrill is lost (1% anyway) but Gholdengo stays healthy for Gengar-Mega Shadow Tag late-game.

Send in Gengar to Mega Evolve into Shadow Tag, trapping both Milotic (35% HP, +2 SpA) and Scrafty (82% HP). Gengar-Mega outspeeds both foes and is unaffected by Intimidate. Tyranitar is 4x weak to Scrafty Drain Punch and would be Intimidated on entry, making it a poor choice. Shadow Tag prevents the opponent from switching Milotic out to preserve the +2 SpA threat or to bring in a counter.
Protect Milotic from Excadrill’s immediate Sand Rush pressure while Snarl covers an Excadrill Protect attempt, removes Excadrill if it attacks, and weakens Gholdengo for the following turns.

Double Shadow Ball into Milotic guarantees a KO (combined min ~40.6% > 35% HP) while Mega Evolving Gengar activates Shadow Tag to trap both foes. Gengar-Mega (Speed 200) outspeeds Milotic and hits first with boosted SpA 222 Shadow Ball; Gholdengo cleans up. Milotic's Protect has reduced success rate from last-turn use, and even if it Recovers between hits, Shadow Tag prevents escape and we finish next turn. This removes the +2 SpA Milotic threat immediately and locks Scrafty in for Sludge Bomb next phase.

Preserve boosted Milotic from likely focused special damage while bringing Garchomp in safely; Snarl immediately suppresses both special attackers and compounds Gholdengo’s existing Special Attack drop.

Gengar-Mega outspeeds Garchomp (200 vs 134-169) and Shadow Ball KOs it at 10% before Earthquake can fire (which would guarantee-KO Gengar and possibly Gholdengo). Gholdengo Protects to dodge Scrafty's Snarl (17-32% to Gengar, survivable) and avoid dropping to -3 SpA, staying fresh for the 4th foe arriving after Garchomp faints. Next turn: Taunt Scrafty to lock it out of Snarl/Protect, then wear it down with Sludge Bomb while handling the new entrant.
Protect preserves Garchomp through the immediate double-target threat while Snarl further suppresses both special attackers for the Milotic/Floette endgame.

Gengar-Mega (200 Spe) outspeeds and guaranteed-KOs Garchomp (10% HP) with Shadow Ball before it can Earthquake, which would KO Gengar (121-173%) and possibly Gholdengo (72-105%). Gholdengo Shadow Balls Scrafty for safe 7-14% chip (NVE but guaranteed progress) rather than risking a reduced-success-rate Protect or wasting Recover at 92%. Next turn Gengar Taunts Scrafty, locking it to Drain Punch (immune to both Ghosts) and neutralizing it while we handle the 4th foe under Shadow Tag.
Preserve the 11% Garchomp by switching to Milotic; Snarl further suppresses both special attackers while Milotic is the safer pivot into their reduced-power attacks.
Snarl maintains special-attack pressure while Earthquake is the only available Garchomp action that can immediately remove Mega Gengar and heavily punish Gholdengo if an opening arises.
Bring in Milotic: it is the safest pivot into the heavily reduced special attackers and preserves Floette-Eternal from immediate Steel- and Poison-type pressure.

Both my Pokémon are at -3 SpA, making special attacks useless (Gholdengo Shadow Ball does only 11-18% to Milotic, can't KO). Switch Gholdengo to Tyranitar for physical damage (unaffected by SpA drops), sand refresh via Sandstream+Smooth Rock (8 turns), and Snarl immunity in practice (NVE 0.5x, only 1.4-3.4% damage). Gengar Protects to avoid potential KO from Scrafty's Snarl (17.5-32.1% vs 27% HP = possible KO) and preserves Shadow Tag, preventing the opponent from switching to their unknown 4th Pokémon. Next turn: Tyranitar Rock Slide both foes while Gengar Taunts Scrafty to lock out Protect.
Snarl plus Scald guarantees the Mega Gengar KO if it does not Protect while further suppressing both special attackers; their heavily reduced damage makes proactive removal better than Recover.

Tyranitar must Protect: Scrafty Drain Punch does 69.6-106.3% (4x SE, potential KO from 98%) and Milotic Scald does 30-44.4% (2x SE, +2 Competitive). The opponent's optimal play is double-targeting Tyranitar to KO the win condition. Protect guarantees survival. Gengar at 21% will die to Snarl+sand regardless, so instead of a reduced-success Protect it should Taunt Milotic (guaranteed to move first at 200 Spe vs 78-110). Taunt locks Milotic out of Recover/Protect for 3 turns, stranding it at 35% HP. If opponent double-targets Tyranitar (most likely), both attacks are blocked and Gengar survives unharmed with Milotic Taunted — best outcome. If Scrafty Snarls instead, Gengar dies but Milotic is still Taunted. Sandstorm ends after this turn, preserving Tyranitar as the healthy win condition going forward.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.
Scald guarantees the Mega Gengar KO if it does not land its reduced-success consecutive Protect, while Drain Punch gives the best Tyranitar pressure and recovery.

Milotic is Taunted at 41% HP and cannot Protect or Recover — this is the optimal turn to guarantee her KO. Crunch (31.7-60%, 100% acc) + Shadow Ball (25.7-44.7%, 100% acc) = 57.4% minimum combined, guaranteed KO from 41%. Tyranitar is almost certainly dying to Drain Punch+Scald (99.6% min combined) regardless of our choice, so maximizing value by removing Milotic is paramount. Protect is only ~50% reliable and doesn't pressure Milotic; Rock Slide risks 10% miss. With Milotic gone, Gholdengo (immune to Drain Punch) faces only Scrafty+4th, and can Recover-stall while chipping with Shadow Ball. If Tyranitar somehow survives (opponent mispredicts), we keep a 98% Tyranitar for next turn.
Snarl further suppresses Gholdengo while Scald makes substantial progress on Tyranitar; this preserves the strongest stable endgame against their special attacker.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Tyranitar is guaranteed KO'd by Floette's Light of Ruin or Scrafty's Drain Punch if it doesn't Protect, and Floette outspeeds it so it can't even attack first. Protect Tyranitar to waste the opponent's likely Tyranitar-targeted moves. Gholdengo Make It Rain hits both foes for 43-74% on Floette (2x SE) and 22-39% on Scrafty (neutral), putting both in KO range next turn. Even if Scrafty predicts and Snarls Gholdengo instead, damage is only 12-23% and Gholdengo survives comfortably.
Mega Moonblast secures Tyranitar while Snarl further suppresses Gholdengo; it also covers a Tyranitar Protect by still lowering Gholdengo.

Tyranitar is guaranteed KO'd by Floette this turn. Protect (reduced rate) is the only way Tyranitar can possibly survive — if it works and only Floette targets Tyranitar (likely, since Scrafty at 27% may Protect or Snarl Gholdengo rather than waste Drain Punch on a potential Protect), Tyranitar lives at 48% and can Ice Punch the chipped Scrafty next turn for a guaranteed KO. Gholdengo's Make It Rain chips both foes critically: Scrafty to 7-16% (KO range next turn) and Floette to 66-82%. Even if Tyranitar dies as expected, the chip damage is essential for Gholdengo's endgame path — it resists all Floette moves at 0.5x and has Recover/Leftovers to outlast a 1v1. The SpA drop to -6 is acceptable since Gholdengo's damage is already minimal and the chip is what matters.
Moonblast is a guaranteed KO on Tyranitar if it does not Protect, while Snarl further suppresses Gholdengo’s already heavily reduced Special Attack and advances the safe endgame.

Gholdengo is in a 1v2 at 59% HP with SpA at -6 (floor). Floette outspeeds and Light of Ruin can KO from 59% (42.8-59.3%). Make It Rain only max-rolls to KO Scrafty (8.7-15% vs 15% HP) and Recover risks death before healing. Protect (+4 priority) guarantees survival, wastes both foes' attacks, and Leftovers heals to ~65%. Up 1-0 in the series, no need to coin-flip Gholdengo's life — stall for an opening next turn.

Light of Ruin is the only available attack with a direct KO chance on the weakened Gholdengo before it can Recover; Snarl adds damage if it attacks rather than recovering and maintains special-pressure control.

Recover is the safest survival play. Floette-Mega outspeeds and hits first, but Light of Ruin (max 59.3%) cannot KO Gholdengo from 65% alone. If Scrafty is slower than Gholdengo (uncertain 78-110 vs 104), Recover resolves before Snarl, guaranteeing survival at 33-60% HP. If Scrafty is faster, the KO risk is the same as Make It Rain, but Recover at least heals if I survive. If opponent uses Moonblast (100% acc, 28.9-40.2%) instead of Light of Ruin to avoid recoil, combined with Snarl (12.4-22.7%) = 41.3-62.9% < 65%, guaranteeing survival and healing to near full. Make It Rain only KOs Scrafty on max roll (~5%) and always eats both hits first. Protect is unreliable after last turn. Recover keeps me alive to chip with Make It Rain on future turns while Floette's Light of Ruin recoil slowly self-damages, potentially bringing Floette into KO range.
Apply maximum immediate combined pressure: Light of Ruin has the best KO chance at this range, while Snarl adds crucial damage and keeps Gholdengo’s Special Attack suppressed.

Floette outspeeds Gholdengo and Light of Ruin (42.8-59.3%) likely KOs from 46% before Gholdengo can act. Floette would self-KO from recoil at 36% HP, but the opponent wins anyway since Scrafty survives at 15%. Protect is the only safe play: blocks Light of Ruin + Snarl, wastes Floette's limited PP, and Leftovers heals to ~52%. Gholdengo can stall out Light of Ruin PP (likely 3 left) with 6 Protect PP, then out-heal NVE Moonblast/Energy Ball with Recover while Scrafty's Snarl PP also depletes. Any non-Protect play risks ~65% instant game loss.
Light of Ruin is the only immediate likely KO on Gholdengo; Snarl provides the best fallback damage if it misses.

Gholdengo is alone at 53% HP with -6 SpA facing two foes. Make It Rain does only 8.7-15% to Scrafty (15% HP, unreliable KO) and 14.4-25.5% to Floette (36% HP, survives). Floette's Light of Ruin does 42.8-59.3% to Gholdengo — a possible KO from 53% this turn. Even if I Recover to full, at -6 SpA I cannot deal meaningful damage to either foe, and the opponent can wear me down with recoil-free Moonblast + Snarl. No win path exists in this 1v2. Series score is 1-0 in my favor; forfeiting game 2 to reset for game 3 is correct.
Light of Ruin is the only direct KO line into Gholdengo’s current range; Snarl adds follow-up damage if it survives and preserves the strongest path through a failed Protect or low roll.

reflections.summary: Scrafty's Snarl was super-effective against both Gengar and Gholdengo, repeatedly dropping their SpA while chipping them down. By the time Floette-Mega arrived, Gholdengo's SpA was -6 (Snarl + Make It Rain self-drops stacked), making it unable to threaten anything. Tyranitar also carelessly Crunched Milotic, triggering Competitive (+2 SpA). Gengar-Mega never trapped anything useful and died to Scald after being worn down by Snarl. Floette-Mega swept the helpless endgame.
reflections.adjustment: Never let Gengar or Gholdengo sit in against Scrafty — Snarl is SE on both and destroys their offense. Use Gengar's Taunt on Scrafty to shut down Snarl, or pivot to Tyranitar/Excadrill to hit Scrafty with physical attacks. Stop using Make It Rain once SpA drops begin accumulating. Do not use stat-lowering moves on Milotic (Competitive). Prioritize trapping Floette with Shadow Tag before it Mega Evolves and sweeps.

reflections.summary: Won by bringing the right four—Scrafty, Milotic, Garchomp, and Mega Floette—and using Scrafty’s repeated Snarl to suppress the opponent’s Mega Gengar/Gholdengo special core. Mega Floette was the correct evolution and gave the decisive Gholdengo endgame pressure with Fairy Aura-boosted Light of Ruin. Piloting was mostly solid, though Drain Punch into the newly revealed Gholdengo on turn 2 wasted Scrafty’s action.
reflections.adjustment: When Gholdengo is on the field, prioritize Snarl rather than Drain Punch: it deals effective spread damage, lowers its Special Attack, and avoids its Ghost-type immunity. Keep Mega Floette preserved for the weakened-Gholdengo endgame.

events.text: Floette used Light of Ruin → Gengar

decisions.rationale: Lead Gengar-Mega + Excadrill per plan: Gengar Mega Evolves turn 1 for Shadow Tag (traps Floette if present) and Taunts Scrafty to block Snarl/Fake Out disruption. Excadrill Focus Sash guarantees survival; at 154 Speed it outspeeds Scrafty/Milotic/Metagross and can Rock Slide (SE on Garchomp/Talonflame) or High Horsepower Scrafty. Backline Tyranitar provides Sand Stream for Excadrill's Sand Rush when switched in, plus Rock Slide spread pressure. Gholdengo is the late-game cleaner: Make It Rain is SE on Floette-Fairy, but must stay benched until Scrafty is removed to avoid Snarl + self-drop compounding to -6 SpA.

Lead Mega Floette plus Scrafty to pressure Tyranitar, Tauros, and Mega Gengar while giving immediate Snarl control into the Gengar/Gholdengo core. Garchomp supplies crucial Ground pressure into both Steel-types, and Talonflame provides Tailwind, Taunt, and Fire coverage for Gholdengo.

Mega Gengar SpA 222 Sludge Bomb is 2x SE STAB on Floette, estimated ~70-123% with Mega stats — very likely OHKO removing the Light of Ruin threat. Gengar Speed 200 outspeeds both foes so Sludge Bomb resolves before any Snarl. Excadrill Protects to block Scrafty's Fake Out (priority +3, targets Excadrill since Gengar is Ghost-immune), preserving Focus Sash and 100% HP. Shadow Tag traps both non-Ghost opponents for future cleanup. If Floette survives, Excadrill finishes next turn with Iron Head; if KO'd, pivot to Taunt+High Horsepower on trapped Scrafty.
Mega Light of Ruin maximizes immediate pressure on Gengar while Fake Out prevents Excadrill's Iron Head and preserves Floette's attack.
Preserve Garchomp’s endgame pressure while Talonflame can establish priority Tailwind from full HP and immediately threatens the weakened Mega Gengar with Gale Wings Brave Bird next turn.

Gengar at 25% is guaranteed KO'd by Talonflame's Gale Wings Brave Bird (priority +1, 50-79% of max HP). Protect (priority +4) is the only way to survive and maintain Shadow Tag. Excadrill Rock Slide chunks Talonflame to 11-52% (removing Gale Wings for next turn since no longer full HP) while hitting Scrafty for chip. Next turn: Gengar outspeeds Talonflame (200 vs 160-195 without Gale Wings priority) to Taunt Scrafty, Excadrill finishes Talonflame. If Talonflame Tailwinds instead, Rock Slide still chunks it and Gengar can Protect again next turn while Excadrill KOs the weakened Talonflame.
Use Gale Wings Brave Bird to guarantee Mega Gengar’s KO unless it Protects, while Drain Punch makes progress on Excadrill through its Focus Sash.

Gengar outspeeds and guaranteed-KOs Talonflame with Sludge Bomb before it can act, preserving Gengar at 25%. Switching Excadrill to Gholdengo is strictly optimal: Gholdengo is immune to Scrafty's Drain Punch (Ghost typing), tanks Snarl for only 12-23%, and if Scrafty targeted Excadrill's slot with Drain Punch the move fails entirely. This preserves Excadrill on bench for later Sand Rush with Tyranitar while bringing in a fresh Gholdengo. Shadow Tag maintained if Gengar survives Snarl (~50% chance); even if Gengar falls, Gholdengo at ~85% HP is a strong position with Tyranitar in back.

Flare Blitz guarantees Excadrill’s removal before it can act if Talonflame survives Gengar’s attack, while Snarl pressures Mega Gengar and lowers its Special Attack for the ensuing endgame. This line remains useful even if Gengar moves first or Protects.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Opponent has only Garchomp + Scrafty left (no switches), so Shadow Tag is worthless — sacrifice Gengar's slot to bring Tyranitar (100% HP, survives EQ at 61-87%, sets Sand for Excadrill's 308 Spe). Gholdengo Protects because Garchomp Earthquake does 72-105% to it (possible OHKO). Preserve the 3v2 advantage and set up sand for Excadrill cleanup next turn.

Earthquake plus Snarl guarantees Mega Gengar is removed if it does not Protect, while giving the best immediate chance to KO Gholdengo; Scrafty survives the allied Earthquake and Snarl provides useful Special Attack control afterward.

Tyranitar Protects (first use, reliable) to survive at 12%. Gholdengo Make It Rain chunks both foes: 35-64% on Garchomp (to 26-55%), 33-59% on Scrafty (possible KO from 50%). If opponent Earthquakes, Scrafty takes 30-64% collateral + Make It Rain = guaranteed faint, leaving 3v1 — but Gholdengo risks OHKO (72-105%). However, Earthquake is a losing play for the opponent (loses Scrafty), so they likely use NVE Dragon Claw/Rock Slide on Gholdengo instead, keeping it safe. Next turn: switch Tyranitar→Excadrill (Sand Rush 308 Spe) to outspeed and finish chunked Garchomp. Ice Punch was rejected because Tyranitar (81 Spe) is outsped by Garchomp (134-169) and likely by Scrafty (78-110), dying before it can attack.

Excadrill under Sand Rush outspeeds both foes and is the only Pokémon with a winning path: Rock Slide flinch chance on Garchomp (30%) lets Tyranitar survive to Ice Punch (4x SE) for the KO, then Iron Head (2x SE) cleans up Scrafty. Gengar-Mega at 6% dies to Sandstorm chip and has no SE moves or bench to trap with Shadow Tag. Not forfeiting because this is decisive game 3 and the flinch line gives a real, if slim, win chance.
Earthquake guarantees Tyranitar’s KO while retaining a possible immediate KO on Gholdengo; Protect prevents allied Earthquake damage and covers Make It Rain.

Both attacks target Garchomp for a guaranteed KO (Iron Head 27-48% + Ice Punch 72.6-131% = 99.6% min > 80% HP). Iron Head's 20% flinch chance is the only defense against Garchomp's Earthquake which would KO both my Pokemon. If Garchomp doesn't EQ (flinch, Protect prediction, or Scrafty collateral concern), both hits land and Garchomp is eliminated, leaving Excadrill + Tyranitar vs Scrafty alone which is winnable. High Horsepower offers no flinch protection and lower accuracy.

Both Tyranitar and Excadrill are fainted; Gengar-Mega at 6% is my only remaining Pokémon. Sending it out rather than forfeiting because Gengar (Speed 200) outspeeds both foes and Shadow Ball is a guaranteed KO on Garchomp (34.9-62.3% vs 26% HP). After that, Gengar moves first vs Scrafty and Sludge Bomb (36.6-65%) has a real chance to KO from 38%. Slot 1 switches Gengar in; Slot 2 passes since no other Pokémon remain.
Earthquake guarantees both opposing active KOs after Excadrill’s move; Scrafty’s Protect is the only way to preserve it from allied Earthquake for the remaining Mega Gengar endgame.

1v2 with Gengar at 6% — any hit KOs me, but Gengar outspeeds both foes. Shadow Ball is a guaranteed KO on Garchomp (34.9-62.3% at -1 SpA > 26% HP). After that, Scrafty's only KO move is Snarl; Fake Out and Drain Punch are both immune to Ghost, leaving a sliver of hope if the opponent misplays. This strictly maximizes win probability over forfeiting (0%) or targeting Scrafty (Sludge Bomb not guaranteed KO at 36.6% min vs 38%, and Garchomp KO's Gengar with any move).
Protect Garchomp while Scrafty uses Snarl; Mega Gengar cannot avoid sandstorm chip at its shown HP, and this prevents a possible Sludge Bomb KO on Garchomp.

reflections.summary: Lost Game 3 and the series because Garchomp's Earthquake devastated an Earthquake-weak core: Tyranitar (4x), Excadrill (2x), and Gholdengo (2x) all fell to Earthquake across turns 5-6 while Scrafty consistently Protected to avoid friendly fire. Gengar was crippled on turn 1 by Floette-Mega's Light of Ruin (75% damage) and then chipped to 6% by Snarl, leaving it unable to finish Garchomp at 26% because Garchomp read the Shadow Ball and Protected on the final turn. The sand core (Tyranitar + Excadrill) was a poor structural fit against a team with Garchomp Earthquake + Scrafty Protect, since both sand members are Ground-weak and Excadrill was already at 32% from Drain Punch before sand was even set. Bringing Grimmsnarl over Tyranitar would have provided Prankster support, a Dark/Dragon resist, and no Ground weakness. The Mega Gengar choice was reasonable for trapping and Sludge Bomb did remove Floette via recoil, but the overall four brought were too Earthquake-fragile.
reflections.adjustment: Against this opponent in a future series, do not bring two or more Earthquake-weak Pokemon alongside each other when Garchomp + Scrafty Protect is a known combination. Replace Tyranitar with Grimmsnarl (Prankster screens/Taunt, resists Snarl and Dragon Claw, immune to Earthquake via typing matchup pressure) or Paldean Tauros Aqua (Intimidate to cut Garchomp's Attack, Water STAB for Garchomp). Keep Mega Gengar for trapping but preserve its HP better—avoid tanking Light of Ruin if possible, since Gengar at low HP cannot clean up late game.

reflections.summary: Won game 3 and the series 2-1 because the Gengar/Excadrill lead was pressured into defensive lines while Mega Floette's sacrifice left Mega Gengar at 24%, allowing Scrafty Snarl to reduce it to 5%. Talonflame then absorbed the key attacks, and the Garchomp/Scrafty endgame converted repeated Earthquake pressure into KOs on Gholdengo, Tyranitar, and Excadrill before Scrafty finished Gengar. The between-game approach helped: Scrafty's Intimidate, repeated Snarl, and Protects gave Life Orb Garchomp the protected turns it needed. Piloting was clean with no recorded errors. At preview, Floette/Scrafty/Talonflame/Garchomp was a suitable four: Floette forced immediate damage into Gengar, Scrafty was crucial utility, Talonflame provided expendable tempo, and Garchomp was the decisive win condition. Mega Floette was a reasonable evolution choice despite being immediately removed; it created the Gengar endgame threshold. For series preparation, the registered six fit well: Garchomp and Scrafty were especially strong into the revealed Steel/sand core, while Floette gave a direct Mega Gengar pressure option. Nothing in the unused roster is evidenced to have been a materially better game-3 alternative; Metagross, Milotic, and the unused seasonal options have no revealed matchup advantage strong enough to displace the winning four.
reflections.adjustment: For a future series, retain the Garchomp/Scrafty-centered plan against this opponent's Mega Gengar, Gholdengo, Tyranitar, and Excadrill structure. Respect Excadrill Protect when using Fake Out and avoid relying on Talonflame to survive Rock Slide; treat it primarily as a tempo or sacrifice piece. Preserve Garchomp through the midgame with Scrafty Protect and Intimidate so Earthquake can clean the sand endgame. If Mega Gengar is exposed, prioritize bringing it into Ground- or Snarl-finishing range rather than trying to preserve Floette after it has achieved that damage.

events.text: Light Screen up on P2's side

decisions.rationale: Lead Mamoswine and Farigiraf to threaten Metagross and Dragapult while Armor Tail protects Trick Room from Fake Out. Armarouge supports the Trick Room mode with Wide Guard and strong spread-safe pressure, while Archaludon provides immediate special coverage into Rotom-Wash, Clawitzer, and opposing Dragon targets.

Lead Incineroar + Dragapult: Intimidate weakens Sneasler/Mamoswine; Dragapult outspeeds the entire opponent team (213 Spe) and Psychic Fangs is a guaranteed OHKO on Sneasler (Focus Sash leaves it at 1 HP). Incineroar's Darkest Lariat hits Farigiraf for 2x (60.8–113.8%, possible OHKO). Armor Tail blocks our Fake Out and Prankster, so Klefki stays in back to set Light Clay screens after Farigiraf is removed. Mega Metagross cleans late-game with Tough Claws STABs once priority blockers are gone.
Use priority Ice Shard to pressure Dragapult before it acts, while Farigiraf establishes Trick Room for the slow-mode core and preserves the option to punish Incineroar next turn.

Keep Mamoswine in play while replacing the fainted Farigiraf with Armarouge. Armarouge provides a strong Fire attack into Metagross, resists Incineroar's Fire pressure, and preserves Wide Guard protection against spread attacks.

Farigiraf is the Trick Room setter and must be eliminated before it moves. Dragapult U-turn (43.6-80%) + Incineroar Darkest Lariat (60.8-113.8%) guarantees the KO with combined minimum 104.4%. Both moves resolve before Trick Room (priority -7). U-turn also pivots Dragapult out of Mamoswine's Ice threat. If Farigiraf Protects we lose momentum, but Mental Herb makes the opponent confident enough to click Trick Room turn 1.

Incineroar must stay in (only Pass/Forfeit options). Darkest Lariat guarantees KO on Farigiraf (38%) before Trick Room goes up, since TR is -7 priority. Metagross is the superior switch: it Mega Evolves with Tough Claws, resists Ice Shard, survives any single hit from -1 Mamoswine, and Meteor Mash threatens Mamoswine (67-123% into 90%). Klefki is too passive and leaves us without offensive pressure if Incineroar falls to Helping Hand + High Horsepower.
Protect preserves Mamoswine from Incineroar and Metagross pressure while Armarouge targets Metagross with the strongest super-effective attack and has a possible OHKO.

Metagross outspeeds both foes and Mega Evolves for Tough Claws, making Meteor Mash a likely OHKO on Mamoswine (~87-160% into 90% HP). Incineroar Darkest Lariat into Armarouge deals 57-105%, threatening a KO or leaving it in range for Dragapult later. Armarouge's Armor Cannon OHKOs Metagross in return, but this trade removes Mamoswine (the bigger long-term threat with LO High Horsepower) while damaging Armarouge. If Mamoswine Protects, we still pressure Armarouge and Incineroar remains healthy. Parting Shot is rejected because it goes last and Armarouge already attacks before the drop applies; switching loses Incineroar's offensive pressure.

Switching to Dragapult is too risky: Mamoswine's Ice Shard (priority +1) guarantees a KO on 38% Dragapult before it can move. Klefki survives any single hit from Mamoswine (High Horsepower 68-97%, Ice Shard negligible) and Armarouge is almost certain to Protect at 20% HP fearing Darkest Lariat, so Klefki won't face Armor Cannon. Klefki then enables Prankster Reflect to shore up our defense against the remaining physical threats.

Protect Armarouge against Incineroar's priority pressure while Mamoswine targets Klefki with super-effective High Horsepower. This creates the best chance to remove Klefki without exposing the weakened Armarouge; Armor Cannon is then available to finish if High Horsepower misses the KO.

Light Screen goes up at Prankster +1 priority before Armarouge moves, halving Armor Cannon into Klefki to ~54–78% so Klefki survives. Incineroar's Darkest Lariat is a guaranteed OHKO on the 20% -1 Def Armarouge. If Armarouge Protects, we still get Light Screen and lose nothing critical; if it attacks, we trade our move for their Pokémon while Klefki lives. This line covers both opponent options cleanly.

High Horsepower should finish the heavily weakened Klefki, while Wide Guard protects both Pokémon from Dazzling Gleam and preserves Armarouge against spread pressure. This maintains pressure on Incineroar and avoids redundant targeting.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Darkest Lariat OHKOs Armarouge (57-105% into 20% HP, -1 Def) unless its reduced-rate Protect succeeds. Thunder Wave permanently paralyzes Mamoswine before it moves — quarters Speed and adds 25% full-para chance — extracting maximum value from Klefki before it falls to High Horsepower. Dragapult enters for free afterward and with para support can outspeed and threaten Mamoswine.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Double-target Dragapult: Mamoswine's priority Ice Shard may finish it before it acts, while Archaludon's Draco Meteor guarantees the KO if Ice Shard falls short. This also preserves pressure on Incineroar afterward.

Dragapult is guaranteed KOed by Mamoswine Ice Shard (+1 priority) before it can move. Incineroar Flare Blitz on Mamoswine has a roll to KO (41.5–75.7% into 70% HP); if it KOs, the game becomes Incineroar vs Archaludon, which is winnable with Sitrus Berry and Light Screen. Dragon Darts on Mamoswine is the best contingency if the opponent unexpectedly does not Ice Shard (e.g., doubles Incineroar), as Dragon Darts + Flare Blitz near-guarantee the KO on Mamoswine. No other move combination offers a better path to victory.

reflections.summary: Won by combining Mamoswine’s priority pressure with disciplined Protect and targeting: Ice Shard removed Dragapult, Armor Cannon immediately eliminated Mega Metagross, and Archaludon finished Incineroar. The four brought were generally well suited to the matchup, especially Mamoswine, Armarouge, and Archaludon; however, Farigiraf was exposed to heavy turn-one pressure and contributed little. No Mega Stone holder was brought or evolved, which was appropriate for this roster.
reflections.adjustment: Next game, preserve Farigiraf from turn-one double targeting by leading Mamoswine with Armarouge or protecting/switching Farigiraf while focusing Dragapult. Continue prioritizing the fast threat before committing to longer-term setup, and account for Klefki’s Prankster screens.

reflections.summary: The game was lost primarily due to a turn 2 misplay where Metagross targeted Mamoswine with Meteor Mash into Protect, allowing Armarouge to KO Metagross with Armor Cannon. This cost us our Mega Evolution and gave the opponent a significant advantage. Additionally, Klefki wasted a turn using Thunder Wave on immune Mamoswine.
reflections.adjustment: In the next game, prioritize KOing Armarouge with super effective moves (e.g., Zen Headbutt from Metagross) when it is on the field, and avoid using status moves on immune targets. Consider leading with Sneasler to Taunt Farigiraf and prevent Trick Room, and be cautious of bringing Metagross against Armarouge's Fire coverage.

decisions.rationale: Lead Mamoswine and Armarouge to pressure Dragapult, Incineroar, and Metagross immediately while preserving strong spread protection through Armarouge's Wide Guard. Bring Archaludon as durable special pressure in the back, with Sneasler providing fast Fake Out, Taunt, and Coaching support.

Incineroar brings Intimidate, Darkest Lariat for Farigiraf, and Parting Shot pivoting. Dragapult is our fastest mon with Will-O-Wisp for Mamoswine/Sneasler, U-turn momentum, and Dragon Darts pressure. Rotom-Wash adds bulk, a second Will-O-Wisp, Hydro Pump for Armarouge, and Ground immunity. Clawitzer is the special wallbreaker: Mega Launcher Dark Pulse threatens Farigiraf/Sinistcha, Aura Sphere hits Mamoswine/Archaludon super-effectively, and Water Pulse covers Armarouge. Metagross is left behind due to Fire/Ground weaknesses into Armarouge and Mamoswine; Klefki's Prankster is blanked by Farigiraf's Armor Tail.
Ice Shard pressures the fast Dragapult while Wide Guard protects both Pokémon from Dragon Darts and preserves the core against spread pressure.

Dragapult outspeeds Mamoswine and burns it with Will-O-Wisp before it moves, halving its Attack on top of the existing -1 Intimidate. This turns Icicle Crash from a possible OHKO (89.7-127.9%) into a safe 2HKO. Simultaneously, Incineroar Fake Outs Armarouge to prevent Wide Guard (which would block future spread moves) and Armor Cannon pressure. Even if Armarouge Protects, the burn still lands on Mamoswine. Farigiraf is not on the field, so Armor Tail does not block Fake Out.

Clawitzer's Mega Launcher-boosted Water Pulse OHKOs Mamoswine (94-184%) and Dark Pulse threatens Armarouge (81-151%, possible KO from 87%). Clawitzer also has Protect for scouting and Aura Sphere for potential Archaludon. Rotom-Wash is safer defensively with Levitate but lacks the immediate offensive pressure to flip the 0-1 deficit. Incineroar must stay in to maintain board presence and threaten with Flare Blitz/Darkest Lariat.

Switch Mamoswine to preserve the pressure core and avoid its severe vulnerability to Clawitzer's super-effective attacks; Protect Armarouge to deny a likely double-target while bringing Archaludon safely into position for the next turn.
Switch to Sneasler to preserve the Focus Sash and bring in a fast Fake Out user while Armarouge passes; this gives the best chance to regain tempo after Armarouge is likely targeted.

Both foes outspeed us. Mamoswine's High Horsepower into Incineroar does 66.8-96.5% (survivable with Sitrus Berry), and Armarouge's Expanding Force into Clawitzer does 37.6-53.9% (survivable). We retaliate with Darkest Lariat into Armarouge (57.3-105%, possible KO from 87%) and Aura Sphere into Mamoswine (85.3-163.2%, likely KO from 90%). Spreading damage threatens both slots; even if one foe Protects, the other takes heavy damage. This preserves both Pokémon and seizes momentum.

Sneasler acts before Incineroar and applies maximum immediate pressure with Close Combat, while Armarouge Protect prevents either foe from removing it this turn and preserves the core for the next turn.

Parting Shot on Sneasler debuffs its Atk/SpA and pivots Incineroar into Rotom-Wash, while Water Pulse on Armarouge forces the opponent into a dilemma: if they Fake Out Clawitzer to save Armarouge, Parting Shot succeeds and Rotom-Wash enters with Sneasler at -1; if they Fake Out Incineroar, Water Pulse KOs Armarouge anyway. Either outcome leaves us in a strong position with Rotom-Wash threatening both remaining foes.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Sneasler acts first and pressures Clawitzer with Close Combat, while Armarouge must attempt Protect because either opposing Water move can remove it from 3% HP. This preserves Mamoswine as the remaining endgame pressure option.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Sneasler cannot Fake Out (not its first turn out) so both my Pokémon will act. Clawitzer's +4 priority Protect guarantees it survives any double-target attempt; Sneasler + Armarouge doubling Clawitzer with Close Combat (52.8–75.8%) and Expanding Force (37.6–53.9%) could otherwise KO before Clawitzer moves. Rotom-Wash Volt Switch into the 3% Armarouge is a guaranteed KO (20.3–37.5% minimum), removing the special attacker. If Armarouge Protects at 33% success it lives, but Clawitzer remains safe and we enter turn 5 with both Pokémon healthy. This preserves a 2v2 endgame against Sneasler (Sash intact) and backline Mamoswine.

Sneasler's Close Combat pressures Clawitzer immediately while Mamoswine Protects from both opposing Water attacks, preserving the key endgame win condition. Clawitzer's reduced Protect success makes this the best balance of progress and safety.

Double into Sneasler to guarantee a KO through Focus Sash. Hydro Pump (47.1–89.7%) breaks Sash, Water Pulse (58.3–111%) finishes; combined minimum 105.4% ensures Sneasler faints if Hydro Pump connects. Sneasler cannot OHKO either of our Pokémon, and Mamoswine's Ice Shard + Sneasler CC cannot KO Clawitzer before it moves. Worst case they double Clawitzer with High Horsepower, but even then Sneasler's Sash breaks and Rotom-Wash can clean up 1v2 with favourable matchups.
Sneasler is fainted, so pass. High Horsepower guarantees the KO on Clawitzer, removing the immediate Water threat and maximizing Mamoswine’s endgame pressure.

Clawitzer at 26% is threatened by both Icicle Crash and High Horsepower (guaranteed KO). Protect at +4 priority blocks any attack into Clawitzer. Rotom Hydro Pump into Mamoswine does 64.5-124.3%; even if it misses or rolls low, both my Pokémon survive to turn 7 where Clawitzer Water Pulse guarantees the KO. This line dominates: if opponent targets Clawitzer it's blocked; if they target Rotom, Clawitzer lives and KOs next turn; Ice Shard cannot KO either mon. Double-attacking risks Clawitzer fainting before moving, leaving a 1v1 where Hydro Pump may not KO.

reflections.summary: Lost because the four brought lacked a reliable answer to the opponent’s Rotom-Wash and Clawitzer core; once Archaludon and Armarouge were removed, Mamoswine and Sneasler could not finish through sustained Water pressure. The preview plan was only partly suitable: Sneasler was valuable against Incineroar, but bringing both Armarouge and Archaludon exposed too much of the team to Clawitzer and Rotom-Wash. No Mega Stone holder was brought or evolved.
reflections.adjustment: Next game, bring a dependable Water-resistant or Water-immune answer and prioritize removing or neutralizing Rotom-Wash and Clawitzer before committing Mamoswine as the endgame attacker; do not rely on Mamoswine alone to close while both remain active.

reflections.summary: won because Clawitzer’s critical Aura Sphere eliminated Archaludon early, and Rotom-Wash walled the remaining grounded threats with Levitate + Leftovers, while opponent's Wide Guard Armarouge lead offered no offensive pressure.
reflections.adjustment: start Rotom-Wash over Dragapult to avoid an immediate Ice Shard KO, and preserve Dragapult as a cleaner with Parting Shot cycling for Intimidate.

decisions.rationale: Lead Archaludon and Farigiraf to deny priority with Armortail, establish Trick Room, and provide immediate special pressure. Sinistcha is the reliable Water counter with Grass spread damage and sustain, while Mamoswine is preserved as a strong Trick Room attacker and Electric-immunity pivot.

Incineroar + Metagross lead: Intimidate softens physical attackers, Fake Out pressures non-Farigiraf leads, Parting Shot pivots out of Trick Room. Metagross Mega Evolves for Tough Claws Zen Headbutt (4x into Sneasler) and Earthquake (SE on Archaludon/Armarouge). Back Dragapult outspeeds everything, Psychic Fangs 4x OHKO threat on Sneasler, U-turn maintains momentum, Will-O-Wisp cripples Mamoswine. Rotom-Wash Levitate blanks Mamoswine's High Horsepower, spreads burns, Volt Switch pivots, Hydro Pump threatens Mamoswine and Armarouge. Covers both fast mode (Sneasler+Archaludon) and Trick Room mode (Farigiraf+breaker).
Archaludon acts before Metagross and pressures Incineroar with Draco Meteor, while Farigiraf Protects to block the expected Fake Out and preserve its ability to use Trick Room next turn.

Farigiraf is the Trick Room setter and must be removed before it warps the game. Armor Tail blocks Fake Out and Bullet Punch, so the best line is double-targeting Farigiraf with Darkest Lariat + Mega Meteor Mash. Darkest Lariat does 60.8–113.8%; Mega Metagross Tough Claws Meteor Mash does ~44.7–84.0% (90% accurate). Minimum combined 105.5% guarantees the KO if both connect. If Farigiraf Protects, Trick Room stays off the field and we reset next turn. If Trick Room goes up as Farigiraf faints, the setter is gone and we play out 4 turns of room with Archaludon alone. Mega Evolving also ensures Metagross outspeeds Archaludon (143–178 vs 105–137).

Helping Hand resolves before opposing priority and boosts Draco Meteor enough to give the best chance of removing Incineroar immediately, while Archaludon can still act after Mega Metagross's likely Earthquake.
Keep Archaludon in and bring Sinistcha rather than exposing Mamoswine while Metagross remains boosted; preserve Mamoswine for later Ground and Ice pressure after opposing Water threats are weakened.

Double-targeting Farigiraf with Darkest Lariat + Meteor Mash guarantees a KO before Trick Room resolves (both are faster than Trick Room's -7 priority). Combined minimum damage is 108.4%, so even with Protect at 1/3 success rate, the opponent cannot safely set Trick Room. If Farigiraf switches, Trick Room is still denied this turn and the switch-in takes heavy damage. This is the most reliable play to prevent the opponent's win condition.
Archaludon safely finishes the exposed Incineroar with Draco Meteor, while Sinistcha Protects to deny Flare Blitz and preserve its defensive utility; Metagross's spread Earthquake is survivable.

Parting Shot into Sinistcha covers both RagePowder (redirected, debuffs Sinistcha) and non-RagePowder lines. Meteor Mash into Sinistcha deals 62.9–115.1% and is also RagePowder-proof. If they RagePowder: Sinistcha eats both moves, gets debuffed and damaged, then Incineroar pivots safely to Dragapult. If they MatchaGotcha: Incineroar may fall before Parting Shot, but Meteor Mash still connects and Dragapult enters for free. Dragapult outspeeds the entire opposing field and brings Will-O-Wisp, Dragon Darts, and U-turn for future turns. Preserving Incineroar for a second Intimidate cycle is valuable but not worth risking a direct switch that forfeits the Parting Shot debuff.

Thunderbolt pressures the 9% Incineroar and may KO before it can act, while Strength Sap targets Metagross's boosted Attack to reduce its Earthquake threat and improve the board's longer-term survivability.

Parting Shot into Sinistcha gives value against both likely opponent lines: if Sinistcha Rage Powders, it redirects and gets -1 SpA while Incineroar pivots to Dragapult; if Sinistcha Matcha Gotchas, Incineroar faints but Metagross still lands Meteor Mash (62.9–115.1%) before Dragapult enters for free. Meteor Mash is chosen over Zen Headbutt for higher damage and the Attack-boost chance. Targeting Sinistcha with both ensures pressure on the opponent's most threatening remaining piece regardless of redirection.

Dragapult is the clear switch-in: it outspeeds both foes (213 vs 105–137 and 90–122), Dragon Darts pressures both targets and doubles onto Sinistcha if Rage Powder is used, Clear Body blocks Strength Sap's Attack drop, and it resists Matcha Gotcha. Rotom-Wash risks being outsped by Sinistcha and offers less immediate KO pressure. Metagross stays in; next turn Meteor Mash + Dragon Darts into Sinistcha gives a strong KO range (83–153% if Rage Powder redirects both Darts hits, ~63–115% otherwise) before Sinistcha can heal.

Use Rage Powder to draw Dragapult's single-target pressure into Sinistcha while Archaludon fires the strongest available attack into Dragapult. This creates immediate super-effective damage and preserves Archaludon from targeted attacks; Metagross's spread Ground pressure is resisted by Sinistcha and does not prevent the play.

Dragon Darts into Archaludon + Meteor Mash into Sinistcha maximizes pressure on the opponent's win condition (Sinistcha). If Sinistcha uses Rage Powder, both attacks redirect to it: Dragon Darts hits twice (40-77%) and Meteor Mash adds 43-77%, giving a strong chance to KO through redirection. If Sinistcha Protects, Dragon Darts still lands both hits on Archaludon (36-63%) as a fallback. Dragon Darts targeting Archaludon is strictly better than targeting Sinistcha when Protect is up, and equivalent under Rage Powder. Archaludon at -4 SpA is negligible offensively, so Sinistcha removal is the priority.

Sinistcha Protect preserves its utility and blocks the likely immediate double-target pressure while Archaludon uses its strongest available attack to punish Dragapult. Draco Meteor's super-effective damage is the best chance to create a favorable follow-up despite its accuracy risk.

Split targets to beat both Rage Powder and Protect: Dragon Darts into Archaludon gets redirected to Sinistcha if it Rage Powders (guaranteed KO), and still chips Archaludon if Sinistcha Protects. Bullet Punch into Sinistcha KOs before Strength Sap resolves if it stays in and doesn't Protect; if it Rage Powders, Bullet Punch also redirects and KOs. Either attack landing on 19% Sinistcha is a guaranteed KO.

Thunderbolt reliably removes the 1% Dragapult without risking another Draco Meteor miss. Rage Powder redirects Dragapult's remaining attack away from Archaludon while preserving the chance to survive Metagross's pressure.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Sinistcha is the opponent's win condition with Strength Sap healing and Rage Powder redirection. Metagross-Mega outspeeds Sinistcha and Meteor Mash is a guaranteed KO from 25% (90% accurate). Dragapult's Will-O-Wisp on Sinistcha provides insurance against the 10% miss chance — even if Meteor Mash misses, burn cripples Sinistcha's recovery and adds chip. Rage Powder is irrelevant since both attacks already target Sinistcha. Protect has only ~33% success after consecutive use. Dragapult avoids Life Orb recoil by using a status move, preserving it at 2% for potential future sacrifice. Archaludon at -6 SpA is harmless.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Mamoswine Protects to avoid the combined Hydro Pump and Metagross pressure, preserving its potential High Horsepower KO on Metagross next turn. Archaludon uses Thunderbolt to chip Rotom-Wash while remaining outside immediate KO range from Earthquake.

Metagross-Mega (178 Speed) is guaranteed to move before Mamoswine. Meteor Mash into Mamoswine does 91.2–166.5% (OHKO likely), and Hydro Pump adds 64.5–124.3%. Combined minimum 155.7% guarantees the KO if both hit. Even in the worst case—Meteor Mash minimum roll leaving Mamoswine alive, Mamoswine winning the speed tie and OHKOing Metagross-Mega with High Horsepower—Rotom-Wash cleans up Mamoswine with Hydro Pump and then easily handles Archaludon at -6 SpA alone. If Mamoswine Protects, both attacks are blocked but consecutive Protect fails often, and we repeat the pressure next turn. No other target makes sense: Archaludon at -6 SpA is harmless, and Rotom-Wash has no bench to pivot to with Volt Switch.

Mamoswine must protect to avoid Rotom-Wash's threatening Hydro Pump while preserving its late-game Ground pressure. Archaludon uses Thunderbolt into Metagross-Mega for safe chip without exposing itself to Rotom's likely attack; Mamoswine's reduced Protect chance is preferable to sacrificing it.

Bullet Punch (priority +1, 100% accuracy) goes first and does 41.5–75.7% to Mamoswine. Hydro Pump adds 64.5–124.3%. Combined minimum 106% guarantees the KO if Hydro Pump hits (80% chance). Mamoswine never gets to move. Archaludon at –6 SpA is harmless (Thunderbolt does 7–10% to Metagross). No other play offers a higher probability of removing the only remaining threat immediately.

Double-target Metagross-Mega: Mamoswine's High Horsepower has a realistic KO chance, while Archaludon's Thunderbolt adds necessary damage despite its severe Special Attack drops. Protecting would leave Metagross active and risk losing Mamoswine to Hydro Pump without meaningful progress.

Double into Mamoswine to remove the only remaining threat. Metagross (178 Speed) is guaranteed faster than Mamoswine (90–118); Meteor Mash has 90% accuracy and OHKO range 91–166%, so if it connects Mamoswine faints before moving. Hydro Pump provides backup: if Meteor Mash misses, Hydro Pump still has an 80% chance to KO (64–124%). Archaludon at –6 SpA is harmless and can be cleaned up afterwards.

Draco Meteor is Archaludon's strongest available attack into Rotom-Wash despite the severe Special Attack drops; Flash Cannon is heavily resisted, while Thunderbolt is weaker. Mamoswine has no available action.

Rotom-Wash is unkillable: Archaludon at –6 SpA does at most 19.7% with Draco Meteor (3 PP left) and even less with Thunderbolt/Flash Cannon, all fully recovered by Leftovers. Hydro Pump 5 PP needs only 2–3 hits to KO 55% Archaludon; opponent cannot stall forever because consecutive Protect fails. Clicking Hydro Pump every turn is the fastest guaranteed path to victory.
Use Draco Meteor because it is the strongest neutral attack available into Rotom-Wash; Flash Cannon and Thunderbolt are resisted. Mamoswine is fainted and must pass.

Hydro Pump into Archaludon is the only sensible play. Archaludon at –6 SpA deals 1.9–2.5% with Flash Cannon, which Leftovers (6.25%/turn) outheals effortlessly. Hydro Pump does 16.8–32.7%; even if it doesn't KO this turn, repeated use guarantees the win with zero risk. Metagross is fainted and must pass.

reflections.summary: Lost the game and series mainly because the four brought could not consistently convert pressure into a win against the Rotom-Wash endgame. Archaludon eventually helped remove Dragapult and Metagross, while Mamoswine’s High Horsepower finished Metagross, but Rotom remained largely healthy and outlasted the weakened Archaludon. Draco Meteor misses into Incineroar and Dragapult cost substantial momentum, although there were no recorded decision errors and the late-game loss was not primarily a piloting mistake. The preview plan was mixed: Archaludon, Sinistcha, and Mamoswine all had useful roles, but Farigiraf was exposed to Metagross plus Incineroar pressure, and Mamoswine was a poor long-term answer to Rotom. No own Mega Stone holder was brought or evolved, so there was no Mega choice to evaluate. The registered six had relevant tools, but the supplied evidence does not establish that any of Altaria, Meowstic-Female, Qwilfish, or Dedenne was a materially better replacement; Armarouge and Sneasler were also untested, so the series loss cannot be attributed to a proven superior unused roster. There is insufficient evidence to judge whether between-game adjustments helped or backfired; in this game, the adjustment toward Sinistcha and Mamoswine produced useful progress but did not solve the matchup.
reflections.adjustment: Against this opponent, prioritize a reliable, accurate way to pressure or remove Rotom-Wash before committing Archaludon to an attrition endgame. Preserve the Rotom answer rather than using Mamoswine only as a Metagross check, and avoid relying on repeated Draco Meteor connections when a safer line is available. Farigiraf should not be left to absorb simultaneous Metagross and Incineroar pressure without stronger protection or immediate speed-control value. Re-evaluate the four from the full roster only if the unused Pokémon have verified tools against Rotom and Mega Metagross; no such advantage is demonstrated by the supplied data.

reflections.summary: Your game plan of applying immediate pressure while denying Trick Room paid off early when Farigiraf fainted turn 2. A key sequence of double protect reads from the opponent around the Sinistcha switch-in stalled your momentum and cost you Incineroar. A critical Thunderbolt onto Metagross on turn 10 turned a likely 2v1 endgame into a 1v1, but Rotom-Wash had such a commanding special-defensive advantage over the heavily debuffed Archaludon that the endgame was unwinnable for the opponent.
