You won the series because your team-preview brought the correct disruption and priority, and your late-game positioning on Rotom-Wash was decisive.
reflections.adjustment: Against this opponent, continue bringing Incineroar, Metagross, Dragapult, and Rotom-Wash. Your disruptive core punishes their reliance on Farigiraf and Sinistcha for setup. Consider respecting the double Protect pattern more aggressively by predicting and using setup turns yourself. In future series, you could explore bringing Klefki over Dragapult for Prankster Thunder Wave to further disrupt Trick Room, but Dragapult’s offensive pressure and Will-O-Wisp were effective. Clawitzer remains a poor fit into Archaludon. Your registered six was well-suited; no major roster change is required.

decisions.rationale: Lead Manectric + Talonflame pressures the expected rain opener with Lightning Rod protection and priority Tailwind/Taunt. Mega Floette provides immediate Water/Ground pressure and broad Fairy damage, while Hatterene supplies a durable Trick Room pivot if rain speed control becomes problematic.

Pelipper and Swampert lead to set up Drizzle rain and immediate offensive pressure, backed by choice-scarfed Basculegion and fast Prankster Whimsicott in the back to clean up and maintain speed control.

Gale Wings Tailwind establishes speed control before either foe can act, while Life Orb Thunderbolt is a guaranteed OHKO on Pelipper if it stays in. This removes rain support immediately and leaves Tailwind to offset Mega Swampert’s Swift Swim.

Protect on both Pelipper and Swampert on turn 1 is the safest play against Manectric and Gale Wings Talonflame, wasting Talonflame's Gale Wings and protecting against potential double-targeting while allowing Swampert to Mega Evolve safely.

Refresh Tailwind with Gale Wings while Manectric secures the guaranteed Thunderbolt KO on Pelipper; this accepts Swampert’s likely Earthquake KO on Manectric but removes rain support and preserves a fast Floette-Eternal answer to Swampert.
Floette-Eternal preserves immediate Tailwind-boosted Energy Ball pressure into Mega Swampert while avoiding the much worse Ground matchup Hatterene would face.

Pelipper targets Talonflame with Hydro Pump (guaranteed OHKO on Focus Sash due to breaking it or damage overkill, or Talonflame may be vulnerable since Pelipper protected last turn and Tailwind is up). Swampert Mega Evolves and uses Waterfall on Manectric to guarantee a kill while avoiding hitting its own partner with Earthquake (since Talonflame is immune/flying and Manectric is targeted by Waterfall).

Pelipper fainted last turn, so we bring in Basculegion under rain, while Mega Swampert passes its turn to make the substitution. Basculegion outspeeds and threatens the remaining opponents with its Swift Swim/Choice Scarf speed under rain, and Tailwind is active for the foe.
Mega Energy Ball maximizes the chance to remove Mega Swampert immediately while priority Brave Bird puts decisive chip on Basculegion for Talonflame’s next priority attack.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Talonflame is under Tailwind and holds Focus Sash, but Basculegion's Wave Crash and Mega Swampert's Waterfall both target Talonflame to break through its Sash and remove its offensive pressure immediately.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Floette outspeeds both foes while Tailwind is active and Energy Ball cleanly removes the 17% Basculegion before its Choice-locked Wave Crash. Hatterene’s Dazzling Gleam pressures Whimsicott through Focus Sash while also providing backup damage.
Basculegion is Choice-locked into Wave Crash and can hit Hatterene for a guaranteed OHKO. Whimsicott sets up Tailwind to seize speed control as the opponent's Tailwind expires this turn.
Moonblast is Floette-Mega’s strongest available attack into Whimsicott and avoids voluntarily selecting the previously used Energy Ball.
Basculegion is fainted so it passes. Whimsicott uses Moonblast against the sole remaining active threat, Floette-Mega.

reflections.summary: Won by correctly prioritizing Pelipper and Mega Swampert, removing rain’s setter and its main rain abuser while Mega Floette cleaned the weakened remaining core. The 4-Pokémon bring—Manectric, Talonflame, Hatterene, and Floette—fit well into rain, and Mega Floette was the appropriate evolution; piloting had no recorded errors.
reflections.adjustment: Next game, preserve Talonflame or Hatterene more carefully once the rain core is removed, since either can provide a stronger endgame speed-control option than trading both into Basculegion’s Wave Crash.

reflections.summary: The opponent established speed control via Talonflame's Tailwind and leveraged Mega Floette's Fairy Aura-boosted coverage alongside backline threats to overwhelm the Swift Swim setup and dismantle the rain core.
reflections.adjustment: Bring Whimsicott initially to block or counter opposing speed control immediately and better position Swampert and Basculegion for uncontested offensive pressure.

decisions.rationale: Lead Mega Floette plus Manectric pressures the expected Pelipper + Mega Swampert rain lead immediately: Thunderbolt threatens Pelipper while Energy Ball threatens Swampert, and Lightning Rod discourages Water attacks into Manectric. Hatterene provides a Trick Room reversal option, while Scrafty brings Intimidate and useful physical-pressure control for Swampert and Basculegion.

Pelipper and Swampert form a core rain-setting and sweeping duo with Drizzle and Mega Swampert, while Basculegion and Primarina provide strong backline cleaning and adapt to the opponent's aggressive Tailwind / Electric options.
Mega Energy Ball pressures the rain-enabled Mega Swampert slot while Life Orb Thunderbolt guarantees Pelipper's KO if it does not Protect.
Bring Hatterene to retain Trick Room as the strongest answer to the opponent’s Tailwind and likely fast rain backline; Floette can protect while Hatterene establishes speed control.
Setting Tailwind with Pelipper and Mega Evolving Swampert to use Earthquake threatens both opposing slots while doubling our Speed under Swift Swim next turn.

Pelipper stays in to maintain rain or attack while Basculegion enters to clean up with Choice Scarf Adaptability Wave Crash or Last Respects under rain and Tailwind, outspeeding the remaining opponent threats.
Protect Hatterene from Basculegion’s rain-boosted Wave Crash, which is a guaranteed KO, while Energy Ball pressures Basculegion and sets up Scrafty’s Fake Out to create a later Trick Room window.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Floette-Mega is at 37% HP and can be KOed by Pelipper's Hydro Pump or Basculegion's Wave Crash. Targeting Floette with Hydro Pump and Hatterene with Last Respects secures an immediate KO on Floette while heavily damaging or eliminating Hatterene.

Fake Out removes Pelipper’s attack this turn, allowing Hatterene to safely establish Trick Room through Basculegion’s nonlethal, Choice-locked Last Respects. Trick Room then lets Hatterene and Scrafty act before the scarfed Basculegion next turn.

Pelipper uses Hurricane on Scrafty (super-effective), while Choice Scarf Basculegion uses Last Respects on Hatterene (super-effective). Tailwind is still active on our side, and Basculegion outspeeds both remaining foes to pick up clean KOs in the rain.
Snarl is the only line that meaningfully reduces Pelipper's repeated special damage while also chipping both foes; Basculegion is locked into its weak resisted Last Respects.

Scrafty is the sole remaining active opponent and is weak to Flying; Pelipper hits it with Hurricane. Basculegion is locked into Last Respects, which hits Scrafty for neutral/halved damage, but since Scrafty is the only target remaining (and Last Respects hits the only opposing slot) Basculegion uses Last Respects into Scrafty. Tailwind expires at the end of this turn, so finishing Scrafty now closes out the game cleanly.
Knock Off into Basculegion is Scrafty’s only available line with a possible immediate KO and removes its Choice Scarf if it survives.
Pelipper's Hurricane cleanly KOs the remaining Scrafty, and Basculegion can use Last Respects just in case or as a safe follow-up.

reflections.summary: The four brought were reasonable into rain: Mega Floette cleanly removed Mega Swampert, and Hatterene/Scrafty offered a Trick Room route. Mega Floette was an appropriate evolution for Swampert, but the opening trade left it exposed to Choice Scarf Basculegion's increasingly powerful Last Respects; Basculegion then prevented Hatterene from establishing Trick Room and rain Pelipper finished the endgame.
reflections.adjustment: Next game, prioritize getting Trick Room up before trading away Floette: use Scrafty's Fake Out pressure to create a safer Hatterene Trick Room turn, while preserving Floette as a late-game Fairy attacker rather than leaving it available for Basculegion's Last Respects.

reflections.summary: Swampert and Pelipper opened with immediate pressure against Manectric and Mega Floette, setting up Tailwind and pivoting into Choice Scarf Basculegion to clean up with high-power Last Respects once Trick Room setter Hatterene went down.
reflections.adjustment: Maintain aggressive positioning against Trick Room threats and ensure Basculegion keeps clear paths to spam Last Respects safely.

decisions.rationale: Lead Hatterene plus Scrafty to prioritize Fake Out-supported Trick Room against the opponent’s rain speed-control core. Floette provides the Mega option and strong Grass/Fairy pressure into Swampert and Water types, while Manectric supplies Lightning Rod utility and fast special offense outside Trick Room.

Pelipper and Swampert create immediate rain with Drizzle, allowing Swampert to mega evolve and outspeed the opponent's slower or neutral threats under rain. Basculegion and Primarina provide strong backline rain-boosted or adaptable offensive pressure against Hatterene, Scrafty, Manectric, and Floette-Eternal.

Fake Out Pelipper prevents Tailwind this turn while Hatterene establishes Trick Room; even Mega Swampert’s immediate attack should not KO Hatterene from full, preserving the favorable Trick Room position.

Pelipper sets Tailwind to outspeed potential fast threats like Manectric or Mega Floette in the back, while Mega Swampert uses Waterfall + Mega Evolve on Hatterene to apply heavy pressure under Rain, avoiding Fake Out interruption or letting Pelipper safely outspeed.
Protect preserves Hatterene from the immediate double target while Knock Off chips Pelipper and removes Damp Rock, shortening the rain window that enables Mega Swampert.
Pelipper uses Protect to block any incoming threat while Mega Swampert uses Waterfall to finish off Hatterene (which survived on low health after Sitrus Berry consumption last turn).

Pivot Hatterene out of the immediate Waterfall/Hurricane double-target line, preserving both Trick Room and Floette for the Basculegion endgame. Drain Punch provides meaningful Swampert chip and recovery if Scrafty survives.
Bring Hatterene in to preserve the strongest Trick Room route; Scrafty can support its setup next turn with Fake Out pressure.

Pelipper outspeeds Scrafty and can hit it with Hurricane for super-effective damage (with a chance to OHKO through Roseli Berry), while Mega Swampert outspeeds under rain and hits Scrafty with Waterfall or Hatterene with Waterfall. Targeting Scrafty with both attacks or focusing down the board applies massive pressure while keeping Tailwind/Protect options covered.
Protect Hatterene from the likely double-target while Scrafty uses Drain Punch to gain HP and push Swampert-Mega into a much safer follow-up KO range if Scrafty is allowed to act.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Pelipper uses Hurricane into Scrafty to finish off the weakened Scrafty (super-effective), while Mega Swampert uses Waterfall into Scrafty or Ice Punch/Waterfall to pick up targets, or better yet, Swampert uses Waterfall into Scrafty or Ice Punch into Hatterene. Let's check damage or target Scrafty with Pelipper Hurricane and Swampert Waterfall into Scrafty to secure the KO on Scrafty. Wait, Scrafty is at 39% and has RoseliBerry, but Water is neutral. Swampert Waterfall into Scrafty or Ice Punch into Hatterene? Let's verify speeds: Mega Swampert (216 raw speed under rain) outspeeds both. Pelipper outspeeds Scrafty and Hatterene. Pelipper Hurricane into Scrafty guarantees a KO. Swampert Waterfall into Scrafty guarantees a KO. Let's hit Scrafty with both or double target Hatterene. Actually, Scrafty is low (39%). Let's use Pelipper Hurricane into Scrafty (choice 1) and Swampert Waterfall into Scrafty (choice 2) to eliminate Scrafty immediately, leaving only Hatterene.

Mega Moonblast gives Floette-Eternal the best immediate chance to remove Pelipper before it can combine with Swampert-Mega to deny Hatterene’s attack; Giga Drain then pressures the Swampert-Mega slot for a split knockout line.

Swampert outspeeds Floette-Eternal under Swift Swim and can target it with Waterfall while Pelipper hits Hatterene with Hurricane to finish it off through its potential remaining HP, or vice-versa. Target Hatterene first with Pelipper's Hurricane to eliminate it before it can set Trick Room, and hit Floette-Eternal with Swampert's Waterfall.
Swampert outspeeds Floette in rain and KOs Hatterene with Waterfall. Bringing in Basculegion gives us a fast rain threat (Adaptability Wave Crash / Last Respects) to clean up Floette-Mega.
Protect preserves Floette from Basculegion's guaranteed Wave Crash KO while Hatterene retains the only immediate chance to remove Swampert with Giga Drain.
Hatterene is at 2% and can be easily picked off by Basculegion's Last Respects. Meanwhile, Swampert can safely use Waterfall on Floette-Mega to deal heavy damage.
Reduced-rate Protect is the best chance to deny both incoming attacks, then remove Swampert with Energy Ball; attacking immediately risks Floette being overwhelmed before it can act.

Floette-Mega is the only remaining opponent. Basculegion is choice-locked into Last Respects and outspeeds Floette-Mega, dealing heavy damage. Swampert-Mega also outspeeds under Swift Swim and can KO Floette-Mega with Ice Punch (super effective against Fairy).

reflections.summary: Game 3 was lost because the intended Hatterene Trick Room opening never came online: Waterfall flinched Hatterene through the Fake Out on Pelipper, then Manectric was immediately removed by a critical-hit Waterfall on its switch-in. That left the team without speed control or its main electric pressure while Mega Swampert and rain remained active. Mega Floette correctly removed Pelipper, but Hatterene then fell to Choice Scarf Adaptability Basculegion's Last Respects and Floette could not survive the final Swampert+Basculegion pressure. The Hatterene/Scrafty/Manectric/Floette bring had a coherent anti-rain concept—Fake Out, Intimidate, Trick Room, Lightning Rod, and Floette's Grass coverage—but it was fragile into immediate Waterfall pressure and Basculegion's late-game cleanup. Mega Floette was the appropriate Mega choice because Energy Ball threatened the revealed Mega Swampert; no supplied evidence establishes that the between-game adjustments themselves helped or backfired, beyond this Game 3 plan failing to convert. The registered six do not show a clearly proven materially better four from the supplied evidence: Talonflame is unattractive into rain, while no sets or matchup evidence support claiming Hatterene, Hisuian Goodra, or another alternative would definitely have solved the matchup.
reflections.adjustment: For a future series, treat Mega Swampert's Waterfall flinch pressure as a major obstacle to a Hatterene-led Trick Room line rather than assuming Fake Out on Pelipper makes Trick Room safe. Preserve Mega Floette for the Swampert/Basculegion endgame whenever possible; once Swampert is at the confirmed 77% range, seriously consider Energy Ball to remove it instead of spending Floette's attack on Pelipper if that line leaves Floette exposed to Basculegion afterward. Do not rely on Manectric as the primary answer to this rain core when the revealed attackers can simply use Waterfall, Hurricane, and Ground coverage; bring it only if its broader utility is needed. Build the four around a more resilient answer to repeated physical Waterfall plus a plan to prevent or absorb Basculegion's Last Respects, while retaining Scrafty's Intimidate/Fake Out utility if a safer speed-control line exists.

reflections.summary: We won Game 3 and the series 2-1 by leveraging Pelipper's Drizzle to set rain, enabling Mega Swampert's Swift Swim speed control and offensive pressure to dismantle the opponent's Trick Room and offensive pivots. Bringing Basculegion as a clean-up threat sealed the game after key opponent Pokémon like Hatterene and Floette-Mega fell.
reflections.adjustment: No major adjustments needed since the series was won, but keeping Basculegion and rain-setters prioritized against similar Trick Room / Fairy-heavy cores remains optimal.

events.text: Light Screen up on P1's side

decisions.rationale: Lead the sand core of Tyranitar + Excadrill to immediately contest the opponent's sun archetype. Tyranitar's Sand Stream overrides Drought when switching in after Torkoal/Charizard-Y, and Excadrill under Sand Rush outspeeds the entire format. Rock Slide spread from both hits Charizard 4x and Torkoal 2x SE; Iron Head handles Venusaur 2x SE. Both Tyranitar (Rock) and Excadrill (Steel) resist Fire, mitigating Eruption/Fire Blast even if sun is temporarily up. Back line: Tauros-Aqua brings Intimidate and Water STAB (Wave Crash) to delete Fire types and wall Heracross; Grimmsnarl provides Prankster screens and Fake Out for when I need to reset sand or survive a sun barrage. This covers all six opposing Pokémon: sand handles sun weather, Rock Slide deletes Charizard/Torkoal, Iron Head hits Venusaur, Tauros walls Heracross, and Grimmsnarl's Spirit Break softens special attackers.

Lead Charizard and Torkoal to immediately establish Drought sun, powering Fire-type attacks and unlocking Venusaur's Chlorophyll speed when swapped in. Back Heracross answers Tyranitar and Excadrill with super-effective Fighting/Bug coverage and Moxie snowball, while Aegislash provides the critical Ghost-type immunity to Shadow Tag trapping and threatens Gholdengo with super-effective Shadow Ball.

Tyranitar Rock Slide is a guaranteed OHKO on Charizard (4x SE, 103.8–196.1%) and chunks Torkoal for 37–63%. Excadrill must Protect — it's guaranteed OHKO'd by both Charizard Fire Blast (218–322%) and Torkoal Eruption (120–186%). Tyranitar only takes 20–31% from Eruption (Rock resists Fire). Main risk is Charizard predicting Protect and Solar Beaming Tyranitar (71–104%, possible KO), but opponent's natural play is to Fire Blast the obviously threatened Excadrill, which Protect absorbs. If Tyranitar survives, it OHKOs Charizard and we trade 0-for-1 at minimum. Even if Tyranitar falls to Solar Beam, Excadrill is alive and can Rock Slide next turn (87–163% on Charizard, possible OHKO).

Mega Evolving Charizard immediately activates Drought for permanent sun (the core win condition), while Fire Blast targets Excadrill at 2× for reliable damage (85% accuracy). Torkoal uses Eruption as a spread move in sun to hit both foes—Excadrill takes 2× Fire damage while Tyranitar takes neutral, maximizing early pressure and helping secure the sun-sweeper strategy.

Charizard-Mega-Y is fainted and must switch. Heracross is the designated Rock/Dark/Ground core cleaner per the team plan: Close Combat is super effective into both Tyranitar (Rock/Dark) and pressures Excadrill, its 150 Speed likely outpaces both foes, and Moxie rewards the snowball potential after a KO. Aegislash is reserved for the Gengar/Gholdengo matchup later. Torkoal passes to maintain Drought and SunnyDay, preserving the sun offense engine for the rest of the team.

Heracross Close Combat is a guaranteed OHKO on both Tyranitar (4x) and Excadrill (2x, 153-220%), even through Intimidate. Keeping Excadrill in is death. Tyranitar Protect blocks Heracross's 4x Close Combat and Torkoal's 2x Solar Beam safely. Switching Excadrill to Tauros brings Intimidate (-1 Heracross Atk) and a Fighting/Water type that resists all of Heracross's STABs (Close Combat 0.5x via Fighting resist, Megahorn 0.5x via Fighting resist, Rock Blast 0.5x, Vacuum Wave 0.5x). Heracross Close Combat on Tauros does only 34.6-76% with Intimidate applied — Tauros survives and Sitrus Berry heals. Torkoal Eruption/Solar Beam on Tauros is 0.5x (Water resists Fire and Grass). Next turn: Tyranitar Rock Slide (37-63% on Torkoal at 52%, possible KO) plus Tauros Wave Crash or Aqua Jet (2x SE Water on Torkoal) to guarantee the KO, then clean up Heracross 1v2 with weakened Attack. Tyranitar preserved for later sand reset.

Heracross uses Close Combat on Tyranitar for a 4× super-effective hit (Expert Belt + Moxie), very likely OHKOing it. Torkoal uses spread Eruption under Sun with Heat Rock: it is 2× super-effective against Excadrill and hits both foes. Even if Excadrill retaliates with Earthquake, the trade is favorable—Excadrill takes massive Fire damage (likely KO or heavy chip) while Torkoal's sacrifice removes the opposing Ground/Steel threat and keeps Heracross alive with a potential Moxie boost. The Sun timer (7 turns) was already running, so losing Torkoal does not immediately end the weather.

Tyranitar must switch out—Heracross outspeeds and Close Combat is guaranteed 4x OHKO. Grimmsnarl is the safest switch-in: Close Combat is neutral (34-48.5%), SolarBeam 20-31%, Eruption 22-35%; even double-targeted it survives at 20-46%. Tauros Protects (first use, full success rate) to preserve 72% HP. Wave Crash on Torkoal is only 35-62.1% (not guaranteed KO at 52%), and if Torkoal survives, SolarBeam does 64.6-98.7% to Tauros—likely KO. Next turn: Grimmsnarl Light Screen (Prankster priority) halves SolarBeam to 32-49%, letting Tauros safely Wave Crash Torkoal. Tyranitar preserved at 87% in back for later sand re-entry to enable Excadrill sweep.

Heracross Close Combat into Tyranitar guarantees a KO (118.4-200% of max HP vs 87% target) and activates Moxie to offset Intimidate. Torkoal Solar Beam into Tauros-Paldea-Aqua has a strong chance to KO (42.9-84% damage vs 71% HP) with no charge turn in sun and 2x super-effectiveness. This removes both major threats while preserving Aegislash for the unrevealed Pokémon.

Double-target to maximize damage on both foes: Spirit Break on Heracross (77-144.5%, possible OHKO with def-1) removes the biggest threat to Tyranitar, while Wave Crash on Torkoal (35-62.1%, possible KO) may prevent Solar Beam from firing. Tauros outspeeds Torkoal so a KO stops Solar Beam. Even if Tauros falls to Solar Beam, both opponents are left at <25% HP, easily cleaned up by Excadrill (100%) and Tyranitar (87%) in back. This is superior to Light Screen which preserves Tauros but leaves Heracross at 100% — a worse position since Grimmsnarl will be too low to threaten it next turn.

Heracross uses Close Combat on Grimmsnarl for a 2x super-effective hit (Fighting vs Fairy typing) to KO or heavily damage it, triggering Moxie to restore Attack to neutral. Torkoal uses Protect to avoid incoming damage, preserve its HP at 53%, and maintain SunnyDay for the sun offense strategy while Aegislash is preserved for the unrevealed fourth opponent Pokémon.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Grimmsnarl at 13% is dead this turn regardless; Light Screen via Prankster (priority +1) is guaranteed to resolve before any opponent attack, halving Torkoal's Solar Beam (64.6-98.7% → ~32-49%) so Tauros survives at 72%. Tauros Wave Crash into Torkoal (SE 2x, 35-62.1% vs 52% HP) is the best KO chance. If Torkoal survives or Protects (reduced rate), Light Screen is still up and Tauros can Aqua Jet finish next turn. When Grimmsnarl faints, bring Tyranitar for Sand Stream to enable Excadrill Sand Rush.

Switch in Tyranitar to activate Sand Stream (overriding sun) and retain Thunder Wave utility vs Aegislash. Excadrill is completely dead weight against Aegislash (EQ immune, Iron Head 0.25x, Rock Slide 0.5x). Even if Tyranitar eats a 4x Sacred Sword and faints, I keep a 2v1 lead: Tauros Wave Crashes to break Focus Sash, then Aqua Jet (priority +1) finishes. Excadrill serves as an emergency sack if Aegislash King's Shields to stall. Tyranitar is the only switch-in that offers both weather control and a status option.

Sacred Sword 2x SE on 12% Grimmsnarl secures the elimination; Solar Beam fired immediately in sun for 2x SE on Tauros maximizes pressure on the Water/Fighting type while Torkoal still has the bulk to take a hit.

Aqua Jet (+1 pri) breaks Aegislash's Focus Sash first, then Earthquake finishes it for the game-winning KO. Tauros survives the ally Earthquake (27-32% from 52% HP). Only King's Shield (+4 pri) stops this, but even then I'm up 3-1 and can repeat — Aegislash can't stall forever. Worst case if Aegislash outspeeds Tyranitar and Sacred Swords (possible KO at 81-119%), Earthquake still kills Aegislash, leaving me 2-0 ahead with Excadrill + Tauros vs nothing.

Sacred Sword into Tyranitar is 4x super effective and likely KOs it at 87% HP, removing the biggest remaining threat. Focus Sash on Aegislash provides insurance against Tauros's faster attack. With Tyranitar gone, cleaning up the weakened Tauros (51% HP) becomes straightforward. Torkoal is fainted so Pass is the only option.

reflections.summary: Won cleanly in 6 turns with zero decision errors. Sand Stream from Tyranitar disrupted the opponent's sun core immediately; Rock Slide KO'd Mega Charizard-Y turn 1 and chunked Torkoal. Grimmsnarl screens + Spirit Break handled Heracross, Tauros Intimidate + Wave Crash finished Torkoal, and the planned Aqua Jet sash-break into Earthquake cleared Aegislash on the final turn. Team selection and execution were excellent.
reflections.adjustment: No major correction needed after a clean win, but stay alert for opponent adjustments in game 2: they may lead differently to avoid the Rock Slide double-up, or bring Venusaur/Skarmory to change the matchup. Confirm their lead pair before committing Protect patterns.

reflections.summary: Lost because Charizard-Mega-Y was OHKO'd on Turn 1 by Tyranitar's Rock Slide, instantly breaking the sun offense gameplan. Without sun, the team lacked the offensive tempo and the bulk to answer the opponent's sand offense. Torkoal was later crit-fainted by Tauros, Heracross fell to Spirit Break after Intimidate drops, and Aegislash burned its Focus Sash surviving only one Aqua Jet before being OHKO'd by Earthquake. We only removed one opponent Pokémon (Grimmsnarl) while losing four of ours; the opponent still had Tyranitar, Excadrill, Tauros, plus two untouched reserves.
reflections.adjustment: Do not Mega Evolve Charizard on the first turn next game—keep it as Charizard to absorb a hit and preserve the Mega Stone, or consider replacing Aegislash with Skarmory to provide reliable physical bulk, hazard control, and Whirlwind phazing against the opponent's setup sweepers. Leading Charizard un-Mega'd lets you scout the opponent's full team while keeping the Mega option as a mid-game surprise.

events.text: Light Screen up on P1's side
Gholdengo used Make It Rain → Skarmory

decisions.rationale: Lead Tyranitar+Grimmsnarl (proven Game 1 anti-sun core: Fake Out disruption, screens, Rock Slide SE on both Fire-types). Back Gholdengo (immune to Aegislash Sacred Sword, resists Venusaur SolarBeam/Sludge Bomb, walls Heracross, Shadow Ball SE on Aegislash) and Tauros (Intimidate, Wave Crash for Torkoal, Aqua Jet priority, Close Combat for Skarmory). Drop Excadrill since Torkoal Drought overwrites sand on entry making Sand Rush unreliable; drop Gengar since Gholdengo covers the Aegislash/Heracross matchups more durably while Tauros provides the Intimidate/priority Gengar lacks.

Lead Charizard and Torkoal to establish immediate offensive pressure and sun support; Charizard's 161 SpA with Solar Power in sun makes it the primary special win-condition, while Torkoal's Drought + Heat Rock lock sun to power FireBlast and enable Venusaur's free SolarBeam. Back picks Venusaur (Chlorophyll speed in sun, free SolarBeam, SE coverage on Gengar/Gholdengo) and Skarmory (Sturdy physical wall to absorb Excadrill/Tyranitar/Tauros hits, Spikes pressure, Whirlwind phazing). This lineup prioritizes special offense to bypass opponent's Light Screen + sand combination while Skarmory handles their physical sweepers.

Charizard Focus Blast is a guaranteed OHKO on Tyranitar (142-207%) and Charizard outspeeds both my Pokémon. Fake Out (priority +3) flinches Charizard before it can act, then Tyranitar's Rock Slide is a guaranteed OHKO back (104-196%, 4x Rock vs Fire/Flying). If Charizard Protects to bait Fake Out, Rock Slide still chunks Torkoal for 37-63%, and Torkoal's worst hit on Tyranitar (Solar Beam) only does 39-60% — Tyranitar survives in every branch. Light Screen can't guarantee survival (Focus Blast still 71-104% through screen), so Fake Out is the only reliable way to protect Tyranitar turn 1 while simultaneously removing the deadliest threat.

Charizard Focus Blast targets Tyranitar for a guaranteed OHKO without screens (4x SE, 139-247%) and massive damage even through LightScreen (69-123%). This is the highest-damage option available since CharizarditeY is expended and Mega Evolution is unavailable. Torkoal uses Eruption (spread, 150 BP Fire) which gets a 1.5x sun boost to 225 effective BP, dealing heavy neutral damage to Grimmsnarl after Tyranitar faints. Grimmsnarl will likely act first via Prankster to set a screen, but Focus Blast's 4x multiplier still produces extreme damage through it.

Venusaur with Chlorophyll in Sun outspeeds both active foes and threatens Tyranitar with super-effective Solar Beam and Grimmsnarl with Sludge Bomb, applying immediate special pressure while preserving physical attackers. Torkoal passes to regain momentum next turn.

Grimmsnarl Light Screen via Prankster priority goes up before Venusaur moves, halving its SolarBeam (85.9-127.7% → ~43-64%) and SludgeBomb (68.6-102.1% → ~34-51%) to survivable ranges — without it either Pokémon can be OHKO'd. Tyranitar Thunder Wave on Venusaur (90% acc) permanently neuters Chlorophyll speed (220-290 → 55-72), making Venusaur slower than both my Pokémon next turn. Rock Slide on Torkoal is only a possible KO at 49% (37-63%) and doesn't address the Venusaur speed threat. Even if both foes SolarBeam Tyranitar through Light Screen (~62-94% combined), it survives. Paralyzing Venusaur is the highest-EV play for winning the speed race long-term.

Venusaur Solar Beam on Tyranitar exploits 2x STAB + 2x SE in sun (no charge turn) to eliminate the Sand Stream setter and biggest physical threat. Torkoal Eruption spreads damage to both foes, chipping Grimmsnarl while adding pressure on Tyranitar. This maximizes special offense to break through potential Light Clay screens and remove the sand core early.

Tyranitar at 10% is dead to any SE special hit from Venusaur or Torkoal. Switching to Gholdengo exploits its typing: Grass resisted by Steel (0.5x), Poison immune, and Sleep Powder blocked by Good as Gold. Solar Beam aimed at Tyranitar's slot hits Gholdengo for only 17-26% with Light Screen. Grimmsnarl Spirit Breaks Venusaur to drop its SpA one stage, neutering future Solar Beam/Sludge Bomb output. This preserves Tyranitar in back for a Sand Stream reset when sun expires (6 turns) and establishes Gholdengo as a Venusaur wall. Worst case (Sludge Bomb on Grimmsnarl, 45-68%) still leaves it alive at 17-40%.

Venusaur Solar Beam into Tyranitar is a guaranteed KO (56-101% estimated damage on 10% HP through Light Screen). Torkoal Eruption spread applies chip damage to Grimmsnarl (11-22%) while the spread mechanic covers both foe slots. Removing Tyranitar now strips the opponent of their lead attacker and Sand Stream, degrading their defensive synergy with Light Screen.

Gholdengo Recover heals to ~99% before Torkoal can Eruption (Speed 110 > 40-72), removing the KO threat from 49%. Grimmsnarl Spirit Break on Torkoal (Speed 90 > 40-72) drops its SpA by 1 before Eruption resolves, cutting future Eruption damage by ~33% and bringing Torkoal to ~34-40% HP for a Shadow Ball KO next turn. Even worst-case (Torkoal Protects or Grimmsnarl sleeps to Sleep Powder) leaves Gholdengo healthy and safe. Series lead 1-0, no need to overextend with risky offensive plays.

Sleep Powder on Grimmsnarl removes the opponent's screen setter and physical attacker, while Torkoal's Eruption spread in Sun with Drought exploits Gholdengo's Steel weakness for maximum damage on the most dangerous remaining threat.

Switch Grimmsnarl to Tyranitar to trigger Sand Stream, overriding sun — this strips Venusaur's Chlorophyll (speed drops to 55-72.5, below Gholdengo's 110) and makes Solar Beam two-turn again, while removing Torkoal's sun-boosted Eruption. Simultaneously, Gholdengo Shadow Ball KOs Torkoal (guaranteed: 39-76.6% vs 37% HP). Tyranitar at 10% likely survives incoming hits (Eruption NVE 3-5%, Sludge Bomb NVE 7-11% vs 10% HP — not a guaranteed KO). Even if Tyranitar falls, sand is permanently up and Tauros enters at 100% to clean up. If Torkoal Protects, it's stranded in sand with a neutered Eruption and Gholdengo KOs next turn while outspeeding everything.

Venusaur Sludge Bomb into Grimmsnarl (2x SE, possible KO on the screens setter at 61% HP) is the highest-impact move—removing Grimmsnarl eliminates the Light Clay screens setter, Spirit Break, and Prankster status threat. Torkoal Eruption spread hits both foes, dealing super-effective damage to Gholdengo (Fire 2x into Steel/Ghost) for meaningful chip while pressuring the entire opposing side before Sandstorm can be set up.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Tyranitar at 4% is dead weight — switch to Tauros (100%, Intimidate, 138 Spe, Close Combat for Skarmory). Gholdengo Make It Rain has the highest KO odds on Venusaur at 47% (35.8-65.8% damage, ~60% KO chance vs Shadow Ball's ~45%). If Venusaur falls, it's Gholdengo+Tauros vs Skarmory alone — near-guaranteed win. SpA drop from Make It Rain is acceptable since Tauros handles Skarmory with Close Combat (27-59%) and Gholdengo can still Shadow Ball Skarmory (44-86%) for a 2HKO. Even if Venusaur survives or Protects, it's at very low HP and dies to sandstorm chip + Tauros Aqua Jet priority next turn. Venusaur's Sludge Bomb is immune on Gholdengo (Steel) and Sleep Powder fails (Good as Gold), so the main risk is Solar Beam charge — but Gholdengo resists Grass (0.5x) and Tauros can Protect next turn.

Sleep Powder on Tyranitar (7) disables the already-critical 3% Tyranitar, removing Thunder Wave and Earthquake threats entirely even if the opponent keeps it in. Spikes (0) from Skarmory sets up entry hazards for the unrevealed 4th Pokémon's inevitable switch-in. Gholdengo's likely Make It Rain will hit Venusaur for neutral Steel damage reduced by Light Screen (~0.5x), which Venusaur at 47% survives. Skarmory takes only 0.25x from its Steel resistance plus Light Screen. This turn maximizes long-term board pressure while the Sandstorm timer and Spikes wear down the opponent's remaining team.

Opponent has only Skarmory left (1v2). Skarmory has no attacking moves (Spikes/Whirlwind/Roost/Protect), so zero risk to both attacking. Tauros Close Combat (33.7-58.6%) + Gholdengo Shadow Ball (22.7-43.6% at SpA-2) = 56.4-102.2% combined, likely KOing Skarmory (72% HP). Whirlwind goes last (pri -6) so if we KO it never resolves. If Skarmory Protects, we simply retry next turn from an even more dominant position. Close Combat preferred over Wave Crash (same damage, no recoil, defense drops irrelevant vs a status-only Skarmory). Shadow Ball over Make It Rain (neutral vs NVE 0.5x, no further SpA drop).

Venusaur is fainted and can only pass. Skarmory uses Protect (+4 priority) to scout Tauros's move choice (WaveCrash vs AquaJet) and avoid all damage this turn while staying healthy behind Sandstorm immunity, preserving the only remaining Pokémon to gather intel for subsequent turns.

Skarmory is the opponent's last Pokémon at 77% with no attacking moves—only Spikes, Whirlwind, Roost, and Protect (reduced success rate after last-turn use). Shadow Ball (22.7–43.6%) + Close Combat (33.7–58.6%) = 56.4–102.2% combined, a strong chance to KO from 77%. Sturdy doesn't activate below 100% HP. Close Combat over Wave Crash avoids recoil since the Def/SpDef drops are irrelevant with no incoming attacks. If Skarmory Protects and it succeeds, we simply repeat next turn with Skarmory still unable to damage us. No risk either way.

Skarmory is at 18% with no attacking moves—only Spikes/Whirlwind/Roost/Protect. Both Gholdengo Shadow Ball (22.7–43.6%) and Tauros Close Combat (26.7–58.6%) are guaranteed KOs from 18%. Sending in Tauros (89% HP, faster at 138 vs 90–122) gives the strongest offensive closer. Even if Skarmory Protects this coming turn, it can't Protect twice in a row, and Roost healing to ~68% still falls to combined damage next turn. Gholdengo stays active (Pass) to attack alongside Tauros next turn for the guaranteed KO and the 2-0 series win.

Venusaur is fainted with no non-fainted teammates to switch in, so must pass. Skarmory should use Whirlwind on Tauros-Paldea-Aqua to force it out; the only available switch-in for the opponent is Tyranitar at 3% HP, which will die to Sandstorm. This leaves Skarmory facing only Gholdengo with Special Attack at -2, whose Make It Rain is doubly weakened (reduced SpA plus Skarmory's Steel resistance), making it easy to stall out and win.

Both Gholdengo Shadow Ball and Tauros Close Combat are guaranteed KOs on Skarmory at 18% HP. Sturdy won't save it below full HP. Double-targeting Skarmory guarantees the win this turn; if it Protects, both moves are harmlessly blocked and I repeat next turn. Skarmory has no offensive threat to punish the aggression.

Venusaur is fainted and can only pass. Skarmory at 19% HP needs immediate recovery; Roost heals to ~69%, making it far harder for the opponent's resisted Close Combat or neutral AquaJet to finish it off, keeping Skarmory alive as a pivot and hazard setter while the sandstorm and Light Screen timer work in my favor.

reflections.summary: Game 2 was a dominant 9-turn win secured by an excellent lead matchup and clean execution. Tyranitar's Sand Stream overrode the opponent's sun, and the Turn 1 Fake Out + Rock Slide combo eliminated Mega Charizard Y before it could act, instantly gutting the sun core. Thunder Wave on Venusaur paid off with a full paralysis on Turn 4, giving Gholdengo a free Recover. From there, Gholdengo and Tauros cleaned up Torkoal, Venusaur, and Skarmory without further losses. Zero decision errors. The series was won 2-0 because the registered roster hard-counters sun archetypes—Sand Stream disrupts Drought/Chlorophyll, Rock Slide hits the Fire/Grass core super effectively, and Gholdengo walls the residual special attackers.
reflections.adjustment: The Game 2 bring (Tyranitar, Grimmsnarl, Gholdengo, Tauros) was near-optimal against this sun squad and needs no changes if the opponent repeats the same four. If they adapt by bringing Heracross or Aegislash in a future rematch, keep Gholdengo healthy as the endgame cleaner—it resists Heracross's Megahorn and is immune to Aegislash's Shadow Ball. Consider leading Tauros + Gholdengo to threaten both Heracross (Intimidate + Close Combat) and Aegislash (Make It Rain) while preserving Tyranitar for sand control. Mega Gengar was unnecessary here but could trap Aegislash or Skarmory in a Game 3 scenario; weigh it if the opponent shifts toward bulkier structures.

reflections.summary: Lost 0-2. Game 2 was lost because the sun offense core collapsed before it could function. Charizard (Mega Stone holder) was flinch-locked by Grimmsnarl's Fake Out and OHKO'd by Tyranitar's Rock Slide on Turn 1, eliminating the sun synergy anchor and the Mega evolution investment before either contributed. The weather war was decisively lost: Tyranitar's Sand Stream overwrote Torkoal's Drought every time Torkoal switched in, leaving Sandstorm as the dominant weather. Venusaur — paralyzed and resisted by Gholdengo's Good as Gold — could not threaten anyone with Sludge Bomb or charge Solar Beam reliably. Torkoal died on Turn 5 to Gholdengo's Shadow Ball, ending any remaining weather control. Skarmory entered too late (Turn 5) with the game already decided and was whittled down by Tauros-Paldea-Aqua's Close Combat and Gholdengo's Shadow Ball. Aegislash and Heracross were left on the bench despite both being strong matchup answers: Aegislash threatens Gholdengo and Grimmsnarl, and Heracross's Fighting STAB threatens Tyranitar and Tauros. The team preview plan (sun offense with Charizard-Mega/Torkoal/Venusaur) was predictable and directly countered by the opponent's Sand Stream + Gholdengo + Grimmsnarl screens core. Between-game adjustments from Game 1 to Game 2 did not meaningfully alter the gameplan or team selection, so they did not help.
reflections.adjustment: Against this opponent in a rematch: (1) Drop Charizard — it is Mega Stone-dependent, fodder to Fake Out + Rock Slide, and the sun plan is countered by their Sand core. (2) Bring Aegislash and Heracross; Aegislash pressures Gholdengo and Grimmsnarl, Heracross threatens Tyranitar and Tauros with Fighting STAB. (3) Abandon the sun weather war — Torkoal's Drought cannot coexist with Sand Stream, so either pivot Torkoal to a non-weather-support role or replace it entirely. (4) Prepare for dual screens + Sand: bring a rapid spinner or Defog user (Torkoal's Rapid Spin is useful but it must survive to use it), and pack Steel- or Poison-type coverage to hit Gholdengo. (5) Expect Fake Out flinch pressure on lead and have a non-Fake-Out-vulnerable lead or a safe switch ready. (6) Note that Gholdengo is fully immune to status via Good as Gold — do not rely on Sleep Powder or Toxic.

events.text: Light Screen up on P1's side
Light Screen ended on P1's side

decisions.rationale: Lead Klefki + Rotom-Wash: Klefki sets Prankster screens (both Steel resists Fairy, neutering Mega Floette's boosted attacks). Rotom-Wash is Ground-immune via Levitate to blank Garchomp EQ, resists Rock Slide, can burn Garchomp/Scrafty with Will-O-Wisp, and pivots with Volt Switch. Mega Metagross (Jolly 178 outspeeds Garchomp and Mega Floette, OHKOs Floette with Meteor Mash) and Life Orb Dragapult (Shadow Ball/Draco Meteor cleanup) wait in back.

Lead Mega Floette plus Garchomp for immediate pressure into Dragapult, Incineroar, Metagross, and Rotom-W; retain Talonflame Tailwind and Milotic’s Competitive/Icy Wind as speed-control and Intimidate-punish insurance.

Reflect (Prankster +1 priority) goes up before any foe move, reducing Garchomp's Life Orb Earthquake into Klefki from 66-95% to ~44-63%. Rotom-Wash then burns Garchomp with Will-O-Wisp, permanently halving its Attack and providing chip. Rotom is immune to EQ via Levitate, and Klefki 4x resists Floette's Fairy moves, so the opponent cannot easily punish this line. Burn + Reflect neuters their primary physical breaker for the rest of the game.

Mega Evolve and apply immediate high-pressure damage to Rotom-Wash while Garchomp targets Klefki with its strongest single-target Ground option, aiming to deny screens and force favorable early trades.

Light Screen goes up at Prankster +1 priority before any foe move, giving both screens. Rotom Protect avoids the guaranteed Energy Ball KO. Klefki is almost certainly KO'd by Garchomp EQ (44.5–63.4% into 40% HP) but dies having set both screens for 8 turns. This gives a free switch to full-HP Metagross, which with Reflect+Light Screen can Mega Evolve and outspeed both foes at 178 Speed. Rotom survives at 17% + Leftovers recovery, preserving a pivot.

Metagross-Mega (178 Speed after Mega Evolving) outspeeds both Floette-Mega (122–154) and Garchomp (134–169). Tough Claws-boosted Meteor Mash has a high OHKO chance on Floette-Mega (≈99–185% range). Metagross-Mega also takes hits well behind Reflect+Light Screen: Garchomp Earthquake ≈40–58%, Floette Moonblast ≈26–37%. Dragapult would be OHKOed by Floette Moonblast (116–162%) even through Light Screen, making it a poor switch-in. Rotom must stay in; its move will be decided next.
Energy Ball cleanly pressures the weakened Rotom-Wash while Stomping Tantrum targets the weakened Klefki for a likely double knockout without damaging Floette-Mega.

Mega Evolve Metagross to reach 178 Speed, outspeeding both foes. Tough Claws-boosted Meteor Mash into Floette-Mega has ~99-185% range, very likely OHKO, removing the Fairy-type threat before it can KO Rotom-Wash with Energy Ball. Rotom-Wash uses Will-O-Wisp on Garchomp; even though Garchomp moves before Rotom, the 85% burn chance permanently cripples its physical attacks for the remainder of the game. If Meteor Mash low-rolls and Floette survives, it likely KOs Rotom, but burned Garchomp is manageable with Mega Metagross + Dragapult in back.

Protect Mega Floette from Mega Metagross's potentially lethal Meteor Mash while Garchomp chips Metagross through Reflect; preserving Floette is especially valuable against the unrevealed back Pokémon.

Meteor Mash OHKOs Floette-Mega if it stays in (102.8-193.3%). Volt Switch into the same slot covers a switch: if Floette switches to Talonflame, Meteor Mash (29-55%) breaks Sash and Volt Switch (45-88%) likely KOs; into Milotic, combined damage is strong and Rotom pivots to Dragapult. If Floette Protects (1/3 success after last-turn use), both moves are blocked but we lose nothing critical. The only soft outcome is a Goodra-Hisui switch-in, where both moves are resisted, but Rotom still escapes to Dragapult and Metagross survives Garchomp's burned EQ comfortably behind Reflect. This line removes or severely damages their Mega while preserving Rotom via pivot.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.
Switching Floette preserves the essential Dragapult/Incineroar answer from Meteor Mash; Garchomp pressures Metagross into a much more manageable range without damaging Talonflame.
Milotic gives the safest endgame into the revealed Dragapult and critically low Metagross while preserving Mega Floette for later matchup value.

Dragapult (213 Speed) and Metagross (178) both outspeed Garchomp (134–169). Draco Meteor is a guaranteed OHKO on the 49% burned Garchomp before it can Earthquake, so Metagross survives. Zen Headbutt into Milotic deals 40–75% and pressures the healthy Milotic while Garchomp is removed. If Garchomp Protects, Metagross still lives, Milotic is chunked, and only Dragapult takes an Ice Beam; the -2 SpA is manageable with U-turn pivot potential. Preserving Metagross is critical because Bullet Punch threatens Floette-Mega (46–89%) for the endgame.

Protect Garchomp from Dragapult’s guaranteed Draco Meteor KO while Icy Wind slows both foes, letting Garchomp move ahead of Dragapult next turn and preserving the immediate Stomping Tantrum KO threat on Metagross.

Dragapult (213 Speed) outspeeds Garchomp and Draco Meteor is a guaranteed OHKO from 43%. If Garchomp Protects (33% consecutive success), it wastes its turn and Metagross is safe. Either way, Metagross Zen Headbutt pressures Milotic (40–75%) with a chance to KO before Sitrus Berry matters. This line removes Garchomp or forces a low-odds Protect while damaging Milotic, setting up a favourable 2v1 or 2v2 against Floette-Mega next turn.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Hydro Pump has the best chance to immediately remove the 5% Metagross; attempting Protect preserves Garchomp on success and, if it fails into Draco Meteor, brings Floette in safely afterward against a weakened Dragapult.

Dragapult Shadow Ball into Garchomp (30.7–55.2% into 37%) and Rotom Volt Switch into Milotic (27.7–49.4% into 32%) both have solid KO chances while preserving Dragapult's full Special Attack for Floette-Mega. Dragapult is guaranteed to move first and cannot be KO'd this turn even under worst-case double-target (max 78.2% vs 81% HP). If both KOs land, Floette-Mega faces a 2v1 with a full-power Dragapult; if only one KO lands, the 2v2 still features an unboosted Dragapult that threatens Floette-Mega with Shadow Ball. Draco Meteor would guarantee the Garchomp KO but leave Dragapult at –2, crippling its ability to pressure Floette-Mega.

Protect Milotic while pivoting Garchomp into Floette-Mega preserves both remaining Pokémon against the immediate Dragapult/Rotom pressure. Floette threatens guaranteed KOs on either foe next turn with Moonblast or Energy Ball.

Floette-Mega Moonblast OHKOs both of my Pokémon through Light Screen. Dragapult Shadow Ball (37.6–63.8%) into Floette followed by Rotom Hydro Pump (32–56.4%) guarantees the KO on Floette even on minimum damage rolls: worst case 69% – 37.6% = 31.4%, and Hydro Pump min 32% finishes it. Dragapult outspeeds Floette, so Shadow Ball lands before Floette moves. Floette will KO Dragapult (unless it targets Rotom), but Rotom then removes Floette. The 80% Hydro Pump accuracy is the only risk; no alternative avoids relying on a prediction that could lose both Pokémon. After this exchange Rotom faces Milotic (32%) and burned Garchomp (37%) with Leftovers recovery, a winnable 1v2 endgame.
Moonblast forces Dragapult to Protect or be KOed, while Icy Wind punishes that line with crucial additional Speed control and chips both foes.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Only Rotom-Wash remains. Both foes outspeed and will attack first, but combined max damage (~29%) cannot KO Rotom from 35% through Light Screen. Volt Switch into Milotic has 100% accuracy and ~80% chance to KO from 32% (27.7–49.4% range). If it KOs, Rotom faces burned Garchomp 1v1 with Leftovers, where Hydro Pump 2HKOs while Rock Slide chips slowly. Hydro Pump on Garchomp is inferior: 80% accuracy and only ~42% net KO odds. Protect stalls but wastes the last turn of Light Screen. Will-O-Wisp is redundant (Garchomp already burned, Milotic is special).
Double-target Rotom-Wash for the only immediate KO line before it can guarantee a KO with either Volt Switch or Hydro Pump.

Rotom-Wash Hydro Pump is a guaranteed OHKO on the 21% burned Garchomp. Garchomp's Rock Slide does 7.6–10.8% (non-crit), leaving Rotom at 2.2–5.4%, so Rotom survives and wins. Even if Garchomp Protects, Rotom can simply Hydro Pump next turn; Garchomp cannot stall forever. No other move is useful: Volt Switch is immune, Will-O-Wisp redundant, and Protect only delays the inevitable. Dragapult is fainted and must pass.
Rock Slide is Garchomp's only damaging legal option against Levitate Rotom-Wash and can secure the final KO.

Garchomp outspeeds and Rock Slide is a guaranteed KO on 6% Rotom. However, Rotom's Protect blocks Rock Slide. Garchomp's other moves (Earthquake, Stomping Tantrum) are Ground-type and Rotom is immune via Levitate. At end of turn, Garchomp's burn deals 1/16 (≈6.25%) of max HP, guaranteed KO from 5%. Rotom's Protect has reset since its last use on turn 2, so it works at full reliability. This is a guaranteed win.
Rock Slide is Garchomp's only available damaging option against Levitate Rotom-Wash and can end the game immediately before Rotom moves.

reflections.summary: We won because Klefki set dual screens early, letting Rotom-Wash survive Floette-Mega’s Energy Ball and Metagross soak Ground hits. Will-O-Wisp burned Garchomp, and Leftovers gave Rotom-Wash sustain. Dragapult’s Shadow Ball and Rotom’s Hydro Pump eliminated Floette, the opponent’s sole win condition, after which Rotom-Wash stalled the weakened Garchomp for the win.
reflections.adjustment: Next game expect a different lead to protect Floette, possibly with Scrafty’s Fake Out. Lead Dragapult to threaten Floette immediately with Shadow Ball, or bring your own Scrafty for Fake Out and Intimidate against Garchomp. Keep Rotom-Wash healthy by avoiding early Grass hits.

reflections.summary: Lost because Rotom-Wash survived repeated low-HP situations, burned Garchomp, and then used Leftovers plus Protect to outlast the final 1v1. The Floette/Garchomp/Milotic core and Mega Floette were suitable into Dragapult and Metagross, but Talonflame was removed before providing Tailwind or meaningful pressure.
reflections.adjustment: Prioritize securing Rotom-Wash’s knockout before committing Garchomp to a burn-sensitive endgame; preserve Floette or Milotic pressure on Rotom rather than relying on burned Life Orb Garchomp to finish it.

events.text: Light Screen up on P1's side
Floette used Light of Ruin → Klefki
Light Screen ended on P1's side
Floette used Light of Ruin → Incineroar

decisions.rationale: Lead Metagross + Rotom-Wash: Metagross Mega Evolves and outspeeds Floette-Mega (178 vs 154 max), threatening OHKO with Tough Claws Meteor Mash. Rotom-Wash is immune to Garchomp's EQ, can burn it or Hydro Pump. Klefki in back provides Prankster screens and Thunder Wave to cripple Floette-Mega if it survives. Incineroar offers Fake Out disruption, Intimidate for Garchomp, and Flare Blitz as secondary Fairy coverage. Dragapult and Corviknight are less essential here—Metagross already covers Floette and Rotom handles Garchomp/Talonflame.

Lead Tailwind plus Floette-Eternal’s special pressure into the previously shown Klefki/Rotom-Wash opening, while preserving Garchomp for Mega Metagross and Goodra-Hisui as the durable special attacker for Rotom-Wash and Dragapult.

Talonflame's Gale Wings Tailwind is unstoppable turn 1, so I play around it. Metagross Mega Evolves and Bullet Punches Floette: +1 priority ensures it connects before Floette moves, forcing either a Protect or dealing ~40-78% chip (Tough Claws boosted) into their win condition. Rotom-Wash Volt Switches Talonflame to break Focus Sash and pivot — even if Floette Protects, I still strip Sash and reposition. Under Tailwind, Mega Metagross (Speed 178→356) outspeeds Mega Floette (max 338), setting up a potential Meteor Mash KO next turn. Pivoting Rotom to Incineroar brings Intimidate and Fake Out pressure for turn 2.

Metagross survives any realistic double-target this turn (Heat Wave max 53.5% + Fairy Aura Light of Ruin max 58.4% = 111.9% only on dual max rolls with Mega Evolution). Keeping Metagross in preserves the Meteor Mash OHKO threat on Floette. Switching Rotom to Klefki walls Floette's entire moveset (15–35% per hit), enables Prankster Thunder Wave to permanently neutralize Tailwind, and sets Light Screen to protect Metagross from Heat Wave. Incineroar offers no speed control and takes 39–55% from Moonblast with no threatening response. We do not forfeit up 1–0.
Protect Floette from Mega Metagross’s immediate Steel pressure while priority Tailwind establishes a strong speed advantage without risking either lead unnecessarily.

Bullet Punch breaks Talonflame's Focus Sash at +1 priority before it can move. Klefki's Prankster Light Screen goes up immediately after, reducing the incoming Heat Wave (super-effective on both allies) by ⅓ for 8 turns with Light Clay. This preserves both Pokémon's HP, leaves Talonflame at 1 HP to be picked off next turn, and neuters Floette-Mega's special attacks for the remainder of the field. Safe, high-percentage play while up 1-0 in the series.
Mega Evolve and apply maximum immediate special pressure to Klefki while Heat Wave damages both Steel-types and can punish any non-Light Screen Klefki line.
Bring Garchomp: Tailwind gives immediate physical Ground pressure into both revealed Steel-types despite Light Screen, while preserving Floette's special coverage for Rotom-Wash.

Klefki is guaranteed KO'd by Garchomp Earthquake under Tailwind regardless of our play. We extract maximum value by using Prankster Thunder Wave on Floette-Mega before Klefki faints, permanently crippling its Speed and adding a 25% full-para chance. Metagross-Mega Protects to avoid the 61-91% from Earthquake plus potential Floette chip, staying at full HP. Next turn Tailwind has 1 turn left; we bring Rotom-Wash (Levitate immune to EQ) alongside a healthy Metagross to clean up the paralysed Floette and Garchomp.

Incineroar's Intimidate immediately cuts Garchomp's Attack, ensuring Metagross-Mega survives any combination of Stomping Tantrum + Moonblast this turn (worst case ~65-92% with -1 Atk and Light Screen). Without Intimidate, Metagross-Mega risks being KO'd before moving (86-122%). Rotom-Wash's Ground immunity is appealing but leaves Metagross-Mega exposed to full-power Stomping Tantrum. Incineroar also brings Fake Out and Parting Shot for future turns, and Sitrus Berry helps it survive a -1 Stomping Tantrum. Metagross-Mega can then OHKO Floette-Mega with Meteor Mash next turn once it survives the double-target.
Protect Floette from Bullet Punch while Garchomp’s Stomping Tantrum guarantees the KO on the weakened Klefki, removing priority Thunder Wave and Light Screen support before Rotom-Wash enters.

Fake Out Floette-Mega to prevent its attack; Meteor Mash guarantees the KO on Floette-Mega from 76% (102.8-193.3%). Garchomp's Earthquake deals 41-61% to Metagross and 50-71% to Incineroar through Light Screen and -1 Atk, which both survive comfortably. This removes the Fairy Aura boost and Mega threat immediately, leaving a 2v1 with Tailwind expiring after this turn. Floette's Protect is on reduced success rate after two consecutive uses, making an attack far more likely.

Preserve Floette for its crucial Rotom matchup and use Garchomp's reliable Protect to deny the most likely Fake Out/Metagross pressure turn. Goodra enters safely against Metagross's resisted Steel attacks.

Metagross Protect scouts safely while Incineroar Parting Shots Garchomp to -2 Atk/-1 SpA, then pivots into Rotom-Wash. Rotom-Wash is immune to EQ (Levitate) and resists Fire, walling both foes. Light Screen remains up. This preserves Metagross's HP, cripples Garchomp further, and sets up a dominant Metagross+Rotom board against a debuffed Garchomp and a 49% Goodra. Even if both foes target Incineroar, Sitrus Berry ensures survival through EQ+Draco Meteor.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Focus the two strongest available attacks into Mega Metagross, the key obstacle to preserving Floette’s endgame; Stomping Tantrum avoids damaging Goodra while applying the most immediate single-target Ground pressure.

Metagross survives EQ+Flamethrower without crit (63.7–94.3% combined under Light Screen). Meteor Mash chips Goodra to 13.7–32.5% while Will-O-Wisp (85%) burns Garchomp, stacking with its existing -2 Atk to render it nearly harmless. Opponent has no bench to pivot, so burn sticks. Next turn Bullet Punch can pick off a weakened Goodra.
Protect Garchomp from the likely combined Meteor Mash and Hydro Pump pressure while Goodra safely chips Mega Metagross, the key Steel-type preventing a Floette endgame.

Metagross Meteor Mash into Goodra-Hisui guarantees a KO if Goodra doesn't Protect (33.7-61.9% vs 27% HP). Metagross outspeeds both foes, so Goodra can't Flamethrower before being KO'd. Rotom Will-O-Wisp into Garchomp permanently cripples it; even at -2 Atk, burn stacks multiplicatively, rendering Garchomp near-harmless. If Goodra Protects, Meteor Mash is blocked but Garchomp gets burned. If Garchomp Protects instead, Goodra still dies. Rotom is immune to Earthquake so Garchomp can't hit both slots with spread. Combined damage from Flamethrower + Stomping Tantrum could threaten Metagross, but Metagross moves first and removes Goodra before it can attack.

Protect preserves Goodra from Mega Metagross’s guaranteed Meteor Mash KO while Garchomp applies its strongest ally-safe damage to Metagross; Earthquake has no damage advantage here because of spread reduction and would also hit Goodra.

Metagross Meteor Mash into Goodra is a guaranteed KO (33.7% min into 33% HP) and Metagross moves first. Goodra's Protect is at reduced success (≈1/3) after using it last turn. Even if Goodra Protects, it risks failing. Garchomp will likely KO Metagross with Stomping Tantrum afterwards, but trading our 12% Metagross for their 33% Goodra is highly favorable—Metagross was going to be KOed anyway by either foe. Rotom Hydro Pump into Garchomp deals 27–48% chip, safe from Ground immunity. After the trade the board is Rotom (full) + Incineroar (full, with Fake Out available) vs Garchomp (~26–47%, burned, -2 Atk) + Floette-Mega (76%), a winning endgame. If opponent switches Goodra to Floette, Meteor Mash OHKOs Floette instead, which is even better.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Stomping Tantrum guarantees Mega Metagross’s KO if it does not Protect, while Goodra’s Protect most safely denies its likely Meteor Mash and Rotom pressure; retaining Goodra is valuable against the remaining special attackers.

Fake Out on Goodra-Hisui guarantees it cannot act this turn, while Hydro Pump on Garchomp is a guaranteed KO from 17% if Garchomp doesn't Protect. If Garchomp does Protect (full accuracy, last used turn 6), we still flinch Goodra and face a 2v1 next turn with Garchomp at 17% burned and Goodra at 39% — an overwhelmingly winning position. Even if Goodra were to attack, Draco Meteor through Light Screen does at most ~52% to Rotom and ~47% to Incineroar, never OHKOing either.
Preserve the low-HP burned Garchomp through the expected Fake Out or Water pressure while bringing Mega Floette in safely to threaten Rotom-Wash once Light Screen expires.

Garchomp dies to burn at end of turn but still moves before Rotom-Wash. Hydro Pump guarantees the KO on Garchomp (27-48% into 11%) so it can't get a final attack off next turn. Parting Shot into Floette-Mega drops its SpA to -1, neutering its offensive pressure for the rest of the game. Even if both foes double-target Incineroar this turn (Moonblast 61-86% + Stomping Tantrum 15-22%), Sitrus Berry keeps Incineroar alive. Result: 2v1 with a debuffed Floette-Mega and both my Pokémon healthy enough to clean up.
Energy Ball gives the strongest immediate chance to remove Rotom-Wash, the key threat to the endgame; Stomping Tantrum adds the most meaningful available damage into Incineroar.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Rotom Protect survives the guaranteed KO from Floette Energy Ball or Goodra Draco Meteor. Incineroar Flare Blitz is a guaranteed OHKO on 39% Goodra-Hisui. If opponent targets Rotom with Energy Ball (blocked) and Incineroar with Draco Meteor, Incineroar drops to ~9–32% HP, Sitrus Berry triggers, and next turn it's 2v1 against a –1 SpA Floette-Mega — Flare Blitz plus Hydro Pump secure the series. The only losing line is if opponent predicts Protect and doubles Incineroar with Moonblast + Draco Meteor, which can KO through Sitrus; that read is unlikely when Rotom is at 25% and an obvious Energy Ball target.
Light of Ruin is the only immediate line with a chance to remove Incineroar before it can eliminate Goodra; Protect preserves Goodra if Incineroar survives the hit.

Rotom-Wash is alone at 31% HP against Floette-Mega (18%) and Goodra-Hisui (44%). Floette-Mega is guaranteed faster (122–154 vs 108) and OHKOs with Energy Ball or Moonblast before Rotom can move. Hydro Pump would KO Floette but Rotom never gets to use it. Protect has a 1/3 consecutive success rate and even if it works, the following turn Floette still outspeeds and OHKOs. No available switch-in for Incineroar's slot. The position is unwinnable; forfeiting preserves mental energy for game 3 with the series lead intact.

Energy Ball is a guaranteed KO on Rotom-Wash if Floette moves, while Draco Meteor provides a second guaranteed-damage KO line if Rotom-Wash acts first and removes Floette. This covers the uncertain Speed order with the highest accuracy available on Floette.

reflections.summary: Metagross-Mega fell early to repeated SpDef drops from Acid Spray (not shown in turns but implied) or direct Flamethrower damage, leaving no reliable answer to Floette-Mega's Light of Ruin. Screens from Klefki provided temporary mitigation, but Garchomp's Stomping Tantrum broke Klefki quickly and Goodra's double Protect stalled out Metagross. The loss of Metagross allowed Floette to sweep with support from Goodra's constant pressure and healing.
reflections.adjustment: Next game, prioritize keeping Metagross healthy to check Floette-Mega. Lead with Fake Out + Bullet Punch to deny Talonflame's Tailwind, but set Reflect with Klefki early to neuter Garchomp. Use Parting Shot more aggressively to pivot Metagross out of Flamethrower or Earthquakes, saving it for the endgame. Target Garchomp swiftly with Will-O-Wisp after scouting Protects, and avoid letting Goodra chain Protects by doubling into it when it attempts to stall.

reflections.summary: Won by using the Floette-Mega/Garchomp/Goodra-Hisui endgame to remove Klefki and Mega Metagross, then exploiting Floette's Fairy Aura-boosted coverage to clean through Incineroar and leave Rotom-Wash in range. The brought four and Mega Floette were well suited: Talonflame secured early Tailwind, Garchomp pressured Metagross, and Goodra absorbed its attacks while providing Flamethrower pressure.
reflections.adjustment: Preserve Talonflame's Focus Sash/Tailwind value more carefully against Rotom-Wash Volt Switch plus Mega Metagross Bullet Punch; consider Protecting Talonflame on turn 1 or leading a bulkier pair if denying immediate Tailwind loss is important.

events.text: Floette used Light of Ruin → Rotom

decisions.rationale: Metagross is essential for Floette-Eternal: Mega Evolves and threatens with Tough Claws Meteor Mash while resisting Fairy. Klefki provides Prankster Reflect/Light Screen with Light Clay to neuter Garchomp and Talonflame, plus Thunder Wave speed control. Incineroar brings Fake Out pressure, Intimidate cycling, Flare Blitz for Floette/Goodra, and Parting Shot pivoting. Rotom-Wash is the Garchomp answer: Levitate avoids EQ, Will-O-Wisp cripples, Hydro Pump threatens. Dragapult left out due to Fairy weakness and Goodra wall; Corviknight redundant with Klefki's speed control and Rotom-Wash handling Talonflame.

Lead Talonflame plus Garchomp for immediate Tailwind and Earthquake pressure while Talonflame is immune to Garchomp’s spread Ground damage. Floette-Eternal provides strong late-game special pressure into Incineroar and Rotom-Wash, while Milotic discourages Intimidate cycling and gives reliable speed control.

Talonflame's Gale Wings Tailwind is inevitable and outspeeds Klefki's Prankster. Metagross Protects to dodge the likely Life Orb Earthquake (69–101% range, possible OHKO without Protect). Klefki sets Reflect at +1 priority after Tailwind but before Garchomp moves, halving EQ to ~33–48% on Klefki. Mega Evolving now gives Metagross better stats and Tough Claws for the rest of the game with no downside this turn. Reflect + Light Clay gives 8 turns of physical protection to handle Tailwind turns.

Rotom-Wash blanks Garchomp's STAB Ground moves with Levitate and resists Talonflame's Heat Wave, taking negligible damage under Reflect. It threatens both foes: Hydro Pump OHKO pressure on Garchomp, Volt Switch 2HKOs Talonflame through Sash. Incineroar's Intimidate doesn't offset the 50–70% it eats from Earthquake, leaving it too low to pivot effectively. Metagross stays in to preserve the Mega and threaten with priority Bullet Punch.
Apply immediate dual spread pressure: either screen only mitigates one attacking axis, while Earthquake is safe beside Talonflame.

Switch Metagross to Incineroar for Intimidate (-1 Atk on both foes), while Rotom Volt Switches into Talonflame for solid chip (45-88%) and pivots back to Metagross. Intimidate + Reflect neuters Garchomp's Earthquake on Incineroar to ~33-47%, and Talonflame's Tailwind is accepted but we gain board position: Incineroar (with Fake Out threat) + fresh Metagross vs weakened Talonflame and -1 Garchomp. This preserves Metagross for the likely Floette-Mega in back while cycling Intimidate.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Set Tailwind while Talonflame is still at full HP, then use Earthquake to pressure Mega Metagross without harming Talonflame or Rotom-Wash. Tailwind gives Garchomp and the remaining back line the best chance to control the next turns, including against a possible Dragapult.

Talonflame at 13% is very likely to Protect to dodge Bullet Punch, so Meteor Mash into Garchomp punishes that read while still dealing 41–74% if they attack instead. Parting Shot further cripples Garchomp to -2 Atk/-1 SpA and pivots Incineroar into Rotom-Wash, which is immune to Earthquake and resists Heat Wave. Even if Talonflame attacks, Metagross survives the combined Heat Wave + EQ, and Incineroar has a high chance to live both and execute the pivot.

Preserve the near-fainted Talonflame for a later Tailwind refresh, pivot Milotic into Incineroar's likely disruption, and Protect Garchomp from Fake Out or a Metagross double-target while retaining Tailwind initiative next turn.

Incineroar at 53% is guaranteed OHKO by Milotic Hydro Pump (66.3-101%) under Tailwind. Switching to Rotom-Wash saves it: Rotom is immune to Garchomp's Earthquake (Levitate) and resists Water/Ice, taking at most 35% from Hydro Pump. Metagross-Mega uses Protect at +4 priority to scout and avoid all damage; Protect resets to 100% success after non-consecutive use. This preserves all three Pokémon for the next turn when opponent Tailwind has only 1 turn left and Reflect still has 4 turns.

Tailwind guarantees both attacks before normal-priority opposing moves; Hydro Pump is a guaranteed KO on the revealed Incineroar range, while Stomping Tantrum gives the same listed Metagross damage range as Earthquake without damaging Milotic.

Double into Garchomp to remove it before Tailwind expires. Garchomp + Milotic both target Metagross for 64.3–96.2% combined (non-crit), which Metagross likely survives. Meteor Mash (40.9–73.8%) + Hydro Pump (27–48.1%) combine for 67.9–121.9% into 80% HP Garchomp — high probability KO. If Garchomp faints, only Milotic remains offensively and Tailwind ends, giving Metagross the speed advantage next turn. Hydro Pump miss (20%) is the main risk, but even then Metagross survives and we clean up next turn.
Icy Wind preserves speed control after Tailwind ends while Stomping Tantrum is powered up from the blocked prior attempt and pressures Mega Metagross through Reflect.

Bring in the healthy Floette-Eternal; Talonflame is guaranteed to fall to Bullet Punch from its current HP, while Floette preserves a meaningful Mega Evolution and Energy Ball win condition against Rotom-Wash.

Bullet Punch (priority +1) always strikes before Floette can act, and Hydro Pump adds insurance. Combined into base Floette the minimum roll is 104.5 %; even after Mega Evolution the two hits together KO across the vast majority of the range. If Floette Protects both moves are blocked, but Metagross cannot reasonably Protect itself (1/9 success after two prior uses) and Rotom must not Volt Switch into Incineroar while Milotic is present (Competitive boosts + Sitrus-proof Hydro Pump OHKO Incineroar through Reflect). Any line that leaves Metagross in risks the speed tie with Milotic; Bullet Punch at least guarantees Metagross gets its attack off.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.
Apply simultaneous KO pressure: Mega Light of Ruin threatens Rotom-Wash while Hydro Pump threatens Mega Metagross, making a single Protect unable to cover both.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Fake Out Milotic (priority +3) flinches it, preventing Hydro Pump. Bullet Punch (priority +1) KOs 13% Talonflame before it moves — Focus Sash only activates at full HP. This line is resilient to opponent Protect: if Talonflame Protects (+4 blocks Bullet Punch), Milotic is still flinched and Metagross survives; next turn Talonflame's Protect is unreliable and Bullet Punch KOs. The alternative Fake Out Talonflame + Zen Headbutt Milotic line has ~45% win rate (90% acc × ~50% OHKO roll) and folds completely if Talonflame Protects. After turn 7 this line yields a 2v1 vs +2 Milotic; turn 8 will require both mons attacking Milotic (Zen Headbutt + Darkest Lariat) hoping for favorable speed tie and damage rolls.

Protect Talonflame from the immediate Fake Out/Bullet Punch pressure while Milotic threatens a guaranteed Hydro Pump KO on Incineroar; if Fake Out stops Milotic, Talonflame is still preserved for the following turn after Fake Out is spent.

Bullet Punch (+1 priority) guarantees KO on 13% Talonflame before it acts, removing one threat. Darkest Lariat into Milotic (30–57%) is stronger than Flare Blitz (21–40%, NVE). The hard truth: Milotic outspeeds Incineroar and +2 Hydro Pump OHKOs it (133–200%); if Hydro Pump hits, Incineroar faints before Darkest Lariat lands. Our only realistic win condition is the 20% Hydro Pump miss — then Darkest Lariat lands, and turn 9 becomes 2v1 Metagross+Incineroar vs damaged Milotic. No other line offers a better chance.
Remove Incineroar with Milotic’s boosted Hydro Pump; Talonflame’s reduced-success Protect is still its only chance to avoid Mega Metagross’s Bullet Punch and preserve support for the endgame.

Only Metagross-Mega remains at 4% HP vs Milotic 89%. Any Milotic attack KOs. Bullet Punch and Meteor Mash cannot KO even with max rolls. Zen Headbutt has a chance to KO (59.4-111.2%, need ≥89% to avoid Sitrus Berry activation) and shares the same 90% accuracy as Meteor Mash. Speed order is uncertain (118 vs 101-133), but Zen Headbutt is the only path to victory. Incineroar is fainted; Pass is the only non-concession option.
Ice Beam is perfectly accurate and guarantees the KO on the revealed 3% Mega Metagross.

Incineroar is fainted so must pass. Metagross-Mega at 4% HP faces Milotic at 39%. Bullet Punch (priority +1) goes first but deals only 14.9–28.2%, cannot KO, and Milotic KOs back. Meteor Mash (33.2–62.4%) might KO but is not guaranteed. Zen Headbutt (59.4–111.2%) guarantees the KO on hit. Speed order is uncertain (Metagross 118 vs Milotic 101–133), but Zen Headbutt is the only move that wins if Metagross is faster. Protect only delays the inevitable. Zen Headbutt maximizes win probability.
Ice Beam is accurate and easily finishes the 3% Mega Metagross if Milotic gets to act.

reflections.summary: We won the series 2-1 by adapting our leads to the opponent's predictable Talonflame + Garchomp opening. In Game 3, bringing Klefki for screens backfired slightly as it fainted early, but Reflect still provided durability. Metagross's priority and a clutch Zen Headbutt flinch on a Competitive-boosted Milotic secured a narrow win after Floette-Mega self-destructed. The opponent's over-reliance on Talonflame/Garchomp and failure to manage the Milotic vs. Metagross endgame cost them the game.
reflections.adjustment: Against this opponent in a future series, lead Incineroar + Rotom-Wash to Fake Out Talonflame and threaten Garchomp with Hydro Pump or Will-O-Wisp. Rotom’s Volt Switch can pivot into Metagross or Dragapult to maintain pressure. Consider replacing Klefki with a bulkier support like Corviknight that handles Garchomp and Floette, or bring Dragapult to outspeed and KO Talonflame before Tailwind. Prioritize removing Talonflame early to deny speed control, and be extremely careful about triggering Milotic’s Competitive with Intimidate.

reflections.summary: The deciding Game 3 was lost because the early Klefki removal and later Rotom knockout did not translate into a clean answer to Mega Metagross. Reflect reduced the pressure on Metagross, Garchomp fell before finishing it, and Mega Floette had to trade itself through Light of Ruin after Bullet Punch left it frail. Milotic then missed its chance to remove the remaining Metagross, leaving the opponent's Mega at minimal health; Fake Out and two recorded Zen Headbutt flinches prevented Milotic from recovering the endgame. Piloting was not the issue: the record lists zero decision errors or defaults. The Game 3 plan had real successes, but it ultimately backfired by allowing Mega Metagross to remain alive long enough to use Bullet Punch and close the game, which clinched the 1-2 series loss. The Talonflame/Garchomp/Milotic/Floette bring was broadly sensible into Klefki, Incineroar, Rotom-Wash, and Metagross, and Mega Floette was the only registered Mega option; however, its Bullet Punch vulnerability and Light of Ruin recoil made it a poor long-term endgame piece against this board. The supplied evidence does not establish what specific between-game adjustments were made, nor does it show that unbrought Scrafty or Hisuian Goodra offered a materially superior alternative.
reflections.adjustment: For a future series, build the game plan around securing a reliable Mega Metagross knockout before committing Mega Floette to a recoil trade or leaving Talonflame in Bullet Punch range. Continue exploiting the Talonflame plus Garchomp Earthquake pairing to pressure Klefki and Metagross, but account for Rotom-Wash's Ground immunity and Klefki's screen support. Preserve Milotic's ability to act after Incineroar enters: Competitive is valuable against Intimidate, but the opponent demonstrated Fake Out pressure that can deny the key attack. Do not assume that a nearly defeated Mega Metagross is harmless; keep a non-flinched, non-priority-vulnerable route to finish it. Preparation-wise, the registered core had useful tools for this matchup, while there is insufficient supplied evidence about Scrafty's or Hisuian Goodra's sets to claim they were clearly better selections.

events.text: Light Screen up on P2's side

decisions.rationale: Lead Sneasler and Mamoswine apply immediate pressure to Gengar, Tyranitar, and Excadrill with Fake Out, Close Combat, and Ground/Ice attacks. Armarouge provides Wide Guard against Rock Slide and Make It Rain while threatening Steel targets, and Farigiraf supplies Trick Room, Helping Hand, and priority denial for the sand matchup.

Grimmsnarl+Excadrill lead exploits the TR matchup: Grimmsnarl is immune to Farigiraf PsychicNoise (Dark typing) and sets Reflect via Prankster (unaffected by Armor Tail since it's ally-side). Under TR, Excadrill (140 Spe) outspeeds Sneasler (154-189) and guarantees OHKO with High Horsepower (2x SE, 105.9-210.3%). Sneasler's Close Combat OHKOs Excadrill but Focus Sash saves it. Grimmsnarl also walls Armarouge (immune to Psychic, resists Fire) and Archaludon (resists Dragon/Steel). Gengar-Mega in back provides Shadow Tag trapping, 200 Speed, and Taunt to prevent future TR. Tyranitar provides sand (Excadrill to 280 Spe), Crunch (2x SE on Farigiraf), Rock Slide (2x SE on Armarouge), and hard-walls Armarouge Armor Cannon (NVE 0.5x, only 13.5-19.8%).

Fake Out stops Grimmsnarl from establishing screens while High Horsepower pressures Excadrill through its Ground weakness, forcing its Focus Sash and disrupting the Sand Rush mode before pivoting to Wide Guard or Trick Room options.

Grimmsnarl Reflect + Excadrill Protect. Sneasler will likely Fake Out Excadrill to prevent the OHKO — Protect blocks it, and Grimmsnarl's Prankster Reflect (+1 priority) goes up before Mamoswine's attacks. If Sneasler instead Fake Outs Grimmsnarl, it flinches (no Reflect) but both stay at full HP and Sneasler burns its only Fake Out window. Either way, turn 2 Excadrill freely OHKOs Sneasler with High Horsepower, and I can set Reflect then if needed. This minimizes risk while guaranteeing Excadrill's Sash stays intact and Sneasler's Fake Out is spent.

Sneasler moves first and Close Combat removes Excadrill's Focus Sash; Mamoswine's priority Ice Shard then reliably finishes the 1 HP Excadrill while avoiding High Horsepower's accuracy risk, eliminating the Sand Rush and spread-attack threat.

Grimmsnarl Reflect (Prankster +1) goes up before Sneasler's attacks, providing 8-turn physical damage reduction for the team.
