Excadrill High Horsepower guarantees the OHKO on Sneasler (105.9-210.3%, no Sash). Even if the opponent doubles into Excadrill, Sash saves from Sneasler's hit, Excadrill KOs Sneasler, and I trade Excadrill for the opponent's most dangerous Pokemon while keeping Reflect active. Switching to Gengar is too risky — Mamoswine HH OHKOs Gengar-Mega (2x SE Ground vs Poison, 148.9-211.7%). Spirit Break on Sneasler is only neutral (28.9-56.8%) and doesn't remove the threat.

Send in Gengar, not Tyranitar. Sneasler Close Combat vs Tyranitar is a guaranteed OHKO (109.7-158.5% through Reflect) — Tyranitar is a pure sack with zero upside. Mamoswine HH vs Gengar through Reflect is 99.3-140.9% — not a guaranteed OHKO, giving Gengar a real survival chance. If Gengar lives, it Mega Evolves next turn for Shadow Tag (game-changing). If it faints, we still have Grimmsnarl+Tyranitar at 2v4 (playable). The Tyranitar route leads to 2v4, then Gengar faces the same HH threat later, risking 1v4 collapse. Sneasler also cannot meaningfully damage Gengar (Fighting immune, Poison resisted), so only Mamoswine threatens it.

Sneasler should pressure Grimmsnarl with super-effective Dire Claw while Mamoswine targets Gengar with High Horsepower, the strongest immediate threat and a possible OHKO. This preserves both active attackers and avoids wasting attacks into immunities.

Mega Evolve Gengar with Protect to safely activate Shadow Tag — Gengar cannot risk High Horsepower (99.3-140.9% through Reflect, ~75% KO). Grimmsnarl Spirit Breaks Mamoswine to break Focus Sash (21.2-38.9%), setting up a clean Shadow Ball KO next turn while both foes are Shadow Tag trapped. Grimmsnarl survives even worst-case double-target (23.3-33.7% + 38.1-55.9% = 61.4-89.6% from 87% HP). If Mamoswine Protects, it wastes its turn and remains trapped. Sneasler is completely helpless vs Gengar-Mega (Fighting immune, Poison 0.25x).

Dire Claw guarantees the KO on Grimmsnarl, removing Prankster and Reflect support. High Horsepower then pressures Gengar-Mega for a possible knockout while preserving the chance to win the active exchange despite Gengar moving first.
Keep Sneasler active to threaten the weakened Grimmsnarl, while switching Mamoswine's slot to Farigiraf, which is immune to Gengar's Shadow Ball and preserves the Trick Room option.

Grimmsnarl must Protect — Sneasler's Dire Claw is a guaranteed KO from 35% HP and Sneasler outspeeds, so Grimmsnarl cannot act before fainting. Switching to Tyranitar is fatal (Close Combat guaranteed OHKO). Gengar Shadow Balls Mamoswine: KOing Mamoswine removes the only threat to Gengar (HH 78.8-113.9% possible OHKO), and if Mamoswine falls, Sneasler is trapped by Shadow Tag and cannot damage Gengar at all — near-guaranteed win. Targeting Sneasler instead still leaves Mamoswine free to OHKO Gengar this turn, making Mamoswine the priority elimination target.
Dire Claw reliably KOs Grimmsnarl from 35%, while Helping Hand boosts Sneasler before it attacks and Farigiraf remains immune to Gengar's Shadow Ball.

Grimmsnarl uses Light Screen (Prankster priority, guaranteed before damage) to halve Farigiraf's Psychic Noise from possible OHKO range (78.8-115.3%) to survivable 39-58%. Gengar Shadow Balls Sneasler at -1 SpD for a possible OHKO (61-116.1%); if Sneasler faints, it cannot Dire Claw Grimmsnarl, so Grimmsnarl survives at 35% and can Spirit Break Farigiraf next turn (21.6-40.5% + SpA drop) alongside Gengar Sludge Bomb (41-75.9%) for a combined 62.6-116.4% double-target KO on Farigiraf. If Sneasler survives, it still cannot damage Gengar at all, and Gengar outspeeds Farigiraf to Taunt it next turn before any Trick Room. Shadow Tag keeps both foes trapped regardless.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Close Combat threatens an immediate 4x knockout on Tyranitar, while Trick Room establishes the speed mode for Armarouge against opposing sand pressure and avoids exposing Farigiraf to an unnecessary attack this turn.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Gengar Shadow Ball KOs Sneasler at 3% before it can Close Combat Tyranitar (Gengar 200 > Sneasler 154-189). Tyranitar Crunch hits Farigiraf for 51.1-95.4% (2x SE). If Sneasler Protects (priority +4), Shadow Ball is wasted but Tyranitar still Crunches Farigiraf; under TR next turn Sneasler Close Combats Tyranitar (OHKO) but Gengar KOs Sneasler and Tyranitar finishes Farigiraf with a second Crunch (102-190.8% combined = guaranteed KO). Both active foes are eliminated in every scenario. Taunt on Farigiraf is useless because Mental Herb cures it immediately, so preventing TR isn't possible — but eliminating both foes under TR is the win path. Best case: Sneasler doesn't Protect, Tyranitar survives, both foes fall over two turns. Worst case: Sneasler Protects, Tyranitar falls, but both foes still die and Gengar faces the 4th Pokémon alone at 42-100%.

Farigiraf acts before Gengar under Trick Room. Psychic Noise damages Gengar first, then Helping-Hand-free Armor Cannon provides enough combined damage to guarantee the KO from 94% across the shown ranges, removing the immediate Shadow Ball threat while preserving Wide Guard for later spread pressure.

Under TR, Armarouge moves before Gengar and Farigiraf's Helping Hand (priority +5) can boost Expanding Force to potentially KO Gengar (91.2-132.1%). Tyranitar Crunch guarantees KO on 17% Farigiraf (51.1-95.4% vs 17% HP). Gengar Protect (priority +4) blocks Armarouge's boosted Expanding Force regardless of Farigiraf's action. If Farigiraf doesn't Protect, it dies and next turn is 2v1 vs trapped Armarouge (Shadow Tag) for the game. If Farigiraf Protects, Gengar stays safe and Farigiraf drops to ~10% from sandstorm chip — repeat next turn. Protecting Gengar is critical: losing it means losing Shadow Tag and the opponent can bring a 4th Pokémon.

Under Trick Room, Armarouge acts before Gengar. Expanding Force is the only listed attack with a realistic chance to KO Gengar before it can retaliate; Tyranitar is immune to it, while Armor Cannon cannot reliably finish Gengar. Farigiraf has no available action.

2v1 endgame: only Armarouge (93%) remains. Under TR, Tyranitar (81 Spe) moves first and Crunches for 47.9-87.5%, dropping Armarouge to 5.5-45.1%. Gengar's Shadow Ball (79.2-150%) then easily finishes. If Armarouge Protects, both whiff but I keep dominant 2v1 with 2 TR turns left. If Armarouge attacks Gengar with Expanding Force (61.3-88.3%, possible KO), Gengar may fall but Armarouge is already weakened — Tyranitar KOs next turn since Expanding Force is 0x into Tyranitar (Dark) and Armor Cannon is 0.5x NVE + Light Screen. No losing scenario exists.

reflections.summary: The game was lost mainly because Trick Room was established too late: Mamoswine and Sneasler were removed before Farigiraf could support Armarouge, while attacks were spent into Mega Gengar's Protect and the opponent's screens and sand compounded the disadvantage. The four brought were strategically workable—Sneasler and Mamoswine supplied immediate pressure, while Farigiraf and Armarouge fit the Trick Room plan—but the sequencing did not let that plan function. No Mega Stone holder was brought or evolved on your side; Armarouge was still the appropriate slow-mode attacker, but it needed earlier Trick Room support.
reflections.adjustment: Lead Sneasler with Farigiraf and use Fake Out to deny the opposing setup or Mega Gengar while setting Trick Room immediately. After Trick Room is active, avoid committing attacks into Gengar's Protect; use Armarouge's Wide Guard or Protect when appropriate and redirect pressure toward Tyranitar or the non-protected target.

reflections.summary: Won through Gengar-Mega Shadow Ball cleaning up weakened Mamoswine and Sneasler, then Tyranitar Crunch (2x SE) finishing Farigiraf and Armarouge. Opponent's Trick Room backfired: under TR, slow Tyranitar outsped and KO'd Armarouge before it could act. Screens from Grimmsnarl and well-timed Protects minimized damage during setup. No decision errors recorded.
reflections.adjustment: Excadrill fell early to Sneasler Close Combat + Mamoswine Ice Shard after only absorbing one Protect. Consider leading Tyranitar alongside Grimmsnarl to threaten Sneasler with Rock Slide and discourage Fake Out, preserving Excadrill for Sand Rush cleanup if Trick Room appears again.

decisions.rationale: Lead Farigiraf and Sneasler to use Helping Hand or Fake Out support while establishing Trick Room. Bring Armarouge to preserve Wide Guard against Rock Slide and Make It Rain, plus Archaludon as a durable special attacker that benefits from Trick Room.

Lead Gengar+Tyranitar for Shadow Tag trapping, Taunt to stop Farigiraf TR, and immediate Sand Stream for Excadrill's SandRush. Gengar is immune to Fake Out/Fighting, shielding Tyranitar. Back line Excadrill (sand sweeper, answers Archaludon/Dedenne/Mamoswine) and Tauros (Close Combat 2x vs Archaludon/Farigiraf, Intimidate vs Sneasler/Mamoswine physical attackers). Covers all 6 opponent mons including expected Game 2 adjustments bringing Archaludon/Dedenne.

Set Trick Room while Sneasler uses Close Combat to heavily pressure or KO Tyranitar. Farigiraf's Mental Herb preserves the Trick Room attempt against Taunt, and this avoids wasting attacks into a possible Gengar Protect.

Mega Evolve Gengar for Shadow Tag (traps both foes, prevents switching to TR sweepers) and Taunt Farigiraf to block Trick Room (if no Mental Herb per notebook) or burn Mental Herb for permanent lock next turn. Tyranitar Protects because Sneasler's Close Combat is a guaranteed OHKO (164-238%) and Fake Out would flinch it — Sneasler must target Tyranitar since Gengar is immune to all its Fighting moves. This preserves Tyranitar at full HP for turn 2 while establishing Shadow Tag control.
Psychic Noise pressures Mega Gengar with a possible KO while Close Combat guarantees the Tyranitar KO; this also punishes either foe Protecting instead of allowing both threats to remain unchecked.

Under TR, Tyranitar is likely faster than Farigiraf and Crunches it (51-95%, possible KO from 93%). Tyranitar dies to Close Combat regardless (guaranteed OHKO). Gengar Protects to guarantee survival against Farigiraf's Psychic Noise (79-115%, real OHKO chance at 94% HP). Gengar is our win condition with Shadow Tag trapping both foes; Sneasler cannot meaningfully damage Gengar (Fighting immune, Poison NVE). Next turn: bring in Tauros (Intimidate) or Excadrill alongside healthy Gengar to clean up weakened Farigiraf + trapped Sneasler.

Bring Tauros over Excadrill: Intimidate weakens Sneasler's Attack, and Tauros's 140 Speed moves before Sneasler (154-189) under TR, whereas Excadrill's Sand Rush (280 effective) would move last under TR. Next turn: Tauros Close Combat + Gengar Shadow Ball on Sneasler = 96.3% min combined > 88% HP = guaranteed KO if both land. Farigiraf at 18% likely Protects (priority +4 always first), letting both attacks hit Sneasler. Shadow Tag keeps both foes trapped. Sneasler cannot damage Gengar meaningfully.

Double-target Tauros with super-effective Psychic Noise and Close Combat to maximize the chance of removing the active physical threat while preserving Trick Room pressure; Gengar's Shadow Ball cannot affect Farigiraf.
Keep Farigiraf in play to preserve Armor Tail and Trick Room pressure, while switching in the preferred slow special attacker. Preserve Armarouge for Wide Guard against spread threats.

Aqua Jet's priority +1 guarantees Tauros moves before Farigiraf's Psychic Noise (priority 0), even under TR. With Farigiraf at 18% HP, Aqua Jet has ~73% chance to KO it before Psychic Noise fires, protecting Gengar and preserving Shadow Tag. If Farigiraf Protects (priority +4), Aqua Jet is blocked but Gengar is safe since Farigiraf didn't attack. Gengar's Shadow Ball targets Sneasler for 61-116.1% damage (~51% solo KO, otherwise heavy chip). This plan protects Gengar in nearly all scenarios versus the alternative of both targeting Sneasler, which guarantees Sneasler's KO but exposes Gengar to a 75% Psychic Noise KO risk — losing Shadow Tag would be catastrophic. Sneasler CC only does 40-57% to Tauros (survives), and Sneasler cannot meaningfully damage Gengar.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.
Helping Hand boosts Archaludon's Dragon Pulse enough to guarantee the KO on Gengar-Mega from its current HP, removing the most dangerous opposing threat before Excadrill acts under Trick Room.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Under TR, Farigiraf moves first and threatens Psychic Noise (78.8–115.3% of Gengar's max HP, ~75% KO from 82%). Gengar must Protect to survive and preserve Shadow Tag. Excadrill KOs 11% HP Farigiraf with High Horsepower (neutral, 95% acc), eliminating the Psychic Noise threat permanently. Archaludon's options are all NVE vs Excadrill (Dragon Pulse/Flash Cannon 0.5x, Snarl 0.5x + only lowers SpA which Excadrill doesn't use), so Excadrill stays healthy. After this turn: Farigiraf gone, Gengar safe at 82%, Shadow Tag maintained, TR 1 turn remaining.

Concentrate both attacks on Gengar-Mega while Trick Room gives Armarouge and Archaludon the first actions. Expanding Force has a possible KO, and Dragon Pulse guarantees the knockout if Expanding Force rolls low, while avoiding Excadrill's immediate pressure next turn.

Armarouge Expanding Force is a guaranteed KO on Gengar (77% HP) and Armarouge moves first under TR. Gengar must Protect — even at reduced success rate (~33%), it's the only way Gengar survives Expanding Force. If Gengar attacks instead, it dies before moving. Excadrill targets Armarouge with High Horsepower (SE 2x, 76–136.3% — possible OHKO) to remove the Expanding Force threat permanently. If Armarouge attacks rather than Protects, Excadrill gets the hit. Focus Sash guarantees Excadrill survives Armor Cannon. Next turn TR and Sandstorm expire, giving Gengar (200) and Excadrill (140) the speed advantage over both opponents.

Armarouge can only pass after fainting. Snarl is the best remaining play because it damages both foes, is super effective into Gengar-Mega, and reduces both opponents' Special Attack while preserving a chance to survive.

Archaludon is the last foe standing in a 2v1 where both my Pokémon outspeed it. Its only survival tool is Protect (priority +4, beats Taunt this turn). Gengar Taunts Archaludon so it cannot Protect next turn, while Excadrill High Horsepower (62-107%, possible OHKO) hits for damage now. If Archaludon Protects this turn, it's Taunted and can't Protect next turn — guaranteed KO with both attacks. If Archaludon attacks instead, HH may OHKO (62%), and even if not, Gengar survives Dragon Pulse (49-71%, Gengar at 77%) or Snarl (32-45%). Win is locked by next turn regardless of opponent's choice.

Armarouge has no legal action remaining. Dragon Pulse into Gengar-Mega is the only available attack with a guaranteed KO if Gengar does not Protect; Snarl cannot KO Gengar reliably and cannot meaningfully pressure Excadrill.

Both Pokémon outspeed Archaludon and each has a guaranteed KO at 22% HP. Sending both attacks at Archaludon ensures the kill even if High Horsepower's 95% accuracy misses, since Shadow Ball is 100% accurate. Archaludon is Taunted so no Protect; it never moves. This closes game 2 and the series 2-0.

reflections.summary: Lost primarily because the chosen Trick Room mode could not convert its early advantage: Mega Gengar repeatedly used Protect and Taunt while Excadrill applied decisive Ground pressure, leaving Farigiraf and both slow attackers unable to sustain momentum. Armortail and Sneasler's early pressure removed Tyranitar and Tauros, but Sneasler could not threaten Gengar, and the opposing Protect cycles denied key attacks. No between-game adjustment is evidenced, so its effect cannot be credited or blamed; the game-2 plan itself ultimately backfired against Gengar plus Excadrill. The four brought were serviceable but not ideal: Farigiraf was valuable for Trick Room and Armortail, while Armarouge's Wide Guard and Archaludon's Snarl were relevant options, but the composition lacked a reliable Gengar answer and was highly vulnerable to Excadrill. No Mega Stone holder was evolved, and no supplied evidence shows that any registered Pokémon had a Mega Stone. The registered six had useful anti-priority and spread-control tools, but their sets did not adequately cover Taunt, Protect stalling, Ghost immunity interactions, and Ground pressure. The four omitted Pokémon might have offered a better alternative, but their sets are not supplied, so a materially superior replacement cannot be established.
reflections.adjustment: For a rematch, do not rely on a single slow Trick Room line. Preserve Farigiraf long enough to control Taunt and speed, bring a direct way to pressure or deny Mega Gengar, and avoid spending Sneasler's main attack into Gengar's immunity. Force value through Protect with double-targeting, disruption, or defensive positioning rather than repeatedly attacking into it. Keep Wide Guard available for Excadrill and Tyranitar spread attacks, while respecting Excadrill's Focus Sash and Ground pressure. If the omitted roster has a proven Gengar answer or Ground immunity, test that Pokémon over the least effective member; otherwise retain the core but alter the opening so Gengar cannot freely Taunt and stall Trick Room.

reflections.summary: Won game 2 and the series 2-0. The sand core of Tyranitar + Excadrill provided strong speed control against the opponent's Trick Room + slow attacker strategy. Mega Gengar's Taunt pressure and Shadow Tag were pivotal, and Excadrill's High Horsepower cleaned up after sand was set. The opponent's Farigiraf used Mental Herb to cure Taunt and still set Trick Room on turn 1, but the team's Protect sequencing and raw damage output overwhelmed the TR window. Tauros contributed Intimidate support but fell early to Psychic Noise after Aqua Jet was blocked by Armor Tail. Excadrill's crit on Armarouge on turn 5 was fortunate but the position was already winning. Gengar finished the weakened Archaludon cleanly. No decision errors were recorded.
reflections.adjustment: The same four (Gengar, Tyranitar, Excadrill, Tauros) were brought for game 2 after winning game 1, and the choice held up well. In a future series, consider whether Gholdengo over Tauros adds value: Gholdengo resists Archaludon's Dragon Pulse and Armarouge's Expanding Force, and provides Make It Rain spread damage. However, Tauros's Intimidate and Ground-type coverage for Archaludon are real assets. The current bring is solid; the main tweak would be better Protect sequencing around Farigiraf's Mental Herb Trick Room, perhaps doubling into Farigiraf on turn 1 instead of splitting Taunt + Protect.

events.text: Toxic Spikes up on P1's side
Stealth Rock up on P1's side
Toxic Spikes up on P1's side

decisions.rationale: Lead Pelipper and Swampert to immediately set up rain via Drizzle and Mega Evolve Swampert for Swift Swim speed control and offensive pressure against their sun/balanced core. Bring Whimsicott in the back for Tailwind backup and Prankster utility, and Basculegion to clean up with Choice Scarf Adaptability.

Toxapex and Skarmory lead to absorb rain-boosted Water/Ground pressure while setting Toxic Spikes and dual hazards (Stealth Rock + Spikes). Aegislash backs up as the dedicated Mega Ampharos and special-attacker switch-in with 202 SpD and Expert Belt leverage. Meowscarada with Choice Scarf at 190 Speed provides late-game cleaning and revenge-kills the opponent's fast special attackers (Whimsicott, Basculegion).
Pelipper targets Skarmory with Hurricane while Swampert targets Toxapex with Liquidation without Mega Evolving yet, keeping matchup options flexible against Skarmory and Toxapex.

Stacking Toxic Spikes + Spikes on Turn 1 maximizes chip damage on the rain team's frequent switch-ins, directly executing the hazard-wear-down plan to enable Meowscarada as the late-game win condition.

Pelipper targets Skarmory with Hydro Pump for a guaranteed KO through its remaining 67% HP, while Mega Swampert uses Earthquake with Mega Evolve to hit both opponents (doing heavy damage to Toxapex and pressuring the board while immune to Skarmory).

Baneful Bunker (priority +4) shields Toxapex from Swampert's Earthquake and poisons on contact, preserving its longevity. Stealth Rock is the highest-value hazard to set against a rain squad—Water and Flying switch-ins take 25% chip, accelerating the wear-down plan before Meowscarada sweeps.

Meowscarada with Choice Scarf (Speed 190 → ~285) outspeeds both opponent's Pelipper (85–117) and Swift Swim Swampert-Mega (180–244), letting it strike first with super-effective LeafStorm on Swampert-Mega to threaten a KO and remove the biggest offensive threat. Toxapex should pass and stay in to remain as a defensive wall, keeping Toxic Spikes pressure while Meowscarada executes the win condition.

Meowscarada outspeeds our whole team due to Choice Scarf (effective Speed 235-288 vs Mega Swampert's 180). Pelipper targets Meowscarada with Hurricane for a super-effective hit, while Mega Swampert targets Meowscarada with Liquidation (or we can hit Toxapex with Earthquake, but Meowscarada threatens Swampert severely with Grass moves). However, Meowscarada resists Earthquake and is weak to Ice. Let's use Pelipper's Hurricane into Meowscarada and Swampert's Ice Punch into Meowscarada to secure a KO on the dangerous Choice Scarf Meowscarada.
Swampert fainted last turn, so we must replace it. Basculegion enters in rain with Choice Scarf and Adaptability to clean up remaining threats, while Pelipper maintains board position.

Toxapex uses Recover to fully heal back to 100% HP, maintaining its role as the defensive backbone against the rain core's physical threats. Meowscarada uses Leaf Storm targeting Swampert-Mega for the 4x super-effective hit (Grass vs Water/Ground), aiming to eliminate the opponent's most dangerous attacker and Mega Evolution outright. Even accounting for Leaf Storm's -2 SpA drawback, removing Mega Swampert significantly weakens the opposing rain team and accelerates Meowscarada's sweep path.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.
Pelipper targets Aegislash with Hurricane to pressure it, while Choice Scarf Basculegion hits Aegislash with Last Respects for super-effective damage (Aegislash is Ghost/Steel).

Baneful Bunker protects Toxapex from Basculegion's Water coverage (FlipTurn/WaveCrash, both not very effective) and poisons any contact attacker. King's Shield protects Aegislash from Basculegion's super-effective Ghost moves (PhantomForce/LastRespects) and drops Basculegion's Attack by two stages, crippling its physical damage for the rest of the game. Both moves have +4 priority, ensuring they execute before Basculegion's Choice Scarf speed advantage. This preserves Aegislash as the essential Mega Ampharos answer and lets Basculegion's poison plus hazard chip finish it off over subsequent turns.
Pelipper stays in and uses Hurricane into Aegislash, while Basculegion switches out to Whimsicott to reset its Choice lock and avoid King's Shield penalty.

Toxapex layers Toxic Spikes to pressure future foe switch-ins. Aegislash uses Shadow Ball on Basculegion: it is super-effective (2x) and Basculegion is at 63% HP, giving a real chance to outright KO the Choice-Scarfed threat. Even if it doesn't KO, Aegislash at 100% HP survives Last Respects (max 55% damage) and can finish Basculegion next turn.

Pelipper uses Hurricane on Aegislash-Blade (which caused confusion last turn and is vulnerable), while Whimsicott sets Tailwind to secure the speed advantage and offensive presence for the rest of the game.

Toxapex stacks Toxic Spikes to upgrade switch-in poison to toxic for Basculegion and other foes; Aegislash uses King's Shield to safely block Pelipper's Hurricane, preserve its 82% HP for the Basculegion switch-in, and prepare to block Last Respects next turn.

Aegislash is currently confused and slower under Tailwind, and we can switch Whimsicott out to Basculegion while Pelipper hits Aegislash with Hurricane to pressure past its Ghost/Steel typing. Basculegion can then enter safely to clean up.

Baneful Bunker protects Toxapex (full HP) from Whimsicott's likely Moonblast and scouts opponent intent; King's Shield is the safest Aegislash option given confusion—its +4 priority blocks Pelipper's guaranteed Hurricane before Whimsicott can act, preserving Aegislash's 82% HP for the critical Basculegion matchup next turn.

Pelipper targets Aegislash with Hurricane while Basculegion uses Last Respects on Aegislash. This double-targets Aegislash to break through King's Shield / damage it while ignoring Toxapex's Rindo Berry and Baneful Bunker/Recover loops. Tailwind is active so we outspeed, and Rain boosts Water moves or Weather Ball if needed, but Hurricane and Last Respects hit Aegislash effectively.

Aegislash Shadow Ball guarantees a KO on Basculegion (26% HP, super-effective, 61.2-111.8% damage range covers target entirely). Aegislash survives both Basculegion's Last Respects (37.7-55.3%) and Pelipper's Hurricane (12.6-18.9%) at 82% HP, ending at roughly 8-32% HP. Removing Basculegion is the stated priority. Toxapex uses Haze as the highest-value safe option—Recover is wasted at full HP, Toxic Spikes are already layered, and Baneful Bunker has reduced success rate with no incoming contact threat.
Pelipper uses Hurricane to chunk Toxapex while Basculegion fires off Last Respects. Tailwind expires this turn, so we maximize offensive output.

Toxapex sets Toxic Spikes to pressure the opponent's remaining grounded Pokémon (Primarina, Forretress) and support Meowscarada as the late-game win condition; Basculegion is nearly dead from poison and Choice-locked, so hazards will wear down switches. Aegislash is fainted and must Pass.
Pelipper's Hurricane cleanly KOs Toxapex from 16% (guaranteed). Basculegion uses Last Respects into Toxapex just in case or as a backup, though Hurricane alone finishes it.

Toxapex at 16% HP needs immediate recovery to remain an effective defensive wall. Recover brings it to ~90%, allowing it to absorb Pelipper's incoming hits (Hydro Pump is resisted 0.5x, Hurricane is neutral but manageable) while continuing to spread hazards. Basculegion at 1% HP poisoned will almost certainly faint from residual poison before acting, so there is no urgent incoming threat requiring Baneful Bunker's protection this turn. Aegislash is fainted with no other option than Pass.

reflections.summary: The game was won by overwhelming the opponent's defensive setup core (Skarmory, Aegislash, Toxapex) with sustained rain offense from Pelipper and Swampert early, followed by cleaning up with Basculegion's Last Respects once the defensive threats were isolated.
reflections.adjustment: Be mindful of timing protection moves (King's Shield and Baneful Bunker) from the opponent's defensive pivot pieces to avoid wasting attacking turns.

reflections.summary: Lost primarily because Basculegion's Last Respects snowballed out of control after powering up through multiple KOs, overwhelming my team once Aegislash fell. My hazard advantage (Spikes/Stealth Rock via Skarmory) was negated by opponent's own hazard stack (Spikes + Stealth Rock + Toxic Spikes) grinding down Toxapex to 16% before Basculegion delivered the finishing blow. Meowscarada was an ineffective pick—died immediately to Hurricane in Pelipper's rain without contributing meaningfully. I also never Mega Evolved any Pokémon, leaving a Mega Stone slot wasted when the opponent successfully Mega Evolved Swampert for early pressure.
reflections.adjustment: Replace Meowscarada or adjust the fourth slot to include a dedicated Basculegion/Last Respects check—ideally a Pokémon that resists Ghost/Fighting or can threaten Basculegion on the switch (e.g., a Normal-resistant or Fighting-resistant pivot). Additionally, Mega Evolve Aegislash on the turn it predicts a Last Respects or Hurricane, gaining offensive pressure to punish the opponent before Basculegion reaches 3–4 Last Respects uses, or use the Mega slot proactively to break through Pelipper and disrupt rain earlier.
