Toxic Spikes up on P1's side

decisions.rationale: Pelipper and Swampert provide an instant Drizzle + Mega Swampert rain core, threatening the opponent's team (especially Heracross, Aegislash, Skarmory, and Toxapex) with Swift Swim speed and massive Water/Ground power. Whimsicott and Primarina offer powerful backline support with Tailwind, Moonblast, and Hyper Voice to clean up.

Drop Venusaur (Chlorophyll useless in opponent's rain) and Aegislash (less impactful here). Lead with Toxapex (ToxicSpikes, Recover, BanefulBunker stall, Regenerator, 224 Def tanks physical Ghost hits) and Skarmory (Spikes/StealthRock, Whirlwind phazing, Sturdy+211 Def walls physical attackers). Back carries Heracross (141 Spe, CloseCombat OHKOs Ghost types, Moxie snowballs) and Meowscarada (Choice Scarf 190 Spe outspeeds Scarf Basculegion, Protean provides type flexibility). Prioritize eliminating Basculegion before Last Respects stacks become unanswerable; ToxicSpikes from Toxapex wear down the entire opposing team to reduce that threat.

Pelipper targets Skarmory with Hurricane to deal heavy special damage while avoiding resistance on Toxapex. Swampert Mega Evolves and uses Liquidation on Skarmory or Toxapex (targeting Skarmory to pick up immediate pressure while Pelipper handles Skarmory's weak side). Wait, let's check damage or options; Swampert Mega Liquidation on Skarmory is solid or Earthquake avoiding ally if Pelipper protects, but Swampert can just attack Skarmory directly. Let's make sure Swampert uses Liquidation on Skarmory + Mega Evolve (choice 5) and Pelipper uses Hurricane on foe 2 Skarmory (choice 7).

Stacking Toxic Spikes and Spikes on turn 1 maximizes hazard pressure against the opponent's entire team. Toxic Spikes poisons both active Water-type foes (Pelipper and Swampert) and every grounded non-Poison/Steel switch-in, critically threatening Basculegion which must be eliminated before it snowballs with LastRespects. Spikes adds another layer of passive damage on all switch-ins. Toxapex's bulk (224 Def) lets it survive Swampert's Earthquake even at 2x, and Skarmory is immune to Earthquake, so both Pokémon are safe this turn while setting the hazard stack that wins the long game.

Swampert-Mega outspeeds Skarmory under Swift Swim and easily finishes off the 15% HP Skarmory with Liquidation. Pelipper can safely target Skarmory with Hurricane to ensure the KO if anything unexpected happens, or hit Toxapex, but targeting Skarmory with Hurricane guarantees a clean double-up on slot 2 while keeping options open.

Stacking Toxic Spikes (now 2 layers) and Spikes (now 2 layers) maximizes entry hazard damage on the opponent's side. Basculegion (Water/Ghost, the identified primary win-condition) takes significant chip from both hazards every time it switches in, which is critical to eliminate it before turn 6. Both of the opponent's active Pokémon have limited options against our duo—Swampert-Mega's Earthquake is immune to Skarmory and only hits Toxapex neutrally despite the 2× bonus, and Pelipper's Hurricane and Hydro Pump are both resisted. Skarmory at 15% should survive another turn of resisted hits, and Toxapex's Regenerator plus its massive defenses let it shrug off Earthquake.

Toxapex passes to maintain the defensive backbone and preserve its bulk against the rain core; Skarmory slot switches to Meowscarada whose Choice Scarf Speed of 190 lets it threaten Swampert-Mega with 4x super-effective Grass coverage and pivot via Uturn to maintain offensive pressure toward the Basculegion elimination window.

Pelipper targets Meowscarada with Hurricane for a guaranteed OHKO. Swampert-Mega targets Meowscarada with Liquidation (or Ice Punch) as a secure offensive option since Meowscarada outspeeds both under Choice Scarf and threatens Swampert with Grass moves.

Toxapex uses Recover to restore full HP, maintaining its role as a durable physical wall with Regenerator and Rindoberry. Meowscarada uses Giga Drain on Swampert-Mega for the 4x super-effective Grass hit while healing 75% of damage dealt, preserving its stats and longevity for the critical Basculegion matchup ahead. Leaf Storm's higher base power is offset by the -2 SpA self-drop, which would cripple Meowscarada if it survives the incoming hits from Swampert-Mega's Ice Punch and Pelipper's Hurricane.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Pelipper uses Hurricane on Heracross (foe 2), which is 4x super-effective and almost certain to KO Heracross before it can move. Mega Swampert uses Ice Punch on Heracross (foe 2) or protects/attacks; wait, Heracross is weak to Ice Punch (2x) or we can target Heracross with Ice Punch to ensure it goes down if Hurricane misses or to chunk it reliably while Pelipper secures the 4x super-effective Hurricane KO. Meanwhile Toxapex is frozen and confused.

Swampert has fainted and needs to be replaced. Bringing in Whimsicott provides great speed control options like Tailwind or taunt against a frozen Toxapex, wrapping up the game easily. Pelipper passes its action or stays active.

Toxapex is frozen and likely cannot act; Recover is the best move if it thaws, restoring crucial HP. Heracross must eliminate Swampert-Mega (10% HP) with Knock Off—a guaranteed KO that also removes the Swampertite, preventing re-Mega. Regardless, Pelipper's Hurricane will OHKO Heracross (4× super-effective), so the priority is removing the Earthquake threat to Toxapex and reducing the opponent to Pelipper + one unknown.

Toxapex is frozen and at 47% HP, but could thaw or use recovery/haze if it thaws. Pelipper's Hurricane threatens a potential KO on Toxapex and deals neutral damage without the water resistances, while Whimsicott sets Tailwind to ensure full speed control for the rest of the game and endgame positioning against any remaining threats.

Toxapex is frozen and cannot act; Recover is selected as the most self-beneficial move if the freeze ever breaks. Heracross is fainted in the active slot with no benched Pokémon available to switch to, so Pass is the only legal option.

Toxapex is alone at 55% HP and confused. Hurricane from Pelipper hits hard despite resisting, and Whimsicott can Taunt Toxapex to prevent Recover/Baneful Bunker/Toxic Spikes while rain and Tailwind are active.

Toxapex is confused at 56% HP facing Tailwind-boosted foes. Baneful Bunker (priority +4) protects from damage this turn, can poison any contact attacker, and scouts opponent's move without risking self-inflicted confusion damage. Heracross is fainted and can only pass.
Switch Pelipper to Primarina and use Whimsicott's Taunt on Toxapex to prevent it from using Recover, leaving Toxapex unable to heal while Primarina enters.

Toxapex should set Toxic Spikes to stack hazard pressure—opponent already has one layer from turn 1, so a second layer upgrades to bad poison on any grounded switch-in like Basculegion, which is the primary win-condition to eliminate. Heracross is fainted so must pass.
Toxapex is alone and taunted. Primarina uses Hyper Voice (Liquid Voice gives it STAB Water typing) and Whimsicott uses Moonblast to finish off the remaining 55% HP Toxapex safely under Tailwind.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

reflections.summary: We won the game and series 2-0 by leveraging Pelipper's Drizzle to power up Mega Swampert in the rain, swiftly overwhelming Skarmory, Meowscarada, and Heracross. Even though Swampert fell to Heracross's Knock Off, Pelipper's relentless Hurricanes and a clean-up crew of Whimsicott and Primarina easily dismantled the remaining Toxapex.
reflections.adjustment: No major adjustments needed since the 2-0 sweep proves the current team and piloting strategy were fully effective against this opponent's core.

reflections.summary: Lost because Toxapex played too passively and was worn down by residual damage (confusion + Toxic Spikes stacking on both sides). It set up two layers of Toxic Spikes but never attacked, letting the opponent's rain core (Pelipper Hurricane + Mega Swampert Liquidation) freely pressure my team. Skarmory died in two turns to that pressure. Meowscarada was OHKO'd by rain-boosted Hurricane. Hercross did KO Mega Swampert (revealing Moxie) but also fell to Hurricane. Once Whimsicott Taunted Toxapex on Turn 7, its only remaining moves were Struggle and switching — it couldn't Recover or Bunker, and the accumulated toxic/confusion damage finished it on Turn 8. The core issue: four passive or frail picks against a fast, disruptive rain offense with no dedicated wallbreaker or consistent offensive pressure.
reflections.adjustment: Against this opponent's rain + Whimsicott disruption core: (1) swap at least one frail pick (Skarmory or Meowscarada) for Venusaur — it resists Liquidation, threatens both Water types with Giga Drain, and has enough bulk to switch into non-super-effective hits. (2) Consider bringing Aegislash instead of one of the weaker picks; its mixed offenses and Stance Change can punish Whimsicott and pressure Pelipper. (3) Never leave Toxapex idle for multiple turns — attack with Toxic Spikes already up to force switches and chip, don't just Recover/Bunker and wait to get Taunted. (4) Prioritize eliminating Whimsicott early; once Focus Sash is broken, Tailwind + Taunt is the win-condition enabler. (5) Mega Evolve proactively if Mega Charizard Y is brought — sun invalidates their rain and Charizard's Fire STAB threatens Pelipper and bulky Water types.

decisions.rationale: Lead Tyranitar+Excadrill sand core: Sand Stream gives Excadrill 280 Spe outspeeding everything, High Horsepower is 2x SE on Metagross/Klefki/Incineroar, Tyranitar resists Dragapult's Shadow Ball (0.5x) and Fire Blast (0.5x) while Excadrill is immune to Thunderbolt. Focus Sash protects Excadrill from Fake Out. Back: Mega Gengar for Shadow Tag trapping and Energy Ball to answer Rotom-Wash (Levitate blocks Excadrill); Houndoom for Flamethrower on Metagross/Klefki and Dark Pulse on Dragapult, with Flash Fire to absorb Incineroar Fire moves aimed at Tyranitar.

Dragapult outspeeds the entire opponent team (213 vs max 200 Mega Gengar) and threatens OHKO on Gengar with Life Orb Shadow Ball. Rotom-Wash walls Excadrill completely (Levitate immune to High Horsepower, resists Iron Head 4x, neutral Rock Slide) and threatens both Tyranitar and Excadrill with 2x Hydro Pump. Incineroar in back provides Intimidate cycling, Fake Out disruption, and Parting Shot pivoting to handle Tauros-Aqua and physical threats. Mega Metagross brings Bullet Punch priority and Tough Claws Psychic Fangs to guarantee OHKO on Gengar while offering Steel-type bulk.

Excadrill Protects to preserve Focus Sash and full HP against potential double-targeting (Fire Blast 82-123% breaks Sash, then Hydro Pump KOs). Tyranitar Crunch hits Dragapult for 58.5-108% — possible OHKO, always heavy damage. If Dragapult Protects, only Crunch is wasted; Excadrill stays pristine for sand sweeping. Tyranitar survives Hydro Pump (47-70%) and remains functional. This hedges against the most common Turn 1 Protect from fast frail Dragapult while still applying maximum pressure.

Dragapult must Protect to avoid the 90.9–127.3% Crunch OHKO from Tyranitar. Rotom-Wash Hydro Pump threatens Tyranitar for 46.4–82.3% while Rotom easily survives any combination of foe attacks (max ~76% from Crunch + Rock Slide). Switching Incineroar risks a High Horsepower OHKO (83.2–116.8%); staying in with Dragapult unprotected risks losing it immediately. This line preserves both mons and pressures the sand core.

Guaranteed KO on Dragapult: Excadrill HHP (44.6-84.7%, goes first at 280 Spe) + Tyranitar Crunch (58.5-108%, 2x SE) = 103.1-192.7% combined, killing Dragapult at 93% HP. Dragapult's Protect is at reduced success rate so they likely attack — Fire Blast on Excadrill is absorbed by Focus Sash (Excadrill survives at 1 HP, immune to Sandstorm as Steel-type). Rotom likely Hydro Pumps Tyranitar (46.4-69.6%, leaving TTar at ~30-53%) — acceptable cost to remove the opponent's fastest Life Orb threat. Even if opponent double-targets Excadrill, Dragapult still dies to Crunch and Tyranitar stays full. Removing Dragapult shifts the game firmly in our favor with sand rush Excadrill still threatening at 280 Spe.

Switch in Gengar (Mega Evolves → Shadow Tag). Gengar-Mega Energy Ball does 49.7-92.8% to Rotom-Wash (pre-Mega calc; 170 SpA post-Mega will be even higher), and with Tyranitar Helping Hand it becomes a guaranteed KO. Shadow Tag traps Rotom-Wash, preventing Volt Switch escape. Gengar's Ghost typing grants Fake Out immunity if Incineroar comes in, and Taunt shuts down Klefki screens. Houndoom's best option (Dark Pulse 38.2-72%) cannot KO Rotom-Wash from 88%, and Flamethrower is NVE (21.7-40.8%). Tyranitar stays active at 100% HP.

Double-target Excadrill to guarantee KO through Focus Sash: Fire Blast (64.5–123.8%) + Hydro Pump (85.7–160%) = minimum 150.2%. Excadrill moves first and can damage Dragapult, and Tyranitar Crunch likely KOs Dragapult afterward, but eliminating Sand Rush Excadrill is worth the trade. Rotom-Wash then dominates Tyranitar 1v1 with Hydro Pump, and Incineroar + Metagross wait in back. Switching Dragapult risks Excadrill predicting with High Horsepower (83–117% on Incineroar, possible OHKO); staying in and trading is more consistent.

Metagross is the optimal switch: it resists Rock Slide (10-15%), threatens Tyranitar with Tough Claws-boosted Meteor Mash (likely OHKO range after Mega), and Psychic Fangs OHKOs any Gengar switch-in. Mega Metagross outspeeds Tyranitar and doesn't take Sandstorm chip. Incineroar's Intimidate+FakeOut is weaker here — Rock Slide still does 45-63% and Fake Out chip is negligible. Metagross establishes immediate offensive pressure and pairs well with Rotom-Wash's Hydro Pump to secure the KO on Tyranitar if it stays in.

Metagross Psychic Fangs is a guaranteed OHKO on Gengar (149-212%), so we must Protect. Mega Evolving activates Shadow Tag, trapping both foes and shutting off Rotom's Volt Switch. Tyranitar Crunch does 43-74% to Metagross (SE 2x) as chip damage with a 20% Def drop chance. Next turn: Helping Hand + Energy Ball on trapped Rotom for the KO, then focus fire Metagross.

Double-target Gengar with priority Bullet Punch (Mega, Tough Claws: 32.6–67.5%) + Dark Pulse (49.1–96.3%). Combined range 81.7–163.8% gives ~75–85% chance to KO Mega Gengar before it can trap us permanently with Shadow Tag. Bullet Punch goes first (+1 priority), so even if the opponent uses Helping Hand + Shadow Ball, Gengar faints before firing if the combined damage KOs. If Gengar falls, Metagross survives Tyranitar's single hit; if not, we trade Metagross for a heavily damaged Gengar and still have Rotom-Wash + Incineroar against Tyranitar + unrevealed. Mega Evolving Metagross maximizes Bullet Punch damage via Tough Claws.

Gengar (200 Spe) outspeeds Metagross/Metagross-Mega (90-162), so Shadow Ball KOs Metagross at 31% HP (77% min dmg) before it can use Psychic Fangs (which would OHKO Gengar). Only Bullet Punch (+1 pri) could precede, but 40 BP neutral won't KO Gengar. Splitting Tyranitar's Crunch onto Rotom (28.7-53.6% neutral) guarantees value from at least one slot regardless of which foe Protects, and preserves Gengar + Shadow Tag for the 2v1. Double-targeting Metagross risks both moves wasted to a Protect; Helping Hand+Energy Ball on Rotom risks total whiff if Rotom Protects and Metagross then KOs Gengar.

Metagross at 31% dies to any attack from either foe. Protect (+4 priority) blocks all incoming damage. Mega Evolving now gives Tough Claws for next turn. Rotom Volt Switch into Gengar-Mega deals chip (29–53%) and pivots to Incineroar despite Shadow Tag — Volt Switch's text explicitly bypasses trapping. Incineroar's Intimidate then drops Tyranitar's Attack, and next turn Fake Out can flinch Tyranitar while Mega Metagross threatens Gengar with Tough Claws-boosted Bullet Punch.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Bullet Punch (pri +1) is a guaranteed KO on Gengar at 37% before Shadow Ball can resolve. Gengar must Protect to survive. Tyranitar Crunches Metagross (26.7-43.9% vs 31% HP — possible KO). If Crunch KOs, we're in great shape with Gengar alive. If not, Metagross is at ~0-4% and easily finished next turn. Shadow Tag traps both foes regardless. This preserves Gengar (our key win condition with Shadow Tag + Energy Ball for Rotom) while making progress on Metagross.

Fake Out (+3) flinches Tyranitar before it can Crunch Metagross. Bullet Punch (+1) hits Gengar before its Shadow Ball, with ~71.5% chance to KO from 37%. If Bullet Punch KOs, Metagross survives and we have 2v1 vs Tyranitar. If not, Gengar KOs Metagross but is then alone and weakened vs Incineroar + Rotom. No other line gives Metagross a chance to live through this turn.

Gengar at 31% is guaranteed KO'd by Metagross Bullet Punch (priority +1) before it can act, and Protect's success rate is reduced after consecutive use. Switching Gengar to Houndoom is guaranteed safe: Houndoom walls both active foes (Bullet Punch 25-35.5%, Meteor Mash 55.9-78.9%, Darkest Lariat 30.3-44.7%, Flare Blitz immune via Flash Fire, Psychic Fangs immune via Dark typing). Tyranitar Crunch on Metagross (26.7-43.9% vs 31% HP) has a real chance to KO; even if it doesn't, Houndoom Flamethrower is a guaranteed KO on Metagross next turn (71.1-127.7%). If opponent Bullet Punches the Gengar slot (most likely since they know it's a KO), it hits Houndoom for negligible 0.5x damage. Worst case: opponent predicts switch and Meteor Mashes Tyranitar (64.7-92.8%), but Tyranitar survives at 96% HP.

Metagross Protect blocks both Gengar Shadow Ball and Tyranitar Crunch, which would otherwise OHKO Metagross. Incineroar Darkest Lariat guarantees the KO on Gengar-Mega (73-142% into 31% HP), removing the faster Ghost-type threat. Gengar's Protect is only ~33% after two consecutive uses; even if it works, Metagross remains safe and we maintain board control. This preserves our Mega and eliminates their special attacker, leaving a 2v1 against Tyranitar and the unrevealed mon.

Houndoom Flamethrower guarantees KO on Metagross-Mega at 31% (71.1-127.7%). Metagross just Protected last turn so consecutive Protect is unreliable — it will likely attack, and Meteor Mash on Tyranitar does 64.7-92.8% (drops to 3-31%). Tyranitar Protect blocks this, preserving HP for the Rotom-Wash endgame. Even if Metagross targets Houndoom with Bullet Punch instead (25-35.5%), Houndoom survives and still KOs Metagross. If Incineroar Parting Shots to Rotom, Tyranitar avoids the stat drop via Protect.

Metagross is guaranteed to be KO'd by Houndoom this turn (Flamethrower/Dark Pulse both OHKO from 31%). Bullet Punch (+1 priority) guarantees chip on Tyranitar (34.8-61.7%) before Metagross falls. Incineroar's Parting Shot onto Houndoom lowers its SpA/Atk by 1, neutering its threat to incoming Rotom-Wash, then pivots Incineroar out safely. Rotom enters against a debuffed Houndoom and damaged Tyranitar; Hydro Pump OHKOs Houndoom and Dark Pulse OHKOs the back Gengar-Mega from 31%. This preserves Incineroar as a late-game win condition while Rotom cleans up.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Helping Hand (priority +5) always resolves before Fake Out (priority +3), guaranteeing the boost even if Tyranitar is flinched. Houndoom (Speed 161) outspeeds Rotom-Wash (106-138), so boosted Dark Pulse (38.2-72%) lands before Rotom can Hydro Pump. Even if Houndoom falls to Hydro Pump, Rotom is left at 5-39% (+Sitrus = 30-64%), easily cleaned up by Gengar's Energy Ball (61-114%) or Tyranitar next turn. If opponent instead Fake Outs Houndoom, Houndoom survives at ~32% and Fake Out is consumed — next turn Houndoom attacks freely. Tyranitar at 96% is preserved for endgame in all scenarios. Switching to Gengar loses tempo (can't act on switch-in turn) and drops Houndoom's damage to 25.5-48% without Helping Hand.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Fake Out on Tyranitar prevents Rock Slide spread damage and Helping Hand. Hydro Pump on Houndoom guarantees a KO whether Houndoom stays (OHKO), Protects (wastes PP but Tyranitar flinched), or switches to Gengar-Mega (Hydro Pump also OHKOs Gengar-Mega). Houndoom moves before Rotom-Wash but its attacks are manageable (max ~38% Dark Pulse to Rotom). This line maximizes our advantage regardless of opponent's response.

Gengar at 31% is KO'd by any SE Dark move from either foe, so Protect is mandatory for survival. The opponent's most likely play is Rotom Protect + Incineroar Darkest Lariat on Gengar; if Gengar attacks instead, Energy Ball is wasted into Protect and Gengar dies for nothing. By Protecting, we waste both their turns while Tyranitar Rock Slide chips Incineroar (17.8-32.9% SE at -2 Atk) and Rotom (10.2-19.2%). Shadow Tag traps both foes, letting us repeat this pattern to grind down Incineroar. If the opponent instead attacks Tyranitar, Tyranitar survives (92% HP, NVE from Incineroar) and we still make progress. Next turns: alternate Gengar Protect/Energy Ball based on reads to eventually catch Rotom without Protect for the KO.

Gengar-Mega threatens to OHKO Rotom-Wash with Energy Ball (65-90.4%) and is faster. Rotom-Wash Protect (+4 priority) blocks any Gengar-Mega attack or Taunt. Incineroar Darkest Lariat guarantees the KO on Gengar-Mega (73.1-142.2%) if it doesn't Protect. If Gengar-Mega Protects, both my Pokémon survive and we reset with Gengar-Mega's Protect degraded. Tyranitar at -2 Atk does limited damage (Rock Slide 23.8-32.7% to Incineroar). This line preserves Rotom-Wash, which is essential for handling Tyranitar with Hydro Pump afterward.

2v1 endgame: only Rotom-Wash (49%) remains, trapped by Shadow Tag. Gengar-Mega (200 Spe) outspeeds Rotom-Wash (106-138) and Energy Ball is a guaranteed KO from 49%. Tyranitar Protects to stay safe from Hydro Pump (SE 2x) in case Rotom's reduced-rate Protect succeeds — if so, we simply repeat next turn with even lower Protect odds. Cleanest path to closing game 1.

Gengar-Mega outspeeds and OHKOs Rotom-Wash with Energy Ball regardless of my move. Dark Pulse on Gengar-Mega is the only play that punishes an opponent misclick (Shadow Ball, Taunt, or Protect), letting me KO Gengar-Mega and then attempt to 1v1 the -2 Atk Tyranitar with Hydro Pump. Protect is only a 1/3 delay into the same losing position. Incineroar is fainted so Pass is forced.

reflections.summary: Won through sand control and Mega Gengar Shadow Tag trapping Rotom-Wash for the KO. Excadrill traded favorably for Dragapult early, Houndoom removed Metagross with Flamethrower, and Tyranitar's crit Rock Slide eliminated Incineroar. Clean piloting with zero decision errors; team preview and Mega Gengar choice were correct for this opponent's four.
reflections.adjustment: Opponent may adjust their bring for game 2 — if they add Klefki or Serperior, keep Houndoom healthier (it was spent removing Metagross here) and consider leading Tyranitar+Excadrill again to pressure screens/Contrary setups before they stabilize.

reflections.summary: The game was lost because Rotom-Wash ended up trapped by Shadow Tag Gengar-Mega in the 1v2 endgame; Gengar's Energy Ball OHKO'd Rotom, and even with Tyranitar at -2 Attack, there was no path to victory. Earlier positioning mistakes allowed Gengar to survive, and a critical Rock Slide on Incineroar removed the only way to pressure Gengar.
reflections.adjustment: Swap Rotom-Wash for Gholdengo to avoid Shadow Tag trapping and threaten Gengar-Mega with a super-effective Shadow Ball that it cannot trap. Lead Incineroar + Metagross to exert immediate pressure on Tyranitar while pivoting Incineroar with Parting Shot to preserve Fake Out for when Gengar stays in.

decisions.rationale: Gengar+Tyranitar lead for Shadow Tag trap + Sand Stream; Excadrill back as Sand Rush sweeper hitting Metagross-Mega SE with High Horsepower and outspeeding everything under sand; Houndoom back as dedicated Serperior/Klefki answer (resists Grass, SE Flamethrower, Sucker Punch priority). Covers all opponent adjustments after Game 1 loss.

Lead Dragapult + Rotom-Wash to handle both likely opponent leads. Rotom-Wash's Levitate blanks Excadrill's Ground STAB, while Dragapult outspeeds Gengar-Mega and breaks Excadrill's Sash with Fire Blast. Against TTar+Excadrill: Dragapult Fire Blast into Excadrill (breaks Sash), Rotom-Wash Hydro Pump into TTar. Against Gengar+TTar: Dragapult Shadow Ball threatens Gengar, Rotom-Wash pressures TTar. Metagross in back threatens TTar and can OHKO Gengar with Psychic Fangs after Mega Evolving. Incineroar provides Intimidate cycling and Fake Out for mid-game tempo.

Dragapult Shadow Ball is a guaranteed OHKO on Gengar (110-165%) and Dragapult likely outspeeds Mega Gengar (213 vs ~199), so Gengar must Protect. Mega Evolving simultaneously gets Shadow Tag active this turn, trapping both foes. Tyranitar Crunch on Dragapult deals 58.5-108% (possible OHKO) — if Dragapult targets Gengar (blocked by Protect), this is a free heavy hit. Even worst case of double-target on Tyranitar (Thunderbolt 15-22% + Hydro Pump 46-70% ≈ 61-92%), TTar's 207 HP bulk likely survives. Next turn: Shadow Tag locks opponents in, Mega Gengar at full HP — primary wincon secured.

Switch Dragapult to Incineroar before Gengar Mega Evolves and traps it with Shadow Tag. Incineroar's Intimidate weakens Tyranitar, and its Dark typing resists Gengar's Shadow Ball to only ~13-20% (even Helping Hand boosted ~21-30%). Rotom-Wash chips Gengar with Dark Pulse for 49-96%, putting it in KO range for later. This preserves Dragapult—my fastest mon and Gengar answer—while gaining board control with Incineroar's Fake Out threat next turn.

Incineroar Darkest Lariat is a guaranteed KO on Gengar (96-140%), so the opponent will almost certainly target Gengar to remove Shadow Tag. Gengar Protect (50% after consecutive use) is the only play that can potentially keep Shadow Tag active — if it works, it blocks Darkest Lariat, Dark Pulse, AND Parting Shot all targeting Gengar, while TTar Rock Slide chips both foes (SE on Incineroar 24-44%, neutral on Rotom) with flinch chance. If Protect fails, Gengar dies but TTar still gets Rock Slide damage — no worse than attacking and letting Gengar die. Switching Gengar out saves it but permanently loses Shadow Tag, and Houndoom has all-NVE matchups against both foes. The 50% coin flip for keeping the wincon active is the highest EV play.

Gengar-Mega's Shadow Tag traps both my Pokémon. The opponent's most lethal play is Helping Hand + Energy Ball from Tyranitar and Gengar into Rotom-Wash, which is a guaranteed KO. Rotom-Wash Protect (+4 priority) blocks that combo regardless of Gengar's speed advantage. Meanwhile, Incineroar's Darkest Lariat threatens Gengar-Mega for 73-142% — a strong chance to KO from 94%, especially since Gengar's consecutive Protect has only ~33% success. If Gengar does Protect successfully, we scout it and degrade its Protect further; Incineroar comfortably tanks Rock Slide (30-43%) and Shadow Ball (17-24%). This line covers both the aggressive Helping Hand + Energy Ball and the safe Protect + Rock Slide from the opponent.

Switch Dragapult into the fainted Incineroar slot. Dragapult (213 Speed) outspeeds Gengar-Mega (165–200) and uses Shadow Ball for 74.9–138.5% into 88% Gengar—a solid chance to OHKO before Gengar acts. Rotom-Wash stays trapped (Shadow Tag) and uses Dark Pulse on Gengar-Mega (43.1–80%). If Dragapult KOs Gengar, Shadow Tag vanishes and Rotom is safe. If Dragapult misses the KO, Rotom's Dark Pulse finishes Gengar provided Rotom survives the opponent's attacks. This double-target maximizes the odds of removing the trapper this turn, which is essential to freeing Rotom and staying in the game.

Dragapult Shadow Ball is a guaranteed KO on Gengar-Mega from 88% (91-137%), and Dragapult is likely faster (213 vs 200). Keeping Gengar in is near-certain death — Protect is unreliable at streak 2 (~25%). Switching Gengar to Excadrill preserves Shadow Tag for later re-entry while bringing in a 280-Speed Sand Rush sweeper with Focus Sash. Tyranitar Crunch hits Dragapult SE for 38-74%, putting it in Excadrill Iron Head KO range (37-71%) next turn. Even worst-case double-target on Tyranitar (Thunderbolt 15-22% + Hydro Pump 46-70% = 61-92%) leaves it alive. Excadrill's Ground typing also blocks Rotom Volt Switch targeting it.

Double-target Gengar-Mega with Shadow Ball + Dark Pulse guarantees the KO (min combined 118% vs 88% HP). Dragapult outspeeds Gengar-Mega and moves first; if Shadow Ball KOs outright, Dragapult survives and we have a 2v1. If it low-rolls, Gengar retaliates and KOs Dragapult, but Rotom-Wash's Dark Pulse finishes Gengar. Either way, Shadow Tag is removed, freeing switches for later turns. Removing Gengar-Mega is essential to enable Metagross to enter safely later.

Excadrill Protects to survive at 4% — it's the only Pokémon that outspeeds Dragapult (280 vs 178-213) to safely KO it before it can Shadow Ball Gengar. Dragapult is forced to Protect (attacking kills it via Life Orb + sandstorm: 15%-10%-6.25%<0), so targeting it wastes attacks. Tyranitar Crunches Rotom for 20-36% chip (Rotom 82%→46-62%), while Tyranitar survives Hydro Pump (46-70%). Plan: Protect Excadrill again turn 5 (Dragapult drops to 2.5%), then turn 6 Excadrill Iron Heads Dragapult at 280 Spe — if it Protects it dies to sandstorm, if it attacks Excadrill KOs first. Gengar then switches in safely with Shadow Tag intact.

Switch Dragapult to Metagross to preserve it and bring a fresh threat. Metagross Mega Evolves; Bullet Punch (+1 priority) outspeeds and KOs 4% Excadrill before it moves — Focus Sash only triggers from full HP. Rotom-Wash Hydro Pumps Tyranitar for 46–82%. This removes the Sand Rush sweeper without taking an attack from it, leaves Metagross-Mega healthy to answer Gengar-Mega with Psychic Fangs, and keeps Dragapult alive on the bench.

Both active Pokémon face guaranteed KOs: Excadrill (4%) dies to Metagross Bullet Punch priority, Tyranitar (38%) dies to Meteor Mash or Hydro Pump. Switching Excadrill to Houndoom brings in a Pokémon immune to Psychic Fangs and resistant to all Steel moves; the opponent's natural play (Bullet Punch on Excadrill's slot, Hydro Pump on Tyranitar) hits Houndoom for only 18-26% NVE and is blocked by Tyranitar's Protect. Next turn Houndoom Flamethrower (80-151% on Metagross) plus Tyranitar Crunch (29-50%) guarantees Metagross KO, leaving a 2v1 vs Rotom with Dragapult unable to attack at 15% HP.

Protect + Mega Evolve on Metagross blanks the likely Helping Hand + High Horsepower OHKO attempt. Dark Pulse from Rotom-Wash into Excadrill breaks Focus Sash, leaving it at 1 HP. Next turn Mega Metagross Bullet Punch (+1 priority) KOs Excadrill before it moves. If opponent instead switches Excadrill to Gengar-Mega, Dark Pulse lands super-effective (43-80%) and Metagross Psychic Fangs OHKOs Gengar-Mega next turn. This preserves Metagross as the Gengar-Mega answer while safely removing Excadrill's Sash.

Switch Tyranitar (38%, too slow to survive) to Gengar-Mega (200 Spe, Shadow Tag traps both foes). Gengar Shadow Ball (67-120%) + Houndoom Flamethrower (71-128%) = 138-248% combined, guaranteed KO on Metagross before it can act (Gengar always outspeeds at 200). Rotom likely Hydro Pumps Houndoom for the KO, but Houndoom's damage is already done. Next turn: Gengar + Tyranitar clean up Rotom while Dragapult is a dead sack (can't attack without dying to LO recoil + sand). Only risk is Metagross Protect (reduced rate), which still leaves a winnable position.

Send in Tyranitar (38% HP) over Excadrill (4% HP). Next turn, Tyranitar's Helping Hand (priority +5) fires before Gengar's Energy Ball, boosting it to ~91-171% — guaranteed KO on Rotom-Wash at 63%. Excadrill's matchups into Rotom are poor (High Horsepower immune via Levitate, Iron Head NVE, Rock Slide neutral) and 4% HP is too fragile. Tyranitar is also Rock-type (immune to sand) and more durable. Dragapult at 15% is a permanent dead sack (LO recoil + sand > HP), so after Rotom falls it's a clean 2v0 win.

Shadow Tag prevents switching and Volt Switch pivot. Metagross always outspeeds Houndoom (162 vs 126–161). Meteor Mash guarantees KO on Tyranitar (78.3–134.9%); Hydro Pump guarantees KO on Houndoom (90.1–169.3%). Both foes are removed this turn. The only counterplay is Tyranitar Helping Hand (+5 priority) boosting Houndoom's Flamethrower into a guaranteed OHKO on Metagross, but even then both foes fall and Rotom + Dragapult face Gengar-Mega + Excadrill with sand ticking down. If opponent forgoes Helping Hand, Metagross has a ~15% survival chance on Flamethrower's low roll, yielding a dominant position. Protect on Metagross is only ~50% reliable after consecutive use and risks losing with nothing gained. This line maximizes expected value against all opponent options.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Helping Hand (priority +5) goes first, boosting Gengar-Mega's Energy Ball to guaranteed KO range (91-171%) on Rotom-Wash at 63%. Dragapult at 15% dies to Life Orb + sand (16.25% > 15%) if it attacks; if it Protects it survives at ~8.75% but remains Shadow Tag-trapped for an easy cleanup next turn. Even if Rotom Protects, we maintain a dominant 2v1 or 2v2 position with all win conditions intact. This is the cleanest forced-win line.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Double-target Gengar-Mega with Dragapult Shadow Ball (74.9–138.5%) + Rotom-Wash Dark Pulse (43.1–80%) guarantees a KO from 82% HP (combined min 118%). Dragapult always moves before Gengar-Mega, so Gengar cannot Energy Ball Rotom-Wash before taking both hits. Dragapult faints to Life Orb recoil afterward; Tyranitar's Crunch does 35–50.3% to Rotom-Wash, leaving it healthy enough to Hydro Pump Tyranitar next turn for the guaranteed KO. Loses only if Gengar-Mega Protects, but that is the opponent's less obvious line given the apparent Energy Ball OHKO on Rotom-Wash.

Protect Tyranitar to block Rotom-Wash's guaranteed Hydro Pump KO (Rotom outspeeds Tyranitar 106-138 vs 81, so Tyranitar would die before acting if it attacks). Excadrill Rock Slide chips Rotom to 24-39% before sandstorm drops it to ~18-33%. If Rotom attacks into Protect, both my Pokémon survive and Tyranitar Crunch (28.7-53.6%) guarantees KO next turn. If Rotom Protects, it's at 50.75% facing 2v1 with no sandstorm next turn — still heavily favorable. This dominates HH+Rock Slide (85% win if Rotom attacks) and Crunch+Rock Slide (~50% win if Rotom kills Tyranitar first).

Hydro Pump OHKOs Tyranitar from 31%. Excadrill moves first (Sand Rush) and may Rock Slide for 17.8–26.1% with 30% flinch. If no flinch, Rotom KOs Tyranitar (speed tie determines whether Tyranitar gets a Crunch off first). The resulting 1v1 vs Excadrill is favourable: its attacks deal only ~10–26%, giving Rotom multiple Hydro Pump attempts. Targeting Tyranitar over Excadrill removes the bigger threat (Crunch 35–50.3%) and maximises survival odds.

Excadrill (Speed 140) outspeedes Rotom-Wash (106-138) and Rock Slides for 17.8-32.8% — 39% to KO from 27%. If it connects but doesn't KO, Rotom drops to 0.1-9.2% HP, creating a checkmate: Rotom's Hydro Pump (80% acc) KOs one of my Pokémon, but the survivor finishes — Excadrill outspeedes and Rock Slides for guaranteed KO from ≤9.2%, or Tyranitar Crunches for guaranteed KO (28.7-53.6%). Even if Excadrill misses (10%), Rotom must hit Hydro Pump on Tyranitar (80%) and then Excadrill still has a 39% shot next turn. ~94% win probability, strictly superior to Helping Hand which leaves Tyranitar unable to attack and removes the double-threat checkmate.

Hydro Pump into Tyranitar is the only winning path. If Tyranitar speed ≤107, Rotom moves first and KOs it; Excadrill's unboosted Rock Slide maxes at 26.1% and cannot KO Rotom from 27%, so Rotom survives and KOs Excadrill next turn. If Tyranitar speed ≥109 and uses Crunch, Rotom faints regardless of target choice. Protect only delays the same speed tie without improving odds. Hydro Pump into Excadrill always loses because Tyranitar Crunch KOs Rotom. Volt Switch fails to KO Tyranitar. The 80% accuracy is unavoidable risk.

reflections.summary: Series won 2-0. Game 2 was a fast 9-turn affair decided by favorable trades and two luck swings: a critical-hit Rock Slide that KO'd Incineroar on turn 2 (it was at 3% from the crit alone, effectively removing the opponent's Fake Out/Intimidate pivot early) and a Metagross Meteor Mash miss on turn 6 that let Houndoom survive to KO Metagross with Flamethrower. The sand core of Tyranitar+Excadrill closed out the endgame cleanly: Tyranitar Protect blocked Rotom's Hydro Pump on turn 8, then Excadrill's Rock Slide finished Rotom on turn 9. The one clear misplay was turn 7 Helping Hand into Gengar—Gengar fainted to Dragapult Shadow Ball before using the boosted move, costing the slot unnecessarily; a double-attack would have been strictly better. Team preview was strong: Mega Gengar's Shadow Tag plus Tyranitar sand and Excadrill sash created pressure the opponent couldn't answer, and Houndoom's Fire STAB was the correct Metagross answer.
reflections.adjustment: In a future series, keep the Gengar-Mega + Tyranitar + Excadrill + Houndoom core against this opponent—it matched up well. Fix the turn-7 type of error: when two attackers both threaten KO on a lone foe, double-attack instead of Helping Hand so the survivor always finishes. Consider Shadow Ball on predicted Rotom Protect turns rather than committing Helping Hand. The opponent may adapt to the sand+Shadow Tag pattern, so have a backup plan if they lead differently.

reflections.summary: We lost the series 0-2 because our team lacked consistent answers to the opponent's Shadow Tag Gengar-Mega + sand core. In game 2, early flinch hax on Incineroar and a crucial Meteor Mash miss on Gengar-Mega prevented us from executing our plan. Even without the hax, the opponent's trapping and speed control overwhelmed our pivots and limited our offensive windows. The between-game adjustment to preserve Rotom-Wash and use Dragapult only after Gengar was removed was sound in theory, but in practice it left us unable to deal with Gengar-Mega efficiently and made us vulnerable to bad luck.
reflections.adjustment: In a future series, I would bring Klefki for Thunder Wave and screens to disrupt the opponent's speed advantage and reduce chip damage. I would drop Serperior and maybe swap Incineroar's item or spread, but keeping Intimidate and Fake Out is still valuable. I would avoid leading Incineroar into Gengar+Tyranitar to prevent early flinch KOs, and I would ensure Dragapult is positioned to snipe Gengar-Mega before it can trap key threats.

decisions.rationale: Mimikyu and Palafin as the lead pair provide immediate offensive pressure: Mimikyu can Swords Dance into Play Rough to delete Fairy leads like Floette-Eternal and threaten Hatterene, while Palafin's Aqua Jet priority and Flip Turn pivot enable the Hero-form sweep that is the core win condition. Aegislash and Toxapex on the back bench cover the defensive needs — Aegislash walls physical attackers with King's Shield and checks Psychic/Fairy types, Toxapex absorbs Garchomp's Earthquakes and provides Haze as a safety net. Glimmora and Skarmory (bench 5-6) enter later to stack hazards once safe, supporting the Palafin sweep plan.

Lead Talonflame and Garchomp for immediate Gale Wings Tailwind pressure and strong spread damage into likely Skarmory/Glimmora leads. Milotic provides the safest Palafin answer and speed control backup, while Mega Floette is retained as a fast late-game cleaner once Steel-types are weakened.

Palafin's Aqua Jet at +1 priority outspeeds and hits Talonflame super-effectively before it can Tailwind or Taunt, applying crucial early pressure on the fastest foe. Mimikyu uses Swords Dance to set up its sweep potential; Disguise negates the first incoming hit (e.g., Garchomp's Earthquake), letting Mimikyu safely boost and threaten Fairy/Psychic targets next turn.
Priority Taunt denies Mimikyu’s Swords Dance while Protect shields Garchomp from the immediate Fairy/Ice pressure, preserving the stronger midgame board against Palafin.

Mimikyu is under volatile Taunt but can still use attacking moves; Play Rough into Garchomp exploits the super-effective Fairy coverage and Garchomp's reduced-accuracy Protect from last turn. Palafin uses priority Aqua Jet into Talonflame to finish off the 43% HP Fire/Flying threat with a guaranteed super-effective hit before Talonflame can Tailwind or attack.

Double-switching preserves both threatened attackers while placing Water-resistant Milotic into Talonflame’s slot and Fairy-type Floette into Garchomp’s slot, making the most likely Water and Fairy attacks unfavorable.

Mimikyu Play Rough guarantees a KO on 36% Floette-Eternal (37-73% damage range eliminates all legal defense spreads), removing the Energy Ball threat that could OHKO Palafin. Palafin Flip Turn on Milotic deals damage, switches Palafin out to activate Zero-to-Hero form on reentry, and avoids leaving Palafin in against Floette-Eternal's super-effective Energy Ball. Speed order: Palafin (120) acts first with Flip Turn (+1 priority), then Floette-Eternal's retargeted move hits Palafin's substitute (Toxapex/Aegislash) at neutral damage, then Mimikyu (116) cleans with Play Rough.

Mimikyu-Busted can only pass or forfeit; passing preserves board presence with its boosted Attack and Play Rough coverage while Milotic acts first. Switching Palafin's fainted slot to Toxapex brings in a Water-type pivot that resists Milotic's Muddy Water, threatens Garchomp with neutral Ground coverage while taking reduced Earthquake, provides Regenerator longevity, and carries Haze to reset Milotic's Competitive boosts and any future setup.
Mega Floette gets its strongest available Palafin pressure before Mimikyu can remove it, while Icy Wind breaks Disguise and gives enduring Speed control over both foes for the remaining endgame.
Bring Talonflame to preserve Garchomp and establish Tailwind pressure while Milotic remains healthy against the unrevealed backline.

Double-target Talonflame (43% HP, FocusSash broken) to eliminate the Gale Wings priority threat before it can fire off a devastating Brave Bird or Flare Blitz. Toxapex's Liquidation is super effective (2x) against Talonflame, and Mimikyu's Shadow Claw hits neutrally. Removing Talonflame's Gale Wings priority is the most urgent defensive play, after which Aegislash can pivot in to safely bring Palafin for the Hero-form sweep.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Double-target Mimikyu before it can set up or pressure Garchomp; Talonflame moves first and Milotic follows before either foe, giving the best immediate chance to remove it while Talonflame is likely lost to Toxapex afterward.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

King's Shield (priority +4) protects Aegislash from Garchomp's Earthquake and drops Garchomp's Attack by 2 stages, dramatically reducing the super-effective spread damage Toxapex would also take. Toxapex's Liquidation (100% accuracy, neutral 1x damage) reliably chips Garchomp while Shell Bell provides passive recovery. This combination mitigates the biggest immediate threat (Garchomp's Earthquake) while maintaining offensive pressure, setting up a favorable position to eventually pivot to Palafin once physical threats are managed.
Earthquake is the only strong simultaneous pressure into both foes; Recover restores Milotic after the allied spread damage.

Aegislash uses King's Shield (priority +4) to block Garchomp's expected Earthquake, which would KO Toxapex regardless. A successful shield leaves Aegislash at full HP with Garchomp's Attack crippled by -2, making Aegislash very difficult to break next turn. Even if the shield fails (reduced success rate), Aegislash may survive the combined Earthquake + Muddy Water damage. Toxapex at 12% HP is almost certainly KO'd by Garchomp's spread Earthquake before acting, so Toxic targeting Milotic is chosen as the highest-value contingency — poisoning Milotic cripples the opponent's primary recovery and special attacker if Toxapex somehow survives or if the opponent's plan changes.
Protect Garchomp from Liquidation and safely let Milotic’s faster Muddy Water remove the critically low Toxapex before it can Recover; this preserves Garchomp to pressure Aegislash afterward.

Aegislash uses King's Shield to block Garchomp's incoming attack and drop its Attack to -3, neutralizing Earthquake and setting up a Flash Cannon KO next turn. Toxapex at 1% uses Recover to attempt to survive the turn as a Regenerator pivot, since foes act first and any other action wastes its remaining HP without saving it.
Earthquake guarantees Toxapex is removed even if Muddy Water misses, while Muddy Water adds pressure into Aegislash; Milotic survives the allied spread damage.

King's Shield is the optimal move for Aegislash. It has priority +4 so it resolves first, protecting Aegislash from both Garchomp's Earthquake and Milotic's Muddy Water. Garchomp's Earthquake is a contact move, so King's Shield will drop Garchomp's Attack by 2 stages on top of the existing -1 from Liquidation, bringing it to -3. This effectively neuters Earthquake and sets up a Flash Cannon 2HKO next turn, which is the stated win condition. Toxapex has fainted so the only legal action is Pass.

Recover preserves Milotic through toxic and allied Earthquake while Garchomp applies the only meaningful immediate pressure to Aegislash; it also covers a successful King’s Shield without sacrificing Milotic.

King's Shield is the critical play: it has priority +4 so it fires before Garchomp's Earthquake. If it lands, it blocks the super-effective Earthquake entirely and drops Garchomp's Attack by 2 stages (on top of the existing Def -1), crippling Garchomp's offensive threat and setting up a Flash Cannon KO next turn. Toxapex is fainted so the only legal action is Pass.
Pressure the heavily reduced consecutive King’s Shield chance with Earthquake while Recover keeps Milotic available through friendly spread damage and poison.

King's Shield is the only move that protects Aegislash from Garchomp's Earthquake and drops Garchomp's Attack by 2 stages, setting up the Flash Cannon 2HKO plan next turn; none of Aegislash's attacking moves can KO Milotic at 37% tox given Aegislash's low offensive stats; Toxapex is fainted so pass is forced
Earthquake has the immediate super-effective KO line if King's Shield fails; Recover gives Milotic the best chance to survive Garchomp's spread damage and remain useful if Shield succeeds.

Garchomp's Earthquake at 2x super-effectiveness guarantees a KO on Aegislash at 31% HP (60.6–87.1% damage). Any move other than King's Shield results in Aegislash fainting. King's Shield (priority +4) blocks the incoming Earthquake, drops Garchomp's Attack by 2 stages (neutering its primary weapon for the Palafin sweep), and leaves Aegislash alive to act next turn. Milotic's follow-up hit (Muddy Water ~14–21% or Icy Wind ~2.6–4.5%) is survivable. Toxapex is fainted so only Pass is available.
Earthquake guarantees the KO if Aegislash’s reduced-success King’s Shield fails; Recover is the only available partner action with any potential value.

King's Shield is the only play that can negate Garchomp's super-effective Earthquake while also dropping its Attack by 2 stages. Even with the reduced Protect success rate, the upside—surviving this turn and making Garchomp's Earthquake trivial next turn—is far better than any attacking move, which would let Earthquake hit unopposed and likely OHKO Aegislash at 37%. Toxapex is fainted so Pass is forced.
Earthquake is a guaranteed KO if King's Shield fails; its repeated use has sharply reduced success.

reflections.summary: Aegislash ran out of King's Shield PP (all 8 uses exhausted by Turn 12), leaving it unable to block Garchomp's super-effective Earthquake and resulting in a fatal OHKO. The team preview also proved suboptimal—Palafin and Talonflame were both eliminated early by the opponent's Mega Floette and Garchomp pressure, forcing Aegislash into a frontline role from Turn 4 onward and accelerating its PP drain.
reflections.adjustment: Slot Aegislash into the starting four instead of one of the early-game fainted Pokémon (e.g., replace Talonflame) so King's Shield PP is preserved from the outset against Garchomp. This gives Aegislash more staying power to neuter Garchomp's Attack and survive to clean.

reflections.summary: Won by neutralizing Mimikyu with Talonflame's Taunt, trading efficiently through Palafin, then using Mega Floette/Milotic pressure to establish Garchomp as the endgame win condition. The four brought suited the matchup, and Mega Floette was the correct evolution for immediate Fairy Aura-boosted Palafin pressure, though its early critical-hit KO reduced its value. Piloting was clean; Garchomp correctly kept attacking once Aegislash's repeated King's Shield attempts became unreliable.
reflections.adjustment: Next game, preserve Mega Floette more carefully after it removes or heavily damages Palafin—use Protect or position Talonflame/Garchomp to deter Mimikyu's Play Rough rather than accepting a direct follow-up. This retains stronger endgame coverage against the opponent's Dark-/Dragon-vulnerable targets and reduces reliance on a low-HP Garchomp cleanup.

decisions.rationale: Lead Mimikyu (Disguise free hit, Fairy coverage vs Floette, offensive pressure) and Aegislash (conserve King's Shield PP per notebook, scout/stall Garchomp Earthquake). Bench Toxapex (Water resists Ground, primary Garchomp and Milotic check, Regenerator, Toxic support) and Skarmory (Ground immunity hard-counters Garchomp, Tailwind speed control, Spikes chip damage, Roost longevity).

Repeat the successful Talonflame + Garchomp lead for immediate Tailwind/Taunt pressure and strong Ground damage into the opponent's known four. Preserve Milotic as a bulky midgame stabilizer and Mega Floette-Eternal as the key Palafin answer.

Aegislash uses King's Shield to protect against Garchomp's Earthquake (and any Talonflame move targeting it), dropping the attacker's Attack by 2. Mimikyu uses Play Rough on Garchomp for super-effective damage; Disguise will absorb whichever foe attacks Mimikyu first (likely Talonflame's Brave Bird or Garchomp's Earthquake), letting Mimikyu retaliate cleanly. This pressures the primary win condition while conserving Aegislash's KS PP and leveraging Disguise's free hit.
Priority Taunt denies Mimikyu’s Swords Dance while Earthquake breaks Disguise and heavily pressures Aegislash; Talonflame is immune to the spread damage.

Mimikyu is Taunted so must attack; Play Rough into Garchomp at 5% HP secures a KO on the biggest physical threat. Aegislash uses King's Shield to block Talonflame's likely Gale Wings Brave Bird/Flare Blitz while cutting its Attack, preserving Aegislash's bulk and KS PP for future turns.
Use priority Brave Bird for the immediate chance to remove the taunted Mimikyu while preserving Garchomp by pivoting into the much sturdier Milotic.

Mimikyu-Busted at 14% with broken Disguise is too frail to attack; switching to Toxapex brings in a Regenerator pivot that absorbs incoming spread damage and sustains against the hyper-offensive foe core. Aegislash uses King's Shield to completely avoid damage from both Talonflame and Milotic while dropping their offensive stats, conserving its own HP and KS PP for future Garchomp checks.
Set Tailwind while Muddy Water can remove the weakened Mimikyu and pressure Aegislash; Tailwind improves the next-turn matchup against the opponent’s unrevealed back line.

Talonflame is the most dangerous active threat with Gale Wings priority Brave Bird/Flare Blitz and Tailwind speed doubling. Toxapex uses Liquidation super-effectively into Talonflame to apply maximum damage on the primary win condition. Aegislash uses King's Shield at +4 priority to block the expected Flare Blitz (which is super-effective against Aegislash), protecting itself and dropping Talonflame's Attack stage, which reduces the damage from any follow-up Brave Bird or Flare Blitz.
Exploit Aegislash's reduced consecutive King's Shield success rate: Flare Blitz plus Muddy Water gives the best chance to remove it immediately while still chipping Toxapex.
Bring in healthy Floette-Eternal to preserve Garchomp only if its priority Ground pressure can still matter later; Milotic has no selectable action this turn.

Floette-Eternal is the primary win condition with 100% HP and Fairy STAB threatening both active Pokémon. Aegislash's Shadow Sneak (priority +1) fires before Tailwind-boosted foes and chips Floette before it can act. Toxapex's Toxic applies badly poison for escalating damage across subsequent turns, pressuring the biggest threat while Aegislash is too frail at 8% HP to trade hits.

Aegislash fainted so slot b needs a replacement. Skarmory at full HP walls Milotic's entire movepool (Muddy Water, Icy Wind, Recover, Haze are all neutral or ineffective on Steel/Flying), can heal via Roost, and preserves Mimikyu-Busted's low 14% HP for a later threat. Toxapex should pass to stay on the field and continue pressuring the toxed Floette-Mega and 5% Garchomp.
Mega Evolve and focus Energy Ball pressure into Toxapex while Muddy Water covers both foes; Muddy Water KOs Aegislash if King’s Shield is not used.

Toxapex at 54% HP is the primary wall and should heal with Recover to maximize its longevity—it resists both Floette-Mega and Milotic's STAB moves, so staying in is safe. Skarmory should apply pressure to the biggest remaining threat, Floette-Mega, with Brave Bird; even neutral damage helps chip down the Mega Fairy that is already at 82% with toxic status. The opponent's Tailwind expires after this turn, and both their active attackers hit our team for neutral or worse, so playing for damage and longevity is optimal.
Use the final Tailwind turn to double Toxapex before it can Recover; Energy Ball plus Muddy Water gives the best immediate chance to remove it and prevent its recovery cycle.

Toxapex applies Toxic to Milotic to wear down the bulky 100% HP threat over subsequent turns, while Skarmory uses Brave Bird to attempt a KO on the 11%-HP toxed Floette-Mega. Even if Floette-Mega Protects, Milotic is already pressured by Toxic, and Floette-Mega will likely succumb to poison next turn. Both of Floette-Mega's STAB moves (Moonblast, Energy Ball) are heavily resisted by our typing, reducing the risk of leaving Skarmory in.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.
Moonblast plus Muddy Water gives the strongest line to remove Skarmory immediately and deny Tailwind; Floette is unlikely to survive its toxic timer regardless.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Toxapex's Liquidation targets Milotic (the primary long-term threat and bulky pivot) despite the neutral-bonus reduction, applying crucial chip alongside Toxic status already active. Mimikyu-Busted's Play Rough targets Garchomp for a super-effective hit that should finish it at 5% HP, removing the opponent's main offensive threat and Earthquake spread pressure.
Earthquake gives the only meaningful chance to remove Toxapex before it can resume Recover cycles, while Muddy Water reliably KOs the low-health Mimikyu if it connects.

reflections.summary: Lost 0-2 in the series. Game 2 was lost due to a compounding chain of setbacks: Mimikyu's Play Rough missing Milotic on Turn 2 was the first critical swing, leaving the team without an early KO on the opponent's primary bulky pivot. The burn on Aegislash from Talonflame's Flare Blitz (Turn 4) gutted the King's Shield stall strategy that was the defensive backbone against Garchomp's Earthquake PP break. Aegislash lasted only one more turn after burning. Milotic proved to be the true linchpin of the opponent's team — its Toxic crippled every switch-in, Recover kept it healthy, and it survived the entire game to clean with a final Muddy Water. Mega Floette underperformed as a threat; it was Toxic'd early, took heavy Brave Bird chip from Skarmory, and contributed limited damage before fainting. Toxapex was the MVP with Recover and Toxic but eventually ran out of recovery against stacked chip. In the final turn, Garchomp's Earthquake broke through Toxapex and Mimikyu, and Milotic mopped up. No between-game adjustments meaningfully backfired, but the inability to punish Milotic or preserve Aegislash's longevity were the decisive failures.
reflections.adjustment: For a rematch: (1) Bring Swampert over one of the current six — it is immune to Earthquake and resists Water, making it the ideal Milotic and Garchomp answer while providing its own Ground STAB pressure. (2) Prepare a sun setter (Torkoal) to cripple Milotic's recovery and shift momentum; sun also powers up Meowscarada as a potential surprise offensive pivot. (3) Prioritize removing Milotic early and relentlessly — it is the opponent's true win condition enabler. (4) Avoid relying on Aegislash as the sole King's Shield staller against Garchomp without a burn-proof backup; consider holding a status absorber or pivoting faster. (5) Do not Mega Evolve Floette early if Toxic is on the field — Mega Floette's longevity is overstated and it becomes set-up fodder.

reflections.summary: Won game 2 and the series 2-0 through a well-suited four of Talonflame, Garchomp, Milotic, and Mega Floette. Talonflame's turn-1 Taunt denied Mimikyu's Swords Dance option, while Garchomp's Earthquake broke Disguise and created immediate spread pressure. Although Garchomp was left at 6%, Talonflame and Milotic established the tempo needed for Mega Floette's Energy Ball pressure on Toxapex and Talonflame's Flare Blitz damage on Aegislash. The decisive endgame was using Garchomp's final Earthquake to remove Mimikyu and leave Toxapex in Muddy Water range. Mega Floette was the appropriate evolution: Fairy Aura-boosted Fairy damage and Energy Ball gave the brought four both offensive coverage and a direct Toxapex answer. Milotic was valuable for sustained spread pressure, Tailwind support enabled the midgame, and the lead matched well into Mimikyu/Aegislash. The full registered six fit reasonably well, but the supplied evidence does not establish that an unused member offered a materially better game-2 alternative. There is no game-1 record or stated between-game change, so whether any explicit adjustment helped or backfired cannot be determined; game 2 itself was piloted without recorded decision errors. The 2-0 series result is authoritative.
reflections.adjustment: For a future series, retain the Talonflame/Garchomp/Milotic/Mega Floette core when expecting Mimikyu, Aegislash, and Toxapex. Continue using early Taunt and spread damage to constrain Mimikyu, but preserve Garchomp more carefully when possible because it is an excellent late-game Earthquake closer against the revealed structure. Against Toxapex, commit simultaneous pressure from Mega Floette's Energy Ball plus a second attack rather than relying on Milotic's Muddy Water alone, which allowed Recover opportunities and can miss. Plan for Toxic attrition on both bulky attackers and avoid treating a low-health Toxapex as secured until it is covered through Recover. No roster substitution is supported by the evidence alone; reconsider unused options only if future preview information shows a specific matchup need.

decisions.rationale: Bring Pelipper for Drizzle rain setup, Swampert (holding Swampertite to Mega Evolve) to gain Swift Swim in rain and punch holes with Waterfall/Earthquake, Basculegion in the back as a fast cleaner with Choice Scarf/Adaptability Water/Ghost attacks, and Whimsicott in the back for priority Tailwind or speed control. Opponent brings Sneasler, Archaludon, Altaria, Mamoswine, Sinistcha, Dedenne; rain sweepers handle Mamoswine, Sneasler, Archaludon well while Pelipper + Swampert pressure the board immediately.

Lead Altaria and Sneasler to suppress rain, establish Tailwind, and use Sneasler’s superior Speed and Fake Out to disrupt Whimsicott or another setup lead. Archaludon and Mamoswine provide strong follow-up pressure into the opponent’s Water core and benefit greatly from Tailwind.
Protect on Swampert and switch Pelipper to Whimsicott dodges Sneasler's Fake Out on Swampert while setting up safe positioning.
Set Tailwind while Sneasler uses Fake Out on Pelipper to prevent its Tailwind or Hurricane this turn, establishing speed control and preserving the team’s Water answers.

Altaria's Cloud Nine ignores rain, and under Tailwind the opponent has two fast offensive threats. Both Pelipper and Swampert used Protect last turn, so switching out is optimal. Switching Pelipper to Basculegion and Swampert to Whimsicott brings in two distinct Pokémon to disrupt the opponent's Tailwind and regain initiative.

Helping Hand boosts Sneasler's faster Close Combat into Swampert, maximizing the chance to remove the major Water/Ground threat before it can act while retaining Altaria's Cloud Nine and Tailwind utility.

Sneasler is under Tailwind and faster than Choice Scarf Basculegion, but it used Close Combat last turn (-1 Def, -1 SpD). Basculegion's Wave Crash on Sneasler is a guaranteed OHKO. Meanwhile, Whimsicott is at 21% HP and uses Protect to shield itself from any incoming attacks from Sneasler or Altaria while Basculegion picks up the knockout on Sneasler.

Target Whimsicott with Altaria's Moonblast while Sneasler uses Quick Guard to block Prankster Encore and other priority disruption. This preserves the anti-Whimsicott plan and avoids letting Sneasler be locked into ineffective Close Combat against Basculegion.

Keep Altaria in to maintain Cloud Nine and Tailwind pressure; switch Sneasler to Archaludon, which better handles the revealed Fairy and Water-heavy threats while preserving Mamoswine as a later answer.

Basculegion is Choice-locked into Wave Crash and hits Archaludon (Altaria resists Water), while Whimsicott sets up Tailwind on the turn the opponent's Tailwind expires to regain speed control next turn.
Basculegion is choice-locked into Wave Crash, and Swampert enters under Rain with Tailwind active to threaten both Altaria and Archaludon effectively.

Refresh Tailwind while Archaludon uses Flash Cannon to guarantee the KO on Whimsicott; preserving speed control is more valuable than marginal damage into Basculegion, and Helping Hand is unnecessary for the KO.

Basculegion is Choice-locked into Wave Crash and hits Archaludon (or Altaria). Swampert Mega Evolves and uses Ice Punch into Altaria (which is 4x super effective and KOs through Altaria's Focus Sash since Basculegion's Wave Crash can chip Archaludon or Altaria, or Swampert can pick up KOs cleanly under Tailwind). Wait, let's verify Ice Punch into Altaria vs Archaludon. Altaria is 4x weak to Ice Punch. Archaludon is 71% and resists Wave Crash, but Swampert's Ice Punch into Altaria or Archaludon? Altaria is an active threat with Tailwind/Helping Hand/Moonblast. Let's make sure Swampert uses Ice Punch into Altaria (+ Mega Evolve), option 11 is Ice Punch -> foe 2 (Archaludon) + Mega Evolve, option 9 is Ice Punch -> foe 1 (Altaria) + Mega Evolve. Wait, let's check index 9: Ice Punch -> foe 1 (Altaria) + Mega Evolve. Basculegion uses Wave Crash into foe 2 (Archaludon) (index 1).
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Helping Hand boosts Archaludon's Thunderbolt enough to guarantee the KO on Basculegion despite its faster Wave Crash, while Altaria's Focus Sash preserves it against Swampert's Ice Punch. Removing the Choice Scarf threat lets Altaria establish Tailwind next turn.

Archaludon is at 18% HP and can be finished off by Swampert's Earthquake or Pelipper's Hurricane. Earthquake also damages Altaria heavily, while Hurricane hits Archaludon or Altaria. Swampert outspeeds both opponents under Tailwind and Swift Swim, making Earthquake a devastating spread move that picks up the KO on Archaludon and heavily damages Altaria, while Pelipper can use Hurricane into Archaludon to guarantee its KO through any defensive options.
Protect both to preserve the two remaining Pokémon through the immediate Mega Swampert threat, then establish Tailwind and attack once the opposing Tailwind expires.

Archaludon is at 18% HP and weak to Ground, so Swampert-Mega's Earthquake will easily KO it (and hit Altaria). Pelipper can use Hydro Pump into Archaludon just in case, or finish off Archaludon with Hydro Pump while Earthquake cleans up. Let's use Hydro Pump into Archaludon and Earthquake together to guarantee the double KO or finish off Archaludon through any positioning.
Set Tailwind while Archaludon Protects, preserving it from Mega Swampert's Earthquake and creating the speed-control advantage after the opposing Tailwind and rain expire.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Pelipper uses Hurricane on Mamoswine to deal heavy special damage under rain, while Mega Swampert uses Ice Punch on Altaria to OHKO it with 4x super-effective damage, breaking through its Focus Sash or threatening a KO while bypassing Pelipper's immunity.

Helping Hand boosts Mamoswine's Freeze-Dry to reliably KO Pelipper before it can threaten Mamoswine with rain-boosted Hydro Pump, while preserving Tailwind speed control and leaving Swampert to be handled afterward.

Pelipper is fainted so it must pass. Swampert-Mega is alone against Altaria (at 77% with Focus Sash) and Mamoswine (at 61% with Expert Belt). Mamoswine is weak to Ice Punch and Waterfall, but Ice Punch on Mamoswine deals solid damage or takes it down, while Altaria can be threatened next turn or is immune to Earthquake. Wait, Altaria is immune to Ground and has Focus Sash. Let's check Mamoswine vs Swampert-Mega: Mamoswine has Freeze-Dry which is super-effective against Swampert-Mega. Protect protects Swampert-Mega from Mamoswine's attacks and Altaria's Helping Hand, but Mamoswine used Freeze-Dry last turn and has Icicle Crash / High Horsepower. However, Ice Punch on Mamoswine directly threatens Mamoswine, or Protect stalls out Tailwind (which has 2 turns left, now down to 1 after turn 9). Let's check Ice Punch into Mamoswine (choice 4).
Helping Hand boosts Mamoswine's Freeze-Dry, giving the best chance to KO Mega Swampert while preserving Altaria's Cloud Nine and Tailwind speed control.

reflections.summary: The opponent neutralized our rain strategy using Altaria's Cloud Nine ability to suppress weather-dependent speed advantages and outmaneuvered our offensive pressure with timely Protects, Helping Hand bursts, and Mamoswine's Freeze-Dry.
reflections.adjustment: Bring Basculegion and Whimsicott back while aggressively targeting or positioning around Altaria's Cloud Nine and Cloud Nine interaction before committing to weather-reliant sweepers.

reflections.summary: Won because the brought four matched the matchup: Altaria supplied Cloud Nine, Tailwind, and Helping Hand while Mamoswine converted that support into decisive super-effective Freeze-Dry damage against Pelipper and Mega Swampert. Sneasler and Archaludon also pressured the opponent's support core. No own Mega Stone holder was evolved; that was appropriate because none was needed, while the opponent's Mega Swampert was the key target.
reflections.adjustment: Next game, preserve Mamoswine from opposing Ice Punch pressure and bring it in safely so Helping Hand-boosted Freeze-Dry can immediately remove Pelipper or Mega Swampert; avoid exposing it before that endgame conversion.

decisions.rationale: Pelipper sets Drizzle for Swampert and Basculegion. Swampert mega evolves and benefits from rain (Swift Swim). Basculegion is a strong Swift Swim abuser or fast cleaner. Whimsicott provides Tailwind or speed control support from the back.

Altaria and Mamoswine immediately suppress rain, establish Tailwind, and threaten Pelipper or Swampert with Helping Hand-boosted Freeze-Dry. Archaludon provides a durable special attacker in back, while Sneasler adds fast Fake Out pressure against Whimsicott and other threats.
Protecting Pelipper while Mega-Evolving Swampert and using Ice Punch into Mamoswine (or handling Altaria) lets us weather Altaria's Cloud Nine turn safely while gaining offensive momentum.
Helping Hand-boosted Freeze-Dry guarantees a KO on Pelipper before it can establish Tailwind, while preserving Altaria's Cloud Nine and removing the opponent's rain enabler.

Swampert-Mega outspeeds both foes under Swift Swim and cleanly KOes Mamoswine with Waterfall. Pelipper uses Tailwind to secure long-term speed control against potential backline threats like Sneasler.
Pelipper fainted and must be replaced; sending in Basculegion under rain maximizes offensive pressure against the remaining backline. Swampert-Mega passes its action while the replacement happens.

Helping Hand-boosted Freeze-Dry guarantees the removal of Pelipper if it does not Protect, while preserving Altaria and Cloud Nine. Mamoswine survives another revealed Ice Punch from Mega Swampert, and eliminating the rain setter is the priority.
Keep Altaria active to preserve Cloud Nine and use Sneasler's speed and Fake Out pressure against the incoming replacement while threatening Swampert.

Basculegion uses Last Respects on Sneasler (since Last Respects has 150 base power after Pelipper fainted, and Sneasler takes massive damage or faints). Swampert-Mega uses Waterfall on Sneasler to secure a KO, or we can look at damage: Sneasler is weak to Ground, but Altaria is immune to Earthquake and Sneasler is a major threat with Close Combat/Dire Claw. Wait, Swampert-Mega's Waterfall into Sneasler (choice 2) hits Sneasler hard in rain. Let's check Last Respects into Sneasler (choice 1) and Waterfall into Sneasler (choice 2). Sneasler is weak to nothing from Waterfall, but it's hit neutrally. Wait, Sneasler is Fighting/Poison (weak to Psychic, Flying, Ground). Swampert's Earthquake hits Sneasler super-effectively (2x), but Earthquake hits adjacent ally Basculegion too. Swampert's Waterfall into Sneasler is neutral. However, Basculegion's Last Respects on Sneasler (choice 1) does massive damage. Let's make sure Basculegion targets Sneasler with Last Respects (1) and Swampert targets Sneasler with Waterfall (2) or Protect (7). Wait, Sneasler might use Quick Guard or Protect. But Swampert's Waterfall is contact. Let's check Sneasler's moves: Fake Out, Close Combat, Quick Guard, Dire Claw. If Sneasler uses Quick Guard, it blocks priority (Aqua Jet), but Last Respects and Waterfall are standard priority 0 moves, not blocked by Quick Guard. Thus Basculegion's Last Respects and Swampert's Waterfall will hit Sneasler through Quick Guard. Therefore, Basculegion Last Respects -> foe 2 (Sneasler) [index 1] and Swampert-Mega Waterfall -> foe 2 (Sneasler) [index 2].
Fake Out Swampert-Mega to deny its super-effective Ice Punch and preserve Altaria; Altaria uses Moonblast into Basculegion for safe damage while Basculegion's Water attacks are resisted.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Basculegion is Choice-locked into Last Respects, which hits Altaria hard or Archaludon neutrally. Swampert-Mega can use Ice Punch on Altaria for a massive super-effective hit (Altaria is 4x weak to Ice) or Protect if needed, but Ice Punch on Altaria removes their Dragon/Flying type threat cleanly while Last Respects hits Archaludon or Altaria.

Protect Altaria to block both Basculegion's locked Last Respects and Mega Swampert's lethal Ice Punch, while Archaludon targets Basculegion with super-effective Thunderbolt for the best chance to remove it.

Basculegion is at 5% HP and locked into Last Respects, which is ineffective against Altaria and resisted/ineffective elsewhere or blocked. Switching Basculegion to Whimsicott brings in Prankster Tailwind / support while keeping Swampert safe to use Earthquake, hitting Archaludon super-effectively and bypassing Altaria's immunity safely.
Protect Altaria to preserve it from the fast, Choice-locked Last Respects while Archaludon uses Thunderbolt to remove Basculegion before it can threaten the team further.

Whimsicott uses Moonblast on Altaria while Mega Swampert uses Earthquake to KO Archaludon through Sturdy (since Archaludon is at 30% HP and Earthquake guarantees a KO) and deal heavy damage to Altaria.

Protect Archaludon from Mega Swampert's guaranteed KO while Altaria chips Swampert and preserves both Pokémon. This also limits Whimsicott's Encore value: if it locks Archaludon, the current Protect still blocks Earthquake and Altaria can target Whimsicott next turn.

Whimsicott uses Protect to shield itself from potential attacks while Swampert-Mega uses Ice Punch on Altaria (foe 1) to secure a super-effective knockout on Altaria's low 31% HP. Archaludon used Protect last turn, so it cannot protect consecutively.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Altaria targets the weakened Mega Swampert with Moonblast while Archaludon removes Whimsicott with super-effective Flash Cannon. This secures both KOs despite Swampert's faster Earthquake, since Altaria is immune to it.

Whimsicott outspeeds and OHKOs Altaria with Moonblast (2x super-effective), while Basculegion outspeeds both opponents with Choice Scarf and can KO Altaria with Last Respects. Targeting Altaria with both secures the KO through its Focus Sash or avoids any disruption.

Protect Altaria from Whimsicott's guaranteed-KO Moonblast while Archaludon uses Thunderbolt to remove the dangerous Choice Scarf Basculegion. Basculegion's Aqua Jet is also blocked, and Whimsicott's priority Encore cannot prevent Altaria's higher-priority Protect.

Altaria protected last turn and its Protect success rate is reduced, but more importantly, Altaria is at 31% HP and Whimsicott outspeeds. Moonblast into Altaria (foe 1) guarantees a KO through any remaining focus sash or HP, and Basculegion is fainted so it passes.
Double-target Whimsicott with Moonblast and super-effective Flash Cannon to remove the remaining fast support threat immediately.

reflections.summary: We lost the series 0-2 because our rain offense cores were systematically neutralized by the opponent's defensive positioning (Cloud Nine Altaria, Sturdy Archaludon, and Protect cycling) and specialized coverage like Freeze-Dry Mamoswine. Pelipper and Mega Swampert fell too early to pressure, and choice-locked Basculegion was walled by smart Protect timing and Archaludon's typing.
reflections.adjustment: Against this opponent's defensive utility and Sturdy/Protect pivoting, we should bring Primarina or Feraligatr for better alternative offensive angles instead of doubling down on straightforward weather setups that get exploited by Cloud Nine and defensive Dragon types.

reflections.summary: Won game 2 and the series 2-0 through a strong matchup plan and clean piloting. Altaria's Cloud Nine removed Pelipper's rain advantage, Mamoswine's Freeze-Dry immediately threatened the Water core, and Archaludon efficiently finished Basculegion and Whimsicott with super-effective attacks. Protect cycling preserved Altaria long enough to deny Basculegion's Choice-locked Last Respects while poison and Moonblast wore down Mega Swampert. The brought four—Altaria, Mamoswine, Sneasler, and Archaludon—were well suited to the preview; Sneasler's Fake Out created useful tempo even though it was traded for Basculegion's attack. No Mega evolution was used, and that was appropriate: retaining Cloud Nine and the Focus Sash/utility set mattered more than introducing an unsupported Mega option. There were no decision errors, and no supplied evidence identifies a specific between-game adjustment, so its effect cannot be credited or blamed; the demonstrated plan itself worked. The registered six fit reasonably well, with coherent anti-rain, anti-Water, speed-control, disruption, and coverage tools. The remaining roster did not show a materially better alternative than the selected four.
reflections.adjustment: Against a future rematch, keep the same core plan and likely the same four, but make Whimsicott a higher-priority target before it can repeatedly use Prankster Tailwind, Encore, or Moonblast. Preserve Altaria when possible, while avoiding overcommitting it to repeated Protect cycles if Whimsicott remains free to pressure it. Maintain dedicated answers to Mega Swampert and Basculegion: Cloud Nine plus Freeze-Dry remains excellent, and Archaludon's Electric and Steel coverage is valuable. No Mega holder needs to be added based on this evidence; do not replace Altaria's Cloud Nine role merely to Mega Evolve.
