Toxic Spikes up on P1's side

decisions.rationale: Rotom-Wash + Dragapult lead: Rotom threatens Palafin with 2x Thunderbolt (67-131% range), Dragapult outspeeds entire roster and pressures Meowscarada (Draco Meteor 72-140%) and Mimikyu (2x Shadow Ball). Back Incineroar provides Intimidate cycling + Fake Out to break Mimikyu's Disguise and neuter physical threats; Mega Metagross offers Tough Claws Bullet Punch priority for cleaning. This core handles the expected Palafin/Mimikyu/Meowscarada/Glimmora bring with speed control and type coverage.

Lead Palafin and Mimikyu as the designated sweeper pair to apply immediate offensive pressure on Dragapult and Incineroar; Mimikyu's Disguise+Focus Sash guarantees a safe setup or hit. Back Glimmora for Stealth Rock/Spikes hazard attrition and Toxic Debris passive damage, and Meowscarada as the fastest Pokémon (192 Spe) for guaranteed revenge-killing with Protean-boosted STAB moves.

Dragapult faces a possible OHKO from Mimikyu Play Rough (71-112%) and heavy chip from Palafin Ice Beam. Protecting Dragapult wastes both of their turns if they double into it. Rotom-Wash Thunderbolt into Palafin deals 67-131%, threatening a KO and forcing Palafin to either take heavy damage or Flip Turn out. This preserves my speed control and Life Orb attacker while pressuring their Water-type.

Mimikyu uses Swords Dance safely behind Focus Sash and Disguise, guaranteeing a free setup boost against likely Dragapult aggression. Palafin targets Rotom-Wash with Close Combat for neutral damage, as Close Combat is completely blocked by Dragapult's Ghost typing. This pairing maximizes Mimikyu's threat for Turn 2 while applying immediate pressure on the less-dangerous foe.

Switch Palafin out to Glimmora to set up Stealth Rock immediately, applying hazard pressure that punishes the opponent's expected switches (especially after Mega Metagross and Dragapult). Glimmora's Rock/Poison typing handles Rotom-Wash's Water moves well and resists Dragapult's Ghost attacks; Toxic Debris will punish Rotom-Wash's special moves. Mimikyu passes because it already has +2 Attack under Disguise and is well positioned to threaten a KO on a future turn with Play Rough or Shadow Sneak once hazards are established.

Switch Dragapult to Incineroar for Intimidate (Mimikyu +2→+1, Glimmora -1 cured by Lum). Rotom Volt Switches into Glimmora for chip and pivots to Metagross, preserving both leads and setting up Metagross+Incineroar. Metagross resists Play Rough; Incineroar resists Shadow Sneak. Next turn Mega Evolve Metagross, Bullet Punch breaks Disguise, and Incineroar pressures with Flare Blitz or Parting Shot. Dragapult is preserved as a fast cleaner.

Switching to Dragapult risks an instant OHKO from Mimikyu's +1 Play Rough (108–165%). Metagross resists Play Rough (18–27%) and can Mega Evolve for better bulk. Incineroar can Fake Out Glimmora to deny Earth Power, leaving only Mimikyu's attack into a resistant Metagross. Dragapult is preserved as a fast cleaner without SR chip for later.

Glimmora sets Stealth Rock to apply critical early-game hazard pressure on all foe switch-ins. Mimikyu uses Play Rough into Dragapult, which is super-effective (2x Fairy) and benefits from the +2 Attack boost while Disguise keeps Mimikyu safe this turn, heavily damaging the series' top threat.

Meteor Mash from Mega Metagross guarantees the KO on Glimmora (78.9-141.8% pre-Tough Claws, even higher with Tough Claws). After Mega Evolving, Metagross hits 162 Speed, always outspeeding Glimmora (116-151), so Glimmora never moves. Incineroar Protects to avoid the likely Play Rough KO from Mimikyu. Metagross takes at most one Shadow Ball from Mimikyu (32.3-58.1%), surviving comfortably from 94%. This removes the hazard setter and preserves both Pokémon for the 2v1 against Mimikyu next turn.

Both active Pokémon target Metagross, the most dangerous remaining threat capable of Mega Evolution. Glimmora's Earth Power is super-effective (2×) and unaffected by its Attack drop since it's special. Mimikyu's Shadow Sneak is super-effective (2×) with priority +1 and boosted by its +1 Attack. Eliminating Metagross before it can Mega Evolve or fire off high-damage moves is the highest-value play.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Metagross Protects to blank the likely Dark Pulse from Meowscarada, which otherwise has a chance to OHKO (52.9–85.2% into 55%). Incineroar uses Parting Shot on Meowscarada; Meowscarada always outspeeds Incineroar, so Brick Break could KO first (40.6–59.4% into 43%), but if the opponent targets Metagross with Dark Pulse or if Brick Break rolls low, Parting Shot connects, dropping Meowscarada's Atk/SpA by 1 and pivoting to Rotom-Wash. Rotom-Wash takes only Stealth Rock (12.5%) thanks to Levitate avoiding Toxic Spikes. Even if Incineroar is KO'd, Metagross is preserved and Rotom-Wash enters safely.

Incineroar's Parting Shot forces a switch. Rotom-Wash is the clear choice: immune to Toxic Spikes via Levitate, resists Meowscarada's Dark Pulse (12–31%), and survives +1 Play Rough (34–82%) with Sitrus Berry recovery. Dragapult is OHKO'd by +1 Play Rough and takes 49–72% from Dark Pulse — far too risky. Metagross-Mega stays in to break Mimikyu's Disguise with Bullet Punch next turn; it survives one +1 Shadow Sneak (31–47%) from 55% HP.

Both Pokémon focus-fire on Metagross-Mega, the biggest remaining threat at 55% HP. Mimikyu's Shadow Sneak (priority +1, Ghost STAB 2x vs Steel/Psychic) strikes first; Metagross-Mega's only faster response is Bullet Punch (also priority +1), but Mimikyu's intact Disguise absorbs it for zero damage. Meowscarada's Dark Pulse (special, 2x vs Psychic) follows at priority 0, giving Metagross-Mega two super-effective hits in one turn and a high probability of KO. Incineroar at 43% is manageable next turn after the primary threat is removed.

Bullet Punch breaks Mimikyu's Disguise at +1 priority regardless of speed ties with Shadow Sneak. Rotom Protect (+4) shields it from Energy Ball and Play Rough, both of which can OHKO or nearly OHKO Rotom. If both foes target Metagross, Dark Pulse + Shadow Sneak deals 68.4–103.9% — Metagross may fall, but that lets Incineroar enter freely with Intimidate. If they split or target Rotom, Metagross survives and Disguise is still broken. Either way we remove Disguise and preserve Rotom, setting up a strong next turn.

Meowscarada's Dark Pulse is 2x super-effective against Metagross-Mega (24.6–46.5% damage) and makes Meowscarada Dark-typed via Protean, immunizing it to Metagross-Mega's Zen Headbutt. Mimikyu's Play Rough targets Rotom-Wash for a possible KO (43.9–81.6% damage vs 67% HP, ~61% KO probability with +1 Atk). Spreading damage across both active foes maximizes immediate pressure and expected value rather than stacking on Metagross-Mega where neither hit alone can KO and the combined KO is not guaranteed.

Metagross at 17% dies to any attack; switching it to Incineroar triggers Intimidate (Meowscarada → -2 Atk, Mimikyu → 0 Atk), absorbs Stealth Rock + Toxic Spikes poison which Lum Berry immediately cures. Rotom switches to Dragapult, taking only Stealth Rock. Both switches resolve before moves, so the opponent's likely Shadow Sneak → Metagross slot hits Incineroar for negligible damage (Dark resists Ghost) and Flower Trick → Rotom slot hits Dragapult for minimal damage (Dragon resists Grass, -2 Atk). This preserves both weakened Pokémon, neutralises Mimikyu's Attack boost, and brings Dragapult safely onto the field.

Mimikyu-Busted Shadow Sneak (priority +1, Ghost super-effective vs Psychic) guarantees KO on 16% Metagross-Mega before it can act. Meowscarada Flower Trick (Grass Physical, super-effective vs Water) targets Rotom-Wash at 67% HP for a possible KO (estimated 41-81% damage). This dual-target strategy can eliminate both active foes in one turn, dramatically shifting the 2v4 board state. Even if Protect blocks one hit, at minimum the faster Shadow Sneak removes the biggest remaining threat.

Incineroar cannot Fake Out (not first turn out). Protect forces Mimikyu's Shadow Sneak onto Dragapult; Dragapult survives the 33–51% roll more often than not, then outspeeds Meowscarada and fires Shadow Ball into Mimikyu for 72–132% — a strong chance to KO the Sash-broken Mimikyu before Meowscarada's Dark Pulse lands. This maximises Dragapult's impact before it falls.

Bullet Punch (priority +1) always goes first, dealing 28.4–55.6%. If Meowscarada targets Metagross with any move, Incineroar survives and Flare Blitz adds 83.1–160.3%; the combined minimum 111.5% guarantees the KO and wins the game. Only Brick Break onto Incineroar prevents Flare Blitz, but that line loses for us regardless of which teammate we send. Sending Metagross punishes every other opponent move choice and gives a slim chance (two high-roll Bullet Punches) even if they Brick Break Incineroar. Forfeiting is premature while a win condition exists.

Play Rough guarantees KO on Dragapult (59.5-111.7% damage on 51% HP target across all legal IVs/EVs). Dark Pulse adds 30.8-57.7% super-effective damage to the same target. Even if Dragapult uses Protect (priority +4 goes first), both moves are blocked but we lose nothing—Protect PP is limited and Incineroar at 5% cannot threaten our position. If Dragapult doesn't Protect, Dragapult is KO'd and we have a winning 2v1 against the 5% Incineroar.

Bullet Punch always goes first due to +1 priority. If opponent targets Metagross with Dark Pulse, Incineroar survives and Flare Blitz lands; combined minimum 111.5% guarantees KO. If opponent Brick Breaks Incineroar, Incineroar faints before moving and we lose, but this is our only win condition — switching Incineroar to Rotom sacrifices Flare Blitz and leaves us unable to OHKO Meowscarada across multiple turns. We must hope opponent chooses Dark Pulse on Metagross over the safer Brick Break on Incineroar.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Brick Break into Incineroar guarantees a KO (5% HP, 2x super-effective, STAB via Protean, even at -2 Atk). After removing Incineroar and its Fake Out priority threat, Meowscarada outspeeds Metagross-Mega (192 vs 130-162) and Dark Pulse cleanly KO's it at 10% HP (guaranteed 24.6-46.5% damage). Mimikyu-Busted is already fainted, so the only legal action is Pass.

Bullet Punch has +1 priority and always goes first, dealing 28.4–55.6% to 49% HP Meowscarada with a chance to OHKO. Thunderbolt adds 20.2–38.4%; combined minimum 48.6% leaves Meowscarada at 0.4% only on double-minimum rolls. In that edge case, Meowscarada KOs one ally next turn but the other finishes it. Any other roll combination KOs outright. Opponent's best response (Dark Pulse into Metagross) is irrelevant if Bullet Punch KOs, and if it doesn't, Thunderbolt cleans up after Metagross falls. Thunderbolt's 100% accuracy avoids Hydro Pump's miss risk.

Dark Pulse into Metagross-Mega secures the KO on the 10%-HP Steel/Psychic target with super-effective damage and Protean STAB. This leaves a favorable 1v1 against Rotom-Wash, whose moves are resisted 0.5x by Meowscarada while my Grass coverage (Energy Ball/Flower Trick) is super-effective with STAB. Mimikyu is fainted and can only pass.

reflections.summary: Early KO on Palafin with Rotom-Wash's Thunderbolt gave a 4-3 lead. Effective use of Protect and pivoting maintained momentum, while Stealth Rock and Toxic Spikes chipped the opponent. Priority Bullet Punch and Shadow Ball cleaned up weakened threats, and Rotom-Wash finished Meowscarada after Metagross brought it to 1%.
reflections.adjustment: Opponent may bring Toxapex or Aegislash next game. Consider a check like a Ground-type or strong special attacker that bypasses King's Shield. Be cautious of hazard stacking; limit switches or bring hazard removal. Preserve Incineroar for Intimidate cycling against physical attackers like Mimikyu and Meowscarada.

reflections.summary: Lost primarily because the opponent's Mega Metagross with priority Bullet Punch overwhelmed my team after Mimikyu's Disguise broke. Dual hazards (Stealth Rock + Toxic Spikes) chipped down my squad, and I had no Mega Evolution to contest the opponent's Mega Metagross. Palafin was a poor lead (took super-effective Thunderbolt and died immediately), and after Glimmora fulfilled its hazard-setting role and Mimikyu lost Disguise, Meowscarada alone could not overcome the combined pressure of priority, hazards, and Rotom-Wash's Thunderbolt.
reflections.adjustment: Bring a Mega Stone holder in the next game to contest the opponent's Mega Metagross. Protect Mimikyu's Disguise by leading with a safer pivot instead of Palafin, and ensure a faster priority user or speed control option is available to handle Bullet Punch.

decisions.rationale: Rotom-Wash + Incineroar lead: Rotom-Wash threatens Palafin/Toxapex/Glimmora with Electric/Water STAB; Incineroar's Fake Out breaks Mimikyu's Disguise, Intimidate weakens physical attackers, Flare Blitz destroys Meowscarada/Aegislash. Dragapult in back provides speed, Shadow Ball for Mimikyu/Aegislash, Thunderbolt for Palafin/Toxapex. Metagross-Mega cleans with Tough Claws Steel moves into Mimikyu/Glimmora and Bullet Punch priority.

Mimikyu leads safely behind Disguise, threatening Dragapult and Mega Metagross with PlayRough and providing priority Shadow Sneak. Meowscarada supplies essential speed control at 192 Speed with Protean-boosted coverage, enabling revenge kills against Dragapult and opposing sweepers. Aegislash is the dedicated Mega counter—its Mega form's Tough Claws-boosted Sacred Sword and Shadow Ball pressure Mega Metagross directly, while King's Shield punishes physical attackers. Toxapex rounds out the squad as a Regenerator physical wall that absorbs Incineroar's attacks and pivots with Recover, giving the team a reliable defensive backbone.

Fake Out on Meowscarada prevents it from hitting Rotom-Wash with a super-effective Grass move (Energy Ball/Flower Trick) while Meowscarada is faster. Volt Switch on Mimikyu breaks Disguise and pivots Rotom-Wash out to a better matchup like Dragapult, who threatens both foes with Shadow Ball. Even if Meowscarada Protects, Disguise still breaks and Rotom pivots safely.

Switch Rotom-Wash to Dragapult to preserve the Electric/Water pivot while gaining a fast Ghost/Dragon that outspeeds both foes. Dragapult resists Meowscarada's likely Grass move (Energy Ball 16-25%, Flower Trick 11-16%) and is immune to Brick Break. The main risk is Dark Pulse (70-110% possible OHKO), but the opponent must predict the switch; if they instead target Rotom's slot with Grass, Dragapult takes minimal damage and threatens both foes next turn with Life Orb Shadow Ball (72-132% on 87% Mimikyu, Focus Sash already consumed) and Draco Meteor (72-140% on 75% Meowscarada). Incineroar has only Pass available.

Both attackers target Rotom-Wash to eliminate a key pivot before it can act. Mimikyu's Shadow Sneak (Ghost +1 priority) hits neutrally and moves first, while Meowscarada's Energy Ball (Grass, super effective 2x) exploits the Water typing for heavy damage. Combining both offenses maximizes the chance of a KO on the faster foe, removing a dangerous Electric/Water pivot and maintaining tempo. Mimikyu's Disguise is preserved for a bigger incoming threat, and Aegislash stays benched for the future Mega Metagross matchup.

Dragapult Protect shields it from Meowscarada's Dark Pulse (70.6-110.4%, possible OHKO) and Mimikyu's attacks. Incineroar Flare Blitz guarantees the KO on Meowscarada (83.1-160.3% from 75% HP). Even if both foes target Incineroar, worst-case damage is Brick Break (40.6%) + Play Rough (25.7%) = 66.3%, which Incineroar easily survives. This eliminates the biggest threat (Meowscarada) while preserving Dragapult for the 2v1 against Mimikyu and the unrevealed back line.

Both Pokémon target Dragapult, the fastest and most dangerous remaining foe. Mimikyu-Busted uses priority Shadow Sneak (Ghost, +1, SE 2x) to hit before Dragapult can act, while Meowscarada fires Dark Pulse (SE 2x) for strong neutral-damage pressure. Eliminating Dragapult removes the opponent's primary speed and offensive threat, giving you tempo control with Meowscarada for the rest of the game.

Toxapex walls both Dragapult and Incineroar effectively—Dragapult's Shadow Ball and Draco Meteor are resisted, and Incineroar's Flare Blitz and Fake Out are also resisted. Regenerator plus Recover plus Leftovers gives excellent staying power, letting Mimikyu-Busted safely use priority Shadow Sneak to pressure Dragapult. Saving Aegislash for the anticipated Mega Metagross matchup preserves the notebook's critical late-game asset. Mimikyu stays in to fire another priority Shadow Sneak before Dragapult can act.

Double-target Mimikyu to guarantee the KO through Focus Sash. Dragapult's Shadow Ball (72–132%) either breaks Sash leaving Mimikyu at 1 HP or leaves it at ~15%; Incineroar's Flare Blitz (43–83%) always finishes it regardless. Mimikyu is the biggest threat with SwordsDance + priority Shadow Sneak that could snowball if left alive. Toxapex gets one free action — worst case is Toxic on Dragapult — but removing Mimikyu now is worth that cost. The Speed order is Dragapult → Mimikyu → (Incineroar/Toxapex speed tie), but Flare Blitz KOs Mimikyu either before or after Toxapex moves.

Mimikyu-Busted is the only Pokémon that safely walls Dragapult (Draco Meteor immune, Shadow Ball resisted) and must press that advantage immediately with Play Rough for heavy neutral-bonus damage before likely being KO'd by Dragapult's Shadow Ball. Toxapex applies Toxic on Dragapult to stack residual with Mimikyu's chip, accelerating the elimination of the series' most dangerous foe.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Dragapult Protects to safely avoid Aegislash's guaranteed-OHKO Shadow Ball. Incineroar uses Parting Shot into Aegislash: as a non-damaging status move it bypasses King's Shield, lowering Aegislash's Atk/SpA by 1 and pivoting Incineroar out. This neuters Aegislash's offensive threat while preserving both of our Pokémon and bringing in a fresh back-line member.

Dragapult stays in to pressure Aegislash with Shadow Ball (51.5-92.6%, 2HKO range) and Toxapex with Thunderbolt. Incineroar's Parting Shot switch brings Rotom-Wash, which threatens Toxapex with super-effective Electric STAB, resists Liquidation (7.6-19.2%), takes Aegislash Shadow Ball neutrally (19.7-36.8%), and can Volt Switch later to regain momentum. Metagross-Mega is strong but Rotom-Wash's type matchups are cleaner here: it isn't weak to any foe move and has reliable 100%-accurate Thunderbolt vs Toxapex. Opponent down to last two Pokémon with no bench; preserving Dragapult and Rotom-Wash while wearing them down is the safest path to close out game 2.

Aegislash's Shadow Ball is 2x super-effective against Dragapult (the priority elimination target) with a possible KO range of 59.5-111.7% on 90% HP. Even if Dragapult retaliates with Shadow Ball (51.1-75.9% damage), Aegislash survives at 24-49% HP. Toxapex's Liquidation is 2x super-effective against Incineroar (Fire/Water weakness), dealing 24.8-47.1% of max HP to the already-weakened 77% Incineroar. This maximizes offensive pressure to eliminate the top threat while keeping Aegislash alive for the Metagross matchup.

Double Thunderbolt into Toxapex guarantees a KO: Dragapult min 46.5% + Rotom min 53.5% = 100% ≥ Toxapex's 92% HP. Toxapex lacks Protect and the opponent has no bench, so this cannot be blocked. Aegislash's Shadow Ball does 55.2–78.5% to Dragapult, leaving it alive at 1.5–24.8% after Life Orb recoil. Next turn it's 2v1 against a -1 SpA Aegislash, which Dragapult Shadow Ball threatens to OHKO. Splitting attacks risks both foes surviving; focusing Aegislash leaves Toxapex free to Toxic Rotom. This line secures a knockout with minimal risk.

King's Shield (priority +4) protects Aegislash from Dragapult's likely super-effective Shadow Ball OHKO attempt and drops Dragapult's offenses by 2 if it attacks. Toxic on Dragapult starts residual chip damage on the priority elimination target. This keeps Aegislash alive and healthy for the upcoming Metagross matchup while steadily wearing down Dragapult.

Aegislash is the opponent's last Pokémon. Dragapult Shadow Ball (51.5–92.6%) + Rotom Thunderbolt (23.4–40.7%) gives a high probability OHKO (74.9–133.3% combined). Both moves are 100% accurate. Dragapult outspeeds Aegislash, so if the combined rolls KO, Aegislash never attacks. Even if we miss the KO range, we have two healthy backline Pokémon to clean up next turn. King's Shield has reduced success rate and doesn't punish special moves.

Shadow Ball on Dragapult is the only super-effective option against the priority elimination target, dealing 40-75% of its max HP. Even if Dragapult retaliates with Shadow Ball (51-76% to Aegislash), Aegislash survives and remains healthy enough for the planned Metagross matchup next turn. Toxapex is fainted so must pass.

reflections.summary: Our lead matchup and pivoting overwhelmed the opponent. Incineroar's Fake Out and Flare Blitz removed Meowscarada early, Rotom-Wash broke Mimikyu's Disguise and pivoted into Dragapult, which cleaned up with super effective Shadow Balls. The opponent's Toxapex and Aegislash couldn't withstand the special pressure. Between-game adjustments—continuing with Incineroar+Rotom lead and bringing Dragapult—worked perfectly against their adapted Mimikyu+Meowscarada lead. The series was won 2-0 due to superior team composition and clean execution.
reflections.adjustment: In a future series, consider a plan for Glimmora hazards, as our team lacks removal. Leading Dragapult or Metagross could pressure it early, or bring Gliscor if it has Defog. Otherwise, the Incineroar+Rotom lead remains strong, and preserving Incineroar's Lum Berry for Toxic is valuable.

reflections.summary: Lost 0-2. The opponent's Dragapult + Rotom-Wash Thunderbolt combination overwhelmed the team; every Water/Ground-type on my roster was 2HKO'd or OHKO'd by Electric coverage. Incineroar's Intimidate plus Parting Shot crippled Mimikyu and Aegislash before they could contribute offensively. Mimikyu's Disguise was burned on the switch to Rotom-Wash (Turn 1), eliminating the best revenge-killer. Aegislash entered after Parting Shot had already lowered its offenses, so it could never threaten. Toxapex was double-Thunderbolted and died. No team member survived long enough to mount a meaningful response. Between-game adjustments (saving Aegislash for Mega Metagross) were never tested because the series ended; the core problem—no Electric immunity and no pivot that could survive two fast special attackers firing super-effective moves—was never addressed.
reflections.adjustment: Swap Palafin and Glimmora slots for a Ground-type immune to Electric (e.g., Swampert with Earthquake/Earth Power/Protect/Flip Turn) and a faster offensive lead that can threaten Dragapult before it sets up (e.g., Spiritomb with Shadow Sneak/Trick to punish Choice items, or Torkoal under Drought to enable Meowscarada's Sun-boosted offenses and reduce Thunder accuracy). Prioritize keeping Mimikyu's Disguise intact by leading it against non-volatile-damage foes, or replace it entirely with the Ground pivot. Against this opponent's pivot-heavy, Electric-spam style, the priority is: (1) an Electric-immune pivot that can absorb hits and chip, (2) speed control or a faster revenge killer, and (3) hazard pressure to punish Dragapult's Life Orb recoil and Rotom's Sitrus recovery.

events.text: Light Screen up on P1's side

decisions.rationale: Lead Tyranitar + Excadrill executes the core game plan: Sand Stream immediately overrides Pelipper's Drizzle rain, shutting down Swift Swim on Mega Swampert, while Excadrill at 280 Spe under Sand Rush outspeeds the entire opposing roster and threatens spread Rock Slide flinches plus Iron Head for Fairies. Tyranitar's Passho Berry cushions Water hits from the rain team. Back Gengar-Mega for Shadow Tag trapping and Thunderbolt OHKO on Pelipper, Sludge Bomb into Primarina, and Shadow Ball into Basculegion. Back Grimmsnarl for Prankster Taunt to shut down Whimsicott's priority Encore/Tailwind (Dark typing makes Grimmsnarl immune to opposing Prankster moves) and dual screens to protect frail sweepers; Spirit Break also softens Primarina's special attacks.

Lead Pelipper and Swampert to immediately overwrite Tyranitar's sand with Drizzle, activate Swampert's Swift Swim upon Mega Evolution, and pressure Tyranitar and Excadrill. Bring Basculegion and Primarina in the back to clean up with Swift Swim/Choice Scarf and powerful rain-boosted water attacks.

Excadrill outspeeds everything at 280 and Rock Slide hits both foes (SE on Pelipper, 30% flinch each). If Swampert flinches, no Earthquake. Tyranitar Protects to avoid Swampert Earthquake (44-66% to Tyranitar). Even if Swampert doesn't flinch and Earthquakes, Excadrill survives at 1 HP via Focus Sash and Tyranitar stays at 100%. This preserves the sand setter while dealing damage and rolling flinches on the fastest slot.
Pelipper sets Tailwind to flip speed control against Sand Rush Excadrill, while Mega Swampert uses Liquidation on Tyranitar to wash away the sand and activate Drizzle rain.

Excadrill Rock Slide outspeeds everything: SE on 50% HP Pelipper (chance to KO) plus 30% flinch on Swampert. Tyranitar Thunder Wave on Swampert provides critical long-term speed control — after Tailwind ends, paralyzed Swampert (45-61 Spe) drops below Tyranitar (81), and 25% full para chance every turn is invaluable. Swampert moves before Tyranitar under Tailwind so TWave won't block this turn's attack, but even if Swampert Earthquakes, Tyranitar survives at 17-40% HP and Excadrill survives via Focus Sash. This play also maintains value if Pelipper Protects (unlike double Rock Slide which would be wasted). Paralyzing the opponent's Mega is the highest-value disruptive play available.

Excadrill fainted; bring Grimmsnarl for priority Reflect (Light Clay = 8 turns) to halve Swampert-Mega's physical attacks (Liquidation/EQ/Ice Punch) while Tyranitar still holds Passho Berry for the first Water hit. This keeps Tyranitar alive to maintain Sandstorm through the 3-turn Tailwind window. Gengar-Mega is better held for post-Tailwind cleanup with Shadow Tag trapping and superior Speed. Pelipper at 1% is trivially handled next turn by Rock Slide or Spirit Break.
Swampert-Mega hits Excadrill or Tyranitar with Liquidation while Pelipper uses Hurricane on Excadrill or Tyranitar (or vice versa), securing heavy damage under Tailwind.

Grimmsnarl Prankster Reflect goes up before Swampert attacks, cutting Earthquake to ~30-42% on Tyranitar (survivable at 100%) and ~20-27% on Grimmsnarl. Tyranitar then Rock Slides: guaranteed KO on 1% Pelipper even at spread 0.75x, 30% flinch chance on Swampert, and NVE chip on Swampert. Pelipper dies to Sandstorm if it doesn't Protect. Passho Berry still held for Liquidation insurance. This sets up for Gengar-Mega Shadow Tag cleanup once Tailwind expires after next turn.

Pelipper is at 2% HP and should protect to preserve presence or stall out Tailwind turns, while Swampert-Mega targets Grimmsnarl with Liquidation to pick up a secure neutral/heavy blow or eliminate Grimmsnarl before it can set up screens or disrupt.

Pelipper has fainted, so we send in Basculegion to clean up. Swampert-Mega passes its action (or we can use an attack, but here we just need to send in our replacement and take our next turn). Wait, Swampert-Mega's slot choice is Pass because Pelipper's slot is a switch choice. Let's make sure Basculegion comes in.

Focus-fire Basculegion to remove the Adaptability Choice Scarf threat. Tyranitar Crunch is SE (56-106%, possible OHKO) and Grimmsnarl Spirit Break adds 24-45%, combining for 80-151% plus Sandstorm chip — high KO probability if both land. Tyranitar survives a double-target with ~98% odds (Wave Crash 64-93 HP post-Passho+Reflect + Earthquake 77-108 HP post-Reflect+spread = 141-201 vs 195 HP). Even if one Pokémon falls, the other still chips Basculegion heavily, and Gengar-Mega enters next turn under Shadow Tag with Tailwind expired. Protecting Tyranitar would leave Basculegion at high HP, risking Gengar-Mega being outsped by Scarf Basculegion (147-195 vs 165-200) next turn — offensive focus-fire avoids that scenario entirely.

Basculegion outspeeds and uses Wave Crash on Tyranitar, while Mega Swampert uses Liquidation on Tyranitar to secure the KO through its Passho Berry in Sand, ignoring Reflect since water hits hard and Tyranitar is the main offensive threat remaining.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Switch Tyranitar (3% HP, dead weight) to Gengar-Mega for Shadow Tag—trapping both foes is the highest-impact play. Grimmsnarl uses Light Screen via Prankster priority (guaranteed to resolve before opponent moves). Moonblast is a guaranteed KO on Grimmsnarl from 47% without screens; Light Screen cuts it to ~38-54%, giving survival chance vs single-target Moonblast and converting several double-target spread combos from guaranteed KO to possible survival. Even if Grimmsnarl dies, Light Screen persists 8 turns (Light Clay) to protect Gengar-Mega from Primarina's special attacks. Spirit Break lacks priority and likely won't resolve if Primarina outspeeds and KOs Grimmsnarl first. Dual screens + Shadow Tag = optimal sweep setup.

Tyranitar is at 3% HP and needs to be cleaned up immediately, and Moonblast + Liquidation guarantees taking it down through Reflect while dealing strong damage to Grimmsnarl. Primarina's Moonblast on Tyranitar and Swampert's Liquidation on Tyranitar ensure no RNG from Rock Slide flinches or misses can save Tyranitar.

Gengar Mega Evolves and Sludge Bombs Primarina — Gengar outspeeds (178 vs 80-112), and Mega SpA boost (~238 vs 182) pushes Sludge Bomb from 58.8-104.5% to ~77-137%, making OHKO very likely. This is the only path to survival: if Primarina acts, Moonblast guaranteed KOs Grimmsnarl (50-72.2% from 47%) and any hit KOs Gengar at 3%. If Primarina falls, Swampert alone cannot KO Grimmsnarl (Liquidation max 41.8% < 47% HP), and Grimmsnarl's Spirit Break chips Swampert from 38% to ~5-19%, setting up an easy cleanup with Tyranitar. Grimmsnarl Spirit Break on Swampert is superior to Taunt (doesn't stop Moonblast) or refreshing screens (already active).
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Swampert-Mega's Earthquake hits both Gengar (at 2% HP, guaranteed KO) and Grimmsnarl (at 46% HP), bypassing Reflect and Light Screen because Earthquake is a physical ground-type spread move. Primarina uses Moonblast into Grimmsnarl (foe 2) to pick up significant damage on Grimmsnarl, ensuring maximum board clearing.

Both Pokémon attack Swampert-Mega at 5% HP — Crunch and Spirit Break are both guaranteed KOs. Swampert outspeeds both and every one of its attacks KOs both my Pokémon (Tyranitar 3%, Grimmsnarl 16%) even through Reflect. Earthquake (spread) KOs both simultaneously and is the opponent's optimal play, which I cannot stop. However, if the opponent uses ANY single-target move instead, one of my Pokémon survives and KOs Swampert — I win. By not Protecting (when the opponent likely expects Tyranitar to Protect at 3%), I bait a potential single-target misread. Protect-based lines are strictly worse: double Protect only delays the Earthquake KO by one turn, and Tyranitar Protect + Grimmsnarl Spirit Break loses to both Earthquake and Liquidation targeting Grimmsnarl.

Swampert-Mega's Earthquake hits both Tyranitar (3%) and Grimmsnarl (15%) for super-effective / normal spread damage that ignores Reflect and Light Screen, guaranteeing KOs on both low-HP foes to close out Game 1. Primarina is fainted and must pass.

reflections.summary: Lost because Swampert-Mega under rain/Tailwind outsped and swept after Excadrill died on turn 2. Thunder Wave on Swampert was wasted (Ground immunity), losing a critical turn of damage. Without Sand Rush speed control, nothing could outspeed Swampert, and its spread Earthquake cleaned up the weakened endgame positions on turns 6-7. Gengar-Mega traded with Primarina but fell to Swampert EQ same turn, leaving no answer to Swampert at 5%.
reflections.adjustment: Do not target Swampert with Thunder Wave (Ground-immune). Prioritize keeping Excadrill alive longer — consider Protect on turn 2 instead of trading into Swampert+Pelipper under Tailwind. Need a cleaner Swampert answer: focus chip from Tyranitar Crunch + Grimmsnarl Spirit Break earlier rather than splitting damage across Pelipper. If Swampert reaches low HP with EQ access, avoid both Pokémon being EQ-vulnerable simultaneously.

reflections.summary: Swampert-Mega and Pelipper established early offensive pressure under Tailwind to remove Excadrill, allowing Swampert to clean up with Earthquake through opponent's screens in the endgames.
reflections.adjustment: Retain Pelipper and Swampert-Mega as core leads to counter the opponent's weather setters and dual screens setup.

events.text: Light Screen up on P1's side

decisions.rationale: Down 0-1, must counter the rain core that beat me in G1. Lead Tyranitar+Excadrill: Sand Stream overrides Drizzle, Sand Rush Excadrill is my only speed answer to Swift Swim Swampert and Choice Scarf Basculegion — but Protect Excadrill early to preserve it. Back Gengar (Mega for Shadow Tag to trap/remove Basculegion or Primarina; Sludge Bomb OHKOs Primarina after chip) and Grimmsnarl (Prankster Taunt shuts potential Whimsicott Encore/Tailwind; Reflect/Light Screen mitigates Swampert EQ spread and Basculegion Wave Crash). Covers all opponent adjustments: same rain core, Whimsicott swap, or Forretress swap.
Lead Pelipper and Swampert to overwrite Tyranitar's sand with Drizzle and pressure with Mega Swampert under rain, bringing Basculegion and Primarina in the back to clean up.

Tyranitar Rock Slide chunks Pelipper for 40-77% (SE spread) while Tyranitar safely survives any combination of Swampert EQ (44-66%) + Pelipper Hurricane (8-13%). Excadrill Protects to preserve Focus Sash and full HP — at 280 Speed it outspeeds the entire rain core even through Tailwind or Swift Swim, making it the decisive threat for next turn. This follows the pre-game plan to shield Excadrill early and maintain sand dominance.
Setting Tailwind with Pelipper lets Swampert outspeed Excadrill under sand (or double rain/speed control) and safely mega evolve and strike Tyranitar with Liquidation.

Swampert-Mega (180-244 Spe with Tailwind) is guaranteed to KO Tyranitar (59% HP) with either Earthquake or Liquidation before Tyranitar can move (81 Spe). Tyranitar must Protect to survive. Excadrill (280 Spe) outspeeds everything; Rock Slide is SE on Pelipper (33.5-63.7%, potential KO from 38%) and hits Swampert NVE with a flinch chance. reflections.summary: Lost 0-2. In Game 2, the Gengar-Mega Shadow Tag plan backfired immediately: Basculegion's Adaptability Wave Crash OHKO'd Gengar on turn 4 before it could Mega Evolve, eliminating the planned win condition. The sand core (Tyranitar+Excadrill) traded poorly against rain Water spam—both are Water-weak and were overwhelmed by Swampert-Mega and Basculegion's raw power even with screens support. Tyranitar's consecutive Protect on turn 7 failed, leaving it exposed to a double-up KO. Hydrapple, which resists Water and was registered, was left on the bench—a critical bring error. The opponent's Tailwind from Pelipper provided speed control that sand override alone couldn't fully neutralize, and their rain team simply outpowered a roster with too many Water-weak picks.
reflections.adjustment: Bring Hydrapple over Gengar against this rain build—its Grass/Dragon typing resists Water and checks Swampert-Mega/Basculegion/Primarina far better. Drop the Gengar-Mega Shadow Tag plan entirely against rain; it cannot safely evolve through Adaptability Wave Crash or rain-boosted Water moves. Consider Vaporeon (Water Absorb) from the bench if available in future series for additional Water immunity. Prioritize Thunder Wave on Basculegion or Swampert early, and avoid consecutive Protect calls that risk failing under pressure.

reflections.summary: You won the series 2-0 by effectively leveraging your rain core (Pelipper, Mega Swampert, and Basculegion) alongside Primarina to break down the opponent's sand-and-screens structure. In Game 2, Pelipper's Tailwind setup and Swampert's heavy physical pressure overwhelmed Tyranitar and Excadrill early, while Basculegion cleaned up Gengar and Excadrill. Though screen support prolonged the game, Primarina and Mega Swampert systematically dismantled the remaining threats to close out the sweep.
reflections.adjustment: No further adjustments are needed since the series is won 2-0. For future matchups against similar sand-and-screen archetypes, continuing to lead weather control and high-offensive-pressure pivots like Pelipper and Mega Swampert remains a winning formula.

decisions.rationale: Lead Mega Alakazam plus Talonflame maximizes immediate anti-Trick Room pressure while retaining Tailwind tempo. Floette-Eternal provides a second Mega option and strong Dragon pressure, while Garchomp covers Armarouge and Archaludon.

Lead Altaria and Mamoswine for immediate Tailwind plus strong pressure into Garchomp and Talonflame. Armarouge provides powerful Fire coverage into Floette and broad special offense, while Scarf Sneasler gives a fast answer to Mega Alakazam and Scrafty.
Mega Protect preserves Alakazam from Mamoswine’s likely Ground pressure while Talonflame’s faster Taunt prevents Altaria from establishing Tailwind or using support this turn.
Set Tailwind while Mamoswine immediately chips Alakazam with priority Ice Shard, preserving offensive pressure and improving the lead's speed position for subsequent turns.
Double-target Mamoswine: Psychic plus Flare Blitz gives the best chance to remove its Focus Sash-supported Ice Shard pressure immediately, preserving Garchomp for the endgame.
Switch Altaria to Sneasler to preserve the fast response to Mega Alakazam while Mamoswine uses priority Ice Shard for guaranteed chip before Alakazam can act.
Switch Mamoswine’s slot to Armarouge, which resists Talonflame’s Fire attacks and provides immediate offensive pressure while preserving Altaria for later support.
Protect preserves Alakazam from either foe’s guaranteed KO pressure while Brave Bird gives the strongest immediate chance to remove the faster Choice Scarf Sneasler.

Switch Sneasler to preserve the fast Alakazam response while Armarouge’s Armor Cannon guarantees the KO on Alakazam; this avoids losing Sneasler to Psychic or Brave Bird and keeps Armarouge positioned against Talonflame’s Fire pressure.
Double-target Armarouge to maximize the chance of removing the immediate guaranteed KO threat to Alakazam-Mega; Shadow Ball plus Brave Bird has the strongest combined removal pressure.
Protect preserves Altaria from Talonflame while Armarouge's Armor Cannon guarantees the KO on Mega Alakazam if it does not Protect.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Protect Alakazam from Scarf Sneasler’s immediate attack while Talonflame removes Sneasler with Brave Bird; preserving Alakazam is preferable to risking it into a potential Helping Hand-boosted Poison Jab.

Helping Hand boosts Sneasler's immediately faster Poison Jab into a guaranteed knockout on Mega Alakazam across the revealed damage range, removing the main Psychic threat while Altaria avoids attacking into Talonflame's resistance.
The position is lost: Altaria cannot meaningfully reverse the two-on-one before being KOed, so concede rather than spend resources.

reflections.summary: Won by denying Altaria’s support with turn-one Taunt and using Mega Alakazam Protect plus Talonflame pressure to safely remove Mamoswine and Sneasler. The critical Shadow Ball KO on Armarouge accelerated the cleanout. Team preview was well suited: Alakazam/Talonflame/Garchomp/Floette was an appropriate four, and Mega Alakazam was the right Mega into their revealed fast offensive-support composition.
reflections.adjustment: In game 2, if Farigiraf is brought, prioritize Mega Alakazam pressure into it (for example Shadow Ball) rather than relying on Talonflame’s priority Brave Bird, which Armor Tail can block; respect Mental Herb making a first Taunt unreliable.

reflections.summary: Lost primarily because the chosen four lacked a reliable answer to Mega Alakazam plus Talonflame's immediate speed and Flying pressure. Team-preview plan was unfavorable: Mamoswine was vulnerable to Talonflame, Armarouge was exposed to Mega Alakazam's Shadow Ball, and Sneasler could not survive Brave Bird; no Mega Stone holder was brought or evolved. Piloting had no recorded decision errors, but the team could not recover after its first two attackers were removed.
reflections.adjustment: For the next game, avoid leading Altaria and Mamoswine together into Mega Alakazam/Talonflame; bring a four with stronger immediate anti-Talonflame and Mega Alakazam pressure, and preserve Sneasler or another fast attacker rather than exposing it to Brave Bird before it can act.

decisions.rationale: Lead Mega Alakazam plus Talonflame to pressure Altaria support immediately while retaining fast Tailwind control. Milotic and Scrafty give a resilient back line into Mamoswine, Armarouge, and Sneasler modes.
Lead Altaria and Mamoswine to establish Tailwind while immediately pressuring Talonflame and Mega Alakazam; reserve Archaludon for reliable Electric coverage and Sneasler as the fast finisher.

Mega Alakazam reliably Taunts Altaria before its support move while Gale Wings Tailwind establishes Speed control; this denies Helping Hand/Tailwind pressure and preserves both attackers’ next-turn options.
Use priority Helping Hand to boost Mamoswine’s Ice Shard into Alakazam, creating the strongest immediate pressure while bypassing likely Taunt and Mega Alakazam’s Speed advantage.
Protect Alakazam from the expected priority Ice Shard while Talonflame starts wearing down Focus Sash Mamoswine; Brave Bird is marginally stronger than Flare Blitz through Thick Fat.

Double-target Mega Alakazam: Moonblast plus Ice Shard is guaranteed to exceed its remaining HP if both connect, removing the fastest immediate threat before it can continue pressuring the team. Mamoswine survives likely Psychic or Brave Bird damage, while Ice Shard also preserves priority pressure if damage rolls vary.

Preserve the low-HP Mega Alakazam by pivoting to Milotic while Talonflame pressures the weakened Mamoswine with Brave Bird; this also exploits the likelihood that their prior attacks remain aimed at Alakazam.

Moonblast applies pressure to the weakened Alakazam while Mamoswine Protects against the opposing priority-free attacks and guaranteed Psychic KO. This preserves Mamoswine for a follow-up Ice Shard attempt and avoids sacrificing Sneasler prematurely.

Renew Tailwind while Milotic targets Mamoswine with Scald, giving the best chance to remove or heavily weaken the immediate physical threat without surrendering speed control for the revealed Choice Scarf Sneasler endgame.

Switch Altaria to Archaludon to escape Taunt and the severe Icy Wind threat while preserving Sneasler as the late-game finisher. Mamoswine should Protect against the likely Scald and Brave Bird double-target; this also lets Tailwind expire while Archaludon enters safely.
Keep Archaludon active and switch Mamoswine's slot to Altaria. Altaria is the safer pivot into Talonflame and Milotic while preserving Sneasler for late-game cleanup.

Taunt prevents Altaria from restoring Tailwind or using Helping Hand, while Icy Wind consumes Yache Berry, chips both foes, and leaves Milotic faster than their reduced Speed ranges next turn. Talonflame is otherwise vulnerable to Archaludon Thunderbolt.
Preserve Mega Alakazam’s fast offensive and disruptive utility; Scrafty is the more expendable switch and can still threaten Archaludon if it survives Altaria’s likely Moonblast.
Helping Hand acts before the opposing moves and boosts Archaludon's Thunderbolt enough to guarantee a KO on Talonflame from 78% HP, removing its Gale Wings threat.

Icy Wind gives durable speed control over both foes while chipping Altaria through Yache; Close Combat applies the strongest immediate pressure to Archaludon. Scrafty survives a single Moonblast, and the Speed drops let Milotic and Scrafty move ahead of Archaludon afterward.
Thunderbolt pressures Milotic for substantial super-effective damage, while Moonblast targets Scrafty with a 4x-effective attack and can potentially remove it despite the range.

Protect preserves Scrafty from Altaria’s guaranteed Moonblast KO while Recover restores Milotic after Archaludon’s likely Thunderbolt, maintaining both endgame pieces rather than trading into Archaludon’s boosted Defense.
Altaria's Moonblast guarantees the Scrafty knockout, while Archaludon's Thunderbolt applies the strongest immediate pressure to Milotic and can also secure a knockout before it recovers.
Recover keeps Milotic healthy through Archaludon's Thunderbolt while Close Combat is Scrafty's only meaningful immediate pressure on Archaludon before Altaria's Moonblast removes it.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.
Thunderbolt can KO Milotic from its current HP while Moonblast guarantees the KO on Scrafty; using both attacks gives the best chance to remove both opposing active Pokémon this turn.
Shadow Ball guarantees the Archaludon KO if it does not Protect, while Icy Wind pressures Altaria heavily and preserves speed control if Archaludon protects.

Protect Archaludon from Mega Alakazam's guaranteed knockout while Altaria uses Moonblast to pressure the critically weakened Alakazam; this preserves both Pokémon and creates a stronger follow-up position.

Icy Wind plus Psychic gives the best chance to remove Altaria immediately while dropping Archaludon below Milotic’s Speed for a crucial subsequent Recover; preserving both remaining Pokémon is stronger than trading Alakazam to guarantee Archaludon damage.

Switch Archaludon to preserve it from Alakazam's guaranteed Psychic KO; Altaria's Moonblast guarantees removing the weakened Alakazam, while Sneasler provides the best chance to retain offensive pressure afterward.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.
Psychic is a guaranteed KO on Sneasler before it can move; Recover keeps Milotic safe from any noncritical Thunderbolt and preserves the endgame.

Archaludon must guarantee the KO on Mega Alakazam, while Sneasler's Poison Jab targets Milotic for additional damage if it moves before Psychic. This preserves the best chance to remove both threats this turn despite the uncertain Sneasler–Alakazam Speed order.
Scald is Milotic’s strongest available damage into the sole remaining foe and is the only direct route to closing the game; Milotic can survive one Thunderbolt from full.
Pass with the fainted Sneasler and use Thunderbolt into Milotic; it is the strongest available attack and exploits the super-effective matchup while Archaludon moves first.
Recover maximizes Milotic’s chance to survive another Thunderbolt and continue attempting the Scald KO; attacking immediately risks losing to the next Thunderbolt if Scald misses the KO range.
Thunderbolt is super effective and is the only damaging option likely to finish Milotic before it can act; Sneasler has no remaining action.
Scald has already shown sufficient damage to finish the burned Archaludon from its current HP, ending the game if it connects.
Sneasler has fainted, so pass. Archaludon should use Thunderbolt into Milotic: it moves first and the super-effective hit may KO before Recover, while Flash Cannon and Dragon Pulse are inferior.

reflections.summary: The 2-0 series win is authoritative; the supplied evidence shows Game 2 was won by a well-suited four and clean execution, with no recorded decision errors. The central game-winning sequence was removing Focus Sash Mamoswine, then using Milotic’s Icy Wind speed control, Scrafty’s Close Combat pressure, and Mega Alakazam’s Psychic KOs on Altaria and Choice Scarf Sneasler to leave Milotic in a favorable endgame against weakened Archaludon. Milotic repeatedly survived Thunderbolt through Sitrus Berry and Recover, then Scald burned and eventually finished the Leftovers Archaludon. Talonflame’s Tailwind and Taunt created early tempo and denied Altaria’s support, even though Talonflame was traded for Archaludon pressure. The Game 2 bring of Mega Alakazam, Talonflame, Milotic, and Scrafty fit the revealed opposing four well; Mega Alakazam was the appropriate Mega choice because it provided the immediate speed and Psychic pressure needed to remove Altaria and Sneasler. The evidence does not provide Game 1 details or explicitly identify between-game changes, so their effect cannot be separately credited or blamed. The registered six appear broadly reasonable from this game, but there is insufficient set information or battle evidence to establish that an unbrought roster member offered a materially better four-Pokemon configuration.
reflections.adjustment: For a future series, retain the basic Mega Alakazam/Talonflame/Milotic/Scrafty structure if the same opposing core appears, but make preserving Milotic for Archaludon the highest priority. Continue to Taunt Altaria early when possible, respect Helping Hand-boosted Ice Shard into Mega Alakazam, and use Icy Wind plus Fighting pressure to force Archaludon into a Recover/Protect cycle before committing Alakazam. Avoid relying on Talonflame to remain on the field once Archaludon is in position to Thunderbolt it; its early Tailwind and Taunt value is often enough. No evidence supports replacing the selected Mega or definitively changing the four from this game.

reflections.summary: You lost because the early pressure on Mega Alakazam and Talonflame did not become a decisive advantage: Milotic repeatedly used Icy Wind and Recover, while Taunt limited Altaria and Scald eventually burned Archaludon. Sneasler was exposed to Mega Alakazam's Psychic instead of being preserved for a safer cleanup, and Archaludon could not finish the Milotic endgame. The four brought were reasonable but imperfect: Mamoswine and Altaria supplied useful Alakazam pressure and support, while Archaludon strongly threatened Milotic; however, the composition was vulnerable to Taunt, repeated speed control, and Psychic pressure. No Mega Stone holder was evolved on your side, so there was no competing Mega plan. There were no recorded decision errors, but the supplied evidence contains no Game 1 or between-game adjustment information, so whether an adjustment helped or backfired cannot be determined.
reflections.adjustment: Against this opponent, preserve Sneasler until Mega Alakazam is removed or unable to target it, and avoid presenting it after Icy Wind has compromised its speed. Build the game plan around denying Milotic repeated Recover turns rather than trading damage into it indefinitely; use the strongest available immediate pressure or double-targeting opportunities before it can stabilize. Treat Altaria's Cloud Nine as unreliable because Mega Alakazam can Trace it, and expect Taunt plus Icy Wind to disrupt its support role. The registered alternatives have no supplied sets or battle evidence, so there is not enough support to claim that the full roster contained a materially better four; replacing a vulnerable slot may be worth testing, but the change should be based on verified sets rather than assumed qualities. No between-game adjustment can be judged from the provided record.

decisions.rationale: Lead Rotom-Wash + Incineroar: Rotom-Wash OHKOs Pelipper with Volt Switch and walls Water attacks; Incineroar provides Fake Out tempo control and Intimidate to weaken physical Swift Swim sweepers. Back Serperior + Klefki: Serperior cleans Water-types with Contrary Leaf Storm after Pelipper falls; Klefki sets Light Clay dual screens to blunt rain-boosted attacks and spreads Prankster Thunder Wave to neutralise Swift Swim speed.
Bring Pelipper and Swampert to lead, setting up Drizzle immediately for Swift Swim Speed and activating Damp Rock. Back them with Basculegion and Whimsicott for strong sweeping and speed control.

Volt Switch OHKOs Pelipper (131-260%) removing their rain setter; Fake Out flinches Swampert to prevent any attack or Mega Evolution this turn. Even if Pelipper Protects, Swampert is still neutralised. If both Protect we reset cleanly. Worst case Pelipper outspeeds for Tailwind before dying — still a winning trade removing Drizzle permanently.

Serperior is the hard counter to Mega Swampert: Leaf Storm is a guaranteed OHKO from 90% (145-252%). Swampert's Ice Punch does only 40-58% and Earthquake a mere 15-21% (Grass resists Ground). Even if Swampert outspeeds the narrow speed tie (Serperior 181 vs Swampert 180-244), Serperior survives any single hit and KOs back. The opponent must hard-read the switch and double-target with Ice Punch plus a strong special Fairy move to have a chance at KOing Serperior before it moves — an unlikely prediction when Waterfall into Incineroar is the obvious play. After the KO, Serperior sits at +2 SpA from Contrary, threatening Basculegion (85-155% Leaf Storm) and snowballing out of control. Incineroar stays in to preserve momentum; its Focus Sash guarantees it lives any single hit, enabling Parting Shot or Flare Blitz next turn.

Pelipper sets Tailwind to outspeed any potential Speed control or fast threats on the opponent's backline, and Swampert Mega Evolves and uses Earthquake to hit both opponents (noting Rotom-Wash is immune via Levitate, but Incineroar takes super-effective damage).

Pelipper has fainted and must be replaced; switching in Basculegion brings in our Choice Scarf Swift Swim cleaner to heavily pressure Incineroar and Serperior in the rain. Swampert-Mega must pass its action since Pelipper fainted and needs a replacement switch-in.

Serperior Leaf Storm into Swampert-Mega: guaranteed OHKO if it doesn't Protect, and Contrary gives +2 SpA either way. Incineroar Protect avoids the likely double-target from Swampert-Mega Earthquake + Basculegion Wave Crash, which would otherwise KO through Focus Sash (EQ breaks Sash, Wave Crash finishes). This preserves both mons and removes or forces Protect from their Swift Swim sweeper.

Basculegion's Wave Crash securely removes Incineroar (breaking through its Focus Sash thanks to Adaptability rain power), while Swampert-Mega's Ice Punch hits Serperior super-effectively to pressure it.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Leaf Storm OHKOs Basculegion through the speed tie while boosting Serperior to +4 SpA via Contrary. Parting Shot debuffs Whimsicott (-1 SpA/Atk) and pivots Incineroar into Klefki, preserving the Focus Sash Incineroar for later. Whimsicott's Prankster Tailwind or Encore both resolve first, but either outcome is manageable: Encore locks Serperior into the Leaf Storm it's already using, and Tailwind gives them speed control but leaves them with a solo debuffed Whimsicott against Serperior + Klefki. Klefki can set Prankster Light Screen next turn to neuter Moonblast. Switch target after Parting Shot: Klefki.

Serperior stays in at +4 SpA with Contrary snowball; forfeiting a dominant 2v1 is absurd. Incineroar at 1% dies to any Moonblast, so switch to Klefki, which resists Moonblast (Steel/Fairy), can Thunder Wave to neutralize Whimsicott's Tailwind speed, and sets Light Screen to further blunt Moonblast damage. Rotom-Wash is also viable but offers no Fairy resist and burn is low value vs a special attacker.

Basculegion is Choice-locked into Wave Crash and hits Incineroar for super-effective damage (Incineroar protected last turn, so it cannot protect again safely or used Protect on turn 2). Whimsicott sets up Tailwind to secure speed control against Serperior (+2 SpA Life Orb Serperior is threatening, and Tailwind ensures we move first next turn).

Whimsicott outspeeds both my Pokémon under Tailwind. Leaf Storm breaks Focus Sash (guaranteed survival at 1 HP due to Sash), Contrary boosts Serperior to +6 SpA, and Klefki's Prankster Thunder Wave paralyzes Whimsicott. If Whimsicott Encores Serperior, it locks into Leaf Storm — beneficial since Contrary keeps boosting. If it Encores Klefki, it fails because Klefki has no prior move this battle. Next turn, +6 Leaf Storm OHKOs even through resistance regardless of paralysis RNG.

Basculegion is fainted and must pass. Whimsicott is faster under Tailwind and can use Encore on Serperior to lock it into Leaf Storm (or whatever it used last, which was Leaf Storm), preventing further setup or attacks, while Klefki is likely to support or screen.

Serperior is Encored into Leaf Storm and must target Whimsicott (the only living foe). +6 Life Orb Leaf Storm is a guaranteed OHKO on 1% Whimsicott even resisted. Klefki's Foul Play also KOs, providing insurance against the 10% miss chance. Whimsicott cannot OHKO Serperior with Moonblast (20-32%), so the game is won regardless of Speed order or Whimsicott's move.

Serperior is locked into Leaf Storm by Encore, which it must use again this turn. Whimsicott resists Leaf Storm (0.5x) and has 1% HP left. Moonblast against Serperior chips it down while Klefki cannot easily KO Whimsicott with Foul Play or screens.

reflections.summary: Serperior's Contrary Leaf Storm snowballed after early KOs on Pelipper and Swampert, and the opponent's Encore only locked it into further boosts, leading to a quick sweep.
reflections.adjustment: Expect Primarina or Ampharos-Mega to counter Serperior. Consider leading Klefki to set screens and slow them with Thunder Wave, and preserve Serperior for late-game after removing Fairy/Dragon threats.

reflections.summary: The opponent's Serperior capitalized on Contrary and Life Orb with unchecked Leaf Storm boosts while Incineroar and Klefki controlled the field, snowballing out of control after neutralizing the Swift Swim and rain offense early.
reflections.adjustment: Prioritize immediate offensive pressure or taunt on Serperior to prevent Contrary Leaf Storm setup, and ensure speed control is established safely against Fake Out.

events.text: Light Screen up on P1's side

decisions.rationale: Lead Klefki + Rotom-Wash. Klefki sets Reflect (Prankster) to blunt physical rain sweepers; Rotom-Wash Volt Switch OHKOs Pelipper and Hydro Pump threatens Swampert. Turn 1 Whimsicott Encore on Klefki fails because Klefki hasn't moved yet. Back Incineroar for Intimidate cycling and Fake Out, Serperior as late-game Contrary sweeper after Fairy/Dragon threats are handled.

Pelipper sets Drizzle on lead to enable Swampert's Swift Swim (via Mega Evolution) and Basculegion/Pelipper water pressure, while Basculegion and Whimsicott backline provide clean-up speed control and power against the opponent's known roster (Serperior, Incineroar, Klefki, Rotom-Wash).

Reflect (+1 Prankster) goes up before Swampert-Mega's Earthquake, halving it to ~28-42% on Klefki. Volt Switch OHKOs Pelipper through rain (132-261%); if Pelipper Protects, Volt Switch fails but Reflect is still up and rain setter is forced to Protect again or switch next turn. Speed tie between Rotom-Wash (116) and Pelipper (85-117) at priority 0 means Volt Switch may even deny Tailwind. This line secures early momentum: either Pelipper dies and we pivot into Incineroar for Intimidate, or Pelipper burns Protect and we have Reflect for the long game.

Klefki stays in (Pass) to continue setting screens or spreading paralysis with Prankster Thunder Wave. Rotom-Wash switches to Incineroar: switches resolve first, Intimidate immediately drops Swampert and the incoming replacement's Attack, and Incineroar threatens Fake Out next turn. Keeping Rotom-Wash healthy in back preserves its rain-boosted Hydro Pump and Volt Switch pivot for later. Serperior stays in reserve until Fairy/Dragon threats are scouted or removed.

Setting up Tailwind with Pelipper while Mega Swampert hits an Earthquake that deals heavy damage to Klefki (immune/levitate for Rotom means Rotom isn't hit by EQ) allows us to gain immediate speed control and pressure Klefki before it sets dual screens.

Pelipper fainted last turn, so we must replace it. Bringing in Basculegion under Rain allows us to threaten strong Water/Ghost pressure alongside Mega Swampert. Swampert must pass its action since it cannot act independently when paired with a fainted slot being replaced.

Thunder Wave onto Basculegion is the only speed-control answer to the Scarf Adaptability sweeper; Prankster guarantees it resolves before Wave Crash or Last Respects. Fake Out onto Swampert prevents Earthquake this turn regardless of Mega Evolution, buying a free turn. Worst case: Swampert Protects and Basculegion connects, but at least Basculegion is paralyzed for the rest of the game. Serperior remains in the back to clean after rain threats are weakened.

Klefki has only Pass/Forfeit options; we never forfeit up 1-0. Serperior is the clear switch: Leaf Storm OHKOs both Swampert-Mega (145-252%) and Basculegion (85-155%), resists both Water and Ground moves, and even if Swampert-Mega outspeeds with Swift Swim and lands Ice Punch (27-38%), Serperior survives and KOs back. Contrary also turns Leaf Storm into a snowball. Rotom-Wash is defensively solid but cannot threaten Swampert-Mega reliably (Hydro Pump 38-84%, Volt Switch immune).

Basculegion's Wave Crash cleanly KOs the weakened Incineroar (at 65% HP) through Reflect under Rain (with Choice Scarf and Adaptability), while Swampert Mega Evolves and uses Earthquake to hit both opponents (Klefki and Incineroar) for heavy damage while Swampert's Swift Swim activates next turn.

Serperior Leaf Storm OHKOs Basculegion through Choice lock (cannot Protect) before it moves, removing the Wave Crash threat. Klefki's Prankster Thunder Wave paralyzes Swampert-Mega, halving its Speed and stripping Swift Swim for future turns while adding a 25% full-para chance this same turn. Swampert's attacks into Serperior are negligible (Ice Punch 27–39%, Earthquake 10–14%) under Reflect and -1 Atk. Next turn, a +2 SpA Serperior OHKOs the paralyzed Swampert, leaving only the unrevealed fourth Pokémon to handle with Serperior, Klefki, and full-HP Rotom-Wash.

Basculegion is Choice-locked into Wave Crash and facing Serperior (resistant) + Reflect. Switching Basculegion to Whimsicott preserves momentum, while Swampert Protects to scout Serperior's Leaf Storm/Dragon Pulse and stall Reflect/Rain turns.

Leaf Storm OHKOs Swampert-Mega guaranteed (288-502%) and also OHKOs Basculegion if it switches in. Light Screen buffers against Whimsicott Moonblast and any special attacks from the back. Whimsicott's Prankster Encore is faster than Klefki, but if it Encores Serperior it locks the Leaf Storm I'm already using; if it Encores Klefki, Thunder Wave still provides value. Swampert-Mega's speed is uncertain vs Serperior (180-244 vs 181), but even if it Ice Punches first, Serperior survives (27-38.8%) and retaliates for the KO, reaching +4 SpA. The double-target risk (Ice Punch + Moonblast on Serperior) maxes at ~86% with Reflect, leaving Serperior alive to sweep.

Whimsicott Protects to block any incoming attack (such as Klefki Thunder Wave / Foul Play or Serperior Leaf Storm) while Swampert-Mega uses Earthquake, which hits both Klefki and Serperior super-effectively/neutrally through Reflect (Klefki is weak to Ground, and Serperior takes heavy damage despite Reflect since Earthquake is physical and Swampert hits hard, or we can pick off Klefki). Wait, let's check Swampert's Earthquake damage or Encore options. Actually, Swampert's Earthquake hits Klefki (2x) and Serperior (0.5x), and Whimsicott protecting prevents friendly fire. Alternatively, Whimsicott Encores Serperior into Leaf Storm (if it used it) or Klefki into Thunder Wave. But Protect on Whimsicott is safe, and Earthquake breaks Klefki's Reflect / damages them both. Let's execute Protect + Earthquake.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Serperior Leaf Storm OHKOs Basculegion (252-461%) and boosts to +6 SpA via Contrary. Klefki Thunder Wave paralyzes Whimsicott for permanent speed control. Whimsicott's Prankster Encore/Tailwind goes first regardless, but locking Serperior into Leaf Storm is harmless when it's at +6 and the only remaining foe is a 37% Whimsicott with Sash. Basculegion Wave Crash can threaten Klefki (60-90%) but even if Klefki falls, +6 Serperior wins the 1v1 against paralyzed Whimsicott.

Whimsicott uses Encore on Serperior (or Klefki if desired, but Encore on Serperior locks it into Leaf Storm or prevents it from pivoting safely if it protected) while Basculegion fires Wave Crash into Serperior to chip through screens or target Serperior.

Klefki is Encored into Light Screen which is already active and would fail; switching to Rotom-Wash escapes Encore and brings in a healthy pivot. Serperior's +6 Leaf Storm is a guaranteed KO on Whimsicott from 37% — Focus Sash leaves it at 1 HP, but Whimsicott is the opponent's last Pokémon and cannot OHKO Serperior through screens (Moonblast does 20–32%). Even if Whimsicott Protects, we repeat next turn with Rotom-Wash and Serperior both healthy behind dual screens.

Klefki is encored into Light Screen and will use Light Screen. Serperior is at +6 SpA and will attack. Whimsicott outspeeds Serperior and can use Moonblast into Klefki to chip it or into Serperior if appropriate; Klefki is vulnerable to Moonblast (though 0.5x, but Serperior resists or takes neutral? Wait, Serperior is Grass, Moonblast is Fairy, neutral). Actually, let's look at Moonblast into Serperior or Klefki. Moonblast into Serperior damages the dangerous threat at +6 SpA. Basculegion is fainted so its slot is pass.

reflections.summary: Game 2 was won by a controlled Serperior sweep after an early KO on Pelipper removed Hurricane pressure and Klefki’s Thunder Wave paralyzed the Scarf Basculegion, preventing it from revenging. Screens enabled Serperior to stack Contrary boosts safely and overpower the entire rain squad. The series win resulted from correctly adjusting to a screen-supported Serperior plan, which the opponent lacked an answer for once Basculegion was disabled.
reflections.adjustment: The between-game adjustment to bring Serperior and Klefki over Mega Metagross and Corviknight was decisive; it exploited the opponent’s rain reliance perfectly. In a future rematch, I would keep the same core but consider slotting Mega Metagross over Incineroar if they start bringing Primarina or Ampharos, as Metagross handles Fairy/Electric types while still providing offensive pressure. Serperior remains the premier win condition, and Klefki + Rotom‑Wash form a resilient screens‑pivot backbone.

reflections.summary: You lost the series 0-2 because Serperior scaled out of control with Contrary Leaf Storm under dual screens and speed control disruption (Thunder Wave), while your aggressive rain offense was dismantled by Rotom-Wash pivoting, Incineroar's utility, and Klefki's support. The team-preview plan of bringing Pelipper, Mega Swampert, Basculegion, and Whimsicott made sense on paper for a rain setup, but the lack of immediate special pressure allowed Serperior to boost freely and sweep.
reflections.adjustment: Against dual screen and Contrary setups like Serperior paired with Prankster Klefki, bring faster taunt or strong physical breakers that ignore screens or punch through them (such as Alakazam or heavier offensive pressure) rather than relying purely on speed-dependent rain sweepers that get crippled by Thunder Wave.

decisions.rationale: Lead immediate special pressure with Mega Alakazam available to outrun and threaten Mega Gengar, while Floette-Eternal pressures Tyranitar and provides strong neutral damage. Garchomp covers the opposing Steel/sand core, and Talonflame supplies priority Tailwind plus disruption.

Lead the Sand core (Tyranitar + Excadrill): Sand Stream activates on entry giving Excadrill 280 effective Speed under Sand Rush, outspeeding the entire opponent roster. Excadrill's Focus Sash insurance + Iron Head (2x Floette), Rock Slide (4x Talonflame, spread), and High Horsepower (2x Garchomp) provide optimal coverage. Tyranitar adds Rock Slide spread and special bulk. Gengar-Mega in back provides Shadow Tag trapping to eliminate Floette-Mega (Sludge Bomb OHKO) and Alakazam-Mega (Shadow Ball) at the right moment. Gholdengo as 4th is the defensive anchor: resists Fairy/Psychic, immune to Fighting (Scrafty), Good as Gold blocks Taunt/TWave/WoW, and Make It Rain hits Floette SE. Against expected Scrafty+Floette lead, Protect Excadrill to block Fake Out while Tyranitar Rock Slides; turn 2 Excadrill Iron Heads Floette before it moves.

Pivot Alakazam out of Tyranitar’s guaranteed Crunch KO while Protect denies Excadrill’s guaranteed Iron Head KO on Floette; Garchomp creates the strongest immediate counterpressure into both opposing actives next turn.

Excadrill Iron Head on Floette (2x SE, 86-169%, potential OHKO) removes the primary threat to Tyranitar. Tyranitar Crunch on Alakazam (2x SE, 89-195%, potential OHKO) removes the speed/Mega threat. Tyranitar survives any single Floette hit (max 70.5% from Light of Ruin), and Alakazam cannot meaningfully damage Tyranitar (Psychic immune, Shadow Ball NVE). Double-targeting both foes at 280 Speed with Excadrill guarantees damage before either opponent moves unless Alakazam-Mega Traces Sand Rush (50% chance). Even then, Excadrill's Iron Head still resolves on Floette, and Tyranitar's Crunch still hits Alakazam-Mega for massive damage.
Preserve both Garchomp and Floette from their immediate guaranteed KO threats; Talonflame can absorb the likely Iron Head while Garchomp safely blocks Ice Punch or other pressure.

Excadrill Iron Head on Floette (~87% KO chance) removes the Fairy threat before Tyranitar acts; Tyranitar Ice Punch on Garchomp (4x SE, 56-101% on 64% HP) likely KOs or cripples it. Garchomp EQ is discouraged (39-91% friendly fire on Floette ally). If Floette falls, Tyranitar survives any single Garchomp hit (Stomping Tantrum ≤80% vs 88% HP) to deliver Ice Punch. Even worst-case (Floette survives, both focus Tyranitar), Excadrill survives via Focus Sash to clean up next turn.
Earthquake maximizes simultaneous damage into both foes while Talonflame pressures Excadrill through Focus Sash and can remove it before Garchomp acts if Rock Slide does not stop Talonflame.
Bring in both remaining Pokémon; Alakazam and Floette together retain immediate pressure on Tyranitar while keeping Mega Alakazam available for a potential Mega Gengar endgame.

Excadrill Rock Slide (280 Spe, guaranteed first since Gale Wings is inactive at 57% HP) guaranteed KOs Talonflame (4x SE, 78-149% vs 57%) and chips Garchomp 7-12% with 30% flinch. Tyranitar Ice Punch hits Garchomp for 4x SE (56-101%); with Rock Slide chip Garchomp drops to ~52-57%, making KO near-certain. Even if Garchomp EQs first (54-80% to Tyranitar who survives at 8-34%, Excadrill saved by Focus Sash), Ice Punch still KOs afterward. If Garchomp Protects (reduced rate), Rock Slide still removes Talonflame. Best expected value: likely double KO, forcing Alakazam+Floette in against our board advantage.
Protect Alakazam from Tyranitar’s guaranteed Crunch KO while Mega Floette uses its strongest Fairy attack to maximize the chance of immediately removing Tyranitar before Excadrill can attack.

Double SE target: Tyranitar Crunch on Alakazam (88.9-195.4%, possible OHKO) and Excadrill Iron Head on Floette (86.2-169.1%, possible KO from 94%). Tyranitar survives any single Floette hit even at 76% (Light of Ruin max 70.5%). Alakazam's damage on both my mons is weak (Psychic immune on TTar, NVE on Excadrill; Shadow Ball NVE on both). Even if Alakazam Megas and Traces Sand Rush (50%), it can't KO Excadrill (max 42%). If Floette Protects, Tyranitar stays at 76% and we adapt next turn with bench options. This is the highest-EV play: two potential KOs with minimal risk.
Reduced-success Protect is the only available action that can prevent the otherwise immediate guaranteed Crunch knockout and preserves the only plausible path through opponent misses or errors.

Opponent has only Alakazam remaining (3/4 fainted). Crunch (88.9-195.4%) + Iron Head (59.3-130%) = 148.2% minimum combined damage, guaranteeing the KO regardless of Alakazam's hidden spread. Iron Head chosen over High Horsepower for 100% accuracy (vs 95%) and flinch chance since Excadrill (280 Spe) outspeeds base Alakazam. Even if Alakazam Mega Evolves and Traces Sand Rush (50%), it can't KO either Pokémon (Shadow Ball max 42% on Excadrill, Psychic NVE). If Alakazam Protects (reduced rate after T4), it only delays the inevitable 1v4. No risk; go for the kill.

reflections.summary: Lost to Tyranitar–Excadrill sand pressure: Sand Rush gave Excadrill the speed advantage, and the Rock Slide flinch plus follow-up Ice Punch removed Garchomp and Talonflame before they could establish offense. The four brought were not well suited to this lead because they lacked a reliable immediate answer to the sand core; Mega Floette was especially vulnerable to Excadrill’s Iron Head. Mega Alakazam would have been the more suitable evolution for speed control versus sand.
reflections.adjustment: Next game, prioritize Mega Alakazam and lead or preserve it with a partner that pressures Tyranitar/Excadrill immediately; do not rely on Talonflame or Garchomp surviving Rock Slide plus Ice Punch to set up Tailwind or attack.

reflections.summary: Sand core of Tyranitar + Excadrill swept through the opponent's entire team in 5 turns. Excadrill under Sand Rush outsped everything, Iron Head KO'd Floette-Mega and Alakazam, while Rock Slide flinched Garchomp T3 enabling the clean double KO. Opponent's Protect-heavy play couldn't generate enough pressure to break the sand speed advantage.
reflections.adjustment: Opponent will likely adapt by bringing Scrafty (Intimidate/Fake Out) or Milotic (Competitive/Icy Wind) to disrupt sand. Consider leading Gholdengo alongside Tyranitar if you expect Scrafty Fake Out, since Good as Gold blocks Snarl and Make It Rain pressures Milotic. Gengar-Mega was unused—only bring if Shadow Tag trapping is needed for a specific lead.

decisions.rationale: Lead Mega Alakazam and Floette-Eternal for immediate speed and high special-pressure options into the opponent’s likely sand lead; bring Garchomp and Milotic as durable backline answers to Tyranitar, Excadrill, and Steel-types. This avoids Talonflame’s dangerous exposure to repeated Rock Slide.

Sand core lead (Tyranitar+Excadrill) remains strongest: Excadrill's Steel typing resists both Fake Out (0.5x) and Brave Bird (0.5x), making opponent's priority disruption ineffective. Focus Sash provides backup safety. Sand Stream triggers on entry so sand is active even if Tyranitar is flinched. Back: Gholdengo for Fake Out immunity + Good as Gold status blocking (switch-in vs Scrafty Snarl/Taunt), and Gengar-Mega Shadow Tag as late-game win condition to trap weakened foes. Opponent likely adapts with Scrafty/Milotic but Excadrill under sand outspeedes their entire team except Alakazam-Mega Trace (which cannot KO Excadrill).

Protect Mega Alakazam while pivoting Floette into Milotic: this denies the opponents’ immediate dual KO routes and brings in a bulkier answer to the sand core. Mega Evolution also gives Alakazam an immediate chance to copy Sand Rush for future speed control.

Crunch Alakazam (SE, possible OHKO 89-195%) and Iron Head Floette (SE, possible OHKO 86-169%). Both attacks are super-effective with OHKO potential. Even if one foe Protects, the other takes massive damage. Tyranitar survives Floette's Light of Ruin (49-70%) and Alakazam's Shadow Ball is negligible on Tyranitar (5-7%) or non-KO on Excadrill (30-42%, Focus Sash safe). This is the highest-EV aggressive opening that punishes the opponent for not Protecting while still being acceptable if they do.
Pivot Alakazam out of the guaranteed Crunch KO into Floette, which resists Crunch, while Icy Wind cuts both foes’ Speed and removes Excadrill’s Sand Rush tempo for the following turn.

Excadrill is the opponent's mandatory kill target (only 280 Speed mon, Focus Sash, 205 Atk). They will likely double-target it with Scald+Shadow Ball, which KOes through Sash since Shadow Ball chips first. Protecting Excadrill wastes their double-target while Tyranitar Crunch (74-149% of max vs 93% HP) likely KOes Alakazam-Mega. Even if Crunch falls short, Alakazam drops to ~19% and is finished next turn. Excadrill preserved at 100% with Sash is our win condition for the remaining matchup.
Floette must Protect against Excadrill’s guaranteed Iron Head KO. Milotic’s Scald pressures Excadrill, can heavily chip or burn it, and avoids letting its Focus Sash remain fully intact for later.

Excadrill Iron Head guarantees KO on Floette at 65% (86-169% range, outspeeds at 280). Floette cannot attack this turn — it either Protects (can't act) or is KOed before acting. Tyranitar Crunch chips Milotic for 24-46%, advancing toward a 2HKO range. Milotic most likely Scalds Excadrill (break Sash, remove fast threat), making Crunch free damage. Even if Milotic targets Tyranitar (24-36%), Tyranitar survives at 60-72% and remains functional. If Floette Protects, Crunch still chips Milotic — no wasted turn. Pressing advantage while up 1-0 in series.

Excadrill acts before Floette and can OHKO it, while Scald is a guaranteed KO on the 25% Excadrill if it does not Protect. Light of Ruin maximally punishes an Excadrill Protect by threatening a Tyranitar KO or leaving it severely weakened; Floette is otherwise likely being traded for Excadrill.
Bring in Garchomp to immediately threaten Tyranitar with Ground damage; Mega Alakazam cannot safely face Tyranitar's revealed Crunch.

Excadrill outspeeds everything (280 Speed) and Iron Head is a guaranteed KO on Floette at 59% (SE 2×). KOing Floette removes the biggest threat to Tyranitar (all Floette damaging moves are SE on Tyranitar). Tyranitar Crunches Milotic for 24–46% STAB chip, putting it in easy 2HKO/KO range for next turn. Excadrill will likely fall to Milotic's Scald afterward, but trading a 25% Sash-broken Excadrill for Floette at 59% plus heavy Milotic chip is an excellent exchange. If Milotic instead Recovers, Excadrill survives and we maintain pressure. Tyranitar at 96% can tank any hit from the 4th Pokémon that switches in after Floette falls.

Bring Gengar to replace Excadrill. Gengar is neutral to Ground, neutralizing the Garchomp Earthquake threat that would hit both Tyranitar (2x) and Gholdengo (2x) as a spread move. Gengar outspeeds Garchomp (178 vs 134-169) with 4x Icy Wind. Gholdengo saved on bench for a clean switch-in vs Alakazam-Mega later (resists Psychic, immune to Taunt via Good as Gold). Tyranitar stays in to pressure Milotic at 28% with Crunch. Alakazam-Mega threatens Gengar with 2x Shadow Ball but is single-target and Gengar at 100% should survive one hit.
Stomping Tantrum guarantees an OHKO on Gengar if Garchomp gets to act, while Protect preserves the low-HP Milotic from likely targeting and avoids Earthquake ally damage.

Garchomp Earthquake is a guaranteed OHKO on Gengar, so Gengar must Protect. Mega Evolving now grants Shadow Tag, trapping both foes — Garchomp cannot switch to Alakazam-Mega. Tyranitar Ice Punch hits Garchomp for 4x (55.8-100.5%, possible OHKO). If Garchomp Protects, Ice Punch is wasted but Shadow Tag is active and next turn Icy Wind + Ice Punch finishes a trapped Garchomp. If Garchomp Earthquakes instead, Tyranitar survives (54-80% from 96%) and then Ice Punches. This is the safest path to removing the biggest threat while gaining permanent trapping value.
