Double-target Mega Gengar: Stomping Tantrum plus Scald guarantees its removal if both attacks connect, while leaving Milotic alive rather than sacrificing it to Earthquake. Removing Gengar is the highest-value immediate line despite its reduced-rate Protect chance.
Send in Mega Alakazam; it can immediately threaten the burned Mega Gengar while outspeeding both revealed foes.

Gengar outspeeds Garchomp and KOs it with 4x SE Icy Wind (guaranteed from 11%). Icy Wind also chips Milotic 5-8.2%, and Tyranitar's Crunch (24.3-45.9%) combined with that chip guarantees the KO on Milotic at 28% (min total 29.3% > 28%). Even if one foe Protects, the other still falls; only a rare double Protect stalls us, and Shadow Tag keeps both trapped regardless.
Psychic guarantees the KO on Mega Gengar before it can move and is the strongest available immediate line.

Opponent has only Alakazam-Mega (93%) left. Gengar at 14% burned is guaranteed KO'd by any Alakazam attack, and speed order is uncertain (187-222 vs 200). Switching Gengar to Gholdengo (100%) is strictly safer: if Alakazam Protects, I still have a dominant 2v1; if it attacks the switch-in slot, Gholdengo survives at high HP; if it targets Tyranitar, Psychic is immune and Shadow Ball NVE. Tyranitar Crunch (SE 2x, 74-149%) may KO outright given Timid Alakazam's likely low defense investment. Even if Crunch falls short, Gholdengo+Tyranitar vs damaged Alakazam next turn is an easy win.

reflections.summary: The 0-2 series loss is authoritative; only Game 2 evidence is available, so the effect of any between-game adjustment versus Game 1 cannot be determined. In Game 2, Milotic successfully removed Excadrill, but the trade cost Floette and left Tyranitar largely intact. Tyranitar's Ice Punch heavily crippled Garchomp, then Gengar's Icy Wind KOed it and Tyranitar's repeated Crunch removed Milotic. This left Mega Alakazam exposed to Tyranitar and facing Gholdengo, which resisted its final Psychic. The brought four had a workable Milotic answer to Excadrill, but Mega Alakazam, Floette, and Garchomp were all poorly positioned into the opponent's revealed Tyranitar pressure and late Gengar/Gholdengo endgame. Mega Alakazam was not a favorable evolution choice once Tyranitar remained healthy, although the available evidence does not establish that Mega Floette would have produced a better result. Preparation was mixed: Milotic fit the matchup well, while the six's shown tools did not establish a reliable plan to preserve pressure against Tyranitar plus Mega Gengar and Gholdengo. Talonflame and Scrafty were available but their sets and matchup value were not revealed, so there is insufficient evidence to claim the full roster offered a materially better four.
reflections.adjustment: For a future series, build the four and Mega choice around a concrete answer to Tyranitar surviving the early exchange and to the Gengar/Gholdengo backline. Do not allow Mega Alakazam to become the last meaningful attacker while Tyranitar can freely Crunch it. Preserve the Tyranitar answer rather than trading all of the team's relevant pieces merely to remove Excadrill, and account for Ice Punch when deploying Garchomp. Re-evaluate Talonflame and Scrafty in testing, but do not assume either is an improvement without confirming their sets and their ability to cover this specific sand-plus-Ghost/Steel structure.

reflections.summary: Won game 2 and the series 2-0 through effective sand-core pressure and a well-executed Gholdengo answer to Mega Alakazam. Tyranitar's Ice Punch proved decisive against Garchomp, and Crunch consistently wore down Milotic and Alakazam. Excadrill traded itself for Floette-Eternal, which was an acceptable exchange given Floette's Fairy typing threatened Gengar. Gengar-Mega's Icy Wind removed Garchomp with a critical hit, and Gholdengo's switch-in on turn 7 perfectly absorbed Alakazam's Psychic while Tyranitar finished it off. The main risk was triggering Milotic's Competitive with Icy Wind, but Tyranitar KO'd it the same turn, neutralizing the threat. No decision errors were recorded; piloting was clean.
reflections.adjustment: The four brought (Tyranitar, Excadrill, Gengar-Mega, Gholdengo) and the Mega Gengar choice were well-suited to this opponent. In a future series, consider whether Grimmsnarl's screens could protect Excadrill from Scald, potentially preserving it longer. Otherwise, the core plan is sound; keep Ice Punch on Tyranitar for Garchomp and maintain Gholdengo as the Alakazam switch-in. Avoid Icy Wind on Milotic unless it will be KO'd the same turn, as Competitive doubles its SpAtk.

events.text: Light Screen up on P1's side

decisions.rationale: Dragapult + Rotom-Wash lead: Dragapult outspeeds everything, threatens Mega Gengar with Life Orb Shadow Ball (85–167% roll), and is Ghost-immune to Shadow Tag. Rotom-Wash walls Excadrill completely (Levitate + resistances), 2HKOs Tyranitar with Hydro Pump, and Volt Switches out of trapping. Klefki in back sets Prankster Light Clay screens to blunt sand-boosted Rock Slides and Thunder Waves Gengar to neutralise its speed. Incineroar cycles Intimidate + Fake Out with Chople Berry to eat Tauros-Aqua Close Combat. Corviknight and Metagross sit out; screens + Intimidate cycling better handles the sand-and-trapping matchup.

Lead the sand core: Tyranitar's Sand Stream triggers on entry, immediately boosting Excadrill to 280 Spe — outspeeding the entire opponent's team including max-Speed Dragapult (213). Rock Slide spread + Focus Sash insurance makes this the safest, most reliable lead. Back: Gengar-Mega (Shadow Tag traps non-Ghost foes like Klefki/Incineroar/Rotom-W/Metagross/Corviknight for late-game elimination, Taunt shuts screens/status, Energy Ball hits Rotom-W SE) and Houndoom (Flamethrower OHKOs Klefki and threatens Metagross-Mega/Corviknight, Dark Pulse OHKOs Dragapult, Flash Fire absorbs Incineroar Fire moves). This covers all six opponent Pokémon across the four brought.

Dragapult is threatened by a likely double-target from Excadrill Iron Head (49–70%) + Tyranitar Crunch (91–127%), which together guarantee a KO before Dragapult can move. Protect at +4 priority negates both attacks safely. Rotom-Wash Hydro Pump into Tyranitar deals 42–75% (2× super effective), applying immediate pressure while Rotom-Wash comfortably tanks anything the opponent throws at it (Excadrill Iron Head does 10–13%, Crunch 35–50%). This preserves Dragapult — my fastest mon and best answer to a potential Mega Gengar — and sets up a strong turn 2 where Dragapult can Fire Blast Excadrill to break its Sash.

Excadrill (280 Spe, guaranteed first) opens Rock Slide hitting both foes for ~17-34% each with 30% flinch on Dragapult and Rotom-W. Tyranitar follows with Crunch on Dragapult (SE 2x, 56-108%). Combined ~79-148% + sand chip very likely KOs Dragapult, removing the faster threat. If Dragapult Protects, Rock Slide still chips Rotom-W. If Rock Slide flinches Dragapult, it can't Protect or attack, and Crunch lands clean. Excadrill Focus Sash covers Fire Blast (81-122%). Tyranitar survives Hydro Pump (36-55%). Best opening to eliminate the speed threat while guaranteeing chip on Rotom-W.

Switch Dragapult to Incineroar for Intimidate (-1 Atk on both foes) while Rotom-Wash burns Tyranitar. This double-dips on Tyranitar's Attack (Intimidate + burn = 0.25x), neutralizing their primary Dragapult answer. Incineroar resists Iron Head and Crunch, taking only ~17-25% and ~16-22% respectively. The main risk is Excadrill predicting the switch with High Horsepower (83-117% into Incineroar), but Iron Head is the more standard play into Dragapult. Even in the worst case, Dragapult is preserved in the back and a burned Tyranitar is crippled for the rest of the game.

Excadrill Protects to preserve Focus Sash and avoid the double-target KO (Dragapult Fire Blast breaks sash, Rotom Hydro Pump guaranteed OHKO after). Tyranitar Crunch is SE on Dragapult (56-108% from 93% HP) — likely KO or leaves it at very low HP for easy cleanup. Even if opponent predicts Protect and pivots to Tyranitar, Thunderbolt is only 11-17% and Hydro Pump 36-55%, so Tyranitar survives comfortably. This preserves our only speed control (Excadrill 280 under sand) while removing the opponent's fastest threat.

Reflect goes first (Prankster +1) and halves physical damage for 8 turns with Light Clay, letting Klefki survive Excadrill's High Horsepower barring a Helping Hand + high roll. Rotom-Wash Hydro Pump into Excadrill breaks Focus Sash or OHKOs, removing the Sand Rush sweeper's integrity. Even if Klefki falls to a Helping Hand + High Horsepower high roll, Reflect remains and Excadrill is left at 1 HP, easily cleaned next turn.

Excadrill High Horsepower is a guaranteed OHKO on Klefki (129–242% even unboosted, and Klefki is at 92% with Def -1), removing the Prankster Thunder Wave / screens threat permanently. Klefki's Prankster Thunder Wave (priority +1) may still fire before Excadrill attacks, but paralysis doesn't prevent the move this turn, so the KO lands regardless. Tyranitar Protects because it's burned (physical damage halved), slower than Rotom (81 vs 106–138, so Rock Slide can't flinch), and Hydro Pump does 35.7–55.1% to Tyranitar — Protect preserves HP for later sand/Intimidate walling. If Rotom redirects Hydro Pump to Excadrill, Focus Sash saves it at 1 HP and we can pivot next turn. Rock Slide chip from burned Tyranitar is only 9.6–18.4% on Rotom, not worth eating a Hydro Pump.

Switch Klefki to Incineroar to trigger Intimidate, weakening both foes' Attack stacks with burn on Tyranitar. Incineroar survives any unboosted hit comfortably through Reflect, and even Helping Hand + High Horsepower is only a roll to OHKO (82–117%). Rotom-Wash Hydro Pump guarantees the KO on 1% Excadrill if it connects (80% accurate), removing the fastest threat. Klefki is preserved for potential Light Screen later.

Double-target Klefki with Tyranitar Crunch and Excadrill Iron Head — both guaranteed KO at 4% even through Reflect/burn. This ensures Klefki dies regardless of Prankster Thunder Wave paralysis on Excadrill. Excadrill at 1 HP is expected to fall to Rotom Hydro Pump after completing its job. Keeping Gengar on the bench preserves it at 100% for a clean switch-in next turn to Mega Evolve with Shadow Tag, avoiding the 65.7–97.1% Hydro Pump risk if it switched in this turn.

Bring in Gengar to Mega Evolve into Gengar-Mega for Shadow Tag, trapping Incineroar and Rotom-Wash and preventing Klefki from switching in for a Prankster Thunder Wave. Gengar-Mega outspeeds both active foes (165-200 vs 80-112 and 106-138) and has Energy Ball SE on Rotom-Wash. Tyranitar stays as burned sand-setting pivot. This matches the pre-game plan of Shadow Tag trapping after Klefki neutralization.

Rotom is at 52% and Gengar-Mega outspeeds and threatens an Energy Ball OHKO range (51–73.9%). Protect keeps Rotom safe. Incineroar's Darkest Lariat into Gengar has a strong OHKO chance (69.5–146.7%) and at worst leaves Gengar in easy cleanup range. Tyranitar is burned, -1 Atk, and its free turn is low-impact (Rock Slide 10–14% on Incineroar through Reflect). This preserves both my Pokémon while heavily pressuring the opponent's Mega.

Double Protect + Mega Evolve safely establishes Shadow Tag, trapping both foes (no switches, no Volt Switch escape). Sandstorm chips Rotom-Wash from 51% to ~45%, below Energy Ball's 49.7% minimum damage — guaranteeing a KO next turn WITHOUT Helping Hand, so Tyranitar can Protect too. This avoids the catastrophic risk of going aggressive now: if the opponent Protects Rotom-Wash and Darkest Lariats Gengar (guaranteed OHKO at 119.7-175.2%), we'd lose Gengar for nothing and face a 2v4. By waiting one turn, we gain Shadow Tag control, sandstorm chip, and information on opponent targeting, while preserving both Pokémon at full health. Next turn: Tyranitar Protect + Gengar-Mega Energy Ball on Rotom-Wash for guaranteed KO, with Tyranitar safe from retaliation.

Rotom faces a likely Helping Hand + Energy Ball from Gengar-Mega that guarantees a KO if it stays in. Switching to Dragapult absorbs Energy Ball comfortably (20-28% unboosted, 31-43% with Helping Hand) while Incineroar's Darkest Lariat has a ~41% chance to OHKO Gengar-Mega outright and severely weakens it otherwise. The opponent must predict the switch with Shadow Ball to punish, but the straightforward play of targeting the threatened Rotom with Energy Ball is more probable. Preserving Rotom for later is crucial.

Rotom-Wash is trapped by Shadow Tag and cannot switch. Gengar threatens Rotom-Wash with Energy Ball (65-90% through Reflect, possible KO). The best counterplay is to double-target Gengar: Darkest Lariat (61-117%) plus Hydro Pump (43-82%) gives a high probability of KOing Gengar before it can claim a second KO. Even if Rotom-Wash falls to Energy Ball first, Darkest Lariat alone has a solid roll to remove Gengar, leaving burned -1 Tyranitar vs Incineroar in a favorable endgame.

Switch Gengar-Mega to Houndoom to dodge Incineroar's guaranteed-OHKO Darkest Lariat (causing it to whiff), bringing in a fresh Houndoom that walls Incineroar (Flash Fire + Dark resist) and outspeeds both active foes. Gengar-Mega is preserved at 94% on bench—Mega Evolution persists through switching, so Shadow Tag returns when re-brought. Tyranitar uses Rock Slide to chip both foes (survives even a double-target: Darkest Lariat 11-16% + Hydro Pump 36-55% = 47-71%, Tyranitar at 77% lives). This keeps 3 Pokémon alive with Shadow Tag available later, far superior to trading Gengar for Rotom and losing Shadow Tag permanently.

Rotom Hydro Pump into Houndoom has a 90.1–169.3% range, likely KOing the biggest offensive threat. Incineroar Protect keeps it safe from the turn's damage. Houndoom is faster than Rotom, but without Helping Hand its Dark Pulse (39.5–57.3%) plus Tyranitar Rock Slide (5.1–7.6%) leaves Rotom a solid chance to survive and fire back. If the opponent uses Helping Hand, Rotom may still barely live a low roll. Incineroar's own attacks are all NVE or immune into both foes, so Protect extracts maximum value.

Switch Tyranitar to Gengar-Mega to activate Shadow Tag, trapping both Incineroar and Rotom-Wash (neither is Ghost-type). Houndoom Protects to avoid the guaranteed-KO Hydro Pump from Rotom-Wash. Any opponent move targeting Tyranitar's slot fails (switched out), and moves targeting Houndoom are blocked by Protect. Next turn: Gengar-Mega Energy Ball is a guaranteed KO on Rotom-Wash (61.1-113.6% from 59% HP), and the opponent remains trapped by Shadow Tag. This preserves both Pokémon at high HP while gaining massive positional advantage.

Rotom-Wash is trapped by Shadow Tag and outsped by Gengar-Mega, whose Energy Ball is a guaranteed OHKO from 54%. Rotom must Protect to survive. Incineroar's Darkest Lariat has a roll to OHKO Gengar-Mega (61–117%); even if it misses the KO, Gengar is heavily damaged. Houndoom cannot KO Incineroar this turn even with both foes targeting it (max ~31% combined). If Gengar falls, Shadow Tag lifts and I can bring Dragapult freely next turn. Incineroar's Protect is unreliable at 1/3 consecutive success, so attacking is higher value.

Gengar Energy Ball guaranteed KOs Rotom-Wash (53% HP, KO from 59%), removing the only SE threat to Houndoom. Houndoom Dark Pulse on Incineroar chips 15-28% and carries 20% flinch chance since Houndoom (161) outspeeds Incineroar (80-112) — the sole way to potentially save Gengar from guaranteed-KO Darkest Lariat while still eliminating Rotom. If Gengar dies, the trade is favorable: Houndoom + Tyranitar vs weakened Incineroar + 4% Klefki + Dragapult, with Houndoom Sucker Punch (29-54% SE priority) as the Dragapult answer.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Houndoom is the only opposing threat that can KO Rotom-Wash before it moves (Dark Pulse 39.5–57.3% into 54% HP). Hydro Pump OHKOs Houndoom (90.1–169.3%). Incineroar's Darkest Lariat adds chip insurance against an 80% Hydro Pump miss and does 18.1–37.3% if Rotom goes down. Tyranitar is burned, -1 Atk, and its Rock Slide does only 14.9–21.3% to Incineroar and 8.3–11.5% to Rotom; once Houndoom falls, Tyranitar alone cannot sweep. Accepting the risk that Helping Hand + Dark Pulse always KOs Rotom, doubling Houndoom is the highest-EV path to a 2v1 endgame.

Klefki can set Light Screen with Prankster priority before being KO'd. Light Screen targets our side, bypassing Dark-type Prankster immunity. With both screens up, Dragapult survives Houndoom's Dark Pulse on turn 11 and the game becomes winnable. Sending Dragapult now risks an immediate OHKO from Dark Pulse before it can contribute. Forfeiting is premature; the position is difficult but winnable with screen support.

Helping Hand (priority +5) boosts Houndoom's Dark Pulse to a guaranteed KO on Rotom-Wash (57-107% from 53%), and Houndoom outspeeds Rotom-Wash (161 vs 106-138) so it lands before Rotom can Hydro Pump (which would guaranteed KO Houndoom). Tyranitar survives even if Rotom Protects (~11%) and Hydro Pumps it (max 55% from 71%). Incineroar's attacks are all NVE/immune on both my mons. Eliminating Rotom-Wash preserves the 2v1 advantage.

Klefki's Prankster Light Screen goes up at +1 priority before any foe attack, halving special damage for 8 turns (Light Clay). Incineroar Protects to guarantee survival through the turn, blocking Tyranitar Rock Slide and any Houndoom attack aimed its way. Houndoom's Flamethrower KOs Klefki regardless, but Light Screen is already set. Next turn Dragapult replaces Klefki, giving us Incineroar + Dragapult vs both foes under Light Screen, where Dragapult outspeeds and Thunderbolt has ~88% chance to KO Houndoom. This is safer than gambling on a ~33% Darkest Lariat KO now while risking Incineroar fainting to Rock Slide.

Klefki's Prankster Thunder Wave fails on both my Dark-types, making it harmless. Incineroar's Darkest Lariat KOs Houndoom from 32% after Life Orb recoil (30.3-44.7% vs 49 HP, guaranteed KO at 34 HP post-recoil), so Houndoom must Protect to survive for the Dragapult endgame. Tyranitar Rock Slide hits both foes: Incineroar (18%) takes 11.4-21.2% + sandstorm ~6.25% = 17.65-27.45%, very likely KO. Klefki (4%) takes 3-6.1% and might survive, but is completely inert (Prankster blocked by Dark typing, Foul Play outsped by Houndoom next turn). Reflect expires after this turn, making cleanup easier.

Klefki at 5% is dead to Houndoom Flamethrower regardless, but Prankster Reflect (+1 priority) goes up before any foe attack, giving Dragapult crucial physical protection for the rest of the game. Switching Incineroar to Dragapult preserves Incineroar on the bench and brings the win condition in safely. The opponent's safest play is Flamethrower into Klefki + Rock Slide; Dragapult takes only ~10–15% from Rock Slide through Reflect and ~18–27% if Flamethrower is redirected, leaving it at ~79–84% with dual screens against a 25% Houndoom and 59% burned Tyranitar. Thunderbolt OHKOs Houndoom next turn.

Helping Hand (priority +5) lets Tyranitar boost Houndoom before anyone else acts, then Houndoom's boosted Flamethrower guarantees KO on Incineroar at 12% (16.8-30.6%). This denies Incineroar's Darkest Lariat (guaranteed KO on Houndoom at 26%) by killing it first, preserving Houndoom for Sucker Punch priority against Dragapult in the endgame. Klefki at 4% survives but is harmless: Thunder Wave fails on Dark types, Foul Play is NVE 0.5x against both my Dark-types. Next turn we KO Klefki and keep Houndoom alive for Dragapult. If opponent switches Incineroar out for Dragapult, Helping Hand-boosted Flamethrower hits Dragapult neutrally for ~47-90% — a huge chunk. If they switch Klefki for Dragapult, Flamethrower still KOs Incineroar and we face Dragapult 2v1 with Sucker Punch ready.

Houndoom at 9% with Life Orb: any damaging attack it makes will cause 10% recoil and self-KO. It must Protect to survive. Dragapult Protect blocks Sucker Punch (and any other attack), neutralizing the opponent's best play. Klefki Foul Play on Houndoom is a guaranteed KO from 9% if Houndoom doesn't Protect; if it does Protect, Foul Play is blocked but Houndoom wastes its turn. Tyranitar's burned -1 attacks do negligible damage through Reflect (Rock Slide 3-4.3%, Crunch 4.3-6.7% on Klefki). Worst case: Klefki faints to Crunch high roll or Flamethrower, but Houndoom self-KOs from recoil if it attacks, and Dragapult remains untouched. Incineroar can enter turn 13 with Intimidate and Fake Out to clean up.

Helping Hand boosts Houndoom's unrevealed Sucker Punch to 42.6-79.8% of Dragapult's max HP. Dragapult at 48% is guaranteed KO'd if it attacks: either Sucker Punch direct KOs (85.5%) or leaves it at ≤5.4% where Life Orb recoil (10%) finishes it. Houndoom faints from its own Life Orb but the trade is decisive — Tyranitar then cleans up Klefki (4%) and Incineroar (12%) with Rock Slide. Opponent has no reason to expect Sucker Punch (unrevealed), making Dragapult attacking the most likely outcome.

Prankster Thunder Wave fails on Dark-type Tyranitar, so Klefki must attack. Thunderbolt (14-24%) + Foul Play (8.2-17.1%) leaves Tyranitar at 5.9-24.8%. Tyranitar's only threatening move is Crunch on Dragapult (30.3-42.4% through Reflect), but only the absolute max roll KOs Dragapult from 42% — roughly a 1/16 chance. Even if Dragapult falls, Incineroar cleans up the weakened Tyranitar. This line maximizes damage while accepting minimal risk.

Rock Slide is the only play that can remove Klefki (4% HP) and its Prankster Thunder Wave threat this turn. Damage range 3-6.1% vs 4% HP isn't a guaranteed KO between accuracy and rolls, but ~61% to kill Klefki is far better than letting it freely Thunder Wave me next turn. If Klefki faints, Incineroar (12%) enters and becomes the next Rock Slide target. Crunch Dragapult chips it to ~6-23% but guarantees Klefki Thunder Waves me, which effectively ends the game. Playing for the small chance to win game 1 rather than forfeiting, since I already have full info on opponent's sets for games 2-3.

Tyranitar is my last Pokémon at 16% with burn (losing ~13 HP/turn). Even though Crunch guarantees a KO on Dragapult (19-36% vs 16% HP), Dragapult moves first and Thunderbolt has a chance to KO Tyranitar outright (11.1-17.4% vs 16%). Even if Tyranitar survives, Klefki's Foul Play (9.2-11.1%) plus burn chip finishes it, and Incineroar waits on the bench. No path to victory exists with 1 burned Pokémon at 16% vs 3 opponents. Forfeiting game 1 to conserve time and reveal nothing new is optimal for the series.

reflections.summary: Incineroar's Darkest Lariat OHKOed Mega Gengar on turn 8, removing the opponent's fastest special threat. Klefki's Light Screen and Reflect coupled with the early burn on Tyranitar allowed the team to weather subsequent attacks, and Dragapult closed out the game with Thunderbolt as the remaining special win condition.
reflections.adjustment: Next game, anticipate more cautious play around Mega Gengar—protects or switches—and a possible shift to the Gholdengo/Tauros-Aqua core. Consider leading with Incineroar and Klefki to apply Fake Out pressure and set screens early, while preserving Dragapult in the back to handle Tyranitar and potential Gholdengo.

reflections.summary: Lost because Tyranitar was burned by Rotom-Wash Will-O-Wisp on turn 2, crippling physical damage for the entire game, while Excadrill fell to back-to-back Hydro Pumps by turn 4. With the sand-rush sweeper gone and Tyranitar weakened, Klefki's screens stalled out remaining damage, and Gengar-Mega was caught by Incineroar Darkest Lariat without Protect on turn 8. Houndoom's Sucker Punch failed into Dragapult Protect on turn 12, sealing the loss.
reflections.adjustment: Lead Gengar-Mega + Houndoom or Gengar-Mega + Excadrill to Taunt Klefki's screens early and avoid feeding Tyranitar to Rotom-Wash Will-O-Wisp. Houndoom's Flash Fire makes it immune to Will-O-Wisp, so use it as the Rotom-Wash switch-in instead of Tyranitar. Preserve Gengar-Mega Protect for Incineroar's Darkest Lariat timing rather than spending it on predicted Rotom Protect.

events.text: Light Screen up on P1's side
Light Screen ended on P1's side

decisions.rationale: Lead Rotom-Wash + Klefki to handle sand mode: Klefki sets Reflect/Light Screen with Prankster, Rotom-Wash threatens Tyranitar and Excadrill with Hydro Pump (2x) while Levitate dodges High Horsepower. Back Dragapult for Ghost-killing speed and Incineroar for Intimidate cycling, Fake Out disruption, and Darkest Lariat into Gholdengo/Gengar. Screens up first gives the back line longevity against spread Rock Slide and special spam.

Lead Gengar-Mega + Houndoom: Gengar-Mega Taunts Klefki before screens and Shadow Tag traps; Houndoom Flash Fire absorbs Rotom WoW (G1 lesson) and threatens Dragapult/Metagross. Back Tyranitar + Excadrill: keep TTar healthy for late-game sand+Rock Slide flinches, Excadrill Focus Sash Sand Rush as wincon once sand is up.

Switch Rotom-Wash to Incineroar to dodge the potential Mega Gengar Shadow Tag trap and bring in a Dark-type that resists or is immune to every attack both foes carry (Flamethrower/Dark Pulse/Energy Ball all NVE, Shadow Ball immune). Intimidate provides minor utility. Klefki sets Prankster Light Screen at +1 priority before any foe move or Taunt, halving special damage for 8 turns with Light Clay. This turn 1 establishes a durable defensive shell while preserving Rotom-Wash for later.

Mega Evolve Gengar for Shadow Tag and Taunt Klefki — Klefki's Prankster gets one screen up first (priority +1), but Taunt then locks it out of its second screen, Thunder Wave, and all future status (only Foul Play remains). Houndoom Protects because Rotom-Wash Hydro Pump is a guaranteed OHKO (111.8-167.1%); Protect wastes that hit and keeps Houndoom alive for Flash Fire utility and Klefki KO threat next turn. This wins the utility war: opponent gets at most one screen, no TWave, and Rotom-Wash is trapped by Shadow Tag (only Volt Switch escapes).

Fake Out fails on turn 2 (not Incineroar's first turn on field). Darkest Lariat into Gengar-Mega has a 61-117% OHKO chance and forces the opponent into a dilemma: either Protect Gengar (wasting its turn) or risk losing it. Switching Klefki to Rotom-Wash preserves the Taunted Klefki and brings in a switch-in that resists Houndoom's Flamethrower (11-27% under Light Screen) while taking manageable damage from either of Gengar's attacks (Shadow Ball 23-50%, Energy Ball 35-76%). Rotom also has Sitrus Berry for recovery. This line keeps pressure on Gengar while safely repositioning.

Both Pokémon are trapped by Shadow Tag. Klefki is Taunted and can only Foul Play. Darkest Lariat (61-117%) + Foul Play (17-46%) into Gengar-Mega has a high combined KO probability. If Gengar Protects, we force the Protect and Klefki absorbs Flamethrower (65-95%), but we maintain board position. If it doesn't Protect, it likely faints, freeing both from Shadow Tag. Foes outspeed us, but both our moves are independently lethal enough that even if Klefki goes down first, Incineroar's Darkest Lariat still threatens the KO.

Incineroar's Fake Out is unavailable (entered turn 1, first-turn-only restriction), so its real threat is Darkest Lariat on Gengar (96.4-140.1%, possible OHKO). Combined with Klefki Foul Play (26.3-32.1%), a double-target on Gengar guarantees the KO. Gengar must Protect to survive. Houndoom Flamethrower on Klefki is 2x SE (63.4-119.7% through Light Screen with Life Orb) — big chunk or possible KO. Even if opponent reads Protect and redirects to Houndoom, both their attacks are 0.5x on Dark/Fire typing, so Houndoom survives and still fires. Both foes are Shadow Tag-trapped (no switching moves), so preserving Gengar maintains positional dominance.

Klefki is Taunted, trapped by Shadow Tag, and at 18% HP — it dies this turn to any special attack from either foe. Its only possible action is Foul Play, and the only worthwhile target is Gengar-Mega (16.8–45.9%). Incineroar's Darkest Lariat into Gengar-Mega deals 61.1–117% with a solid OHKO chance; Flare Blitz is weaker (41.9–82.2%) and cannot OHKO alone. Combined damage (77.9–162.9%) gives a strong probability of removing the opposing Mega and its Shadow Tag, trading Klefki for Gengar-Mega at worst and leaving Incineroar healthy against Houndoom plus two unrevealed backs. Even if Klefki is KO'd before moving, Darkest Lariat alone still threatens the OHKO.

Rotom-Wash is the clear switch: Hydro Pump threatens both Tyranitar (32.9-75.4%) and Houndoom (72.5-169.3%, possible OHKO), while Dragapult takes 66-97% from Houndoom Dark Pulse even through Light Screen and its attacks are all neutral or resisted. Rotom-Wash takes manageable damage (Dark Pulse 20-48%, Rock Slide 19-44%, Flamethrower 11-27%) and has Sitrus Berry recovery. Incineroar must stay in to preserve offensive pressure and avoid giving a free turn.

Gengar switches to Tyranitar to dodge the Darkest Lariat OHKO (96.4-140.1%) and bring Sand Stream for future Excadrill sweep. Both foes are Shadow Tag trapped and can't switch; Klefki is Taunted (only Foul Play). Houndoom Flamethrower guarantees KO on 17% Klefki (63.4-119.7% through Light Screen). Worst case both foes target Houndoom: Darkest Lariat NVE 30-45%, Foul Play NVE 11-13% — Houndoom survives comfortably. If foes target Gengar, moves fail. This preserves Gengar, sets sand, and removes Klefki.

Hydro Pump into Houndoom threatens an OHKO (90-169%) and forces a likely Protect. If Houndoom doesn't Protect and Hydro Pump connects, we remove their special attacker immediately. Incineroar Protects to avoid the near-certain Tyranitar Rock Slide (45-63% to Incineroar), preserving its HP for later. Even if both foes attack Rotom-Wash, the worst case (Sucker Punch + Rock Slide) deals ~62% max, activating Sitrus Berry without a KO. This keeps both of my Pokémon healthy while maintaining offensive pressure.

Houndoom is guaranteed KO'd by Rotom-Wash Hydro Pump (111.8-167.1% from 74%), so it must Protect. Tyranitar Rock Slide hits both foes with physical damage (bypasses Light Screen): 33.7-63.5% on Incineroar (SE, putting it in KO range) and 19.7-36.8% on Rotom-Wash. Even if opponent predicts Protect and double-targets Tyranitar, it survives (Hydro Pump 35.7-55.1% + Darkest Lariat 11.1-15.9% = 47-71% max HP, leaving 17-41% from 88%). This is the safest high-value play: protect the threatened slot while spreading chip to both opponents.

Hydro Pump guarantees a KO on Houndoom if it stays in, removing their special attacker. If Houndoom switches, Hydro Pump still deals heavy damage to the replacement (85.7–160% into Excadrill forcing Sash, 39–70% into Gholdengo, or 24–47% into Tauros-Aqua). Darkest Lariat chips Tyranitar for 10–17% while Incineroar tanks Rock Slide comfortably behind Light Screen and Chople Berry. This preserves Dragapult in the back for Gengar-Mega and keeps the 2v1 field advantage after Houndoom is removed.

Switch Houndoom to Gengar-Mega to bring Shadow Tag online, trapping both foes so neither can switch out. Tyranitar uses Crunch on Rotom-Wash (physical, bypasses Light Screen, 28.7–52.8%) to chip it from 68%. If the opponent targeted Houndoom with Hydro Pump (the expected play since it KOs Houndoom), the move fails because Houndoom left the field. Next turn Gengar-Mega at 200 Speed outspeeds everything and can Taunt Rotom-Wash to block Protect/Will-O-Wisp, then finish it with Shadow Ball. Houndoom is preserved at 68% for later. Main risks: Rotom targets Tyranitar with Hydro Pump instead (survives at ~33–52%) or burns it with Will-O-Wisp; Incineroar Flare Blitz on Gengar-Mega is SE on Poison but requires predicting the switch.

Rotom Protect shields it from Gengar's Energy Ball and Tyranitar's Rock Slide. Incineroar Darkest Lariat KOs Gengar-Mega if it doesn't Protect; if Gengar does Protect, both our Pokémon survive the turn and Gengar is forced to have burned its Protect. Either outcome preserves both our Pokémon and either removes or neutralises the opposing Mega.

Helping Hand (priority +5) boosts Gengar's Energy Ball to a guaranteed KO (60.5-112%) on Rotom-Wash at 47%, and Gengar at 200 Spe outspeeds Rotom (106-138) so Rotom is eliminated before it can Hydro Pump Tyranitar. Incineroar's Darkest Lariat then KOs Gengar at 15% — an acceptable trade of a nearly-dead Gengar for Rotom while keeping Tyranitar at full 76%. Only risk is Rotom Protecting, but opponent has been aggressive with Hydro Pump and hasn't used Protect yet. Result: 3v2 with Tyranitar 76% + Excadrill 100% + Houndoom 68% vs Incineroar 82% + 1 unknown.

Gengar is fainted; bring in Excadrill (100%, Focus Sash, Sand Rush 140 Spe) over Houndoom (68%, Life Orb). Excadrill outspeeds both active foes in sand (Incineroar 80–112, Rotom-Wash 106–138) and Rock Slide hits Incineroar SE while spreading to Rotom. High Horsepower is SE vs Metagross and Incineroar (Rotom immune via Levitate). Focus Sash guarantees survival against Dragapult if it is the 4th mon. Houndoom stays as a strong bench option for later. Tyranitar stays in (Pass) to preserve sand and support next turn.

Excadrill outspeeds both active Pokémon under Sand Rush and OHKOs Incineroar with High Horsepower (83.2–116.8%). Switching Incineroar to Dragapult preserves Incineroar and brings in a faster mon that survives any single Excadrill hit (HH 58.2–83.6%, Iron Head 49.1–69.7%, Rock Slide 23.6–33.3%). Dragapult Fire Blast then outspeeds Rotom and breaks Excadrill's Focus Sash (min 64.5%), after which Rotom Hydro Pump finishes through the broken sash. Tyranitar's Crunch into Rotom (35–50.3%) is a threat but Rotom moves before Tyranitar if Tyranitar's Speed ≤108, which covers most of its range. Even in worst-case scenarios the position remains advantageous.

Excadrill outspeeds everything (280 Spe) and guaranteed KOs Incineroar with High Horsepower (77-139% vs 76% HP), removing the Flare Blitz OHKO threat before Incineroar can act. Tyranitar Crunch into Rotom-Wash deals 28.7-52.8% from its 41% HP for a possible KO; even if it survives, Rotom is at single digits and easily finished next turn. If Incineroar Protects, High Horsepower is blocked but Crunch still chunks Rotom, and Excadrill (immune to sand chip via Ground/Steel typing) survives any single hit via Focus Sash to finish Incineroar next turn. This removes the opponent's biggest threat while simultaneously pressuring their lowest-HP mon.

Excadrill under Sand Rush outspeeds both my Pokémon and Rock Slide KOs both. Switching Dragapult to Incineroar triggers Intimidate (-1 Atk to both foes) before any moves, letting Incineroar survive even double Rock Slide. Rotom Protect keeps it alive. Next turn Incineroar Fake Out (priority +3) flinches Excadrill while Rotom Hydro Pump KOs it, removing Sand Rush and freeing Dragapult to clean later.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Excadrill (Speed 280) outspeeds everything and KOs Dragapult (12%) with Iron Head (100% acc, guaranteed KO). Tyranitar KOs Rotom-Wash (1%) with Crunch (100% acc, guaranteed KO). Both are physical so Light Screen is irrelevant. If one foe Protects, the other still dies. If both Protect, I lose nothing and repeat. Worst case trades 1% Excadrill for a foe, leaving Tyranitar+Houndoom vs Incineroar — a winning endgame.

Fake Out (+3) KOs 1% Excadrill through resist; if Excadrill Protects (+4), Fake Out is blocked but Dragapult's own Protect (+4) shields it from Tyranitar's attack. Either way Dragapult survives the turn. Once Excadrill falls and sand ends (1 turn left), Dragapult becomes the fastest Pokémon and cleans.

Tyranitar Crunch into Dragapult is a guaranteed KO (SE, 37.9-71.2% vs 12% HP). Excadrill Rock Slide hits both foes—chips Incineroar for 20.8-36.5% SE (Chople Berry doesn't apply to Rock) while also hitting Dragapult. If Incineroar Fake Outs Excadrill (KO at 1%), Tyranitar still KOs Dragapult. If Incineroar Fake Outs Tyranitar (flinch), Excadrill Rock Slide chips Incineroar and Dragapult dies to sandstorm/Life Orb recoil. Excadrill at 1% is expendable; Rock Slide chip on Incineroar makes the Houndoom Flamethrower endgame much cleaner.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Dragapult at 6% dies to any attack; Protect gives a ~33% chance to survive since it was used last turn. Protect (+4 priority) outruns Sucker Punch (+1), so if it works both Sucker Punch and Rock Slide are blocked. Incineroar's Darkest Lariat into Houndoom chips it to 31–50%, setting up a potential KO next turn if Dragapult lives. Incineroar survives Rock Slide (29.7–42.6% from 49%) and is not threatened by a KO this turn. Flare Blitz is useless into Flash Fire Houndoom and Darkest Lariat does more than Flare Blitz into Tyranitar.

Dragapult is dead this turn regardless (Life Orb recoil if it attacks, sandstorm if it Protects). Sucker Punch at priority +1 KOs Dragapult before it can fire off Thunderbolt (35-53% on Houndoom), preserving Houndoom's HP. Rock Slide hits both foes—SE on Incineroar for 24-42%, dropping it to ~6-24%. If Dragapult Protects, Sucker Punch fails but Dragapult dies to sandstorm and Rock Slide still damages Incineroar. Next turn is a trivial 2v1 vs Incineroar whose attacks are all NVE or Flash Fire-immune.

Dragapult is dead to any attack and Life Orb recoil; we must maximise its one move. Thunderbolt into Houndoom (28–54%) plus Incineroar Darkest Lariat (18.1–37.3%) guarantees Houndoom faints if both connect. If the opponent uses Sucker Punch, Dragapult falls before moving but Incineroar still has a ~70% roll to KO Houndoom alone. Eliminating Houndoom is the only path to a 1v1, even though Incineroar vs Tyranitar is unfavourable.

Sucker Punch (priority +1) guarantees KO on 6% Dragapult before it can attack (Life Orb recoil would also KO it). Rock Slide hits both foes — SE on Incineroar for 24-42% chip, bringing it to ~6-24% for easy 2v1 cleanup. If Dragapult Protects (heavily reduced at streak 2), Sucker Punch fails but Rock Slide still damages Incineroar, and Dragapult remains stuck at 6% with no switch options for next turn.

Incineroar is guaranteed to be outsped and OHKOed by Tyranitar's Rock Slide before it can move. Even with a Rock Slide miss (10%), neither Darkest Lariat nor Flare Blitz can KO Tyranitar from 76% HP, even with a critical hit. The game is mathematically lost. Forfeiting saves time and preserves focus for game 3 with the series tied 1-1.

1v1 endgame: Tyranitar (76%) vs Incineroar (8%). Rock Slide is SE (2x) and guaranteed KO from 8% HP (23.8-42.4% damage) at 90% accuracy. Crunch is only NVE (0.5x, 7.9-14.7%) and not a guaranteed KO. Even if Rock Slide misses, all of Incineroar's attacks are NVE vs Tyranitar and cannot KO at 76%, giving another shot next turn. If Incineroar Protects, it resets the Protect streak and I simply try again next turn at 90%. Rock Slide maximizes win probability this turn.

reflections.summary: Lost because Dragapult was brought in too early and chipped into Sucker Punch range, allowing Houndoom to remove it before it could threaten Tyranitar. Incineroar was left alone against Tyranitar with no way to break through.
reflections.adjustment: Preserve Dragapult for the late game. Lead with Incineroar and Rotom-Wash to pressure sand with Fake Out and Hydro Pump, and use Klefki screens to enable Dragapult to clean up after sand sweepers are removed.

reflections.summary: Won by removing Klefki early with Taunt + Flamethrower, then grinding down the opponent's team with the sand core. Houndoom's Sucker Punch picked off Dragapult and Tyranitar's Rock Slide finished the 8% Incineroar for the 1v1 win. Gengar-Mega did its job trapping and Taunting but fell predictably to Darkest Lariat.
reflections.adjustment: Gengar-Mega is too fragile against Incineroar's Darkest Lariat; if bringing it again, keep it away from Incineroar or consider a different Mega pick. Also be ready for Dragapult double-Protect sequences—lead Sucker Punch with a different move to avoid wasted turns.

decisions.rationale: Incineroar+Rotom-Wash lead: Intimidate and Fake Out disrupt early, Rotom-Wash Hydro Pump threatens both Tyranitar and Excadrill 2× SE while Levitate blanks Excadrill's Ground moves. Volt Switch enables pivoting. Dragapult (213 Speed) outspeeds even Mega Gengar (max 200) and Shadow Ball OHKOs it; Metagross-Mega brings Bullet Punch priority and SE Psychic Fangs/Meteor Mash against Gengar/Tyranitar. This four covers the expected Gengar+Houndoom lead and the sand backline while retaining late-game cleaning power.

Lead Tyranitar+Gengar to set sand while Gengar-Mega Taunts shut down Corviknight Tailwind and Klefki screens—the two biggest threats to the sand core. Excadrill+Houndoom on bench: Excadrill provides sand-rush offense at 140 Speed, Houndoom covers Metagross-Mega (Flamethrower SE), Corviknight (Flamethrower SE), Incineroar (Flash Fire+Dark resist), and Dragapult (absorbs Fire Blast via Flash Fire, Sucker Punch priority). Gengar-Mega Shadow Ball is SE on Metagross/Dragapult; Shadow Tag traps key targets. Houndoom chosen over Gholdengo (weak to Psychic Fangs/Thunderbolt, no Taunt) and Tauros (Intimidate bounced by Mirror Armor).

Switch Rotom-Wash to Metagross to dodge the expected Helping Hand + Mega Gengar Energy Ball combo that would OHKO Rotom (77.7-110.8% with base Gengar + Helping Hand, likely >100% with Mega). Metagross takes only 14.6-21% from resisted Energy Ball. Fake Out on Tyranitar prevents Rock Slide (though Helping Hand at +5 resolves first). We preserve Rotom-Wash for later and bring in Metagross, who threatens Gengar with a guaranteed OHKO from Psychic Fangs. Turn 2 we can double-target Gengar or pivot based on what the opponent reveals.

Helping Hand (pri +5) resolves before Incineroar Fake Out (pri +3), so Tyranitar safely boosts Gengar-Mega's Energy Ball into 73.9–139.2% range on Rotom-Wash—possible OHKO. Gengar Mega Evolves for Shadow Tag and outspeeds both foes (178 vs 80–112 / 106–138). If Incineroar predicts and uses Darkest Lariat on Gengar (guaranteed OHKO), Gengar still acts first and gets Energy Ball off, trading favorably for Rotom-Wash. Fake Out chip on Tyranitar is only 3.4–5.3%. This is the maximum-pressure turn-1 play that can remove Rotom-Wash and establish Shadow Tag.

Gengar-Mega Shadow Ball OHKOs Metagross (99.4-138.9%) before Metagross can move. Switching Metagross to Dragapult preserves Metagross and brings in the only mon that outspeeds Gengar-Mega (213 vs 165-200). Dragapult Shadow Ball does 74.9-138.5% to Gengar; Incineroar Darkest Lariat adds 61.1-117%. Dragapult moves before Gengar, so if Shadow Ball KOs, Gengar never attacks. If Dragapult rolls low, Gengar OHKOs Dragapult but Incineroar finishes Gengar. Either way Gengar-Mega is removed at the cost of at most Dragapult, leaving Metagross and Rotom-Wash in reserve.

Metagross is trapped by Shadow Tag and Gengar-Mega Shadow Ball is a guaranteed OHKO (99.4–138.9%). Protect saves Metagross while Mega Evolving grants Tough Claws for future turns. Incineroar Darkest Lariat into Gengar-Mega deals 61.1–117%, a possible KO; even if it falls short, Mega Metagross can revenge with Tough Claws-boosted Bullet Punch next turn. This preserves both Pokémon and applies maximum pressure to the opponent's fast special attacker.

Gengar Protects to dodge guaranteed OHKOs from Incineroar Darkest Lariat and Metagross Psychic Fangs, preserving Shadow Tag which is critical for keeping the opponent locked in. Tyranitar Crunches Metagross (SE 2x, 27-48% chip) for insurance. Next turn Gengar Shadow Ball guarantees KO on Metagross from any HP while Shadow Tag remains active, forcing opponent's 4th Pokémon in while Incineroar stays trapped. If opponent predicts and targets Tyranitar instead, TTar likely survives at low HP and Gengar still cleans up Metagross next turn.

Shadow Tag prevents switching. Gengar-Mega Shadow Ball is a guaranteed OHKO on Metagross-Mega (85.4-118.5%). Protect (+4 priority) resolves before Shadow Ball; even at ~33% success after consecutive use, it is the only path to keep Metagross-Mega alive. Incineroar Darkest Lariat into Gengar-Mega (61.1-117%) threatens a KO and is our best damage. If Protect fails, we lose Metagross-Mega but still get the Darkest Lariat chip; if Protect succeeds, we preserve a 2v2 or 2v1 position. The double-Bullet-Punch line guarantees the Gengar trade but sacrifices the 33% chance of a dominant board state, which is worth the variance in a decisive game 3.

Switch Gengar to Excadrill to preserve Shadow Tag user at 88% — opponent most likely targets Gengar (their primary threat), wasting both attacks when it switches out. Tyranitar Crunch chips Metagross from 64% to ~20-38%. Next turn Excadrill at 280 Speed (Sand Rush) outspeeds everything and KOs chipped Metagross with High Horsepower (58.8-100.6%). Even worst case (opponent predicts switch, Metagross Meteor Mash possibly KOs Tyranitar at 81-114%), I'm 3v2 with Gengar preserved. This is strictly better than trading Gengar for Metagross, which leaves 3v2 with no Shadow Tag and no speed control answer to potential Dragapult.

Excadrill under Sand Rush outspeeds both my active Pokémon and OHKOs either with High Horsepower. Switching Incineroar to Rotom-Wash gives me a Levitate pivot immune to Ground, while Metagross-Mega's Bullet Punch (+1 priority) breaks Excadrill's Focus Sash before it moves. Even if Excadrill KOs Metagross with High Horsepower targeting that slot, I break Sash and preserve Incineroar for later Intimidate cycling. Rotom-Wash then threatens Excadrill with Hydro Pump next turn and can Volt Switch to regain momentum. Dragapult remains in the back as a Gengar-Mega answer.

Bring Incineroar for the Intimidate re-apply and fresh Fake Out. Intimidate drops Tyranitar to -2 and Excadrill to -1, neutering their physical pressure. Rotom-Wash passes so the move can be decided with full turn-5 information. Dragapult stays benched as the Gengar-Mega answer.

Helping Hand guarantees Excadrill's High Horsepower KOs Metagross-Mega (87.7-148.4% with HH vs 64% HP, guaranteed KO). Without HH, High Horsepower alone is only 58.8-100.6% — not a guaranteed KO from 64%. Excadrill at 280 Speed moves before both foes, so Metagross is removed before it can act (Meteor Mash was a possible KO on Tyranitar at 81-114%). Incineroar's Flare Blitz is a guaranteed KO on Excadrill at 50% HP regardless, so Excadrill is likely traded — but that's a favorable swap (broken-sash Excadrill at 50% for Metagross-Mega at 64%). Tyranitar stays at 97% and I retain Gengar-Mega (Shadow Tag) and Houndoom (100%) in back for the 3v3 endgame.

Fake Out on Excadrill neutralises the fastest, most threatening spread attacker (Sand Rush Rock Slide). Hydro Pump into Tyranitar deals 41.5–75.4%, pressuring the Sand setter and exploiting the free turn created by the flinch. Even if Excadrill Protects, Tyranitar still eats the Hydro Pump and its -2 Rock Slide is manageable; double Protect wastes both their Protects. Volt Switch is too weak (13.5–24%) and pivoting Dragapult into Rock/Dark moves is unsafe.

Switch Tyranitar to Gengar-Mega to activate Shadow Tag, trapping both foes before they can switch to their unknown 4th mon. Excadrill Protects — opponent most likely targets Excadrill (26% HP, easy KO), wasting both their moves. Next turn pivot Excadrill to Houndoom for free switch-in while Gengar attacks. Endgame: Gengar+Houndoom outspeed both trapped foes, Houndoom resists Incineroar's STABs, Gengar Energy Ball hits Rotom-Wash SE. Switching the 97% HP Tyranitar is far safer than switching the 26% Excadrill to bring in Gengar.

Gengar at 2% almost certainly Protects; Excadrill's High Horsepower has a roll to OHKO Incineroar (54.5–78.2% into 76%). Incineroar Protect blocks that KO. Rotom-Wash Will-O-Wisp burns Excadrill through Protect, permanently neutering its Attack (already -1) regardless of Gengar's action. If Gengar unexpectedly attacks, Rotom risks the Energy Ball KO but Gengar remains at 2% and can be revenged by Dragapult. Next turn Gengar's Protect success is reduced, letting us finish it.

Gengar dies to sandstorm at 3% regardless; both my Pokémon outspeed both foes. Energy Ball is SE on Rotom (61-114% of max HP, ~49% KO chance from 88%) and High Horsepower is SE on Incineroar (52-93% of max HP, ~41% KO chance from 76%). Going for double KO potential is far superior to switching, since Rotom Hydro Pump OHKOs Houndoom (112-167%), making any switch-in extremely risky. Even if no KO, both foes are heavily chipped and I keep Houndoom (100%) + Tyranitar (97%) fresh on bench for cleanup.

Gengar fainted; bring in Tyranitar (97% HP) which resists Incineroar's Flare Blitz (0.5x) and Darkest Lariat (0.5x) and survives Rotom's Hydro Pump (36-55%). Houndoom must stay in back — it's OHKO'd by Hydro Pump (112-167%) and is our best late-game cleaner once Rotom is removed. Excadrill is at 20% burned with -1 Atk and can only Pass; it will likely faint soon, after which Houndoom enters with Tyranitar as a safe pivot. Never forfeit with two healthy mons remaining.

Rotom-Wash Protect (priority +4) blocks all incoming attacks, crucially stopping Tyranitar Crunch which would otherwise OHKO Rotom-Wash (35-50.3%). Excadrill moves before Incineroar but its Rock Slide only does 10.9-15.3% to Incineroar. Incineroar Flare Blitz then guarantees the KO on Excadrill (77.4-149.2%), removing the fastest threat. Rotom-Wash is preserved at 30% to threaten Tyranitar with Hydro Pump (41.5-75.4%) next turn. Worst case: Tyranitar also Rock Slides Incineroar for 44.6-63.4%, total 55.5-78.7% — Incineroar survives except on extreme dual high rolls. This line preserves both Pokémon and secures a KO.

Focus-fire Rotom-Wash (29%): Excadrill Rock Slide (5.7-11.2% chip, moves first at 280 Speed) + Tyranitar Crunch (28.7-52.8%) = 34.4% minimum combined, guaranteed KO from 29% if both connect. Excadrill is dying from burn anyway so extracting value now is essential. Rock Slide also chips Incineroar (10.4-18.2%). If Rotom Protects, we still damage Incineroar and can retry Crunch next turn. Once Rotom falls, Houndoom can safely enter to clean up Incineroar with Flash Fire absorbing Fire and resisting Dark.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Incineroar cannot use Fake Out (not first turn out) so Houndoom is free to move. Houndoom Dark Pulse OHKOs Rotom before it can act. The only play that preserves any winning chance: Rotom uses Protect (~33% consecutive success) while Incineroar switches to Dragapult (switches resolve before moves). If Protect succeeds, Turn 9 presents Rotom+Dragapult vs both foes with Sandstorm gone; Dragapult can Protect to bait Houndoom's Dark Pulse while Rotom Hydro Pumps Houndoom for a possible OHKO. If Protect fails, Dragapult takes only Rock Slide and we lose Rotom, but the alternative plays all lead to certain loss.
Automatic: only one legal joint action.

Houndoom Dark Pulse guarantees the KO on Rotom-Wash at 24% HP (38.2-72% damage) and Houndoom outspeeds Rotom (161 vs 106-138), so Rotom dies before it can Hydro Pump (which would OHKO Houndoom). Tyranitar Rock Slide hits both foes: SE on Incineroar (33.7-63.5%, possible KO at 43% HP) and chips Rotom if it somehow survives. If Rotom Protects (reduced success rate), Rock Slide still punishes Incineroar. This executes the win path: eliminate Rotom this turn, then clean up Incineroar with Houndoom next turn.

Fake Out fails (Incineroar not first turn out). Dragapult cannot OHKO either foe and both foes OHKO it back (Houndoom Dark Pulse 99-147%, Tyranitar Crunch 59-85%). Houndoom's Sucker Punch also threatens 44-68% before Dragapult moves. Dragapult Protect (+4) blocks all incoming damage; Sucker Punch fails against Protect. Incineroar Darkest Lariat chips Houndoom (18-37%) for a sliver of future hope. This preserves Dragapult one turn while dealing chip to the faster, Dark-Pulse-carrying threat.

Double-target Dragapult for guaranteed elimination: Houndoom Dark Pulse is a guaranteed KO (77-149% on 52% HP), with Tyranitar Crunch as backup (38-71%, ~50% KO chance). Neither foe can KO either of my Pokémon this turn. If Incineroar Fake Outs Houndoom, Crunch still chips Dragapult to near-zero, enabling Sucker Punch priority KO next turn. If Dragapult Protects, both miss but next turn Incineroar can't Fake Out and Dark Pulse guarantees the KO. Once Dragapult falls, 2v1 vs Incineroar at 43% is an easy sweep.

Dragapult's Protect has a 1/3 chance to succeed after last turn's successful Protect. If it works, Dragapult survives the double dark-move targeting and Incineroar chips Houndoom with Darkest Lariat (18-37%). Next turn we can double Houndoom for a guaranteed KO (Thunderbolt + Darkest Lariat min 46% > max remaining 39%), leaving Incineroar vs -1 Tyranitar. If Protect fails, Dragapult faints but Houndoom is still chipped, giving Incineroar a slim chance to Protect-stall and pick off a weakened Houndoom. No other line keeps Dragapult alive; attacking with Dragapult guarantees its death and leaves Incineroar alone with less cumulative damage on the foes.

Houndoom Dark Pulse is a guaranteed KO on Dragapult at 52% (77.4–148.5%). Tyranitar Rock Slide hits both foes and chips Incineroar for 24–42% (SE, spread-adjusted), setting up the 2v1 endgame. If Dragapult Protects again (reduced success rate), Rock Slide still lands on Incineroar. Dragapult is faster but cannot KO Houndoom in one hit, so Dark Pulse resolves regardless. After Dragapult falls, Houndoom walls Incineroar (Flash Fire immunity + Dark resist) and Tyranitar's Rock Slide pressure closes it out.

Position is lost with no winning line. Dragapult Thunderbolt guarantees KO on Houndoom, but Tyranitar Crunch OHKOs Dragapult in return. Incineroar at 11% cannot 1v1 Tyranitar from 96%: Flare Blitz does 14-24% and Darkest Lariat 10-17%, neither a 2HKO range before Tyranitar KOs back. Dragapult Protect is only 33% and even if it works, the follow-up turn fails to secure the game. Forfeit is the correct competitive decision.

reflections.summary: The game and series were lost primarily due to a critical piloting error on turn 4, where Mega Metagross was left in against Excadrill and got OHKOed by a Helping Hand-boosted High Horsepower, costing us our Mega early. A subsequent failed Protect on Rotom-Wash (turn 8) led to its KO, leaving an unwinnable 2v2 endgame against Tyranitar and Houndoom. The team composition was reasonable, but these misplays, combined with the opponent's effective use of sand offense and Helping Hand, sealed the loss. Between-game adjustments are unknown, but the brought four were appropriate; the loss stemmed from execution rather than preparation.
reflections.adjustment: In a future series, bring Klefki over Dragapult to set dual screens, which blunts the opponent's special attackers (Mega Gengar, Houndoom) and helps Mega Metagross survive Ground moves. Lead Incineroar + Klefki to safely set screens and cycle Intimidate, then pivot to Rotom-Wash or Metagross as needed. Alternatively, if keeping Dragapult, adjust the game plan to always Protect or switch Metagross when Excadrill is on the field, and avoid consecutive Protects on Rotom-Wash.

reflections.summary: Game 3 was won through superior matchup exploitation and a well-executed sand core. Mega Gengar's Energy Ball chunked both Metagross-Mega and Rotom-Wash for super-effective damage, enabling Excadrill to KO Metagross on turn 4 with a Helping Hand-boosted High Horsepower. Houndoom was the series-clinching bring: Flash Fire made it a complete wall to Incineroar's Flare Blitz, and Dark Pulse threatened Dragapult super-effectively while cleanly KOing Rotom-Wash on turn 8. Tyranitar provided sand, Helping Hand support, and consistent Rock Slide chip. The opponent's Dragapult wasted turns 9-10 on consecutive Protects with a heavily reduced success rate, effectively stalling itself out while Incineroar was whittled to 10%. The endgame 2v1 (Tyranitar 97% + Houndoom 22% vs Dragapult 52% + Incineroar 10%) was mathematically won. Series won 2-1.
reflections.adjustment: The Game 3 bring of Mega Gengar / Tyranitar / Excadrill / Houndoom was optimal for this opponent and needs no changes in a future series. Houndoom as the specialist answer to Incineroar + Dragapult was the decisive adjustment. If anything, consider whether Gholdengo offers value as an alternative to Excadrill if the opponent adapts and brings Klefki for screens, but the current four are the default keep.

reviews.outcome: You finished 6th of 6 in the round robin and missed the playoffs. Your season is over.
reviews.summary: The season was a 0-5, 0-10 last-place finish. The initial sun core built around 20-point Mega Charizard Y was consistently shut down by Cloud Nine and Sand Stream, and even after a mid-season pivot to a weather-neutral roster featuring Palafin, Mimikyu, and Glimmora, the team failed to win a single game across all five series.
reviews.didWell: The mid-season trade window pivot was the right macro decision — correctly identifying that sun was unrecoverable and swapping to Glimmora, Mimikyu, and Palafin gave the team new win conditions and type coverage. Several draft picks held up well regardless: Toxapex at 8 points was excellent value as a Regenerator pivot, Aegislash at 14 was a versatile Ghost/Steel answer to many meta threats, Skarmory at 3 was nearly free hazard control and Defog, and Swampert at 6 cleanly provided the Ground immunity the team desperately needed. The post-FAM roster construction on paper was reasonable with layered hazard pressure, priority, and dedicated Fairy and Psychic checks.
reviews.didPoorly: The 20-point Mega Charizard Y pick was the defining mistake — it consumed a quarter of the budget and locked the entire team into a sun strategy that was countered in week 1 and never became viable again. Venusaur at 13 points was a second dead investment in Chlorophyll speed that meant nothing without reliable sun. Torkoal at 15 points was expensive dead weight once Charizardite Y was expended and Drought became unreliable. Heracross at 3 points was filler that was immediately dropped at the trade window. The result was a 0-10 record — the post-FAM roster looked competent on paper but never translated into a single win, suggesting the remaining budget was too thin or the six selected each week were still exploitable.
reviews.wouldChange: First, never take Mega Charizard Y at 20 — spend those points on a pick that contributes in non-sun games rather than one that becomes a dead slot the moment its mega stone is used. Second, drop Venusaur entirely and reallocate those 13 points toward a second reliable win condition or a deeper defensive backbone. Third, keep Torkoal only if paired with a plan that doesn't rely on Drought — or replace it with a cheaper pivot and spend the saved 15 points on the remaining slots. Fourth, after pivoting at the trade window, the team needed at least one more high-impact pick rather than three mid-tier ones; the 3-point Heracross drop should have been replaced with something that addressed the post-FAM team's still-thin offensive firepower.

reviews.outcome: You finished 5th of 6 in the round robin and missed the playoffs. Your season is over.
reviews.summary: I finished 2-3 and missed playoffs because the roster had a strong weather-and-Trick-Room shell but no dependable answers to several central defensive and disruption problems. The two wins showed the team could execute its intended plan, while the three losses exposed both draft-window gaps and avoidable registration and piloting mistakes.
reviews.didWell: Archaludon, Farigiraf, Sinistcha, Sneasler, Armarouge, and Mamoswine gave me a genuinely flexible core, and Altaria was an excellent one-point pick: Cloud Nine and Tailwind directly enabled the 2-0 win over the sun team and the 2-0 win over the rain team. The Week 1 registration correctly paired Altaria with Mamoswine and Armarouge, and the Week 4 registration used Freeze-Dry, Thunderbolt, Fake Out, and redirection to attack the opponent's actual rain structure rather than forcing Trick Room. Declining Absol itself was defensible because Altaria's Ground immunity, Cloud Nine, and Tailwind were uniquely valuable, and I correctly identified Rotom-Wash and Mega Gengar as problems after facing them.
reviews.didPoorly: The draft left me without a reliable Rotom-Wash or Milotic answer and without a robust anti-Mega-Gengar route; those were draft weaknesses, not problems that every possible registration could have solved. At the window, I overvalued preserving the roster: I made no coach offer, declined the only incoming Absol swap, and made no free-agent change even after the first three weeks had revealed exactly these structural holes. Week 3 was primarily a piloting and registration failure: despite knowing Mega Gengar used Taunt and Protect to stall Trick Room, I brought a six centered on Farigiraf's Trick Room and never established a credible non-Trick-Room plan. Week 5 repeated the issue against Milotic and Mega Alakazam, registering passive or unreliable pressure into Recover and Icy Wind while relying on a Choice Scarf Sneasler whose Unburden plan was inactive and leaving myself without a convincing late-game answer.
reviews.wouldChange: At the draft, I would spend one of the expensive support slots on a direct Rotom-Wash/Milotic answer rather than accepting three overlapping speed-control and support options around Archaludon. At the trade window, I would actively pursue a replacement for either Altaria or a redundant support slot only if it produced concrete Electric-, Grass-, or anti-Gengar coverage; if Absol remained the only offer, I would still decline it, but I would not automatically keep all ten unchanged. Against GLM in Week 3, I would register a fast, non-Trick-Room six with Sneasler and Dedenne pressure, preserve Armarouge's Wide Guard, and treat Farigiraf as optional rather than making Taunt-and-Protect Gengar fight my primary mode. Against Terra in Week 5, I would prioritize a way to deny Milotic's Recover or remove it quickly, bring a more coherent Mega Alakazam answer, and avoid the Scarf Sneasler set unless its speed benchmarks and role were demonstrably better than a normal offensive or utility set.

reviews.outcome: You reached the playoffs as the 4th seed and were eliminated in the semifinals. Your season is over.
reviews.summary: We finished 4th in the regular season at 3-2 and reached the semifinals, where our 0-2 loss to deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro ended our run. While our rain core dominated favorable matchups, structural vulnerabilities to Grass-types like Serperior and weather disruption capped our ceiling.
reviews.didWell: We drafted an exceptionally cohesive rain archetype early, locking down elite offensive powerhouses like Pelipper, Mega Swampert, and Basculegion-Male alongside premium support in Whimsicott and Primarina. This core steamrolled sun and sand teams cleanly, securing solid 2-0 and 2-1 victories against inclusionai/ring-2.6-1t and z-ai/glm-5.2.
reviews.didPoorly: Our draft bench suffered from wasted depth and random fallback picks, leaving us with unplayable roster slots like Castform and underutilized threats like Feraligatr and Alakazam instead of essential anti-grass or anti-dragon defensive pivots. Piloting a linear rain strategy also left us helpless against dedicated counter-picks like deepseek's Serperior and Rotom-Wash cores.
reviews.wouldChange: Draft a diverse defensive backup instead of wasting points on filler Pokémon like Castform and redundant water types like Feraligatr. Bring tailored anti-grass and electric checks like an Amoonguss or a Dragonite rather than relying purely on linear Swift Swim offense. Actively utilize the mid-season trade window to patch our glaring Serperior and Rotom-Wash weaknesses instead of keeping an unadjusted roster.

reviews.outcome: You reached the playoffs as the 2nd seed and were eliminated in the semifinals. Your season is over.
reviews.summary: I finished 3-2, earned the second seed, and reached the semifinals before a 0-2 playoff loss to GLM. The season was successful overall, but the elimination exposed that our excellent Mega Floette/Garchomp core did not always translate into a sufficiently durable plan against GLM’s Tyranitar, sand, Mega Gengar, and Gholdengo endgame.
reviews.didWell: The draft was strong: Mega Floette, Garchomp, Milotic, Talonflame, Scrafty, and the 6-point Metagross/Hisui Goodra values gave us real Tailwind, Trick Room, anti-Intimidate, and alternate-Mega modes. The Week 1 2-1 over GLM and Week 4 2-0 over Ring showed that the Garchomp/Scrafty/Talonflame/Floette structure was genuinely effective into sand, Steel, and slower defensive teams; Week 5’s 2-0 also validated registering Mega Alakazam as a matchup-specific anti-Sneasler and anti-Trick Room option. Declining the Mega Floette-for-expended-Mega-Charizard-Y trade was plainly correct, and keeping the roster was defensible because no listed swap replaced Floette’s role or meaningfully improved the rain, sand, and Metagross matchups at once.
reviews.didPoorly: The Week 2 rain loss was primarily a registration and piloting problem: despite bringing Manectric and a Trick Room mode, we still relied too heavily on fragile Hatterene speed control into Pelipper, Waterfall Mega Swampert, and flinch pressure, then failed to preserve Floette consistently for its confirmed Energy Ball Swampert assignment. Week 3 against the eventual first seed was a roster-window result as much as a series loss: Mega Metagross behind Klefki screens, Incineroar, and Rotom-Wash stressed our physical and Ground-centric answers, and no free-agency adjustment was made to sharpen that matchup. The playoff 0-2 to GLM was the clearest registration/piloting failure: we correctly identified Tyranitar’s Crunch, Excadrill’s sash and Sand Rush, Garchomp’s Ice Punch risk, and the Gengar/Gholdengo backline, but still did not produce a durable Tyranitar plan or keep Mega Alakazam and Milotic safe enough to convert their intended roles.
reviews.wouldChange: At the midseason window, I would have actively pursued a swap or free-agent replacement for one of the redundant slow special pivots—most plausibly Hisuian Goodra or Hatterene—to add a more reliable Tyranitar/Gholdengo/Rotom-Wash answer; keeping all ten unchanged was a window decision that left the eventual GLM rematch too similar to Week 1. For the playoff rematch with GLM, I would register Metagross over one of the two Megas or over Talonflame: Clear Body, Bullet Punch, and its Steel resistance give a more stable board piece against Gengar/Gholdengo than an all-in dual-Mega selection. Against rain, I would build the six around a safer Fake Out plus Trick Room line and treat Mega Floette as a protected Swampert check rather than exposing it early, while using Manectric as targeted disruption instead of assuming Lightning Rod alone solves the Water matchup.

reviews.outcome: You won the final. You are the league champion and the season is over.
reviews.summary: Won the championship at 3-2 in regular season (7-4 games) then swept through two playoff rounds, avenging the week 1 loss to terra and edging deepseek 2-1 in the final — the sand core of Tyranitar + Excadrill was the engine that carried every series, and the trade window swaps (Rotom, Houndoom, Hydrapple) patched enough holes to flip the terra rematch.
reviews.didWell: The Tyranitar (14) + Excadrill (13) sand core at 27 combined points was the best value decision of the draft — it appeared in every single series and provided speed control, weather override, and spread Rock Slide pressure that no opponent could fully answer. The trade window was excellent: all three swaps were upgrades that addressed real structural holes, and Houndoom in particular proved its worth as the Metagross-Mega and Dragapult answer against deepseek in both meetings. The playoff adaptation against terra — adding Rotom for Ground immunity and Grimmsnarl with Adamant Spirit Break to threaten Garchomp — showed genuine learning from the week 1 loss, turning a 1-2 defeat into a 2-0 sweep. Mega Gengar's Shadow Tag was used intelligently as a trapping tool rather than a standalone sweeper, and the movepool flexibility (Energy Ball for Rotom-Wash, Icy Wind for speed control, Taunt for setup denial) kept opponents guessing.
reviews.didPoorly: The original budget picks were dead weight: Absol (1 pt) and Sandaconda (2 pts) were never registered in a single series, and Chandelure was dropped before it could contribute meaningfully — three draft slots producing zero games is a real waste even at low cost. Vaporeon (5 pts) was drafted specifically as rain insurance yet was never brought in any series, including the week 5 loss to gemini's rain team where it should have been most valuable — that 5 points was effectively dead cap. The week 5 loss to gemini exposed a structural Water weakness that no registration could cover: four Water-weak Pokémon (Tyranitar 4x, Excadrill 2x, Houndoom 2x, Gholdengo 2x) meant the rain matchup was lost at draft, not at the battle screen. The week 1 loss to terra was partly a piloting issue — the opponent's Protect reads were called out in prep notes yet still punished.
reviews.wouldChange: I would consolidate the three weakest budget picks (Absol 1, Sandaconda 2, Chandelure 6 = 9 points) into one better Pokémon at the draft rather than waiting for the trade window to fix them — a 9-point Water resist like Gyarados or Milotic would have addressed the rain hole from day one. I would cut Vaporeon entirely, since a 5-point mon that never sees a single series is worse than spending those points elsewhere on the roster. I would have pushed harder for the Altaria trade or found another Ground-immune Pokémon before week 5, since the gemini loss was directly caused by having no answer to Swift Swim sweepers under rain-boosted Water STAB. I would have registered Grimmsnarl in week 1 against terra instead of Tauros, since the prep notes identified Scrafty's Snarl spam and Garchomp EQ as the primary threats — Prankster screens and Spirit Break answered both better than Intimidate alone.

reviews.outcome: You reached the final and lost it. You are the league runner-up and your season is over.
reviews.summary: Finished 4-1 in the regular season and reached the playoff final, but lost to the same Sand + Mega Gengar team twice — the one matchup my roster was never built to solve.
reviews.didWell: The Incineroar–Mega Metagross–Dragapult–Rotom-Wash top four was a superb draft core that carried me through rain, sun, Trick Room, and Fairy Aura matchups. Serperior at 5 points was the steal of the draft, single-handedly winning both rain series against Gemini (4-0 in games) with Contrary Leaf Storm snowballs. My game-planning and set registration were sharp: I correctly identified win conditions for each opponent and adjusted sets week to week — the Life Orb Dragapult pivot set in week 2, the Chople Berry Incineroar for Tauros-Aqua in week 4, and the Expert Belt Gliscor for the sun team in week 5 all show strong metagame reading.
reviews.didPoorly: The bottom three draft picks — Gliscor (3 pts), Clawitzer (4 pts), and Furfrou (1 pt) — combined for 8 points and were registered only twice across seven series, contributing almost nothing. The trade-window decision to stand pat at 3-0 was complacent: GLM-5.2 added Houndoom (a Flash Fire Dark-type that blanked my Incineroar and threatened Dragapult), and I made no counter-adjustment despite knowing they were my biggest threat. The Mega Gengar matchup was never adequately solved — Dragapult's Life Orb Shadow Ball was only a 67–152% roll to OHKO, and Shadow Tag hard-countered the entire pivoting identity of my team (Parting Shot, Volt Switch, U-turn), yet I drafted no backup plan beyond a never-used Furfrou.
reviews.wouldChange: Replace the Gliscor–Clawitzer–Furfrou trio at picks 48/49/60 with a dedicated Shadow Tag answer: a Choice Scarf Dark-type like Krookodile or a Sucker Punch user like Kingambit that could reliably remove Mega Gengar without needing to pivot. Use the trade window to add a Fire-immune Dark-type (Houndoom or Flash Fire Chandelure) after seeing GLM-5.2's roster, dropping Clawitzer whose Mega Launcher niche was redundant with Rotom-Wash and Dragapult already covering special offense. Bring Corviknight over Serperior from the first Gengar series — Serperior was dead weight into sand and I learned that lesson in a 0-2 loss that ultimately cost me tiebreaker positioning for the final.
